messages.content:
Ayesha's necklace snapped in the middle of the dance rehearsal, and small blue beads rolled across the floor in every direction. She dropped to her knees and began gathering them with trembling fingers. The music stopped. Several girls stood around her, and her face grew redder. Then Lisa knelt beside her without a word and began picking up beads too. Soon, six girls were on the floor. Within a minute, every bead was in a cup. Ayesha looked around at all of them and said "Thank you" so softly that only Lisa heard.

Why did Ayesha say thank you so softly?
She was embarrassed but moved by their help. Her face had grown redder as the girls watched, so she spoke shyly.

At Greenfield School, the lunch queue forms outside the dining hall at twenty past twelve. Younger children go first, followed by Classes Four and Five. A teacher stands at the door with a list and ticks off each name. Nobody is allowed to push or skip ahead, and any child who does must go to the back of the line. The queue moves quickly, and by half past twelve, the last children are seated. The whole hall then falls silent for a short grace.

What happens to a child who skips ahead in the queue?
The child must go to the back of the line.

Every morning, Oscar found a small paper star on his desk with a kind word written on it. Some days it said "You are funny" and on others "Great drawing." He looked around the room but could not tell who left it. He began to arrive early, hoping to catch the writer. One day he saw Greta slip in quickly and leave something on his desk before rushing out. Oscar smiled but said nothing. The next morning, he left a paper star on her desk too, with the words "Thank you for the stars" in blue pencil.

Who was the secret star writer, and how do we know?
It was Greta. Oscar saw her slip in early and leave something on his desk, and then he thanked her.

Piyush did not cry when he lost the race. He did not cry when his father scolded him for coming last. But when his small cat jumped on his lap that evening and began to purr, his eyes suddenly filled. He pressed his face into the cat's soft fur and sobbed quietly. After a while, he wiped his nose on his sleeve and laughed at himself. The cat stayed where it was, kneading his knee gently with its paws. Later, he told his mother that he felt much better.

Why did Piyush cry when the cat purred?
The cat's comfort let him finally release the sadness he had been holding in about losing the race and being scolded.

When the river overflowed, the children of the village could not cross the road to school. The teacher, Mr. Das, walked to each house and gave them a bundle of worksheets and a note. At the end of the week, he came back and collected the papers. Only one child had not finished: a boy named Shan, whose home had been filled with water. Mr. Das did not scold him. He sat on the porch and helped him with the first question. Shan's father, watching nearby, wiped his eyes.

Why did Shan's father wipe his eyes?
He was moved by the teacher's kindness, because Mr. Das did not scold Shan and sat down to help him after the flood.

In the home science room, the students of Class Eight learned to make chapatis for the first time. Their teacher, Mrs. Hegde, showed them how to knead the dough with a little water and a pinch of salt. She asked them to let the dough rest for twenty minutes under a damp cloth. Mahesh rolled his chapati into the shape of a map, and Nina's came out almost perfectly round. When the flat bread puffed on the griddle, the children cheered. They took turns eating each other's creations with a little butter.

What did Mrs. Hegde ask the students to do with the dough after kneading?
She asked them to let it rest for twenty minutes under a damp cloth.

Karthik owns a small blue notebook that he keeps in his shirt pocket at all times. In it, he writes down words he does not know, along with their meanings. Last week he collected seven new words, including "curious", "plenty" and "swift". Every Friday, he reads the list to his sister, who tests him. If he gets all the words right, she gives him a sticker. So far, he has collected four stickers, which he has pasted on the back cover.

What does Karthik write in his blue notebook?
He writes down words he does not know, along with their meanings.

At the end of the school year, the Class Nine students make a memory book. Each child contributes a page with a photograph and a few lines about their favourite moment. Lalit took the cover photograph, which shows the whole class on the steps of the main building. Hannah designed the title page with a border of tiny leaves. The book is bound with a red ribbon and kept in the library, where anyone may read it. Memory books from earlier years are stored on the same shelf, one for each batch.

Where is the memory book kept?
It is kept in the library, where anyone may read it.

The final match of the school football league was played on Saturday morning on the main ground. The Blue House team wore sky-blue shirts, and the Red House team wore bright red. The referee was Mr. Costa, the sports teacher. In the first half, Blue House scored a goal from a corner kick. Red House answered five minutes before the break with a long shot. The score stayed one-one until the very last minute, when Emil from Blue House pushed the ball past the goalkeeper. The crowd along the edge of the field shouted for nearly a minute.

Who was the referee of the final match?
The referee was Mr. Costa, the sports teacher.

A boy walked into the corner shop and asked for a pencil that cost eight rupees. He handed over a note, thinking it was a ten, but it was really a twenty. The shopkeeper noticed the mistake. Instead of keeping the extra money, he called the boy back and counted out twelve rupees in change. Then, after a moment's thought, he added a small candy and said it was for being so polite. The boy stared at the candy, thanked him, and walked away slowly, smiling, with a pencil in one hand and a candy in the other.

What do the shopkeeper's actions show about him?
They show that he was honest and kind, since he corrected the mistake and gave the boy a candy for his good manners.

Ms. Kamat wants her Class Four students to carry lighter bags. She has asked each child to bring only the books needed for that day's timetable. Heavy items like atlases and craft supplies are kept in cupboards at the back of the room. Every Friday, the children clean out their bags and throw away old papers. As a result, the weight of the average bag has dropped by almost half, and the children say their shoulders hurt less. Ms. Kamat hopes the other classes will follow the same plan next term.

Where are the heavy items like atlases kept?
They are kept in cupboards at the back of the room.

Bela stared at her drawing of a house and felt it was ugly. The roof was crooked, and the door looked too small. She crumpled the paper and threw it in the bin. Her art teacher, Mr. Pinto, quietly picked it up, smoothed it flat, and pinned it to the board among the others. "Look," he said to the class, "this one has something special. The windows look as though somebody is waving." Bela peered at the paper. She had drawn tiny curtains in the corners, and they did look like hands. For the first time that day, she grinned.

Why did Bela grin at the end?
The teacher pointed out something special in her drawing, so she saw it in a better light.

A big calendar hangs on the wall of Mrs. Gupta's classroom. Each month, a different student draws a picture to place on top of it. March's picture was a field of yellow mustard flowers by Tanya. April's was a kite in a blue sky by Joel. Birthdays are circled in red, and exam dates in green. Next to the calendar is a small chart on which the children place stars for good behaviour. The teacher uses it to remind the class of every coming event, and the children check it each morning.

What colour is used to circle birthdays?
Birthdays are circled in red.

The school's notice board announced a clean-up drive for the first Saturday of next month. Students from Class Six to Class Ten were asked to meet at the main gate at eight o'clock. Each group would be given gloves, bags and a section of the road outside the school to clean. The science club would then separate the plastic from the other waste. At eleven, there would be juice and biscuits for all participants. The principal added that every volunteer would receive a certificate.

What would each volunteer receive?
Every volunteer would receive a certificate.

Kenji always went to his grandfather's room after school and sat on a low stool next to his chair. His grandfather could no longer see well, so Kenji read to him from the newspaper in a careful voice. One day, he got stuck on a long word and stopped. His grandfather, without turning, said, "Say it slowly." Kenji tried again and got it right. After that, his grandfather asked for the long words first. Kenji realised that the old man had been teaching him all along, and he sat up a little straighter.

What did Kenji realise about his grandfather's requests?
He realised his grandfather was teaching him to read hard words, because the old man began asking for the long words first.

On the day of the class photo, everyone wore their best uniform. Mr. Pillai arranged the children in three rows, tall ones at the back. Just as the photographer raised his camera, Nikhil sneezed, and the whole class laughed. They tried again, but Nikhil's face wrinkled, and he sneezed twice more. Finally, the photographer shouted, "Everyone, say cheese!" and clicked at the exact moment when all the children were laughing. When the picture arrived, it was crooked, and everyone had their mouths open. It became the class's favourite photo.

Why did the class like the photo so much?
It showed everyone laughing naturally, which made it a happy and funny memory.

On the morning of the exam, the school bus broke down on the bridge. The driver, Mr. Lal, called the mechanic from his mobile and asked the children to stay seated. Twelve students needed to reach the school by nine o'clock. A parent driving past in a van stopped and offered to take a few. After some thought, Mr. Lal agreed, and he went with them to look after the children. They reached the gate at ten to nine, a little squashed but on time.

Who offered to take some of the students to school?
A parent driving past in a van offered to take a few of them.

Piotr had a collection of football cards, and he loved all of them. One day, a boy from Class Five offered to swap his rare gold card for Piotr's whole bundle of duplicates. Piotr's eyes shone. He agreed at once, and the other boy walked away grinning. At home, Piotr compared the gold card with a picture in a magazine, and his heart sank. It was a printed copy, not a real one. The next day, he told the boy politely that he wanted his cards back. The boy hesitated, then handed them over with a sigh.

What did Piotr discover when he got home?
He discovered that the gold card was only a printed copy, not a real one, so the swap was unfair.

Maria stood by the school gate long after the others had gone home. Her mother had said she would come at four, but the clock above the gate said half past five. The guard asked if he should call someone, but Maria shook her head and said she would wait a little more. She held her bag tightly and kept watching the road. At last, a bus stopped, and her mother ran toward her with a bunch of flowers, her eyes red. She said that the bus had broken down and she had tried to call. Maria threw her arms around her and cried.

Why did Maria cry when her mother arrived?
She had waited and worried for an hour and a half past four, so she cried with relief when her mother finally came.

A loose button fell off Karim's shirt during morning assembly and rolled across the floor. It stopped near the shoe of the girl beside him. She looked down, bent to pick it up, and handed it back with a shy smile. Karim put it in his pocket. In class, his teacher noticed the gap in the shirt and gave him a needle and thread from the cupboard. Karim sewed the button on himself while the others read, and it took him about ten minutes.

Where did the button stop rolling?
It stopped near the shoe of the girl beside him.

The Class Six science teacher showed the children a video about blue whales. She told them that these animals can grow up to thirty metres long, about as long as three buses. They feed mostly on tiny shrimp-like animals called krill, which they swallow in huge mouthfuls. The video also showed how whales sing to each other across the ocean. At the end of the lesson, each child drew a whale and wrote one fact beneath it. Afterwards, the teacher pinned the drawings along the corridor wall, one beside the other.

What do blue whales feed on, according to the teacher?
They feed mostly on tiny shrimp-like animals called krill.

When Daniela saw that Fiona had been given the lead role in the school play, she pulled her bag onto her lap and pressed her lips together. She had practised the lines for a month and knew every word. During the rehearsal, she answered the director in short, flat sentences. Fiona noticed and tried to catch her eye, but Daniela kept looking at her script. Afterwards, Fiona walked up and said that she wished they could swap parts for one scene, because Daniela was so good. Daniela blinked, and for the first time that day, her face softened.

How did Daniela feel when Fiona got the lead role?
She felt jealous and disappointed. She pressed her lips together and gave short, flat answers.

The morning of the school picnic dawned grey and chilly, and Class Five stood at the gate, looking at the sky. The teacher said that if it rained, the trip would be cancelled. Kavya crossed her fingers. Arman kept checking the clouds, and Sophie said she had packed an umbrella just in case. At nine o'clock, a small gap opened in the clouds, and a pale beam of sunlight fell on the road. A cheer went up from the children. The driver started the engine, and everyone hurried to their seats.

Why did the children cheer at nine o'clock?
They saw the sun come out, so they knew the picnic would not be cancelled.

Two weeks before the annual race, Coach Mehta started the morning practice at six o'clock. The students ran around the field five times and then did stretches near the long jump pit. Anil, who was the fastest in Class Eight, finished first almost every day. Meanwhile, the coach gave extra attention to Farah, who was the slowest. He showed her how to swing her arms and how to breathe steadily. By the end of the second week, her time had improved by almost half a minute.

What time did Coach Mehta start the morning practice?
He started it at six o'clock.

Using a large map spread on the floor, the Class Five students were asked to find the town where their classmate Peter had been born. Each child guessed. Priya put her finger on a spot in the north, and Samir tapped a place near the sea. Peter laughed. "None of you," he said. Then he moved his own finger slowly to a small dot among the hills, and said, "Here." The children leaned in to look. A few of them asked how to say its name, and Peter, who was usually quiet, taught them with a proud voice.

What do we learn about Peter from how he taught the children the name?
He was proud of his home town. The passage says Peter, who was usually quiet, taught them the name with a proud voice.

Rehan won first prize in the spelling contest, and his friends cheered and slapped his back. Only Gopal stayed quiet at the edge of the group, staring at his shoes. He had come second, missing a single letter in the word "necessary". Rehan noticed. He walked over, put the small golden trophy in Gopal's hands for a moment, and said, "You were so close. I was lucky." Gopal turned the trophy over slowly. A small smile appeared, and he asked Rehan to help him practise for the next contest.

Why did Rehan let Gopal hold the trophy?
He wanted to cheer Gopal up and be kind, since Gopal was disappointed about coming second.

Mira walked into the classroom on her birthday and saw that nobody looked at her. Her best friend Leela did not even say good morning. Mira felt a sinking feeling and sat down quietly. In the middle of the first period, the teacher said she needed Mira's help in the next room. When Mira opened the door, a chorus of voices shouted "Happy birthday!" The room was hung with paper chains, and a small cake sat on a table. Mira covered her mouth with both hands, and tears came into her eyes.

Why did nobody say hello to Mira in the morning?
They were keeping her birthday surprise a secret, so they acted as if nothing special was happening.

In Class Five, students learn English, Hindi and one regional language. The regional language is Tamil, Marathi or Bengali, depending on where the child comes from. Every Wednesday afternoon, the three groups meet separately in different rooms, and then the teachers bring them together to share one new word each. Last week, the Marathi group taught the word "paus", which means rain. The Tamil group taught the word "mazhai", and the Bengali group offered "brishti". The teachers say the exercise helps the children respect one another's mother tongues.

What does the Marathi word shared last week mean?
The word means rain.

Under the big jamun tree behind Rohit's house, three friends built a small platform from planks of old wood. Rohit's father helped them nail the boards to two strong branches about two metres above the ground. They hung a rope ladder and attached a bucket on a string to pass up snacks. The platform could hold only three children at once, so they made a rule that anyone waiting had to count slowly to one hundred. In the monsoon, they covered it with a plastic sheet.

How many children could the platform hold at once?
It could hold only three children at once.

Mr. Ford took his Class Six students to a pizza place near the school as a treat on the last day of term. They sat at three long tables. Each child chose a topping from a list of six: cheese, mushroom, olives, peppers, corn or tomato. Hitesh picked olives, and Sana chose corn. While they waited for the food, they played a quiz game on paper napkins. Afterwards, each student thanked the staff, and they walked back to school in the afternoon sun.

How many toppings were on the list?
There were six toppings on the list.

At the entrance to Sunrise School, there is a zebra crossing painted in bold white lines. A traffic volunteer stands there every morning from seven to eight to help children cross. He wears a bright yellow jacket and carries a round red sign. When the traffic stops, he raises the sign and nods to the children. The school bus drops the youngest ones right at the crossing so they do not have to walk far. The path beyond it leads to the main gate.

What does the traffic volunteer wear?
He wears a bright yellow jacket.

Tomas fell during the game and scraped his elbow on the gravel. Blood ran down his arm, and he bit his lip to stop himself from crying. The other children stopped playing and stood around him in silence. Chen ran to the water tap and came back with a wet handkerchief. Alicia fetched the teacher. As the teacher cleaned the scrape, Tomas watched his friends, whose faces were pinched with worry. When the teacher finished, he stood up, tried to smile, and said it did not hurt much. Nobody believed him, but they all went back to the game gently.

Why did nobody believe Tomas when he said it did not hurt much?
He had been bleeding and biting his lip to stop himself from crying, so his friends could tell he was in pain.

After a sudden afternoon shower, the children of Class Two ran out to the courtyard. A faint arch of colours had appeared in the sky above the water tank. Lalit shouted that he could count seven stripes. His friend Suhana argued that there were only six. They stood next to each other, pointing and frowning. Their teacher laughed and told them to look again, slowly, from the same spot. After a moment, Suhana's eyes widened, and she pointed to a thin purple band at the edge. "Oh! Seven!" she said, and the two of them started giggling.

What made Suhana change her mind about the stripes?
She looked again slowly and saw a thin purple band at the edge, so she counted seven.

Everyone in Class Two knew that Rahul was afraid of dogs. When a small brown puppy wandered into the school yard one afternoon, he climbed straight onto a bench. The other children laughed and rushed to pat it. The puppy wagged its tail and licked a boy's hand. Rahul watched from above. After a while, the puppy came and sat under the bench, looking up at him with big round eyes. Slowly, Rahul stretched out one finger and touched its ear. He pulled back fast, but then he did it again, and this time he stayed.

How had Rahul's feelings about the puppy changed by the end?
He had become less afraid. He started by climbing on the bench but ended by touching the puppy's ear twice.

A large spider built her web in the corner of the Class Five window, just above the teacher's table. The children saw it first on a Monday, when dew made the threads sparkle. They agreed that nobody would touch it, and the janitor was asked to leave that corner alone. Each morning, they checked the web for insects. After two weeks, the spider laid a small sac of eggs, which she guarded carefully. The teacher took a photograph and pinned it on the notice board.

Where did the spider build her web?
She built it in the corner of the Class Five window, above the teacher's table.

When Gaurav came to school with a small cut on his knee, he told everyone he had fallen from a tree. Only his friend Hari knew that he had actually tripped on the stairs while running late. At lunchtime, a girl asked Hari if the tree story was true. Hari looked at Gaurav and then said, "Ask him yourself." Gaurav turned red, but he laughed and said it was just a silly stumble. Later, he thanked Hari for not telling on him, and Hari shrugged and shared his orange.

What did Hari's answer, 'Ask him yourself', show?
It showed that Hari did not want to lie, but he also did not want to expose Gaurav. He left it for Gaurav to decide.

The bell for recess rang, and Tomas ran out to the playground with his football. Three boys from the other class were already standing near the goalposts. They did not look up when he asked if he could join. Tomas stood still for a moment, holding the ball against his chest. Then a girl named Priya waved from the far corner of the field and called, "We need one more player! Bring the ball!" Tomas smiled and jogged over to her group. By the time the bell rang again, his shirt was wet with sweat, and he was laughing so hard that he could barely tell her the final score.

How did Tomas feel after he joined Priya's game?
He felt happy. The passage says he was laughing so hard he could barely speak about the score.

Mia and her cousin waited at the bus stop for half an hour, but the school bus did not come. The cousin wanted to walk, but Mia said they should wait where the grown-ups could find them. A little later, the neighbour's car pulled up, and the driver explained that the bus had broken down two roads away. Mia and her cousin climbed into the back seat. When they entered the school gate, the bell had just rung. Mia sighed with relief and said she was glad they had waited at the stop.

Why was Mia glad they had waited at the stop?
Because the neighbour found them there and drove them to school, so they arrived just as the bell rang.

The games teacher, Mr. Ibrahim, wears a silver whistle around his neck. One long blast means the children should gather around him. Two short blasts mean it is time to line up, and three blasts mean the game has ended. Last Tuesday, he blew the whistle five times in a row, and the whole field fell silent. A lost kitten had wandered onto the track, and the children had to keep still until it was safely carried away by a student.

What does one long blast of the whistle mean?
It means the children should gather around the teacher.

Hira and Zaid had been friends since nursery, but this year they were put in different classes. At the start of the term, they met at the gate and promised to sit together at lunch. By the second week, Zaid sat with the cricket boys, and Hira sat with the girls from her class. They waved at each other across the canteen. On Friday, Zaid walked over with his plate and said, "Is this seat free?" Hira moved her bag at once. They talked about everything they had missed and did not notice when lunch ended.

What does Hira moving her bag at once show?
It shows she was glad Zaid came and had missed sitting with him. She welcomed him immediately.

When the principal called Taj to the stage to get the prize for the best attendance, he walked slowly, trying not to smile. His mother, in the third row, held her scarf against her mouth. Taj had not missed a single day in the whole year, even when he had a fever and a sore leg. He took the certificate and shook hands. Back in his seat, he stared at the paper without blinking. On the way home, he held it close to his chest in both hands. At the door, he showed his grandmother first.

What does holding the certificate close to his chest show about Taj?
It shows he was very proud of the certificate and valued it greatly.

A rumour spread through the class that Lakshmi had cheated on the spelling test. Nobody asked her directly. They just whispered when she walked by, and a few girls stopped sitting near her at lunch. Lakshmi ate alone for two days. On the third day, Mr. Shah announced the real results and said that Lakshmi had been the only one to spell "necessary" correctly because she had practised it all week. The room went quiet. Afterwards, a girl named Preeti walked to her table with her tiffin and quietly asked if she could sit.

Why did Preeti ask to sit with Lakshmi?
She realised the rumour was false and felt sorry for how Lakshmi had been treated, so she wanted to make up for it.

Dilip sat by the window and looked at the grey sky. The geography lesson droned on about rivers. He watched a raindrop slide slowly down the glass and race another one that joined it. Soon the teacher's voice stopped, and the room went quiet. He turned and saw that every child was looking at him. "Dilip," said the teacher, "can you answer the question?" He had not even heard it. His ears went hot. A boy behind him tapped his back and whispered, "Brahmaputra." Dilip repeated it, and the class gave a little sigh of relief.

Why did Dilip's ears go hot?
He had been daydreaming and had not heard the question, so he felt embarrassed when everyone looked at him.

The school train to Hillside leaves from Platform Three at seven o'clock. Eleven students from the villages near the station take it every morning. They carry their bags on their laps and play card games on the journey, which takes forty minutes. The conductor, Mr. Das, knows them all and lets them stand near the door to watch the fields roll by. When the train arrives, the students walk up a short lane to the school gate. The last train home leaves at half past four, so the children must leave school promptly.

How long does the train journey take?
It takes forty minutes.

Mrs. Sengupta takes her Class Three students to a mango orchard just outside town every May. The trees stand in neat rows, and each one is marked with a number painted on the trunk. The owner, Mr. Hussain, lets the children pick fallen mangoes from the ground, but not the ones on the branches. They carry the fruit in cloth bags to the school kitchen, where the cook turns it into a sweet drink. The trip ends with a picnic under the largest tree.

Which mangoes are the children allowed to pick?
They may pick only the fallen mangoes from the ground, not the ones on the branches.

Last Sunday, Class Six students visited a vegetable farm run by Mrs. Pawar. She grows tomatoes, brinjals, okra and green chillies on two acres of land. The children walked along the rows and learned how to tell when okra is ready to pick. Each child picked ten pods and put them in a basket. The farm has a water tank and a small pump, which Mrs. Pawar switches on at six every morning. On the way out, she gave each child a small packet of seeds.

What did Mrs. Pawar give each child at the end?
She gave each child a small packet of seeds.

The lunch break at Hillcrest School lasts thirty minutes, from half past twelve to one o'clock. The younger children eat in their classrooms with their teachers, while the older ones go to the dining hall. The dining hall has long tables, and each table holds ten students. A bell rings five minutes before the end, as a signal to pack up. Students are expected to wash their hands before eating and to carry any waste to the bins at the door.

How long is the lunch break at Hillcrest School?
It lasts thirty minutes, from half past twelve to one o'clock.

Veer was learning to ride his new bicycle in the lane outside his house. His cousin held the back of the seat and ran beside him, calling out, "Pedal, pedal!" The bicycle wobbled and veered left, and Veer wailed that he wanted to stop. But his cousin laughed and said that he was already going alone. Veer glanced behind him and saw that nobody was holding the seat. He shrieked with joy, nearly lost balance, and rode all the way to the end of the lane. When he turned around, his cousin was far behind, clapping.

What did Veer realise when he looked behind him?
He realised that nobody was holding the seat, so he was riding by himself.

Pia's hands felt cold when the teacher placed the exam paper on her desk. She read the first question twice but could not remember the answer. Her heart beat faster. She looked at the clock and then at the window, where a sparrow sat on the ledge. She took a slow breath, as her mother had taught her, and closed her eyes for a few seconds. When she opened them, she read the question a third time. This time a picture of last week's lesson came to her mind, and she began to write steadily.

What helped Pia calm down and start writing?
She took a slow breath and closed her eyes for a few seconds, and then she could remember the lesson.

There is a small bookshop opposite the school gate, run by a man named Mr. Pinto. It has wooden shelves up to the ceiling and a rolling ladder. A sign on the door says that children can read for free until the closing time at six. Mr. Pinto keeps a stool near the picture books so that younger children can sit. Many students come after school to read comics. Once a month, he organises a story hour on Saturday morning.

Until what time can children read for free at the bookshop?
They can read for free until six o'clock.

Every Monday, the teacher of Class Six chooses a new monitor. This week, it is Bilal, who has to write the date on the board, collect the notebooks and switch off the fans at the end of the day. He also keeps a list of students who talk during class. Last Monday, the monitor was Sneha, and the week before that it was Arjun. The teacher says every child will get a turn before the year ends. Bilal said he was nervous about the job, but his friend promised to remind him about the fans.

What must the monitor do at the end of the day?
The monitor must switch off the fans.

Amrita and Juan were making a mud castle in the corner of the playground during recess. They shaped the walls with their hands and decorated them with small pebbles. Just as they placed the last pebble, the bell rang. Amrita looked at the castle with a worried face and asked if someone might step on it. Juan nodded slowly. Then he grabbed a few sticks and arranged them in a circle around the castle. "That will warn them," he said. They ran to class together, glancing back twice at their fence.

Why did Juan place sticks around the castle?
He wanted to protect it by warning other children not to step on it.

Rukmini's science project was a model of the solar system made of fruits and vegetables. The sun was a big yellow melon, Earth a blue grape, and Jupiter a large orange. She stuck them on thin sticks and arranged them on a wooden board using green tape. It took her three evenings to complete. At school, her teacher asked her to place it near the window so that everybody could see it. By the afternoon, the melon was beginning to smell, and the caretaker had to carry the whole model outside.

What fruit did Rukmini use for the sun?
She used a big yellow melon.

Lena crept down the corridor with a plate of cupcakes, trying not to make any noise. Behind her, three friends carried streamers and a banner that said "Welcome back, Mr. Rahim." The teacher had been away for a month because of an operation, and today was his first day back. They hid behind the classroom door as his footsteps came near. When he stepped in, everyone jumped out and cheered. Mr. Rahim stopped, put his hand on his chest, and blinked hard. Then he laughed and said that he had never felt so welcome in his whole life.

Why were the children so excited about Mr. Rahim's return?
They had missed him during the month he was away for his operation, and wanted to show him he was welcome.

Hugo moved to India from Germany with his parents in July. At his new school in Bangalore, he was put in Class Five. The teacher, Mrs. Murthy, asked a boy named Vinay to be his guide for the first week. Vinay showed him the library, the playground and the canteen. Hugo found the food spicy, but he liked the idlis. In the second week, he began teaching the class to count in German up to ten, and the children enjoyed repeating the words.

Which country did Hugo move from?
He moved from Germany.

The athletics coach set up six hurdles on the track for the Class Seven students to practise. Each hurdle was about knee high and spaced seven metres apart. The children had to jump over them without touching the bars. Arif knocked down two on his first try, while Sheila cleared all six. The coach told them to focus on the take-off foot and to keep their eyes on the finish line. By the end of the hour, even the slowest runners were leaping over most hurdles.

How many hurdles did the coach set up?
The coach set up six hurdles.

During the school's Diwali celebration, each class decorated one corner of the corridor. Class Three made rangoli with coloured sand in the shape of a peacock. Class Four set up a row of clay lamps along the stairs. Class Five made paper lanterns in red and gold. At five in the evening, the lights in the corridor were turned off, and the teachers lit the lamps one by one. Parents walked through the corridors and took photos. The evening ended with sweets, which were handed out by the Class Ten students.

What did Class Three make for Diwali?
They made a rangoli in the shape of a peacock using coloured sand.

A strong storm hit the town on Thursday night, and many trees fell near the school. On Friday morning, the principal sent a message that the building would be closed for the day. Teachers and parents spent the morning clearing branches from the playground. A group of senior students helped to remove a fallen gulmohar tree from the main road. By the afternoon, the gate was open again, and classes resumed on Saturday, the next day. The school also set up a small fund to plant new saplings in the playground.

On which day did classes resume?
Classes resumed on Saturday.

During silent reading, a note travelled from desk to desk and landed in front of Omar. He unfolded the paper. It said that a few children were planning to leave Lucas off the invitation list for the class party. Omar frowned, glanced across the room, and saw Lucas bent over his book with a very still face. Under the desk, Omar wrote on the same note, "That is not fair. I will tell Mrs. Das." He folded it and passed it back. After the lesson, Lucas looked at him with wide eyes, and Omar gave a small, firm nod.

What did Omar think about the plan to leave Lucas out?
He thought it was unfair. He wrote back that he would tell Mrs. Das.

A pair of pigeons nest on the ledge outside the Class Nine window. The children call them Gol and Gappa. Every morning, the birds coo loudly before the first lesson. This month, two small eggs appeared in their nest, and the children have promised not to open that window. The teacher, Mr. Saxena, has put up a note asking other classes not to disturb the ledge. When the eggs hatch, the students plan to take a photograph and add it to the class scrapbook.

What are the names of the pigeons?
They are called Gol and Gappa.

On Sports Day, the students stood in the sun for nearly two hours. The school nurse, Mrs. D'Cruz, set up a table near the water cooler with caps, cold towels and a large jug of lemon water. Any child who felt dizzy was asked to sit under the tent and rest. Three children needed her help, and all were fine after half an hour. In the evening, the principal thanked the staff for looking after everyone. The children were told to drink water often and to wear caps whenever they stood in the sun.

Who set up the table near the water cooler?
The school nurse, Mrs. D'Cruz, set it up.

At the school's winter camp, the children slept in a big hall on mattresses laid in rows. Each child had a numbered mattress, a blanket and a thin pillow. The teachers slept near the door. Lights were switched off at nine, but a few torches kept flickering until Mr. Daniels walked the length of the hall. In the morning, the cook, Mrs. Kamala, served hot porridge with jaggery. The children folded their blankets and stacked them at the end of each row.

What did the cook serve in the morning?
She served hot porridge with jaggery.

Hana fell off her bicycle outside the school gate and scraped her knee. A passing grandmother, who sold peanuts on the corner, brought a small bottle of water and a clean cloth. She wiped the cut, patted Hana's head, and gave her a handful of peanuts. Hana's friend, Rusli, helped her to the bench and waited until her mother arrived. The mother thanked the grandmother and offered her a few coins, but the woman refused and said it was nothing.

Who helped Hana to the bench?
Her friend Rusli helped her to the bench.

A few boys began calling Ben "Spectacles" when he came to school in his new glasses. He tried to laugh, but his smile looked stiff, and he kept pushing the frame up his nose. At lunch, he took them off and hid them in his pocket, squinting at his plate. Noticing this, his friend Arjun put on a pair of cardboard glasses he had made from an old box and wore them all through lunch. Soon the other boys stopped calling Ben names, and some even asked Arjun to make them a pair. Ben took his glasses out of his pocket and put them back on.

Why did Ben put his glasses back on?
Arjun's cardboard glasses made the teasing stop, so Ben felt more comfortable wearing his own.

Every afternoon at half past three, the canteen of Lakeview Junior School sells snacks to hungry children. Mr. Yadav, the canteen man, stands behind a wide steel counter with a tray of hot samosas on one side and a pile of banana chips on the other. A glass jar near the till holds small packets of roasted peanuts. Students pay with coins and move aside quickly so that others can reach the counter. Mr. Yadav knows most of the children by name and sometimes remembers what each one likes best. On Fridays he adds sweet corn cups to the menu, which sell out within ten minutes.

What does Mr. Yadav add to the menu on Fridays?
He adds sweet corn cups.

When the race began, Pavan shot to the front, but halfway round the track, a stitch caught his side. He slowed, and one by one the other runners passed him. He considered stopping. Then he saw his friend Hari at the edge of the track, running alongside the boundary and shouting, "One more lap!" Pavan gritted his teeth and kept going. He finished last, long after the others, but the crowd stood up and clapped for him. Hari handed him a bottle of water and said he was the bravest runner of the day.

Why did the crowd stand up and clap for Pavan?
He kept going and finished the race even though he was in pain and far behind.

On Independence Day, the whole school gathered on the lawn, and the flag was raised at seven-thirty. As the principal unfurled it, a shower of petals fell. The school band played the anthem, and all stood at attention. After that, the children from the junior classes presented a short programme of songs. Sweets were distributed at the gate, and each child received a small paper flag on a stick. Two older students then read out a poem about freedom. The ceremony ended at nine, and everyone went home.

At what time was the flag raised?
It was raised at seven-thirty.

Jaya's pencil was only an inch long, and she had to hold it by the very tip. When Mr. Nelson saw her struggling, he asked why she did not use a new one. Jaya looked at the floor and whispered that her grandfather had given it to her before he went away. The teacher did not say anything for a moment. Then he took a small metal cap from his drawer and fitted it on the end, so that she could hold it better. She looked at him, surprised, and a slow smile spread across her face.

Why would Jaya not throw away the short pencil?
Her grandfather had given it to her before he went away, so it had special meaning for her.

The summer holidays at Hill View School start on the first of May and end on the thirtieth of June. Before the break, every student receives a small booklet with holiday homework: two stories to read, one drawing to complete and a page of tables. Teachers remind the children to keep the booklet safe, away from sunlight and water. When school reopens, the class monitor collects the booklets, and the teacher gives a stamp for work that is neat. Students who forget to return it must stay back for ten minutes on the first day to finish it.

When do the summer holidays at Hill View School end?
They end on the thirtieth of June.

Kabir never raised his hand in class, even when he knew the answer. During a lesson on rivers, the teacher asked who could name the longest river in India, and he whispered the answer to himself. Beside him, his friend Zoya noticed his lips move. She leaned over and whispered, "Say it out loud, I'll help you." Kabir shook his head. After a while, she raised her own hand and said, "Kabir knows it." The whole class turned toward him. His ears went red, but he stood up and said, "The Ganga." The teacher smiled and nodded.

Why did Kabir's ears go red?
He was shy and nervous because the whole class turned to look at him.

The street lights near the school come on at six in the evening. A boy called Rafi, who stays back to practise for the cricket team, usually walks home just as they flicker on. His route takes him past the tea stall, the tailor's shop and a small temple with a yellow flag. He meets the milkman at the corner, who greets him with a nod. By half past six, Rafi is at his door, and his mother has laid a hot dinner on the table.

What does Rafi pass on his way home?
He passes the tea stall, the tailor's shop and a small temple with a yellow flag.

At noon on a sunny day, Mr. Fernando took his Class Six students into the yard with a metre stick and chalk. He asked them to mark where their shadows ended. They then repeated the measurement at two o'clock and four o'clock. At first, the children laughed and played with their shadows. By the third measurement, they noticed that the shadows were shortest at noon and longest at four o'clock. A girl named Ayesha raised her hand and said it must have something to do with how high the sun was. The teacher beamed.

What did Ayesha work out from the measurements?
She worked out that the length of a shadow depends on how high the sun is in the sky.

On school mornings in the Rao household, breakfast is served at seven. Nikhil's grandmother makes idlis on Mondays and Thursdays, upma on Tuesdays and dosas on Wednesdays. On Fridays, the family eats bread and eggs, which is Nikhil's favourite. His sister Ria complains if there is no chutney. Their mother wraps lunch while they eat, and their father reads the paper out loud, mostly the sports news. By half past seven, they are all at the door. On Sundays, they eat later, and there are often guests at the table.

What does the family eat on Wednesdays?
They eat dosas.

The pond at the edge of the village was deep, and the older boys jumped into it from the rock with loud whoops. Rafiq stood at the edge and watched. He had never learned to swim well, and he pretended to be busy looking for pebbles. When his friend Joseph called out, "Come on!" Rafiq shook his head. Joseph swam to the bank and sat beside him. "We can start at the shallow end," he said. For an hour, Joseph showed him how to float, holding him lightly. By evening, Rafiq could keep his head above the water by himself.

What does Joseph's offer to start at the shallow end show?
It shows that Joseph understood Rafiq was afraid and kindly helped him instead of teasing him.

Lukas had trained for the hundred-metre race for two months, but on the day of the final, his shoelace came undone at the starting line. He knelt to tie it while the other runners waited. The crowd groaned. He tied a firm double knot, stood up, and forced himself to take a long breath. When the whistle blew, he was a little behind the others. By the halfway mark, he had caught up with two of them, and in the last twenty metres, he pulled into second place. He crossed the line, bent over his knees, and laughed out loud even though he had not won.

Why did Lukas laugh even though he did not win?
He was proud and happy to have recovered from a bad start and finished second after the lace problem.

Zeynep hummed softly while she did her homework, and her little brother kept asking her to stop. She apologised each time, and a minute later she hummed again, without noticing. At last, he put his pencil down and said that he did not mind. "Actually, the tune is nice," he said. "What is it called?" She told him it was a lullaby her grandmother used to sing. He put his head on his arms and listened. By the time she had finished, he was fast asleep at the table.

Why did Zeynep's brother stop minding the humming?
He realised he liked the tune, and it was a soothing lullaby that made him sleepy.

Seven-year-old Mohan lost his first tooth during break on Wednesday. It came out when he bit into an apple, and he held it up in his fingers with wonder. The teacher gave him a small envelope to keep it in. His classmates crowded around, and a girl named Ruhi asked if the tooth fairy would come. Mohan said he would put it under his pillow that night. At home, he told his mother, who smiled and said that she would wait and see.

When did Mohan lose his first tooth?
He lost it during break on Wednesday, when he bit into an apple.

Every Monday, the monitor of Class Two collects a new box of chalk from the staff room. The box holds twelve white sticks and four coloured ones. Mr. Thomas likes to use the yellow chalk for headings and the blue for important words. When the sticks become short, the children save them in a tin, and on Fridays they use them to draw pictures on the pavement outside. The caretaker sweeps the chalk dust away every evening. When the sticks become too short to hold, the children bring them to the staff room to be thrown away.

How many coloured chalk sticks are in the box?
There are four coloured ones.

Nine-year-old Yara had never spoken in front of the whole school, and now she had to read a poem at the morning assembly. She stood behind the microphone and looked at the rows of faces. Her hands trembled, and the paper rustled. For a long moment she could not begin. Then she saw her small brother in the third row give a thumbs-up. She cleared her throat and read the first line, a bit too softly. By the end of the second stanza, her voice had grown firm, and the whole school listened. When she finished, there was loud clapping.

What gave Yara the courage to begin reading?
Seeing her little brother give her a thumbs-up encouraged her to start.

The chair at the front of Class Five is the biggest in the room, with a cushion and arms. Only the teacher sits in it, except on Fridays, when the Star Reader of the week reads a story from it. This week, the Star Reader was Neela, who picked a tale about a clever mouse. She sat very upright, with her feet not touching the floor. At the end, the class clapped, and she handed the book to the next child.

On which day does the Star Reader sit in the big chair?
The Star Reader sits in it on Fridays.

For their history project, the girls of Class Seven made a model of an old fort using cardboard, clay and small sticks. Divya cut the walls, Ishita painted them in brown and yellow, and Nandini built a tiny gate that opened and closed. They worked on Ishita's balcony for four evenings. On the last day, they added flags made of toothpicks and coloured paper. The next morning, they carried the model carefully to school in a large box, and the teacher placed it on the front table.

Who built the tiny gate for the fort?
Nandini built the tiny gate.

Ritika's blue umbrella has a wooden handle shaped like a duck's head. Her grandfather bought it for her at a fair in Pune two years ago. She carries it to school every day from June to September, even when the sky is clear, because she says she cannot trust the clouds. At the school gate, she leaves it in a tall stand with the other umbrellas, and she ties a yellow ribbon on it so that nobody takes it by mistake. On the last day of the monsoon, she dries it carefully and stores it in the cupboard.

What does Ritika tie on her umbrella so nobody takes it by mistake?
She ties a yellow ribbon on it.

Morning assembly at Hilltop School starts at ten minutes to eight in the open courtyard. The students stand in lines by class, with the youngest at the front. First, they sing the national anthem, then recite a short prayer. A student reads the news headlines from the day's paper, and the principal says a few words. On Mondays, the winning house of the week is announced. Assembly ends by eight, and the classes walk quietly to their rooms. Late students must wait at the gate and write their names in a register before they go in.

At what time does morning assembly start?
It starts at ten minutes to eight.

On Monday morning, Ananya opened her bag in the classroom and found that her maths notebook was missing. She remembered doing the sums at the kitchen table the night before, so she was sure she had finished them. Her teacher, Mrs. Verma, said she could bring it the next day. Ananya felt her face turn warm, but she nodded and sat down. At lunch, her friend Rohan told her to check the dining chair at home, because he sometimes left his own books there. When Ananya reached home that afternoon, she looked on the chair and found the notebook under a cushion. She packed it in her bag at once, next to her water bottle, so she would not forget it again.

Where did Ananya find her maths notebook?
She found it on the chair at home, under a cushion.

A small girl was crying behind the water tank during break. Naveen, passing by, stopped and asked what had happened. She said she had lost her hair clip, a gift from her aunt. Naveen did not say anything for a moment. Then he asked her where she had been playing. She pointed at the sandpit. He walked over, knelt down, and began sifting the sand with his fingers. After several minutes, he held up something small and shiny. She gasped, and her tears turned to a wide smile. He placed it in her palm, grinning.

How did Naveen help the girl?
He asked where she had been playing, searched the sandpit, and found her lost hair clip.

Wei saw Jorge whispering to the teacher and thought he was telling on him for talking in class. He glared at Jorge during recess and refused to share his ball. Jorge looked puzzled and sat by himself. Later, Wei heard that Jorge had been asking the teacher whether the class could hold a surprise party for Wei's birthday. His glare melted into shame. He found Jorge on the steps and said that he was sorry. Jorge shook his head and laughed, saying the party was still on for Friday.

Why did Wei feel ashamed later?
He had wrongly thought Jorge was telling on him, but Jorge was really planning a birthday surprise for him.

A new rule at school said that nobody could bring toys into the classroom. On Monday, Erin discovered a small plastic dinosaur in her pocket and looked at it with alarm. She could hear the teacher calling the register. She slipped it into her shoe and sat down, shifting uneasily. Throughout the lesson, she kept thinking about the dinosaur. During the break, she went to the teacher and held it out in her palm. "I forgot it was there," she said. The teacher asked her to keep it in her bag until home, and Erin nodded, relieved.

Why did Erin go to the teacher during the break?
She felt uneasy about hiding the toy and wanted to be honest, since she had broken the new rule by mistake.

The Class Four students of the village school made a scarecrow for the field beside their building. They stuffed an old shirt with straw, tied a pillowcase for the head and drew a smiling face with a marker. A boy named Kunal donated his grandfather's hat. They stood it on a wooden pole and named it Bhola. The farmer who owns the field, Mr. Reddy, thanked them and said the crows had already moved to the next field. The children visit it every Friday to check that its hat is still straight.

Whose hat was used for the scarecrow?
It was Kunal's grandfather's hat.

Rhea and Tara were working together on a science chart about the water cycle. Tara wanted to paint the clouds grey, but Rhea insisted they should be white and fluffy. Their voices grew louder until the whole table turned to look. Rhea pulled the chart toward herself, and Tara folded her arms and turned away. For a while nobody spoke. Then Tara quietly picked up a pencil and drew a small raincloud in the corner, and said, "This one can be grey." Rhea looked at it for a moment, nodded, and passed her the paintbrush.

What will the two girls probably do next?
They will probably finish the chart together. Tara's raincloud and Rhea passing the brush show they are making up.

Sunil was ashamed of his brother, who sold roasted corn near the school gate. When his friends walked past, he lowered his eyes and pretended not to see. One afternoon, a boy asked loudly, "Isn't that your brother?" Sunil's face burned. But then he saw his brother handing a cob to a small girl with a gentle smile, and realised that the man had worked hard to pay for Sunil's school fees. He walked up to the stall and said, "Hello, bhaiya." His brother grinned, and Sunil bought the biggest cob.

What made Sunil change how he behaved toward his brother?
He realised his brother worked hard to pay for his school fees, so he felt grateful instead of ashamed.

After the argument, Mel did not look at Ivy for the whole afternoon. Ivy tried to catch her eye twice, but Mel always turned to the window. When the final bell rang, Ivy waited at the gate with a folded note in her hand. Mel walked past her at first, and then she stopped. "What is that?" she asked, without turning. Ivy held it out. Mel unfolded it slowly, read it, and her mouth twitched. The note had a drawing of two crying faces and a single line: "Friends again?" Mel sighed, took Ivy's pencil, and drew two smiling faces beneath.

How did Mel answer Ivy's note?
She drew two smiling faces under it, which shows she forgave Ivy and wanted to be friends again.

While cleaning the classroom, Amit found a shiny ten-rupee coin under a desk. For a moment, he held it in his palm and thought of the ice cream at the corner shop. Then he looked around the room and noticed that Bela, who sat at that desk, was searching her bag with an anxious face. Amit walked over and held out the coin. "Is this yours?" he asked. Bela gasped and took it, saying it was her bus fare. After that, she sat next to Amit during the break and shared her peanuts.

Why did Bela sit next to Amit and share her peanuts?
She was grateful that he returned her bus fare when he could have kept it.

Sunita was spending her first night away from home at the school camp. When the lights went out, she lay still in her sleeping bag and heard unfamiliar sounds: crickets, a distant dog, someone turning over. A tear slid into her ear. After some time, the girl in the next bag whispered, "Are you awake?" Sunita whispered back that she was. "Me too," the girl said. "Shall we count the stars through the window?" They counted quietly until they both reached forty and fell asleep without finishing.

Why did the whispered conversation help Sunita?
It showed her she was not alone, and counting the stars distracted her from feeling homesick.

During the relay race, Pooja dropped the baton halfway through the second leg. The next runner, Darius, stopped and stared at it. Their team was already behind, and the crowd groaned. Pooja's eyes filled with tears. Darius ran back, picked up the baton, and gave it to her instead of taking it himself. "Finish your leg," he said. Pooja wiped her face with her sleeve and sprinted the last twenty metres. They came in last, but the teacher stood up and clapped for them as if they had won.

Why did the teacher clap even though they came in last?
The teacher admired how Darius supported Pooja and how she kept going, which mattered more than winning.

Meera's seventh birthday was on a Saturday, and her mother had planned a small party in the garden. There were paper hats, a table of samosas and lemonade, and a cake shaped like a rabbit. Six children from her class came at four o'clock. They played musical chairs on the grass, and Meera's cousin Kabir won the first round. After the game, everyone sat in a circle and sang while Meera blew out the candles. Her grandfather took photographs from a chair under the mango tree. When the guests left, each child carried home a little bag with a pencil and a sticker inside.

What shape was Meera's birthday cake?
It was shaped like a rabbit.

For the school dance, the Class Seven students were asked to work in pairs. Mrs. Almeida read out the names from a list, and each pair received a number. Anita was matched with Jacob, who was the tallest in the class. Malik was paired with Fiona. The pairs practised for forty minutes every Friday, with the music teacher playing a harmonium in the corner. The final performance was set for the first week of December, and all pairs were required to wear white.

What colour were all the pairs required to wear?
They were required to wear white.

Tia had hoped to win the school science prize, but the judges gave it to Marcus for his volcano model. She clapped with the others, though her hands felt heavy. Later, she walked home alone, kicking small stones. At the gate, her mother asked how it went, and Tia only shrugged. In her room, she opened her notebook and began to sketch a new idea, a machine that could carry water uphill. By dinner, her eyes had brightened. She told her mother that next year, she would be ready.

What does Tia's new sketch tell us about her?
It shows she is determined and does not give up easily. She turned her disappointment into a new plan.

Anjali always walked to school with her little brother Pico, who held her hand until they reached the gate. One morning, Pico let go and ran ahead, because he saw his friends playing. Anjali called after him, but he did not look back. For the rest of the day, she felt strangely light and strangely empty. At the end of school, when she came out of the gate, Pico was waiting by the wall. He took her hand again without saying anything, and she gave it a gentle squeeze.

Why did Anjali feel light and empty after Pico ran ahead?
She was used to him holding her hand, so without him she felt free but also a little lonely.

Mrs. Nambiar always keeps a bottle of warm water and a small jar of honey on her desk. During the winter months, many children cough in class, and she offers the honey in a spoon to anyone who needs it. She also asks the children to cover their mouths with a handkerchief. The windows are opened for a few minutes at the start of every period to let in fresh air. Parents are asked to keep children at home if they have a fever.

What does Mrs. Nambiar keep on her desk?
She keeps a bottle of warm water and a small jar of honey.

Every Wednesday, the Class One teacher takes her students for a nature walk around the school. They start at the main gate and walk along the boundary wall to the pond. At the pond, the children look for tadpoles, dragonflies and water lilies. They then cross a small bridge and stop under a banyan tree for a drink of water. Each child carries a small notebook and draws one thing they find on the way. The teacher ends the walk by asking each child to show their drawing and say what they noticed.

Where do the children stop for a drink of water?
They stop under a banyan tree.

At Oakwood School, the children are not allowed to bring mobile phones. In an emergency, parents may call the office on a landline. The receptionist, Mrs. Britto, writes down the message and sends a helper to deliver it to the right classroom. The school also gives each student a small card with their parents' phone numbers, which is kept in the class teacher's drawer. Phones found in bags are kept in the office until the end of term. Parents have said the system works well and gives them peace of mind.

What happens to phones found in the students' bags?
They are kept in the office until the end of term.

Four students stayed back after school on Thursday for talking during the assembly. They sat in room nine with Mr. Alvares and were asked to write a short letter of apology to the whole class. Rina wrote hers in neat cursive. Saif used only three lines. The teacher read each letter silently and then asked them to read them aloud on Friday morning. After they left, he closed the windows and switched off the lights. The teacher told them that the letters would be pinned to the notice board only if the writers agreed.

Why did the four students stay back on Thursday?
They stayed back because they talked during the assembly.

When Pablo came out of the school gate at three o'clock, he could not find his father's car at the usual place. He looked up and down the road and saw only strangers. His chest felt tight, and he held his bag straps with both hands. Then he remembered what his teacher had told them: if you are ever lost, go back to a safe adult. He walked slowly back inside, found the security guard at the gate, and told him his name and class. A few minutes later, his father rushed in, out of breath, saying his car had a flat tyre.

How did Pablo feel when he could not find the car?
He felt scared and worried. The passage says his chest felt tight and he held his bag straps with both hands.

Mrs. Pillai starts every Thursday with a reading hour. The children take out their library books and read quietly for twenty minutes. After that, each student tells the class one thing they enjoyed or learned. Today, Farhan talked about a story with a clever crow, and Eva described a book on sharks. Sunil admitted he had not finished his book yet, and the teacher told him he could take it home for the weekend. The children listened closely, because they could choose a new book from the shelf after the talks.

What did Eva talk about during the reading hour?
She described a book about sharks.

Hassan ran down the lane with his bag bouncing on his back. He had pressed the snooze button twice, and now the gate would close in three minutes. Sweat ran down his neck as he turned the corner. The guard was already pulling the gate across. Hassan waved both arms and shouted, "Wait, please!" The guard paused, looked at his watch, and then opened the gate wide enough for him to slip through. Hassan bent over with his hands on his knees and gasped his thanks. Then he walked into the building, vowing to wake up on time the next day.

Why was Hassan running so hard?
He was late for school and the gate was about to close, because he had pressed the snooze button.

The reading corner in Class Three has a green carpet, six cushions and a low shelf of picture books. Children go there when they finish work early or when they need a quiet moment. A rule on the wall says "Whisper only." Mrs. Thakur changes the books every two weeks, putting the favourites at eye level. Last month, a book about a lost balloon was borrowed so often that she had to buy a second copy. A small lamp stands beside the shelf.

How often does Mrs. Thakur change the books?
She changes them every two weeks.

Lucia noticed that the girl next to her had been wearing the same torn sweater all winter. At home, she opened her cupboard and found a green cardigan that was too small for her. She thought about it for a long time, then folded it neatly and put it in her bag. At school, she slipped it onto the other girl's chair before the lesson began, with no note. When the girl found it, she looked round the room, puzzled. Lucia kept her eyes on her book, and a small smile played on her lips.

Why did Lucia not leave a note with the cardigan?
She did not want attention or thanks. She kept her eyes on her book when the girl looked round, so she could help without embarrassing her.

Before the spelling test, Hannah read her list of twenty words again and again at the dinner table. Her older brother laughed and said it was too much work for a small quiz. Hannah ignored him and wrote each hard word three times in her notebook. At school the next day, Mr. Lewis read the words aloud, and she wrote them without stopping. When he returned the papers, she saw a big gold star on top and a score of nineteen. She pressed the page flat on her desk, smiled quietly to herself, and did not say a word to anyone until the bell.

Why did Hannah do well on her spelling test?
She practised hard. She read the words many times and wrote the difficult ones three times each.

The Class Seven teacher keeps a large dictionary on her desk, and each Tuesday a student is asked to find a new word. Last week the word was "generous". Fatima read out the meaning, and the class gave examples. Suresh said his uncle was generous because he gave his old bicycle away. The teacher wrote the word on the board, and every child copied it into a vocabulary notebook. She likes to say that a small word learned every week adds up to fifty new words in a year.

What word was chosen for last Tuesday?
The word was generous.

The school barber visits on the last Saturday of every month. He sets up a chair under the neem tree and charges five rupees per haircut. Boys in Classes Five to Ten line up on the bench, and the prefects keep order. A mirror hangs from a branch on a piece of wire. Girls may use the same spot to have their fringes trimmed, but only if the teachers allow it. Haircuts end by noon, and the barber stays for a cup of tea in the staff room.

How much does a haircut cost?
A haircut costs five rupees.

Mr. Kapoor teaches science to the fifth class at Green Valley School. Every Friday, he brings one strange object to show the students. Last week it was a piece of black volcanic rock that floated in a bowl of water. The children crowded around the table to touch it. He asked them to write down one question about the rock in their notebooks. Zara wrote about how a rock could be so light. Mr. Kapoor promised they would find the answer together on Monday, when they would study how lava cools and traps tiny bubbles of air.

On which day of the week does Mr. Kapoor bring a strange object?
He brings one every Friday.

Bus number twelve picks up the children of Lotus Colony at seven-fifteen each morning. The driver, Mr. Anwar, always waits at the same corner, under the old banyan tree. He keeps a small steel box of toffees near the steering wheel and gives one to anyone who is early. The bus then passes the post office and the temple before reaching the school gate at eight. On rainy days it comes ten minutes later because the road near the bridge is slow. Mr. Anwar has been driving this route for eleven years.

Where does Mr. Anwar wait for the children each morning?
He waits at the same corner under the old banyan tree.

Zoe's handwriting was very messy. Her teacher often wrote "Please be neater" in red ink beside her answers. One evening, Zoe's older sister sat with her and showed her how to hold the pen lightly and write slowly. They practised a page of letters together. At first, Zoe's lines wobbled, and she wanted to give up. But after a week, her sister held her notebook up to the lamp and said, "Look at this." Zoe looked, and the writing was straight and clear. She hugged her notebook and ran to show her mother.

What helped Zoe improve her handwriting?
Her older sister showed her how to hold the pen lightly and write slowly, and they practised together for a week.

In the Class One music lesson, Miss Fernandes teaches rhythm by clapping. First, she claps a pattern, and the children copy it. Then she makes the pattern longer, with two slow claps and three fast ones. The children sit in a circle, and each takes a turn to invent a pattern for the others. Yesterday, Rani made one with four claps and a stamp. Everyone tried it, and Miss Fernandes added it to the list on the board. The children say it is their favourite part of the day, and the shy ones join in by the end.

What did Rani's pattern include?
It had four claps and a stamp.

A narrow canal runs behind the village school, and the children cross it every morning on a plank of wood. In the monsoon, the water rises almost to the plank, and the teacher, Mr. Chandra, waits on the other side to hold each child's hand. The older students help the little ones to balance. After school, they take their sandals off and wade in the shallow water near the bank, looking for small fish. When the sun begins to drop, they walk home along the paddy field.

Who waits on the other side of the plank during the monsoon?
The teacher, Mr. Chandra, waits there to hold each child's hand.

Mr. Verghese gives a sticker every Friday to the child who has shown the most improvement. The stickers are small silver stars, kept in an old biscuit tin on his shelf. Last Friday, the sticker went to Deepa, who had been struggling with reading since June. Now she can read a whole page without stopping. She put the star on her notebook, next to a drawing of a sunflower. The rest of the class clapped, and Mr. Verghese promised to find a longer book for her.

Who received the sticker last Friday?
Deepa received it.

In art class, Ms. Banerjee gave each child a sheet of blue paper and a small box of chalk. She asked them to draw their favourite place in the world. Hamid drew the sea, with a red boat and three white birds. Lena drew her grandmother's kitchen, with a table and a round clock. Others drew parks, cricket grounds and even a train station. After twenty minutes, the teacher pinned the drawings along the back wall. She said she would leave them there until the parents' day on Friday.

What did Hamid draw in art class?
He drew the sea, with a red boat and three white birds.

The Class Nine students publish a monthly newspaper called The School Bell. It has four pages. The front page carries school news, such as exam dates and winners of competitions. The second page has a column of jokes and riddles. The third is for interviews, and last month's was with the school cook. The back page has sports results. A teacher, Mr. Chakraborty, checks every article for spelling before it is printed. Copies are pinned on the notice board, and a few are sent to the parents of the writers.

What is the name of the students' newspaper?
It is called The School Bell.

After a week of heavy rain, the children of the class were restless and cross. Mrs. Joseph tried a quiet story and a game of dumb charades, but nothing worked. Then she slipped on a wet spot near the door and sat down with a bump, her glasses sliding down her nose. For a moment, no one moved. Then Ankur let out a giggle, and the whole class roared. Mrs. Joseph laughed too, holding her sides. Afterward, the room felt lighter, and the children worked happily for the rest of the day.

How did the teacher's fall change the mood of the class?
It made everyone laugh, including the teacher, and the cross, restless mood turned happy.

Wanjiru's shoes were too small, and her toes pressed against the front whenever she ran. She never told anyone, because her mother had worked extra shifts to buy them. At sports practice, the coach noticed that she stopped before the last lap and held her foot. After practice, he quietly asked her to meet him in his office. He took out a pair of used shoes from a cupboard and said they had been left by students who had outgrown them. Wanjiru tried them on, and they fitted. She walked out of the office with the shoes in her hands and a very big smile.

Why did Wanjiru not tell anyone her shoes were too small?
She knew her mother had worked extra shifts to buy them and did not want to make her feel bad.

The school stationery shop is run by two Class Twelve students, who take turns after the last period. They sell pencils, erasers, glue sticks, rulers and notebooks, each for one rupee more than it costs the shop. Every student receives a small card where purchases are marked. At the end of the term, the shop's earnings are counted and given to the school's charity fund. Last term, they collected eight hundred and twenty rupees, which bought blankets for a nearby shelter. The two students keep a small ledger, which the teacher checks every Friday.

What was bought with the shop's earnings last term?
Blankets for a nearby shelter were bought.

The class was asked to learn a four-line poem about the moon for Friday. Meena learned it on Tuesday while she was brushing her hair. Joseph practised it with his grandfather on Wednesday evening, saying each line aloud after dinner. Several other students wrote the words on their palms and read them on the school bus. On Friday morning, Ms. Craig called them one by one to the front. Meena went first, and she did not forget a single word. Joseph went fourth, and he made her laugh by adding a funny face at the end.

On which day did Meena learn the poem?
She learned it on Tuesday.

The school garden had been quiet for weeks because nobody remembered to water it. One morning, Grade Three students discovered that their bean plants had gone yellow and bent. Sofia touched a dry leaf and sighed. Then she turned to her friends and suggested a list of names, one for each day of the week. Every student would bring a bottle of water on their day. The next Monday, Imran arrived first with a large bottle and poured it slowly around the stems. By the end of the month, small green pods had appeared on the vines.

Why did the bean plants turn yellow?
Nobody watered them for weeks, so they became dry.

The nursery class keeps a white rabbit named Snowy in a cage near the window. Each child takes a turn to bring a carrot or a handful of grass from home. Miss Aguiar explains that the rabbit eats best in the morning and sleeps in the afternoon. The children are allowed to stroke Snowy only when the teacher is present, and only with one hand. Last month, the rabbit had a visit from a vet, who said she was healthy.

What is the rabbit's name?
The rabbit's name is Snowy.

Before the school year began, Meghna and her mother went to the stationery shop on Market Road. They bought five notebooks, a geometry box, three blue pens and a red one. Meghna also picked a purple pencil case with a small zip. The shopkeeper wrapped everything in brown paper and tied it with string. On the way back, they stopped at a juice stall and shared a glass of sugarcane juice. At home, Meghna laid out all her new things on the bed and counted them twice.

What colour pencil case did Meghna choose?
She chose a purple pencil case.

Yusuf was not chosen as captain, and he walked off the field without saying a word. He sat under the neem tree with his chin on his knees. After a while, his friend Bharat came and sat beside him. Bharat did not say anything about the captaincy. He just opened his bag, took out a piece of jaggery, and broke it into two parts. Yusuf took the smaller piece, chewed it for a minute, and then picked up a stick to draw circles in the dust. When the bell rang, he stood up first and offered Bharat a hand.

What does Bharat's silence and the jaggery suggest about him?
It suggests he is a caring friend who knew Yusuf was upset and tried to comfort him without lecturing.

Aisha has a pen friend named Clara who lives in Scotland. They write to each other once a month, using blue envelopes that Aisha's aunt brings from the post office. In her last letter, Clara described the snow and a bagpipe concert. Aisha replied with a drawing of a mango tree and a pressed jasmine flower. She also taught Clara how to say hello in Hindi. Clara answered that she would try to learn a new Hindi word every week.

Where does Aisha's pen friend live?
She lives in Scotland.

The new boy in Class Three, Emeka, brought only a single pencil on his first day. When the teacher asked everyone to take out their colours, he sat with his hands in his lap. Lucy, who sat nearby, noticed. She quietly slid her box of twelve crayons to the middle of the desk and went on drawing. Emeka looked at her, then at the crayons, and took a blue one. Neither of them said anything. After class, Emeka stopped at her desk and handed her a small drawing of a bird. Lucy put it carefully into her bag.

Why did Emeka give Lucy a drawing?
He wanted to thank her for sharing her crayons when he had none.

Behind the curtain, Freya could hear the audience murmuring. She was playing a talking tree in the school play and had only three lines. Her hands were damp, and her leaf costume itched. She whispered the lines to herself again and again. Then the curtain opened, and the bright lights made everything white. Her first line came out as a squeak, and someone in the back row giggled. Freya blinked, straightened her branches, and spoke the next line in a deep, slow voice. The audience laughed with delight, and she felt her fear fade.

Why did the audience laugh with delight at Freya's second line?
She used a deep, slow voice that suited a talking tree, which was funny and charming.

The Class Seven students took a trip to the old lighthouse on the coast. It stands on a rocky point, and its white tower is almost forty metres high. A keeper named Mr. Antony led them up the spiral staircase, which has two hundred and twelve steps. At the top, they could see boats like toys on the sea. He showed them the big lamp and explained how it turns to send a beam of light far over the water. Everyone clapped when they reached the ground again.

How many steps does the spiral staircase have?
It has two hundred and twelve steps.

When the first drops of the monsoon fell, the children of Class One ran into the open yard and spun with their arms out. The teacher watched from under the verandah. Her first thought was to call them back, because they would catch a cold. But she saw how their faces shone, and she remembered doing the same in her own childhood.
