She let them play for five minutes, and then she called them in, one by one, and rubbed their hair with a towel. The children kept giggling and asking for another turn.

Why did the teacher let the children play in the rain for five minutes?
She remembered her own childhood and saw how happy the children were, so she allowed a short time.

Sara's school uniform needed new buttons, so her mother took her to the tailor in the next lane. The shop was narrow and smelled of cloth. A man named Mr. Gopal sat on the floor behind a sewing machine, and a calendar of a mountain hung above him. He measured her shirt with a yellow tape and said it would be ready by Thursday. Sara watched him thread a needle without looking at it. On the way out, he gave her a small button as a gift.

On which day would the shirt be ready?
It would be ready by Thursday.

For the school picnic, each child in Class Two was asked to bring one item to share. Mira brought cheese sandwiches cut into triangles. Joel brought a bag of grapes and a bottle of orange squash. Fatima brought boiled peanuts in newspaper cones, which she had made herself. The teacher had packed napkins, paper plates and a big flask of water. They spread a blue sheet under a mango tree near the lake and ate until the plates were empty.

What did Fatima bring to the picnic?
She brought boiled peanuts in newspaper cones that she had made herself.

Whenever Priyanka's school ended early, she walked to her grandmother's flat, which was only two streets away. Her grandmother always had a small glass of warm milk and a plate of biscuits ready, even if nobody had phoned to say she was coming. One day Priyanka asked how she always knew. Her grandmother smiled and said, "I just listen for your footsteps." Priyanka laughed, but that evening she walked on tiptoe and still found the milk waiting. She gave her grandmother a long hug.

What does the glass of milk waiting every time show about Priyanka's grandmother?
It shows she loves Priyanka and pays close attention to her, so she is always ready for her visit.

Aarav checked the clock on the classroom wall for the fifth time in ten minutes. His foot tapped the floor, and he kept glancing at the door. Today his uncle was coming to take him to the cricket stadium, and the last period was a long grammar lesson. Mrs. Rao noticed him fidgeting and asked whether the clock had done something wrong. A few children giggled. Aarav sat up straight and pretended to read his book. Yet at the first sound of the final bell, he was out of his seat and halfway to the door before the teacher finished her sentence.

Why did Aarav keep looking at the clock?
He was excited about going to the cricket stadium with his uncle and wanted school to end.

The final exam for English began at nine o'clock in Hall B. Students were told to leave their bags at the front and to bring only two pens and a pencil. Ms. D'Souza walked between the rows, handing out the question papers face down. Nobody was allowed to turn them over until the clock on the wall struck nine. The paper had three sections: a reading passage, a short essay, and grammar questions. The students had two hours to finish. Those who completed early could raise a hand and wait quietly, but they could not leave before ten-thirty.

How many sections did the English paper have?
It had three sections: a reading passage, a short essay, and grammar questions.

Mr. Dutta gives homework only from Monday to Thursday. On Friday, the children are free to read whatever they like. In English, they write five sentences using new words. In maths, there are ten sums, usually on fractions or measurement. Science homework is a drawing with labels, to be done once a week. The teacher checks every notebook on the next morning, and he puts a green tick for neat work. Anyone who is absent must copy the homework from a friend and show it to him the next day.

On which days does Mr. Dutta give homework?
He gives homework from Monday to Thursday.

The boundary fence of the school was damaged in a storm, and two long sections fell flat. The principal asked the parents' association to help. On a Sunday morning, twelve fathers arrived with hammers, nails and wooden poles. The children brought water and tea, and one of the mothers made jalebi. By noon, the new fence stood straight again, and the fathers painted it white. The principal thanked them with a short speech at the gate. The old fence had been there for more than twenty years, and the new one is expected to last as long.

Who repaired the fence?
Twelve fathers from the parents' association repaired it.

Class Six went to the botanical garden on Thursday. The bus left at eight and reached the gate around nine-thirty. A guide named Mr. Fernandez led the group along a stone path lined with ferns and orchids. He pointed out a tree that is over a hundred years old, and a pond with red and white lotuses. At noon, the children sat on the grass for lunch. Before leaving, they each picked up one fallen leaf to take back to school for a collection.

What did each child take back from the garden?
Each child took back one fallen leaf for a collection.

At half past six, the alarm rings in Dev's room. He brushes his teeth, puts on his school uniform and drinks a glass of milk. His mother ties his shoelaces while he finishes a banana. At seven, the school van honks outside, and Dev runs down the stairs with his bag. His little sister waves from the window and shouts goodbye. On the way, he usually reads the next chapter of his adventure book. He is often the first student to sit down when the van reaches the school gate.

What does Dev do before the school van arrives?
He brushes his teeth, puts on his uniform, drinks milk and eats a banana.

Sofia saw her friend Daniel slide a small folded paper from his sleeve during the science test. Her stomach turned. She kept her eyes on her own sheet and tried to write, but her pencil kept freezing. After the test, she waited by the gate until Daniel came out. She said quietly that she had seen the paper, and that she was worried about him. Daniel stared at the ground and said he had been afraid of failing. Sofia offered to help him study before the next test. He looked up at her slowly and nodded.

Why did Daniel use the paper in the test?
He was afraid of failing the test.

On rainy afternoons, the children of Class Three are allowed to play indoor games in the activity room. There are four shelves: one with board games, one with building blocks, one with puzzles and one with story cards. Last Wednesday, Ruhi and Kai worked on a puzzle of a map of India, which had a hundred pieces. It took them forty minutes, and they could not find the piece for Goa. They finally found it under the carpet. Both children said the Goa piece was the smallest one in the whole box, and they were proud to have found it.

Where was the missing piece of the puzzle found?
It was found under the carpet.

On the last day before the holidays, Mrs. Dutt asked each child to stand and say one kind thing about the person on their left. Giggles filled the room. Arman said that Kritika always shared her pencils. Kritika said that Dev made her laugh. When the turn came to Rishi, the quietest child, he blushed and said that Manu helped him with sums. Manu looked down and smiled. By the end of the circle, the room felt warm, and nobody wanted the bell to ring. The teacher wiped her eyes quickly and told them to have a wonderful holiday.

Why did the teacher wipe her eyes?
She was touched by the kind things the children said, so she felt emotional.

Before he left for the holidays, Kiran told his friend Mateo that he would send him a postcard from the hill station. Mateo did not believe him. Nobody else had ever kept such a promise. For two weeks, he checked the letterbox every afternoon and found only bills. On the sixteenth day, a card with a picture of snowy mountains lay inside. On the back, in uneven handwriting, were the words "I did not forget." Mateo read it three times, then ran up the stairs and stuck it on the wall above his bed.

What did the postcard show Mateo about Kiran?
It showed that Kiran kept his promise and cared about their friendship, since he really did send it.

By the third period, Kavin's stomach rumbled so loudly that the girl next to him turned and stared. He pressed his hand against it, but it only grumbled again. He had missed breakfast because the bus came early, and his tiffin lay at the bottom of his bag, untouched until lunch. Mrs. Anand noticed his face and walked over. She quietly placed a small banana on his desk and said nothing. Kavin ate it in two bites, hiding behind his open book. For the rest of the lesson, he kept his eyes on the board.

Why did Kavin's stomach rumble in class?
He was hungry because he had missed breakfast, and his lunch had not yet been eaten.

The school library at St. Mary's is on the second floor, next to the computer room. It opens at eight in the morning and closes at four in the afternoon. Each student may borrow two books at a time for one week. If a book is late, the student must pay a small fine of one rupee per day. Mrs. Fernandes, the librarian, keeps a box of bookmarks near her desk and gives one to any child who finishes a book early. This month, the shelf near the window holds new stories about animals and space.

How long can a student keep a library book?
A student can keep a book for one week.

A crow often visits the window of Class Two in the afternoon. The children give it bits of chapati from their tiffin boxes, and it takes them in its beak and flies to the neem tree. Their teacher, Miss Lobo, says the crow is clever and remembers faces. One day, a boy named Tarun left a shiny paper clip on the sill, and the next day the crow left a small stone there in return. The children have named the crow Kaalu.

What have the children named the crow?
They have named it Kaalu.

One evening, while locking the school gate, the caretaker heard a faint hoot from the big tamarind tree. He shone his torch up and saw a round-faced owl staring down. The next morning, he told the Class Three children, who were thrilled. They begged to see it. Mrs. Khanna agreed to stay back with them after school. They sat on the steps in the dusk, whispering and watching. When the owl finally appeared on a branch, no one made a sound. Even the noisiest boy held his breath until it flew away.

Why did the noisiest boy hold his breath?
He was so amazed to see the owl that he stayed silent and still so he would not scare it away.

Eight-year-old Shreya had saved her pocket money for six weeks to buy a pink pencil box. On the way to the shop with her aunt, she saw a smaller girl crying near the gate because she had lost her own money. Shreya stopped walking and looked at the coins in her purse. She counted them, hesitated, then placed half of them in the girl's hand. When she reached the shop, she could not buy the pencil box. Yet she smiled the whole way home, humming a song, and her aunt hugged her.

What does Shreya's smile on the way home show?
It shows that she felt good about helping the crying girl, even though she lost her chance to buy the pencil box.

Dhanush gave each friend a small folded note on the last day of Class Five. He had written the notes the night before, sitting on his bed. Next year, he would be moving to another city, and he had not told anyone. His friend Alka opened hers on the bus and read it twice. Her eyes filled with tears, and she quickly wiped them with her sleeve. At the next stop, she got off and ran back to the school gate, but Dhanush's father was already driving away. She held the note tightly in her hand.

How did Alka feel after reading the note?
She felt very sad. Her eyes filled with tears and she ran back to the gate to see him.

Liam and Joel had been best friends since the first grade, and they always sat together on the school bus. One Tuesday, Liam climbed on and saw that Joel was sitting in the back with a new boy, talking and laughing. Liam walked past them and took a seat near the front. He kept his eyes on the window for the whole ride and did not turn around once. When the bus stopped, he got off quickly, even though Joel called his name twice. At home, he left his dinner half eaten and told his mother he was not hungry.

Why did Liam probably sit near the front of the bus?
He was probably upset or jealous that Joel was sitting with a new boy. He then stared out of the window and would not turn around.

The students of Class Eight were asked to bring their own water bottles to school from the first of July. The principal explained that the old plastic cups in the corridor were being removed. In their place, the school installed a steel water tank with four taps near the playground. Each Monday, a team of two students checks that the taps are working and the area is dry. The team reports any problem to Mr. Bhatt, the caretaker, who fixes it before the end of the day.

Where was the new water tank installed?
It was installed near the playground.

On Sunday mornings, the children of Palm Street meet at the corner field for an informal game of football. The players do not wear uniforms, and there are no referees. They divide into two teams by choosing numbers: those who say odd numbers go to one side, even to the other. The game stops at ten, when the church bell rings and the sun gets hot. After the match, they share a bottle of juice that Ayaan's mother sends with a boy on a bicycle.

When does the Sunday football game stop?
It stops at ten, when the church bell rings and the sun gets hot.

In Class Six, every student must keep five notebooks: one each for English, maths, science, social studies and Hindi. Mrs. Kulkarni asks them to cover each notebook in brown paper and write their name and class on a white label at the front. She checks the labels on the first Monday of the month. If a label is missing, the student receives a small note to take home. The notebooks are collected every Friday and returned on Monday, with comments in red ink.

When does Mrs. Kulkarni check the labels?
She checks them on the first Monday of the month.

Every Sunday, Arun's father gives him twenty rupees for the week. Arun puts ten in a small tin box shaped like a postbox and keeps the rest in his pocket. In the school canteen, he buys one samosa on Tuesday and a bar of chocolate on Friday. By the end of the month, the tin has forty rupees. He is saving for a football that costs two hundred, and his father has promised to add the remaining money if Arun reaches one hundred by December.

How much does Arun put in the tin each Sunday?
He puts ten rupees in the tin.

At lunch, the children of Class Three line up with metal trays. A server places a spoonful of rice, a ladle of dal and a piece of fruit on each tray. The children then find their seats at the long benches. Before eating, they say a short thank-you together. At the end, each child washes their own tray in a large tub of water and stacks it on a shelf. Today's fruit was a small yellow banana for everyone. After lunch, the monitors sweep the floor and wipe the benches before the bell.

What fruit did the children get today?
They each got a small yellow banana.

On Makar Sankranti, the children of Ward Road gathered on the terrace of Mr. Patel's building to fly kites. Jay brought a red kite with a long tail, and his sister Nisha carried a roll of strong thread. The wind was good by ten o'clock, and soon the sky was dotted with yellow, orange and green patterns. A neighbour kept shouting "Kai po che!" every time a kite was cut. At noon, Mrs. Patel sent up a tray of tilgul sweets, and everyone sat on the mats to eat before flying again.

What colour was Jay's kite?
His kite was red, with a long tail.

Two weeks after Arjun's family moved to another country, a package arrived at Sam's door. Inside was a small flag, a picture of a snowy street, and a letter written in Arjun's slanted handwriting. Sam read it three times, laughing at the part about the strange food. Then he took his green pen and began to write back, filling a whole page before dinner. He drew a map of their old street and marked the tree where they used to climb. He pressed the paper into an envelope as carefully as if it were glass.

What does the care Sam takes with the envelope show?
It shows that Sam values the friendship and treasures the letter, so he handles it very gently.

On Saturday morning, Mrs. Dias took her Class Five students to the local vegetable market as part of a lesson on money. Each child was given fifty rupees and a list of three items to buy. Roshan chose tomatoes, onions and a bunch of coriander. Carla bought a cucumber and two lemons. They had to ask the vendors for prices and write them in their notebooks. After half an hour, the class met at the entrance and counted the change they had left over.

What was the lesson at the market about?
The lesson was about money, with each child buying items with fifty rupees.

When the power went out during the school's evening practice, the whole building fell into darkness. Mr. Saldanha found a box of candles in the staff room and lit six of them, placing them in the middle of the hall. The children sat in a circle, and he asked each to say what they liked most about school. Zia said lunch. Hari said the library. Mariam said the way chalk smelled on the first day. After half an hour, the lights came back, and the children groaned because they wanted to continue.

Where did Mr. Saldanha find the candles?
He found them in a box in the staff room.

Everyone stood up when the bell rang, but Ishani stayed seated, staring at her notebook. She had only finished half the page, and the teacher had said that no one could eat until it was done. Her stomach growled. The boy beside her slid his chair closer and whispered, "Let me read you the answer while you write." They did it together, and in three minutes, Ishani was finished. She thanked him, grabbed her tiffin, and ran to the dining hall, two steps behind him, laughing.

Why did Ishani stay seated when the bell rang?
She had not finished her work, and the teacher had said nobody could eat until it was done.

The Dsouza family lives on the first floor of Rose Apartments, and their neighbour is Mrs. Iyer. Every evening at five, Mrs. Iyer waters the plants on the balcony. The Dsouza children, Tia and Neil, often wave to her from their window. On Sundays she bakes ginger biscuits and leaves a small plate outside their door. Last Sunday, Tia left a drawing of a flower in return, and Mrs. Iyer stuck it on her fridge. The children from the building say the biscuits are the best thing about the weekend.

What does Mrs. Iyer bake on Sundays?
She bakes ginger biscuits.

The older boy snatched Nikhil's cap and held it high above his head. Nikhil jumped for it twice, but the boy laughed and tossed it to a friend. A crowd of children watched without moving. Then Sabina, a tiny girl from Class Three, stepped forward and said, "Give it back, or I will call the teacher." Her voice was thin but clear. The boy hesitated, glanced around at the silent crowd, and dropped the cap on the ground. Nikhil picked it up, brushed off the dust, and thanked Sabina, who was shaking a little.

Why did the older boy drop the cap?
He was afraid of being caught. Sabina threatened to call the teacher, and the whole crowd was watching him.

Nora invited three friends to her house for a sleepover on Saturday night. They arrived at six with sleeping bags and pillows, and Nora's father had made a big pot of pasta. After dinner, the girls watched a movie in the living room and then made a tent out of bedsheets between two sofas. At eleven o'clock, Nora's mother told them to turn off the lights. They whispered and giggled for another hour. In the morning, the smell of pancakes woke them up, and they ate breakfast in their pyjamas.

What did Nora's father cook for dinner?
He made a big pot of pasta.

During the school trip to the zoo, the children stood in front of the elephant enclosure for twenty minutes. A young elephant named Raja was playing in a pool, spraying water over his back. The zookeeper explained that elephants eat for about sixteen hours a day. Some students asked why the elephant flapped his ears, and the keeper said it helped him cool down. Before leaving, each child threw a small bunch of grass over the fence, and Raja caught every piece with his trunk.

What was the elephant's name?
The young elephant's name was Raja.

When Mr. Pereira announced a surprise test, Dhruv slumped in his chair and pulled his cap over his eyes. His friend Ravi leaned over and asked whether he had studied. Dhruv shook his head slowly. "I was playing games all weekend," he whispered. Ravi hesitated, then slid his notebook halfway across the desk, opened to a page of notes. "Read this fast," he said. Dhruv skimmed it as the papers were handed out. He looked up, grateful, and whispered, "I owe you." Ravi smiled and put his finger to his lips, pointing at the teacher.

Why did Ravi put a finger to his lips?
He wanted Dhruv to stay quiet so the teacher would not notice that they were sharing notes.

The bus was crowded, and only one seat was left. Jaya, who had a bad cold, climbed into it gratefully. A boy of about five, standing near her with his school bag, was swaying with every turn. He did not complain. Jaya looked at him, then scooted over so that he could sit on the very edge. He sat with a stiff back, then slowly relaxed, leaning his head on his bag. At the next stop, he whispered "Thank you" without looking at her. She sneezed, and they both laughed.

What did the little boy's whisper of thanks mean?
He was grateful that Jaya shared her seat with him, though he was too shy to say it aloud.

Rajiv had been told he could not join the football team because he was too small. Instead of giving up, he stayed behind after school and kicked the ball against the wall. At first, he missed half the time. After a month, he rarely missed. One day, the coach, passing by, stopped and watched for a while. He called Rajiv over and asked him to play in the next friendly match. Rajiv scored twice. Afterwards, the coach said that skill and effort mattered more than size.

What made the coach change his mind about Rajiv?
He saw how hard Rajiv practised after school and how well he kicked the ball.

Hamza was famous in class for his mother's sweet coconut barfi, which he brought on special days. The other children begged him for the recipe. He refused, saying it was a family secret. One day, a new girl named Leela admired the barfi and said it tasted like her late grandmother's. Hamza paused, then softly asked her about the grandmother. They talked about it all through the break, and he ended by writing the recipe on a small piece of paper and sliding it across to her. "Do not tell the others," he said.

Why did Hamza share the recipe with Leela but not with the others?
Leela's story about her late grandmother touched him, so he felt close to her and wanted to help her.

For the craft hour, each student in Class Four received a lump of clay and a wooden stick. They were asked to shape a small animal or a bowl. Hira made an elephant with a long trunk. Marco made a snail on a leaf, and he spent a long time pressing the curl of the shell. The clay models had to dry for two days. After that, the students painted them with poster colours and placed them on the window sill.

What did Marco make from the clay?
He made a snail on a leaf.

Lina dropped one of her red gloves on the way to school and did not notice until she reached the gate. Her fingers were stiff with cold. She turned back to look for it but saw only dirty snow along the road. At lunch, she found a red glove sitting on her desk, with a little note beside it. The note said, "I found this near the bus stop. Hope it's yours. Ravi." She looked across the room at the boy who was drawing quietly at the back. He glanced up, blushed, and returned to his picture.

How did Ravi probably know the glove was Lina's?
He had probably seen her wearing red gloves, and the one he found near the bus stop matched. His note says he only hoped it was hers.

Isla did not like her grandmother's carrot soup, and she pushed her bowl away every evening. Her grandmother did not scold her. One day, she asked Isla to come to the garden and pull a carrot from the ground herself. Isla tugged hard and fell back with a muddy orange carrot in her hand. She laughed. That night, her grandmother cooked the same soup, using Isla's carrot. Isla sipped it carefully, then took another sip. "It tastes sweeter," she said, and she finished the bowl.

Why did the soup taste sweeter to Isla?
She had pulled the carrot herself, so she felt proud and interested in the soup.

In the last match of the term, Diego stood at the penalty spot with the ball in front of him. The score was tied at two goals each, and only five seconds remained. The goalkeeper, a tall boy named Femi, crouched and spread his arms. The whistle blew. Diego kicked low to the left, and the ball slid past Femi's fingers into the net. The spectators leapt up, and his teammates piled on top of him. The coach said later that it was the calmest penalty he had seen.

What was the score before Diego's penalty?
The score was tied at two goals each.

After school, the boys of Lane Seven play cricket in the empty plot behind the temple. They use a flat wooden plank as a bat and a taped tennis ball. Samar is usually the bowler, because he has a quick arm. Yash keeps the score on a scrap of paper with a stub of pencil. When the ball goes over the wall into the neighbour's yard, the rule is that the batsman is out and must fetch it. They stop playing when the street lamps come on.

What do the boys use as a bat?
They use a flat wooden plank as a bat.

The inter-school quiz was held on a Saturday in the town hall. Each school sent a team of three students. Our team had Aditi, Marcus and Pooja, and our coach was Mr. Nair. There were four rounds: general knowledge, science, geography and a rapid-fire round. At the end of the second round, we were in third place. By the last question, we had moved to second. The winners were a team from Rosewood School, who got a silver cup and books.

Which school won the quiz?
A team from Rosewood School won it.

Applications for school clubs open on the first Monday of July. There are six to choose from: drama, robotics, chess, art, debating and gardening. Each club meets once a week, after the last period, for one hour. A student may join only two clubs. To apply, children fill out a small form and ask a parent to sign it. The lists of selected students are put on the notice board on Friday. Robotics is usually the most popular, and the teacher often has to draw names from a box.

How many clubs can a student join?
A student can join only two clubs.

Dear Diary, today was the first day of Class Six, and everything felt big. My new classroom is on the third floor, and I can see the football ground from the window. Our class teacher is Mr. Joshi, who wears a green scarf even when it is warm. I sat next to a girl called Kavita, who has a long plait and a laugh like a bell. At lunch, we shared my aloo paratha and her mango pickle. In the evening, Papa asked how it went, and I said it was okay, but I really think it was wonderful. Good night, Diary.

What colour is Mr. Joshi's scarf?
His scarf is green.

When the new English teacher stepped into the room, the class straightened up. She was tall and wore a plain cotton sari. She did not say her name. Instead, she opened a book and read a short story about a boy who built a boat in his backyard. Nobody moved. When she stopped, there was a pause, and then Priya asked quietly if she could read some more. Soon, everyone was begging for the next page. The teacher smiled for the first time and said her name was Mrs. Thomas. The class would remember her for the story, not for the name.

What did the class think of the new teacher's way of starting?
They liked it. They listened closely and begged her to read more.

Everyone in the choir was told to stand still while the conductor counted them in. Tessa's voice shook on the first note, and she wished she could disappear behind the girl in front. But her friend Leo, who stood next to her, gave a tiny nod. She took a deep breath and tried the second line. Her voice steadied, and she found that she could hear herself blend with the others. By the end of the song, she was smiling. Afterward, the conductor told the choir that they had sounded warmer than ever before.

What helped Tessa feel braver while singing?
Leo's small nod encouraged her, and hearing her voice blend with the others made her feel more confident.

At the corner of the school gate, a group of boys plays marbles every day before the first bell. They draw a circle in the dust with a stick and place ten marbles inside. Each player flicks his own marble from a line and tries to hit those in the circle. Whoever knocks a marble out of the circle may keep it. Imran owns the largest collection, about forty, which he keeps in a cloth bag. The teacher usually reminds them to wash their hands afterward.

How do the boys decide who keeps a marble?
The player who knocks a marble out of the circle may keep it.

The staircase at the north end of the school has forty steps and a metal railing painted green. Children from Class Five and above use it to reach the second floor. A sign at the bottom says "Keep to the left" in large white letters. Every morning, a prefect stands at the landing to remind students not to run. On the wall halfway up, there is a painting of a tall tree, made by the graduating class of last year, with the names of all thirty students on the leaves.

What colour is the railing on the staircase?
The railing is painted green.

Maya always thought her singing was too loud, and she mouthed the words in choir. Mr. Lopes noticed from the front and asked her to stay behind. The other children left. He said he had heard her voice once and thought it was the strongest in the group. Maya stared at the floor. He suggested she try singing the solo in the next piece. She hesitated, then nodded. On the day of the performance, she stepped forward, took a breath, and sang. A hush fell in the hall, and then everyone clapped.

Why did Mr. Lopes ask Maya to stay behind?
He had noticed she was mouthing the words and wanted to encourage her, because he thought her voice was strong.

On the coldest morning of the year, only half of Class Four came to school. The teacher found the room freezing and asked the caretaker for a small heater. Tanvir arrived late, with a woollen cap pulled low over his ears and a dripping nose. He sat at his desk and rubbed his hands. The girl beside him, Kajal, wordlessly took a spare pair of gloves from her bag and passed them to him. His face brightened. By the end of the lesson, Tanvir's nose had stopped running, and he had written his full page of work.

How did Tanvir feel after Kajal gave him the gloves?
He felt better and happier. His face brightened, and he was able to finish his work.

Ten-year-old Leena had been practising the same piano piece for a month. Each afternoon, she played it from beginning to end, and each afternoon, she made a mistake in the same place. Her little brother, who sat on the sofa, could hum the tune by now. On Friday, just before her school concert, Leena played the piece again and reached the difficult bar. Her fingers moved smoothly without stopping. She sat very still for a second, then turned around, and her brother clapped loudly. She grinned and started over from the top.

What can we tell from the fact that Leena's brother could hum the tune?
It shows that she had practised the piece many times, so often that he knew it by heart.

Pia blew out the candles on her cake and made a wish. Her friends clapped, and her father began to cut the first slice. Then Pia noticed that Tobias, who had come late, was standing by the door with a small paper bag. He looked uncertain. She walked over, took his hand, and led him to the table. Tobias opened the bag and took out a small clay animal he had made himself. Pia exclaimed that it was her favourite gift. She put it in the middle of the table, next to the cake, where everyone could see.

Why did Pia put Tobias's gift in the middle of the table?
She wanted to show that she valued his handmade gift and make him feel welcome.

Only ten students could join the swimming class, and twenty had applied. Amy's name was number twelve on the list. She tried to hide her disappointment but could not help staring at the notice board each morning. A week later, a boy dropped out, and then another. On Friday, the coach called her name and told her she could begin on Monday. She walked away calmly, but as soon as she turned the corner, she jumped in the air and whooped. Her friend Neha, who had seen it all, ran after her laughing.

Why did Amy jump in the air once she turned the corner?
She was thrilled to have a place in the swimming class and had been hiding her excitement until she was alone.

For a science project, each student of Class Five planted a bean seed in a paper cup filled with soil. They placed the cups on the window sill and watered them every morning. After four days, Neha's seed produced a small white root. On the seventh day, a green shoot pushed up through the soil. The children measured the shoots every day and recorded the numbers in a table. By day fourteen, the tallest plant, belonging to Kabir, was fifteen centimetres high.

On which day did Neha's seed produce a small root?
It did so on the fourth day.

Dark clouds rolled over the school just before the last period. Mrs. Reddy looked out of the window, then at the clock, and quickly told the class to pack their bags. Outside, the wind bent the thin neem trees, and the first heavy drops struck the tin roof of the bicycle shed. Several children who had come on bicycles gathered near the gate, holding their bags over their heads. A few parents arrived with umbrellas. The teachers decided that no student should leave alone, and they asked everyone to wait in the corridor until the rain slowed.

Why did the teachers ask the students to wait in the corridor?
The rain was heavy and the wind was strong, so the teachers wanted the children to stay safe and not leave alone.

Ms. Alvarez entered the classroom and said nothing. She wrote one sentence on the board and sat down. The children stopped whispering one by one and read the words: "Today we will not talk until the bell rings." At first, someone giggled, and then someone coughed. Soon, only the sound of pencils scratching was heard. After a few minutes, a girl named Rina noticed that the sun made a golden square on the floor. A boy near the window heard a bird's song for the first time that week. When the bell rang, no one wanted to speak at once.

Why did the children hear things they had not noticed before?
The room was quiet because nobody was talking, so they noticed small sounds and sights like the bird and the sunlight.

Dev and Sam were always competing. If one scored ten, the other had to score eleven. During the maths quiz, they tied for first place. The teacher decided on a tie-breaker question, and both stood at the board. Dev knew the answer but noticed that Sam's hand was shaking. He hesitated, and Sam wrote his answer first. It was correct. Dev clapped, and the whole class looked at him in surprise. Afterwards, Sam asked why he had waited. Dev shrugged and said that he wanted a fair fight, and the two of them started to laugh.

What does Dev's waiting for Sam show?
It shows that Dev valued fairness and cared about Sam, even though they were rivals.

In the middle of the school courtyard stands an old clock tower, built over eighty years ago. It has four faces, one for each side, and a brass bell that rings on the hour. The caretaker, Mr. Mathew, winds the clock every Sunday evening using a large iron key. He also oils the hinges of the small door at the base. Visitors often ask to climb inside, but only the senior students may do so, and only once a year, on the last day of term.

How often does Mr. Mathew wind the clock?
He winds it every Sunday evening.

Ravi's grandmother packs his tiffin every morning at six. On Mondays she puts in lemon rice and a boiled egg. On Wednesdays, he gets vegetable sandwiches with green chutney. Fridays are his favourite, because she makes small puris with potato curry. She always wraps a piece of jaggery in a paper napkin and tucks it into the corner of the box. Ravi shares it with his friend Colin, who loves the sweet taste. Some days they also trade snacks and talk about cricket until the bell rings for the next class.

What does Ravi get on Wednesdays?
He gets vegetable sandwiches with green chutney.

For her friend's birthday, Neelam had no money for a present, so she spent an evening making a bookmark from coloured card. She cut a small butterfly and glued it at the top, and wrote "To Sana, my best friend" at the bottom. She worried that it looked too plain compared with the shiny gifts the others would bring. At the party, Sana opened it last. She held it up in the light and said it was her favourite, and she slipped it into the book she was reading. Neelam felt her worry melt away.

Why did Neelam's worry melt away?
Sana said the bookmark was her favourite and used it straight away, so Neelam knew the gift was valued.

Ruchi was painting the sky for the school mural when she spilled a pot of black paint across the blue. She gasped and pressed her hands to her cheeks. The other children stopped and stared. Mr. Prasad came over and studied the stain for a long minute. Then he picked up a brush, added a few lines, and turned the black into a flock of birds. Ruchi's eyes widened. "It looks like they are flying," she said. The teacher nodded and told her that mistakes sometimes made the best parts of a picture.

How did Mr. Prasad fix the spilled paint?
He painted a few lines on the black stain and turned it into a flock of birds.

The trophy for the best class had stood in Class Six's glass cabinet for two years. This term, the rule was changed, and the trophy would go to the class that showed the best teamwork, not the best marks. Class Six scored the highest on exams, but the teachers noted that students kept their work to themselves. Class Five won the trophy because they had a "buddy system" where stronger students helped weaker ones. The Class Six monitor, Lavanya, saw the trophy leave the cabinet and was quiet. The next day, she started a similar system in her own class.

Why did Class Five win the trophy?
They won because of their buddy system, where stronger students helped weaker ones, which showed good teamwork.

Mr. Brown, the school gardener, planted a small tree for the Class Seven students, but a dry summer killed it. When the children saw the bare brown trunk, they stood quiet. Thomas suggested they plant another one, and the rest nodded. They collected money in a jar and bought a young neem sapling. This time, they made a rota to water it, and they put a fence around it. When the first green leaves opened in July, Mr. Brown took off his cap and thanked them one by one, his voice a little rough.

Why was Mr. Brown's voice a little rough when he thanked the children?
He was moved by their care for the new tree, so he felt emotional.

Aditya's pencil box is made of green metal and has a picture of a rocket on the lid. Inside are two sharp pencils, an eraser shaped like a cricket ball, a small ruler and a sharpener. His uncle gave it to him on his eighth birthday. Aditya is very careful with it and never lets anyone borrow the eraser. Every night, he checks that the lid is shut and places the box in the front pocket of his bag. His younger sister would like one just like it, but the shop no longer sells them.

What picture is on the lid of Aditya's pencil box?
There is a picture of a rocket on the lid.

The new whiteboard in Class Eight is bigger than the old blackboard and has a magnetic strip along the bottom. Teachers use coloured markers, and the monitor must clean it at the end of each day with a soft cloth. A box of spare markers is kept in the top drawer of the teacher's desk. Last week, someone left the cap off a marker, and it dried out. The teacher asked the class to be more careful and put up a reminder.

What must the monitor use to clean the whiteboard?
The monitor must use a soft cloth.

Feroz had saved stamps for two years, and he finally owned a hundred and twenty. At school, he laid them on his desk in neat rows to show a classmate named Alina. She looked at each one carefully, touching the edges with a finger. "May I see that one?" she asked, pointing to a tiny blue stamp from Italy. Feroz handed it over, slightly nervous. She turned it over and, with respect, gave it back. "It's beautiful," she said. Feroz relaxed. He decided he would let her borrow the album for a weekend.

Why did Feroz decide to let Alina borrow the album?
She handled his stamps with care and respect, so he trusted her.

When music began in Grade Four, each student received a plastic recorder from Mr. Fonseca. They learned to cover two holes, the thumb hole at the back and the top hole at the front, to play the note B. The sound was thin and squeaky, and a few children burst out laughing. By the end of the hour, the class could play the first four notes of a simple tune. Their homework was to practise for ten minutes each day and to clean the mouthpiece with a soft cloth. Next week, they would add one more note.

How many holes did the children cover to play the note B?
They covered two holes: the thumb hole at the back and the top hole at the front.

Behind the school kitchen, there is a vegetable patch the children call the Green Corner. The Class Five students planted spinach, radish and coriander in rows. Each row is marked with a stick and a small paper label. The students pour water from a tin can every morning before assembly. When the vegetables are ready, the cook uses them in the school lunch, and the leftover leaves are put in the compost pit near the wall. The school cook visits the patch every Thursday to see which vegetables are ready to pick.

What do the students plant in the Green Corner?
They plant spinach, radish and coriander.

Sports Day at Sunrise School begins with a march past at eight o'clock. The students walk in four lines, each dressed in a coloured T-shirt: red, blue, green and yellow. The principal then lights a small torch and declares the games open. After that come the sack race, the lemon-and-spoon race and the long jump. The relay race is the last event, around noon. Parents sit under a large cloth tent along one side of the field, and a cold drink stall near the gate sells lime juice.

Which event is the last one on Sports Day?
The relay race is the last event.

Kofi was good at copying the voices of teachers, and he often made the class laugh behind the principal's back. One afternoon, he did his imitation of Mr. Mishra in the corridor. When he turned around, Mr. Mishra stood a step away, arms folded. The laughter stopped at once. Kofi swallowed. After a pause, Mr. Mishra said, "Very good. Now please do it in the school play." Kofi blinked and then grinned. The class cheered. From that day, he played the narrator, and the teacher was always the first to clap.

How did Mr. Mishra react when he caught Kofi?
He was not angry. He praised Kofi's skill and invited him to use it in the school play.

During the maths test, Oliver noticed that his neighbour's paper was open and the answers were easy to see. His eyes drifted over once and then he turned quickly back to his own sheet. His pencil stopped. He thought about it for a moment, then put his hand up and told the teacher what had happened. The teacher thanked him for being honest and moved him to a desk at the front. Oliver finished the test with fewer answers than he wanted, but his chest felt lighter than before.

What does Oliver's decision to tell the teacher show about him?
It shows that he is honest. He chose to report what he saw even though it cost him some answers.

The school choir travelled by bus to a music festival in a neighbouring town. Twenty-four children went, along with Mr. Lobo and two parents. The bus left at six in the morning, and the children sang on the way. At the festival hall, they waited for two hours before their turn. They performed three songs in front of a panel of judges and about two hundred people. They won second place and returned home by evening with a silver trophy.

Why was the choir probably pleased when they got home?
They had won second place and brought home a silver trophy, so they probably felt proud of their performance.

When Selin heard that her friend Mona was planning to run away from the hostel, she did not know what to do. Mona had made her promise to say nothing. Selin lay awake that night, thinking about the dark road and the cold. In the morning, she went to the warden and said, "Please, I need to tell you something. I am worried about Mona." The warden listened and thanked her. Later, Mona refused to speak to Selin, but she was sitting safe in the common room, and Selin felt sure she had done the right thing.

Why did Selin break her promise to Mona?
She was worried about Mona's safety, so she decided that telling the warden was more important than keeping the secret.

Parth had not done his geography homework, and he knew that Mr. Menon would ask for it first thing. He looked at his bag and decided to tell the truth. When the teacher walked in and asked for the notebooks, Parth stood up. "Sir, I did not finish it," he said. "I was watching TV late last night." The class went still. Mr. Menon looked at him for a moment and said that he appreciated the honesty. He told Parth to complete it during the break and hand it in by lunch. Parth sat down with relief.

Why did Mr. Menon not punish Parth more strongly?
He valued Parth's honesty. Parth admitted the truth at once, so the teacher let him finish it at break.

A girl named Amira joined Class Four on the first day of term. She had moved from another city, and she carried a blue bag with a small elephant keyring. Mrs. Joseph introduced her and asked her to sit next to Dhruv, in the third row. Amira spoke softly and said she liked reading and drawing. During the break, Dhruv showed her where the water cooler was and where to buy sharpeners. By the end of the week, she knew the names of everyone at her table.

Who did Mrs. Joseph ask Amira to sit next to?
She asked her to sit next to Dhruv, in the third row.

The school choir practises in the hall on Tuesday and Thursday. This term, they are learning three songs: a folk song in Marathi, a Christmas carol and a song about rain. The conductor, Mr. Lobo, plays a small keyboard and sometimes taps the desk to keep the beat. About thirty students attend, and the tallest stand at the back. Their first performance will be at the annual function in December, in front of all the parents. Parents have been invited to sit in the front rows, and the school will serve tea afterwards.

When will the choir give its first performance?
They will perform at the annual function in December.

When it rained, the street in front of Anita's school filled with a shallow stream. Anita and her friend Laila made paper boats from old notebook pages. Anita's boat was folded from a sheet of squared paper, and Laila's was made from a page torn from a magazine. They put them in the water at the top of the slope and watched them drift toward the drain. Laila's boat travelled the farthest, passing the lamp post before it sank. They clapped, folded two more, and ran back to the beginning.

What was Laila's boat made from?
It was made from a page torn from a magazine.

On Saturday afternoons, the small children of Green Park colony ride their tricycles around the central garden. They go in a long line, with the oldest at the front ringing his bell. The path is a loop of red brick, about a hundred metres around. Mothers sit on benches near the entrance and talk. When the sun begins to set, a watchman rings a bell, and the children park their tricycles in a row beside the gate. The smaller children wear helmets, which their parents bought from the shop near the gate.

What is the path in the garden made of?
The path is made of red brick.

After the rain stopped, six-year-old Ishaan found a huge puddle at the edge of the school ground. He looked at his shiny black shoes and then at the water. A group of friends was already splashing and shouting. Ishaan took a small step in, and cold water went over his toes. He gasped, then began to giggle. In a minute he was jumping with all the others, and his socks were soaked. Later, when his mother saw him at the gate, she shook her head, but she was also trying hard not to smile.

Why was Ishaan's mother trying hard not to smile?
She was amused. His socks were soaked, so she shook her head, but seeing him so happy made her want to laugh.

The homework club meets in the library from three to four every weekday. About fifteen children attend, mostly those whose parents work late. A teacher, Ms. Roy, sits at the head table and helps with questions. The younger children work at one table, and the older ones at another. At half past three, there is a short break for fruit. Anyone who finishes early may read a book. The club closes at four, and parents collect their children from the gate.

What time does the homework club end?
It ends at four o'clock.

On Teachers' Day, the students of Class Nine decorated the staff room with balloons and paper flowers. Zubin brought a cake from a bakery, and Alisha wrote a thank-you poem on a large chart. At ten o'clock, they invited all the teachers inside and handed each a rose. Mr. Banerjee, the oldest teacher, accepted his with a small bow. The class sang a short song, and the principal gave a speech about how much the students had grown. Afterwards, the teachers cut the cake in the staff room.

What did Alisha write on the large chart?
She wrote a thank-you poem.

A small pond lies behind Sunshine School, next to the sports ground. In summer, it is full of green frogs, and in winter, migrating ducks sometimes visit. The Class Seven eco club cleans it every second Saturday by removing plastic bags and dead leaves. They also keep a notebook near the fence, where anyone can write down the animals they have spotted. Last month's list included two kingfishers, a heron and a very large turtle. Visitors are not allowed to feed the animals, and a sign near the gate says so.

How often does the eco club clean the pond?
They clean it every second Saturday.

Emre sneezed so loudly in the middle of the silent reading hour that a pencil rolled off his desk. A few children giggled, and he went red. He bent down to pick up the pencil, and then he sneezed again, even louder than before. The whole class burst out laughing. The teacher tried to look stern, but her shoulders were shaking. Emre sat up, pinched his nose, and said in a squeaky voice, "I am sorry, I think the dust is trying to read too." The class laughed again, and this time Emre laughed with them.

Why did Emre's joke make him feel better?
It turned the embarrassing moment into something funny, so he could laugh with the class instead of feeling shy.

There are four swings in the park behind Sai's building, and the children line up for them after school. The first swing is the oldest and squeaks loudly, so nobody likes it much. The second and third are new, painted bright orange. The fourth swing is small and meant for toddlers. Last Tuesday, Sai arrived at four o'clock and found a boy named Dev waiting for the second swing. They agreed to take turns, five minutes each, counting slowly in their heads. By the time their mothers called them home, both had had three turns.

How many swings are there in the park?
There are four swings.

Last Friday the school held a book exchange in the hall. Students could bring old story books and swap them for different ones. A table near the door was covered with comics, picture books and a few dictionaries. Each child received a paper ticket for every book they brought. Isabel brought three and took home a thick adventure novel. Pranav gave away a stack of old magazines and exchanged them for a book of puzzles. By the end of the afternoon, only five books were left on the table.

What did Isabel take home from the book exchange?
She took home a thick adventure novel.

Every morning, twelve children from a small island near Kollam cross the backwater by ferry to reach their school on the mainland. The boat leaves the small wooden jetty at seven-thirty, and the boatman, Mr. Joy, counts the children as they step aboard. They wear orange life jackets that the school provides. The crossing takes about fifteen minutes, and the children usually do their last bit of homework on the way. On the other side, a teacher meets them at the landing and walks them up the path.

Who counts the children as they step onto the ferry?
The boatman, Mr. Joy, counts them.

Nine-year-old Sana stood at the top of the tall slide with her hands gripping the rails. Below, the other children were shouting for her to come down. She looked at the long drop, and her knees began to shake. Behind her, a smaller boy named Dev waited quietly. After a minute, Sana stepped aside and said, "You go first, I'll come after you." Dev slid down with a happy shout. Seeing how easy it looked, Sana took a deep breath, sat down, and let go. She landed in the sand with a bump and ran straight back to the ladder.

What does Sana's decision to go back to the ladder show?
It shows she enjoyed the slide and was no longer afraid. She wanted to go down again.

Zara spent the whole Sunday baking a cake for her grandmother's birthday. She measured the flour carefully and whisked the eggs until they were pale. When she opened the oven, the cake had sunk in the middle. Her face fell. Her younger brother, Zane, looked at it and said it looked like a volcano. Zara first frowned, then began to laugh. They filled the hole with whipped cream and strawberries. When Grandma saw it, she called it the most beautiful cake in the world and ate two slices.

How did Zara fix the problem with her cake?
She filled the sunken middle with whipped cream and strawberries.

Mr. Reyes raised his voice when he saw the paper balls scattered across the floor. He asked the class who was responsible, but nobody answered. Elena lowered her head and picked at her sleeve. The teacher paused and then spoke more softly. He said that he was not interested in blaming anyone, but the room must be clean before the next class. A moment later, three boys stood up and began to gather the paper. Elena joined them, and then more students did. Within two minutes, the floor was bare, and Mr. Reyes gave a small nod.

Why did the students start picking up the paper?
The teacher spoke calmly and said the room needed to be clean, so they felt they should help instead of waiting to be blamed.

A goat wandered into the school yard on Monday morning and began eating the leaves of the hibiscus bush. The children giggled, and the watchman tried to shoo it away with a stick. The goat simply moved to the next bush. At last, the cook brought a handful of leftover roti, and the goat followed her out of the gate. Its owner, an old man named Mr. Baig, arrived an hour later and apologised. The principal laughed and said no harm was done.

What did the cook do to lead the goat out?
She brought a handful of leftover roti, and the goat followed her.

The chess club at Oakridge School meets every Wednesday after lunch, in room twelve. It has eleven members, aged from nine to thirteen. The coach, Mr. Singh, starts each session with a puzzle on the board. The children try to find the best move in under two minutes. After that, they play games in pairs, and the winners move to the next table. On the last Wednesday of each month, the club holds a small tournament, and the winner takes home a paper certificate.

How many members does the chess club have?
It has eleven members.

The nursery class at Little Stars School has a corner of wooden blocks, a rug with a map of roads, and a basket of toy cars. During free play, the children build towns. Today, Anil made a tall tower for a fire station, and Chiara placed a toy ambulance near its door. A boy named Ben built a bridge from three blocks. The teacher, Miss Lopez, gently reminded them to take turns with the red car. At the end of play, each child put the blocks back in the basket.

What did Anil build today?
He built a tall tower for a fire station.

Mr. Rao gave each pair a magnet and a small tray of objects: a copper coin, paperclips, a wooden spoon, an eraser and a nail. He asked the children to guess which things would stick. Kiran guessed the eraser, and Becky guessed the coin. They tested them one by one. The paperclips and the nail jumped to the magnet with a click. The coin did nothing. Kiran grinned at his mistake, and Becky said the coin was made of a different metal. They wrote down the results in a neat table and compared them with the class next door.

What do the results suggest about the coin?
The coin is probably not made of iron or steel, since the magnet did not attract it.

On a windy afternoon, the children of Class Three carried a big paper kite to the field. Its string was long, and its tail was made of bits of cloth. Naveen ran with it, and it rose a metre and then crashed to the ground. They tried four more times, each time with the same result. Frustrated, Naveen sat on the grass. Then his sister Shilpa noticed that the tail was too heavy. She tore off half of the cloth and tied the kite again. This time, it climbed high, and the children cheered and ran after it.

Why did the kite finally fly?
Shilpa took off half of the heavy tail, which made the kite light enough to rise.

Somebody had been eating the biscuits from the jar in the staff room, and the teachers could not work out who. Mr. Das placed a sheet of paper on the table and asked the children in the club to investigate. Chitra noticed crumbs on the floor leading toward the music cupboard. Inside it, behind the drum, they found a small grey squirrel nibbling a biscuit and looking up at them with bright eyes. The children burst out laughing. They gently let it out through the window and wrote "Case closed" on the paper.

What was the real cause of the missing biscuits?
A squirrel hiding in the music cupboard was eating them. The crumbs on the floor led the children to it.

Dear Grandma, school has been fun this week, and I made a new friend named Yuki. She does not speak much English yet, so we use drawings to talk. Yesterday she drew a picture of a cat with a hat, and I drew a dog on a skateboard. We laughed so much that the teacher came to see. She then asked if we could teach the class a new word each day. Tomorrow, Yuki will show everyone how to say "good morning" in her language. I think I will learn it too. Love, Maya.

Why did Maya and Yuki use drawings to talk?
Yuki did not speak much English yet, so drawings helped them understand each other.

The annual school fair is held on the second Sunday of November. The Class Eight students run the games stall, where visitors can throw rings on bottles or knock down cans with a ball. Class Seven sells hand-painted bookmarks, and Class Nine sells homemade lemonade. A small stage near the gate hosts dance and music performances from noon until four. All the money collected is used to buy new books for the library. Parents are welcome, and entry to the fair is free for everyone.

What is the money from the fair used for?
It is used to buy new books for the library.

At recess, Jonas sat on the low wall by the water tank, as he did every day, eating his sandwich in silence. He watched the other children laugh, and now and then he pretended to check his watch. A new girl named Anya came out with her lunch box and looked around for a place. She hesitated, then walked straight to the wall and asked if she could join. Jonas nodded, and shifted over. After a minute, he asked what she liked to read. Their conversation lasted until the bell, and neither of them noticed it had ended.

Why did Jonas pretend to check his watch?
He was lonely and wanted to look busy, so nobody would notice he was sitting alone.

Ahmed had been chosen as a prefect, and on the first day he walked along the corridor with his badge shining on his collar. When he saw two younger boys running, he stopped them and told them to walk. They grinned and ran again as soon as he turned away. Ahmed frowned. Later that day, he went to the little ones' classroom, sat down with them, and asked why they ran. One said they were afraid the canteen would close. Ahmed promised to talk to the canteen man about letting them in first.

What did Ahmed learn by asking the boys why they ran?
He learned that they ran because they feared the canteen would close, so he tried to solve the real problem.

Each year, the students of Class Eight choose a class representative by voting. Candidates give a short speech on Monday, and the vote takes place on Tuesday. Every student writes the name of one candidate on a folded slip of paper and drops it into a box. The class teacher and two helpers count the slips after school. This year, there were three candidates: Rohan, Sheetal and Ibrahim. Sheetal won with fourteen votes, and she began her work the next morning by organising the class library.

How does each student vote?
Each student writes one candidate's name on a folded slip and drops it into a box.

At lunchtime, Karan opened his tiffin box and found only two plain chapatis and a little pickle. Across from him, Isha was unwrapping a big paratha stuffed with potato. Karan looked down at his own food and slowly closed the lid. Isha noticed, tore her paratha in half, and pushed the bigger piece toward him without saying a word. Karan hesitated, then took it. The next day, he came to school with an extra bag. Inside were four of his mother's sweet laddoos, which he placed in the middle of the table for both of them to share.

Why did Karan bring laddoos the next day?
He wanted to thank Isha for sharing her paratha, so he brought sweets for both of them to share.

The classroom floor was covered with scraps of paper after the craft lesson. The teacher was called to the principal's room and told the children to wait quietly. When she returned ten minutes later, the room was spotless. The tables were wiped, the scraps were gone, and the chairs were pushed in neatly. She looked at the monitor, Gita, who stood in front of the group. "We decided to do it before you came," Gita said. The teacher was pleased and said she was proud of them, and then she let them go out early.

Why did the teacher let the class go out early?
The children had cleaned the room on their own, so she wanted to reward their responsibility.

Ritu's father had told her the night before that he would come to the school concert. She searched the audience from the stage, row after row, but the seat she had saved stayed empty. The curtains opened, and she began to sing. Halfway through the first verse, she saw the door at the back swing open, and a tall man in a work uniform sat down in the last row, breathing hard. She did not miss a note. When the song ended and the applause began, she found her father's eyes and smiled with her whole face.

How did Ritu feel when she saw her father arrive?
She felt relieved and happy. She smiled with her whole face and kept singing without missing a note.

Samira had not come to school for three days, and her seat by the window stayed empty. On the fourth afternoon, her best friend Jenny stood outside her house with a paper bag. Inside were notes from the lessons, a small card signed by half the class, and a mango from Jenny's tree. Samira's mother opened the door and led her inside, where Samira sat on the bed with a blanket around her shoulders. When she saw the card, she touched each name slowly with a finger. Then she looked up and said that she had been waiting for someone to come.

How did Samira feel when she saw the card?
She felt happy and touched. She read each name slowly and said she had been waiting for someone to visit.

The new canteen at Harmony School opened last week. It sells fresh fruit, idli, sandwiches and curd rice instead of fried snacks. Prices range from five to twenty rupees. A menu is written on a board near the door every morning by the canteen staff. The students line up in single file, and the oldest classes are served first on Mondays and Wednesdays. The principal says the change will help children feel more active in the afternoon. Some students miss the fried snacks, but many say the curd rice is very tasty.

What kind of food does the new canteen sell instead of fried snacks?
It sells fresh fruit, idli, sandwiches and curd rice.

To make a string telephone, the Class Four children each received two paper cups and a long piece of thread. The teacher poked a small hole in the base of each cup, and the children tied the thread through it with a knot. They then walked apart until the thread was tight. One child whispered into a cup, and the other listened with the second cup against her ear. Only when the thread was pulled tight could they hear. Rana and Kumar managed to hear each other from across the whole playground.

What must be done to the thread for the telephone to work?
The thread must be pulled tight.

Idris's kite was torn when it landed in the branches of a tall acacia tree. He looked up and tried to jump for the string, but it hung far out of reach. His younger sister Salma said they should go home and forget it. Idris shook his head. He had spent two evenings making it, and the paper had his own drawing of a tiger. He found a long bamboo stick in the neighbour's yard and tried again. After ten minutes, he hooked the thread and gently pulled the kite free. The tiger was a little crumpled, but still there.

Why did Idris refuse to leave the kite in the tree?
He had spent two evenings making it and had drawn a tiger on it, so it mattered a lot to him.

When the vase in the corridor broke, Dylan was standing right next to it. Mrs. Gomes asked who had done it, and the corridor fell silent. Dylan stared at his shoes. He knew the vase had fallen when his bag swung against it, but his tongue felt stuck. Another boy, Sam, got scolded for being nearby. Dylan's stomach hurt for the rest of the day. After school, he walked up to the teacher's room, knocked, and said, "It was me. I'm sorry about Sam." Mrs. Gomes looked at him for a long moment and then said, "Thank you for telling me."

Why did Dylan's stomach hurt during the day?
He felt guilty because Sam was scolded for something Dylan had done.

Giulia had borrowed her friend Maya's pencil case without asking, and by afternoon one of the zips was broken. She tried to bend it back, but it would not close. At the end of the day, she walked to Maya's desk with her hands behind her back. Maya was packing her bag. Giulia held out the case and said quietly, "I'm very sorry. I will buy you a new one." Maya looked at the zip, then at Giulia's red face, and said it was only a case. She laughed, and Giulia's shoulders finally relaxed.

What does Giulia's red face suggest?
It suggests she felt embarrassed or guilty about breaking the zip.

Four-year-old Noor was building a tower of wooden blocks on the nursery floor. A boy called Aarav came over and silently picked up a red block from her pile. Noor opened her mouth to shout but then saw him looking at the tower with wide eyes. She hesitated, held out another red block, and said, "Put it on top." Aarav carefully placed both blocks together. The tower wobbled but stayed up. Then they cheered at the same time, and the teacher, who had been watching from the door, smiled and went back to her desk.

What does Noor's offer of another block show about her?
It shows she is kind and willing to share. She chose to include Aarav instead of getting angry.

Owen had promised his little cousin that he would build a sandcastle with her at the beach after school. When the day came, his friends invited him to play football instead. He looked at the ball, then at his cousin, who stood near the gate with a plastic bucket. He told his friends he could not come. They rolled their eyes, but he walked off with his cousin and dug in the wet sand until the sun went red. When she hugged him and called him the best cousin ever, he did not regret missing the game.

Why did Owen skip the football game?
He had promised his cousin to build a sandcastle, and he chose to keep his promise.

Camila's chain slipped off her bicycle halfway to school, and she stood by the roadside holding the handlebars. She looked at her greasy hands and then at the clock on the tea shop wall. The first bell would ring in ten minutes. A boy from her class, Tarun, rode up and stopped without being asked. He knelt on the dusty ground, hooked the chain back onto the gear, and spun the pedal twice to check it. Camila wiped her fingers on her handkerchief and thanked him. They rode the rest of the way side by side, and reached the gate just as the bell began.

Why did Camila thank Tarun?
He stopped and fixed her bicycle chain, which helped her reach school on time.

The class trip to the science museum began at six-thirty in the morning at Central Station. Forty students and four teachers boarded the second coach of the morning express train. Each child carried a small bag with water, a snack and a notebook. The journey took about two hours, and the children played word games on the way. At the museum, they were divided into groups and given a worksheet with ten questions to answer during the visit. The teachers counted heads twice at the station, once on the platform and again inside the coach.

How many students went on the trip?
Forty students went, along with four teachers.

Tanvi told Rita a secret about her older sister, and Rita promised to keep it. A day later, in the corridor, a girl from another class winked at Tanvi and mentioned the same secret. Tanvi's face went pale. She spun around and looked for Rita, who stood near the lockers with her mouth slightly open. "I did not tell anyone," Rita said quickly, "except my cousin, but she is far away." Tanvi walked away without answering. That evening, she sat on her bed and looked at the phone for a long time, without making a call.

What do you think Tanvi suspected after the girl mentioned the secret?
She suspected that Rita had broken her promise and told someone, since another girl knew the secret.

Nandini's school bag was always a mess. Pencils rolled loose at the bottom, and pages of old homework were crumpled among her books. One Monday, her teacher asked everyone to take out their geometry boxes for a test, and Nandini spent five minutes searching while the others began. By the time she found it, only half the time remained. She did poorly. That evening, she emptied her bag onto the floor, sorted everything into piles, and bought a few small pouches. From then on, she knew where each thing was.

Why did Nandini clean out her bag that evening?
She lost time during the test searching for her geometry box, and she wanted to avoid that problem again.

Ellie had known for a month that her family would move to another town, but the news felt real only when the packing boxes arrived. Her bedroom filled with cartons, and her posters came off the wall one by one. Her friend Naomi sat on the bed, silently folding clothes into a suitcase. When the last box was taped shut, Naomi took a bracelet off her wrist and slipped it onto Ellie's. They did not say much. Ellie hugged her, and neither of them noticed that the doorbell kept ringing because the movers had arrived.

Why did Naomi give Ellie her bracelet?
She wanted Ellie to remember her and their friendship after the move.

There is a tortoise named Moti in the school garden. He lives in a wire enclosure near the water tank, and the Class Three students take turns feeding him. His main food is lettuce, with a few slices of carrot on Sundays. Last year, the children measured his shell and found it was thirty centimetres long. They drew a picture of him and hung it on the notice board. Every morning, they check that his water bowl is full before they go to class.

What do the students feed Moti?
They feed him lettuce, with a few slices of carrot on Sundays.

The Mohans' rose bush had never bloomed. For three years, Mrs. Mohan watered it, fed it with tea leaves and talked to it each morning. Her husband said it was a waste of time. Then, in the fourth spring, a single bud appeared on the highest branch. Mrs. Mohan stood in front of it for a full minute and said nothing. She went in and came back with her husband. He looked at the bud, scratched his head and said that he would go and buy a small stake to support it. By evening, a bamboo stick stood beside the rose bush.

What does Mr. Mohan's buying a stake show about his attitude?
It shows that he changed his mind and now cares about the plant, supporting his wife's effort.

The power went off on a hot evening, and the whole building came out onto the stairs. Neighbours who had never spoken before sat on the steps with paper fans. A man brought a guitar, and an old woman produced a bag of roasted peanuts. A small boy started to sing, and soon half the staircase was joining in. When the lights returned at ten, nobody moved. Mrs. Pinto from the third floor said, to no one in particular, that it was a shame the electricity had to come back so soon. The others nodded and stayed where they were.

What does Mrs. Pinto's remark show?
It shows that she and the neighbours enjoyed the evening together and were sorry it ended.

Mr. Ibrahim has a toolbox that belonged to his father. It is green, with a rusty latch and a handle wrapped in black tape. Inside are a hammer with a cracked handle, a set of tiny screwdrivers and a tin of assorted nails. When anything breaks in the house, Mr. Ibrahim brings the box to the spot and sits on the floor before he starts. His daughter Zoya has watched him since she was four. She has her own small box now, a gift from her grandfather, with a plastic hammer and a real screwdriver.

What is wrapped around the toolbox handle?
Black tape is wrapped around it.

Three days before the wedding, Neha's cousin Rani sat on the terrace steps with a long face. The house below was full of noise: aunts arguing over the menu, children running through the hall, a band rehearsing in the lane. Rani said she wanted to run away to a quiet place. Neha did not give advice. She went downstairs and returned with two glasses of sugarcane juice and a sheet to spread on the floor. They sat there until the stars came out, hardly speaking. When Rani finally stood up, she brushed her skirt and said she was ready to go back down. She thanked Neha with a quick squeeze of the arm.

What helped Rani feel ready to go back downstairs?
Sitting quietly with Neha, with juice and no pressure, helped her calm down.

The Dutta children have an unusual bedtime custom. Before sleeping, each of them tells the others one good thing and one bad thing that happened that day. They sit cross-legged on the big bed with the lamp lit. Ritwik, the oldest, always talks about cricket. Mithu, the middle one, is usually sad because of a quarrel with a friend. The youngest, Puchki, tells long, mixed-up stories that end halfway. When everyone has spoken, their father puts out the lamp. He says that a day should not be carried into the night without being shared.

How many good things and bad things does each child tell?
Each child tells one good thing and one bad thing.

The Reddy family drove to the beach at dawn so they could see the sunrise. Mr. Reddy packed a flask of tea, a bag of puffed rice and a mat. The road was empty, with only a few trucks. When they arrived, the sand was cold, and the sky was a pale grey. Eleven-year-old Nithin spread the mat while his sister ran toward the water. Slowly a thin red line grew along the horizon, and then the sun lifted out of the sea. Nobody spoke. Nithin's mother whispered that it was the same sun they saw every day, and yet it looked new.

What did Mr. Reddy pack for the beach?
He packed a flask of tea, a bag of puffed rice and a mat.

After her grandmother died, Pooja found a small tin box in the almirah. It held a handful of buttons, some faded ribbons, a thimble and a tiny silver key that fitted nothing in the house. Her mother laughed and said that Grandmother had kept strange things all her life. But Pooja turned the key over and over. She kept the thimble on her desk and sewed the buttons onto a cloth bag. The key she tied on a thread and wore around her neck. She did not know what it opened, and she decided that she preferred not to know.

Why did Pooja wear the silver key around her neck?
She kept it as a keepsake of her grandmother, because it came from the tin box her grandmother left, and she chose not to know what it opened.

Each November, Grandma Ellen bakes an apple pie for the whole street. She starts at six in the morning, peeling a basket of green apples with a small knife. By ten, the kitchen is warm, and the smell drifts out of the window. She makes eight pies in total: one for her family, one for the postman, and six for neighbours who live on either side. Her grandson Peter carries them in a wooden crate and knocks at each door. The neighbours, who know what is coming, wait inside with the door ajar and often have a jar of jam ready in return.

How many pies does Grandma Ellen make in total?
She makes eight pies.

Deepak's family eats dinner at nine o'clock, which his friends think is very late. His mother returns from the hospital at eight-thirty, where she works as a nurse, and cooks while still wearing her uniform. His father, a bus driver, arrives a little earlier and lays the table. Deepak and his sister take turns to wash the vegetables. No one eats until all four are at the table. Over dinner they discuss the day's small events: a funny passenger, a birthday in the ward, a test result. Deepak says that late dinner is not a problem because the conversation is the best part of the meal.

What work does Deepak's father do?
He is a bus driver.

In the Thakur family, birthdays are celebrated with a special breakfast. The birthday person chooses the menu, and everybody else cooks it. Last month, Sunita turned fifteen and chose idli, sambar, banana fritters and a tall glass of rose milk. Her father steamed the idlis, her mother made the sambar and her little brother dropped bananas into the oil. They placed everything on the best table cloth, and Sunita sat at the head, wearing a paper crown. She was allowed to eat first and was not allowed to wash any plates for the whole day.

What did Sunita choose to drink on her birthday?
She chose a tall glass of rose milk.

For a month, Kabir's mother had asked him to clean his cupboard, and each time he said he would do it tomorrow. She stopped asking. One evening, Kabir could not find his school tie anywhere. He turned the room upside down, then pulled out everything from the cupboard in a heap.
