Under a pile of old shirts, he found the tie, creased and covered in dust, along with two missing socks and a library book. He stood there looking at the mess he had made. Then he rolled up his sleeves and, without a word, began to fold the shirts.

Why did Kabir begin folding the shirts?
He had to find his tie, and seeing the mess he made, he finally decided to clean the cupboard.

When Karthik's baby brother started crawling, he went straight for Karthik's schoolbag and pulled out every notebook. Karthik shouted at him, and the baby began to cry. Their mother took the baby away and told Karthik to arrange everything again. He did so, scowling. That evening, he noticed his baby brother staring at him from across the room, with a sleepy, serious face. Karthik sat down on the floor and held out a notebook. The baby took it, turned it upside down and giggled. Karthik giggled too, and they both stayed there on the floor for a long time.

How had Karthik's feelings changed by the evening?
He was angry when the baby pulled out his notebooks, but by the evening he felt warm toward his brother and played with him on the floor.

Before the festival, the Bhatt family paints the house. Mr. Bhatt buys two large tins of cream-coloured paint and a smaller one of green for the window frames. On Saturday, the children move the furniture to the middle of each room and cover it with old sheets. Mr. Bhatt does the high parts with a ladder, and his wife follows with a small brush for the corners. The youngest, Gita, is given a roller and permission to paint the lowest strip of wall. By Sunday evening, there is paint on her hair, her elbows and the family cat, but the walls shine.

What colour is used for the window frames?
The window frames are painted green.

The cold wave lasted eight days, and the Rai family kept a single heater in the living room. Everyone slept there on mattresses, with quilts piled high. In the morning, Mrs. Rai brought tea to each person, and the children drank it with their hands wrapped round the cups. Outside, the water pipe froze, and Mr. Rai had to pour hot water over it each day. On the ninth morning, the sun rose clear, and the pipe ran freely. The family opened all the windows and let the warm light in. The heater was switched off for the first time since the cold began.

How many days did the cold wave last?
It lasted eight days.

The ceiling fan in the living room made a clicking sound, and for weeks the family argued about whose job it was to fix it. Mr. Das said it was a job for the electrician. Mrs. Das said it was the electrician's fault in the first place. Their son Soham, who was thirteen, quietly stood on a chair one afternoon with a screwdriver. He tightened one screw on the housing, and the clicking stopped. He climbed down and said nothing. A few minutes later, his father noticed the silence and looked up. Then he looked at Soham and said nothing either, though he nodded slowly.

What does Mr. Das's slow nod show?
It shows he was impressed and quietly grateful, because he noticed the silence, looked at Soham and nodded without a word.

Dadu keeps his reading glasses on a string around his neck, and he is always looking for them. Whenever he cannot find them, the grandchildren shout in chorus, "On your neck, Dadu!" He pats his chest, finds the glasses and says, "Ah, there you are," as if they had been hiding. This happens at least three times a day. Last week, the youngest, little Bina, drew a pair of spectacles on a piece of paper and stuck it on his forehead. Dadu wore it all day, and said nothing, and the grandchildren giggled until their stomachs hurt.

Where does Dadu keep his reading glasses?
He keeps them on a string around his neck.

Mr. Alvi looked at the grey sky from the doorway and then at the washing on the line. He called to his wife that the clothes were almost dry and would be fine. She looked at him without a word and went to the roof. By the time he finished his tea, she had taken in every shirt and folded them in the basket. Then the first drops fell, and the sky opened wide. Mr. Alvi stood at the window with his empty cup, watching the rain bounce on the roof. His wife passed behind him with the basket and said nothing, which was worse than any remark.

What does the wife's silence show about how she felt?
It shows that she was a little annoyed that she had been right and he had not listened, though she did not say it.

Aunt Rekha came to stay while the family painted their house. She had been told she was a guest, but by the second morning she was holding a brush. Mr. Kumar asked her to sit and rest. She smiled, said that her hands did not know how to be idle, and went on painting the lower edge of the door. The children stopped arguing and began to paint beside her. By the evening, the door was finished, and the children were speckled with green. Aunt Rekha carried the brushes to the tap and washed them one by one, while Mr. Kumar poured her a large cup of tea.

Why did Mr. Kumar pour Aunt Rekha a large cup of tea?
He was thanking her for the help she gave, even though she was a guest.

Gita is thirteen, and her brother Vinay is eight. When they are at home, she bosses him around. But at school, if someone bothers Vinay, Gita is the first to step forward. Last month, a bigger boy took Vinay's lunch box and held it above his head. Gita saw it from across the playground, walked up and looked him straight in the eye. She did not raise her voice or her hand. The boy put the box down at once and walked away. On the way home, Gita went back to bossing Vinay around about his untied shoelaces.

What does Gita's behaviour show about how she feels about Vinay?
It shows that she is protective of him and cares for him, even if she bosses him at home.

Our train to my uncle's town leaves at five in the morning, so we are up at three. My mother packs lemon rice and boiled eggs in a steel tiffin, and my father carries the two big bags. At the station, there is a tea vendor who sells small clay cups of hot tea for five rupees. We find our seats by the window, and my brother takes the upper berth so he can sleep. The journey is nine hours long, with a long halt at a junction where we buy hot vada from a boy on the platform.

How long is the train journey?
It is nine hours long.

When the family's old television finally broke, Mr. Sharma did not want to buy a new one. He said that it was good for the children to read and play outside. The first week was hard, with complaining and boredom. By the second week, the children were building a fort from sofa cushions. In the third week, they started a family newspaper, written on sheets of folded paper. Mrs. Sharma wrote the recipes, Mr. Sharma the jokes, and the children the news from the lane. The paper had four pages and was read aloud on Sunday evenings.

What was the family newspaper written on?
It was written on sheets of folded paper.

At six in the evening, the sun still burned over the courtyard, and the Gomez family had given up trying to stay indoors. The air was thick and still. Mr. Gomez dragged the table outside and put a wet sheet over the window to cool the room. The children lay on the tiles with their cheeks pressed to the stone. Then a small wind rattled the clothesline, and the grandmother lifted her face and smiled. She said that the heat was finally ready to break. Within an hour, the first drops landed on the dusty yard, and the children rushed out shouting.

How do we know the grandmother expected rain?
She smiled at the small wind and said the heat was ready to break, which suggests she knew rain was coming.

Aditi's sister Radha left for college in September, and the house changed. Dinner was quieter, and the bathroom was always free. Aditi found herself standing at Radha's closed door, listening for music that did not come. She started sending long messages every night, though Radha replied only with short lines. At first, Aditi felt hurt. Then Radha called on Sunday and talked for an hour, describing the hostel food, her new roommate and the long walk to class. She said she was sorry for being slow to answer because there was so much to do. Aditi put the phone down and went to eat dinner with a lighter heart.

Why did Aditi feel lighter after the Sunday call?
She realised her sister was not ignoring her but was simply busy, and Radha had taken time to talk.

Everyone in the Okafor family cooks, but only Uncle Emeka is allowed to make the jollof rice for celebrations. He stirs the big pot with a wooden spoon taller than his youngest niece. Last month, for his sister's wedding party, he made enough rice for sixty guests. At the end of the evening, there was not a spoonful left. Several guests asked for the recipe, and Uncle Emeka only smiled and tapped the side of his nose. His sister later whispered that even she does not know the exact amount of pepper he uses. The family joke is that he will take the secret to his grave.

What does the family joke say about Uncle Emeka's recipe?
It says he will never reveal his secret recipe, even taking it to his grave.

The wind had blown the washing line down for the third time that week, and Grandma Peg was fed up. She stood in the yard with her hands on her hips, looking at the pile of muddy sheets. Then she turned to the children and told them that she was going to build a new line, one that would not fall. She spent the afternoon with a hammer, two stout poles and a coil of thick rope. The children carried and held what she asked for. By evening, a solid line stood across the yard, and Grandma Peg gave it a firm shake and nodded.

What does Grandma Peg's behaviour show about her?
It shows that she is determined and practical, because she decided to solve the problem herself rather than complain.

On Saturdays, my brother Chetan and I polish all the shoes in the house. We spread an old newspaper on the veranda and line up the pairs: father's black leather, mother's sandals, grandfather's brown ones and our school shoes. The tin of polish is almost empty, and we have to scrape the sides with a stick. Chetan does the brushing, and I do the rubbing with a soft cloth. When we finish, the row of shoes gleams in the sun. Mother pays us five rupees each, and we run off to buy peppermints.

What do the narrator and Chetan spread on the veranda?
They spread an old newspaper.

Nobody in Farah's house likes cleaning fish, so it is a treat when her father does it. He sits on the back step with a newspaper under the bucket, scraping off the scales with the edge of a spoon. Farah brings him a bowl of water and a lemon. Her mother waits in the kitchen with the pan ready. When the fish is cleaned, he rubs it with turmeric, salt and chilli, and leaves it to rest. Farah's job is to put out the plates. By seven, the whole family is eating crisp fried fish with rice and a little dal.

What does Farah's father rub on the fish before it rests?
He rubs it with turmeric, salt and chilli.

Last Sunday, a big thunderstorm hit our town, and my father went up to the terrace to take the wires off the television aerial. My mother ran around closing windows. My little brother hid under the dining table with a cushion on his head and kept asking if the roof was going to fall. I told him it would not. In about twenty minutes, the thunder moved away, and we heard frogs croaking in the drain. Dad came down with wet hair and gave me a thumbs-up. The electricity returned at nine.

Where did the narrator's little brother hide during the storm?
He hid under the dining table.

Every year on the first night of Navratri, Lata's family sets up a small altar in the living room. Her father brings home nine clay pots and fills them with soil. Lata plants wheat seeds in each pot and places them around the altar. For nine days, she waters them before breakfast. By the last day, the green shoots stand a hand tall, and the room smells of fresh grass. In the evenings, the family goes to the community hall for dancing. Lata wears an embroidered skirt and a mirror-work blouse. She says her legs hurt by the end of the week.

How many clay pots does Lata's father bring home?
He brings home nine clay pots.

When we have guests, my mother brings out the big copper pots from the top shelf. They are heavy, and I have to stand on a stool to help her lift them down. Each pot has to be scrubbed with tamarind and ash until it shines like a mirror. This takes me almost an hour, and my hands turn dark. When I am done, I rinse them and rub them dry with a rough cloth. Mother holds each one up to the light and checks for spots. If it passes, she nods once, and I place it on the stove.

What does the narrator use to scrub the copper pots?
The narrator uses tamarind and ash.

On cold nights, my father heats a brick in the oven and wraps it in a towel to put at the foot of my bed. It stays warm until morning. My mother tucks the quilt tightly under my feet and puts a small dish of water by the bed in case I am thirsty. My brother and I whisper for a few minutes after the light goes out, mostly about nothing. Then the whispers fall apart into long gaps, and the last thing I hear is the clock on the wall.

What does the narrator's father put at the foot of the bed?
He puts a heated brick wrapped in a towel.

Sarita had just come home from the hospital with her newborn son, and the entire neighbourhood had come to see him. Mrs. Dutta brought a packet of soft cotton cloth, Mr. Sharma brought a rattle and a young girl from across the street brought a hand-drawn card. They each peered into the cradle and whispered their opinions. The baby slept through all of it. Sarita's mother kept offering tea and biscuits. By evening, the front room was full of small gifts and the smell of sweets, and Sarita sat in the corner, smiling at everything, too tired to say a word.

Who brought the rattle?
Mr. Sharma brought the rattle.

Our aquarium has seven fish: four orange, two silver and one black. My sister named them after famous cricketers, though I have forgotten which is which. Every morning, she sprinkles a pinch of flakes on the surface and watches them rise. The silver ones are shy and eat only after the others have finished. Once a week, our father scoops out a cup of water and replaces it with fresh. The black fish is the oldest and the largest, and sometimes it rests at the bottom for an hour without moving. We have learned not to worry about it.

How many silver fish are in the aquarium?
There are two silver fish.

My brother and I share a room, and every Sunday we are supposed to tidy it. I usually do the floor, and he does the shelves. Last Sunday we started late because we were playing cards. At noon, our mother called us for lunch, and the room was still a mess. She told us we could eat only after the bed was made and the clothes were off the floor. We worked quickly, and in fifteen minutes the room looked better than it had in months. At lunch, my brother whispered that maybe we should always have a deadline. I told him not to say it loudly.

When are the narrator and the brother supposed to tidy their room?
They are supposed to tidy it every Sunday.

Irfan's little sister Hina followed him everywhere, and he found it annoying. When his friends came to play cricket, she wanted to bat. He said she was too small. She stood on the edge of the field with her arms crossed. After a while, the ball flew over the wall, and no one wanted to go to the dark yard behind it. Hina marched in, came out with the ball and threw it back without a word. The boys stared at her. Then Irfan said, rather quietly, that perhaps she could bat for two overs.

Why did Irfan change his mind about letting Hina bat?
She bravely fetched the ball that no one else wanted to get, and so earned his respect.

Ananya's mother was ill in bed, so Ananya decided to cook dinner. She chose a simple recipe: boiled eggs and plain rice. She put the eggs into cold water but forgot to light the stove properly, and for ten minutes nothing happened. Then the rice stuck to the bottom of the pot and the kitchen filled with smoke. Her father rushed in and opened the windows. Ananya burst into tears. He hugged her and said the eggs looked perfect, which was true. They ate the soft top layer of the rice with plenty of butter and laughed at the black bottom. Ananya said she would try again tomorrow.

What does Ananya's wish to try again tomorrow show?
It shows she is determined and did not let the failure discourage her.

Tomas had been waiting by the window since four o'clock. His older sister had promised to bring home a kite from the market, and he could not think about anything else. When the front door finally opened, she walked in with wet shoes and an empty bag. The kite shop had closed early because of the rain, she explained. Tomas looked down at the floor and said nothing. His sister knelt beside him and said they could build one together from newspaper and thin sticks. She fetched the glue and a ruler from the drawer. Slowly Tomas lifted his head, and a small smile crept across his face.

How did Tomas feel when he heard his sister's idea at the end?
He felt happier, because after looking sad he lifted his head and began to smile.

Rafi and his younger sister Tasnim share one desk by the window. They have drawn a pencil line down the middle, and neither is allowed to cross it. Rafi's side has books, a ruler and a brass paperweight. Tasnim's side holds crayons, a jar of buttons and a small cactus. Last Monday, Rafi's elbow slipped over the line, and Tasnim shouted that he had broken the treaty. Their mother, who was ironing in the next room, called out that they would both sit on the floor if the shouting did not stop. The line stayed, but they now use a thicker pencil.

What does Tasnim keep on her side of the desk?
She keeps crayons, a jar of buttons and a small cactus.

The family was nearly at the station when Dad realised the tickets were still on the kitchen table. He did not say anything for a moment, then turned the car around. Mum looked at her watch and took a long breath. The children were silent in the back seat. At home, Dad ran inside, grabbed the tickets and ran back, his shirt half untucked. They reached the station just as the train was beginning to move. They ran along the platform, and a kind guard held the door open for them. They sat down in the carriage, panting, and everyone burst out laughing at once.

Why did everyone burst out laughing at the end?
They were relieved and amused that they caught the train after such a close call.

Forty guests were expected at the Pandey house on the day of the engagement, and the preparations began at dawn. Mrs. Pandey rolled out puris while her sister fried the potatoes. The men hung strings of marigolds across the front gate and carried borrowed chairs up the stairs. Anil, the youngest boy, was told to stand at the door and greet everyone. He practised his greeting in the mirror, bowing a little too deeply. When the first car arrived at noon, he stepped forward and said "Namaste" in a loud, confident voice, and the guests smiled.

What was Anil's job on the day of the engagement?
He had to stand at the door and greet the guests.

Aisha was fasting for the first time during Ramadan, and she was determined not to tell anyone how hungry she was. By the afternoon, she was rather pale. Her mother noticed that she had stopped talking and sat very still on the sofa. She did not comment. Instead she brought out a book that Aisha liked and put it on her lap. She also quietly closed the kitchen door so the smell of cooking would not drift into the living room. When the call to prayer sounded at sunset, Aisha's mother put a date into her hand first. Aisha ate it and whispered, "Thank you."

Why did Aisha's mother close the kitchen door?
She wanted to stop the cooking smells from making Aisha's hunger harder while she was fasting.

Our Sunday lunch always begins at two, and my aunt's job is to set the table. She spreads a faded cloth with printed mangoes along the border and puts a steel plate at each place. In the middle, she places a bowl of curd, a plate of sliced onions and a small dish of pickle. My mother brings the hot dishes one by one. The last to arrive is the rice, in a big copper pot with a wooden spoon. We wait until everyone has been served before beginning. After lunch, the adults sleep, and the children play carom on the veranda.

At what time does Sunday lunch begin?
It begins at two o'clock.

Every winter, our grandfather wears a grey woollen cap that covers his ears and a long coat that reaches his knees. He takes a walking stick, though he does not really need it, and goes out to the park at six in the morning. The park is empty, and the grass is white with frost. He walks seven laps, stopping at the bench under the tree to blow his nose and look at the sky. When he returns, his face is red, and he drinks two cups of hot ginger tea before he says a single word.

How many laps does grandfather walk in the park?
He walks seven laps.

Whenever Nana Joan's grandchildren asked why she saved empty jars, she said they might be useful one day. The children rolled their eyes. Her shelves were full of jars of every size, with labels peeling. Then the family planned a surprise party for her seventieth birthday. Her daughter asked each grandchild to write a memory on a slip of paper. They dropped the slips into the jars, one slip in each, and lined them up on the table. When Nana Joan came in and saw the glass shining with all the paper, she covered her mouth with both hands.

What was the use the grandchildren found for the jars?
They used them to hold slips of paper with memories written on them, as a birthday surprise for Nana Joan.

Our flat has one window that faces the railway line, and we have learned to live by the trains. The six-fifteen shakes the glass and wakes my father. The eight o'clock goods train is so long that my little sister counts the wagons to forty. At night, the last train rumbles by around eleven, and its yellow light moves across the ceiling like a slow ghost. Guests are always startled the first time, and they grab their cups. We simply keep talking. My mother says that without the trains, the flat would feel empty.

When does the last train pass at night?
It passes around eleven o'clock.

When her baby brother started to walk, Anya was supposed to be happy. Everyone clapped when he took three wobbly steps toward the sofa. Anya clapped too, but she remembered the days when she had been the baby, and everyone had clapped for her. That evening, she asked her mother, quietly, if she had clapped as loudly for her first steps. Her mother laughed and went to the cupboard. She took out a video disc and put it on the television. There was little Anya, wobbling toward the camera. Her mother's clapping on the recording was deafening, and Anya grinned.

How did Anya's feelings change after watching the recording?
She felt reassured and happy, because she saw that her mother had clapped just as loudly for her.

Nobody enjoys sweeping the courtyard of the Pawar house, because the neem tree drops its leaves all day. Mr. Pawar made a rule: each of his three children sweeps for one week, and whoever sweeps in the week of the first rains is excused for the next one. Seema, the eldest, tried to arrange her turn to coincide with the rains, but the monsoon was late that year. She swept for three weeks in a row, grumbling. When the rain finally came, she dropped the broom, ran out and danced in the middle of the wet yard, her hair dripping.

What rule did Mr. Pawar make about sweeping?
Each child sweeps for one week, and whoever sweeps in the week of the first rains is excused from the next one.

When Dylan's family went away for a weekend, they left their goldfish, Captain, with the neighbours. Dylan gave careful instructions: two pinches of food each morning, never more. He wrote them on a card and taped it to the tank. On Monday morning he rushed to the neighbours' flat and found the tank cloudy and the fish hiding behind a plastic plant. The neighbour's young son had fed him a spoonful of food every few hours because he thought Captain looked hungry. Dylan sighed, took the tank home and cleaned it carefully. He decided that next time he would ask the neighbours to feed the fish only while he watched.

What probably caused the tank to turn cloudy?
Too much food, because the neighbour's son fed the fish a spoonful every few hours.

Pranav's father built a small wooden box for herbs and set it on the kitchen windowsill. Pranav planted mint, coriander and basil, and for a week everything went well. Then his family went to visit relatives for ten days. When they returned, the coriander was brown and the basil had folded over. Only the mint stood tall, green as ever. Pranav was puzzled until his father explained that mint grows almost anywhere, even without much care. Pranav replanted the other two, set a reminder on his mother's phone for watering and wrote the word "tough" on a sticky note beside the mint.

Why was the mint the only plant that survived?
Mint is a tough plant that grows without much care, so it lasted through the ten days without water.

Every day after dinner, Rohit's job was to put out the kitchen rubbish. He disliked it because the bin was by the back lane, which was dark. One evening, he walked out, hesitated and put the bag down just outside the door, planning to leave it there. In the morning, the smell had drawn stray dogs, and the bag was torn open, scattering waste across the porch. His father, who had to sweep it, did not say anything harsh. He handed Rohit the broom. Rohit did the sweeping and, from then on, always carried the bag all the way to the bin.

What did Rohit learn from the mess on the porch?
He learned to finish his job properly, because leaving the rubbish by the door caused a worse mess.

When the water pipe burst in the kitchen, the Mehta family had to move out for two nights. Ruchi's father arranged for them to stay with an aunt across town. The aunt's flat had only two rooms, so five people slept on mattresses spread across the living room floor. Ruchi packed her school bag and her favourite book but forgot her toothbrush. Her aunt found a spare one still in its box. In the morning, they all shared a single small bathroom, and the line outside the door grew longer and longer. When they finally returned home, Ruchi hugged the front door and said she would never complain about her tiny room again.

Why did Ruchi say she would never complain about her room again?
After sleeping crowded on the aunt's floor, she realised how much she valued her own room and home.

Omar always asked for a second helping of his aunt's lentil soup, though he claimed he did not like lentils. His aunt noticed but pretended not to. She simply ladled out a little extra each time and said nothing. One evening, Omar's cousin teased him about it in front of everybody. Omar's face turned red, and he put down his spoon. His aunt looked at the cousin sternly and said that a cook is happiest when the pot is empty. Omar picked up his spoon again, a little shyly, and finished his soup. Afterwards, he washed the bowls without being asked.

Why did Omar wash the bowls afterwards?
He wanted to thank his aunt for defending him and for the soup.

After the grandmother's funeral, the house fell silent. The relatives sat in a circle with the lights dim, and nobody knew what to say. Then little Tanvi, who was four, walked into the middle with her drawing book. She held up a picture of a round yellow face with a big smile and said it was Grandma. A few people smiled through tears. An uncle took the picture and propped it against a lamp. Soon the elders began to share stories about the old woman, and the room, at last, filled with quiet laughter.

What did Tanvi's drawing do for the family?
It broke the silence and helped them to remember Grandma with warmth and begin to share stories.

The Tanaka family's apartment is on the eighth floor, and every evening at six, Mrs. Tanaka opens the balcony door and sets a small stool outside. She sits there with a cup of green tea for ten minutes and looks at the rooftops. Her husband knows not to disturb her. The children, Yuki and Hiro, are told to lower their voices. Last Thursday, Hiro, who had been bursting with news about a football match, came to the door three times and went away each time. On the fourth, his mother's tea was finished, and she turned to him with an open face.

What will Hiro probably do next?
He will probably tell his mother his football news now, because her tea break is over and she is ready to listen.

Grandfather Nikhil's hearing had failed, and he now answered questions with a smile and a nod, whatever was asked. The family found it funny at first. One afternoon, his granddaughter Ria asked if he was happy living with them. He smiled and nodded. Then she asked if he wanted to go home. He smiled and nodded again. Ria felt cold. She took a notebook and wrote in large letters: "Do you want to go back to the village?" He read it twice, and tears ran down his face. He shook his head slowly and wrote one word: "No."

Why did Ria write her question on paper?
She realised that he nodded to everything without hearing, and wanted to be sure of his real answer.

On the night before the exam results, Vikram's mother kept busy. She swept the already clean floor, rearranged the spice jars and folded the same towel twice. His father pretended to read the paper but held it upside down for a full minute before noticing. Vikram himself lay on his bed, staring at the fan. Nobody mentioned the results at dinner. They talked about the price of onions and the neighbour's new scooter. When the plates were cleared, his mother put a hand on his head for a moment and went to bed. The house stayed lit until very late.

How were Vikram's parents feeling that evening?
They were anxious and nervous about the results, shown by their restless busyness and the upside-down newspaper.

When the neighbour's kitten climbed up the drain pipe and could not get down, ten-year-old Aarti heard it mewing for an hour. She brought a ladder from the storeroom, but it was too short. Then she tied a basket to a long rope, put a bit of fish inside and lowered it beside the kitten. The animal stretched a paw, hesitated and finally stepped into the basket. Aarti pulled it up slowly, hand over hand. She handed it to the owner, who stood on the lane in tears of relief. The owner asked how she had thought of the basket, and Aarti shrugged.

How did Aarti show that she is resourceful?
When the ladder was too short, she used a basket on a rope with some fish in it to bring the kitten up.

There are five of us in a small flat, so waking up is an organised business. Dad uses the bathroom first at five-thirty. Then Mum makes tea, and my elder brother Kunal takes his turn. Ritu and I share the third slot, which is why we both end up brushing our teeth in the kitchen. The youngest, Baby Tia, wakes last and is carried to the bathroom by whichever of us is free. By seven, we have all left the flat for school or work, and the flat is quiet for the first time of the day.

Who uses the bathroom first in the morning?
Dad uses it first, at five-thirty.

When Aunt Pallavi came to visit from Bengaluru, she brought three suitcases and a cloth bag full of mangoes. She slept in the children's room, so the two boys moved to the living room floor. She woke early every day and went straight to the kitchen to make dosa batter. The boys complained the first morning about the noise. By the third, they were awake before her, sitting at the table with empty plates. On the day she left, she gave each boy a small box of sweets and said she would be back in December. The boys stood at the gate until her taxi turned the corner.

What did Aunt Pallavi bring in the cloth bag?
She brought a cloth bag full of mangoes.

For New Year, Mr. Tan's family eats long noodles, because they believe the length brings a long life. At the reunion dinner, his grandmother's noodles were so long that they hung from the plate. Six-year-old Li bit hers short and chewed happily. Her cousin gasped. He said that she had cut her life short. The grown-ups looked at Li, and then at each other, trying not to laugh. Grandmother patted Li's head and said that clever children make their own long lives. She then lifted a noodle from her own bowl and gave it to Li, who accepted it with great seriousness.

Why did Grandmother give Li a noodle from her own bowl?
She wanted to reassure Li after her cousin said she had cut her life short, so she gave her a long noodle and said clever children make their own long lives.

At six months old, Zoya refused to take medicine from a spoon. Her mother tried a smaller spoon, a funny face and singing, and nothing worked. At last, her grandmother suggested the little dropper that came in the medicine box. Zoya looked at it with interest, opened her mouth and swallowed. Her mother, who had been close to tears, burst out laughing. They never found out whether it was the dropper or her grandmother's soft chant that did it. Her mother simply wrote the word "dropper" on the label of the medicine bottle and held the baby close.

What do we learn about Zoya's mother from the story?
She was worried and nearly in tears before the dropper worked, and then she felt such relief that she laughed.

Nirmal's family keeps a cow named Kamala in a small shed behind the house. Every morning at five, his father milks her into a steel bucket. The milk is warm and frothy, and Nirmal's job is to carry it to the kitchen without spilling. By seven, his mother has boiled it, and the whole house smells sweet. The cow is fed chopped grass, a handful of oil cake and a bucket of water. In the evening, Nirmal takes her to the field behind the school, where she grazes until dusk and then walks home on her own.

Who milks Kamala in the morning?
Nirmal's father milks her.

Before bed, Grandpa Lee winds the old brass clock in the hallway, and it is Nora's job to hold the key. The clock has to be wound twenty-one times, no more, no less. Nora counts aloud, and her grandfather turns. When they reach twenty-one, he closes the glass door with a click and pats the side of the clock as one pats a horse. Then Nora goes to bed. She says the ticking helps her to sleep, and she can hear it from her room if she holds her breath.

How many times is the clock wound?
It is wound twenty-one times.

When the storm knocked out the lights in the Baker house, six-year-old Poppy sat in the corner of the sofa gripping a cushion. Each flash of lightning made her jump. Her older brother Sam saw her face and went to find a torch. He turned it on beneath his chin and told her a ghost story, but with a silly twist: the ghost was afraid of thunder too. Poppy giggled, then laughed. By the time the next flash came, she was holding the torch herself, pointing it at the ceiling to make shadows. The storm kept going, but she did not notice.

Why did Poppy stop noticing the storm?
Sam's silly story and the torch games took her mind off her fear.

Every winter, a stray cat visits the Nair family's back porch. She is thin and orange, with a torn left ear. Mrs. Nair leaves a saucer of milk by the step each evening and goes back inside quickly, so the cat will not be scared. For weeks the saucer is empty by morning, but no one has seen her drink. Last Tuesday, the youngest daughter stayed up late and watched from the window. At nine o'clock, the cat slipped under the gate, drank the milk in a minute and washed her face. The girl whispered the news at breakfast.

Which of the cat's ears is torn?
Her left ear is torn.

When Sneha's maths exam was only two days away, she began to panic. She had read every chapter once but remembered nothing. Her older cousin Arvind noticed her pale face at dinner. He suggested that instead of reading again, she should teach him one chapter. Sneha thought it a silly idea but agreed. Standing at the whiteboard in the hallway, she explained fractions with a clear voice and neat drawings. When she finished, Arvind clapped. Sneha looked at the board and realised, with some surprise, that she knew the chapter perfectly. She asked him to be her pupil for the next chapter too.

Why did teaching Arvind help Sneha?
Explaining the chapter made her go over it carefully, so she learned it well and saw she did know it.

During the harvest festival, the Joshi children are given a set of new clothes. Pallavi, the middle child, always chose the brightest colour in the shop, and this year was no different. She picked a deep orange frock with gold trim. Her mother frowned, as the price was higher than planned, but Pallavi said nothing. She just looked at the frock and then at her mother, and then at the floor. Her mother sighed and said that she would take it, but that there would be no new shoes this year. Pallavi hugged her and said shoes did not matter.

What does Pallavi's mother's sigh show?
It shows that she gave in because she saw Pallavi really wanted the frock, even though it cost more than she had planned.

The rains had failed for the second year, and the water tank behind the Naidu house was nearly empty. Mrs. Naidu measured each bucket and wrote the number on the wall with chalk. Her children bathed with only a mug of water and used the leftover for the plants. When a neighbour offered to sell them an extra tank of water, Mr. Naidu shook his head. He said that they would manage if they were careful, and that the money was needed for school fees. At night, he looked out at the sky, but there were no clouds. He sighed and turned off the light.

What does Mr. Naidu's refusal of the extra water show about him?
It shows he is careful with money and puts the children's school fees first.

Grandma Rose wears the same blue cardigan every winter, even though it has holes at the elbows. Her grandchildren have bought her new ones, but she keeps them folded in the cupboard. When twelve-year-old Mia asked her why, Grandma Rose said that her husband had given her the blue one on their first anniversary. He chose the colour himself, though it was too big. She has mended it so many times that the wool is almost a different cloth. Mia said nothing. The next day, she went to the sewing box and carefully stitched a small round patch over the largest hole.

Why does Grandma Rose keep wearing the old cardigan?
It was a gift from her late husband on their first anniversary, so it holds special memories for her.

Eid at the Rahman house starts with a quiet morning. Sana's father goes to the mosque with her brothers, and Sana helps her mother arrange the sheer khurma in small glass bowls. The kitchen smells of cardamom and roasted vermicelli. When the men return, the relatives begin to arrive, one after another, with plates of biryani and sweets. Sana's mother greets each guest at the door, and the children are given small gifts. In the evening, the house is warm with talking. Sana looks at all the empty bowls and thinks that the whole day went by like one happy minute.

What does Sana's thought at the end show about her day?
It shows she enjoyed the day so much that it felt very short.

On her second birthday, little Tara was given a wooden toy cart with a string. She pulled it all over the house, with a stuffed elephant sitting inside. The cart bumped against doorsteps and table legs, and each time Tara said, "Oops." Her grandfather laughed and said that was the first full sentence she had spoken that week. By the evening, the cart had been to the kitchen, the bedroom, the balcony and even the bathroom. Tara finally fell asleep on the floor with the string still wrapped around her finger.

Who was riding in Tara's wooden cart?
A stuffed elephant was riding in it.

When the guests were late for lunch, Mrs. Fernandez kept the food warm on a low flame. At two o'clock, she covered the dishes. At three, she sat down alone and ate a small plate of rice. At four, she walked to the window, looked up the empty road and came back. At five, the phone rang. The guests had missed their train and would arrive the next day. Mrs. Fernandez did not say much. She put the food into containers, labelled them and slid them into the fridge. Her husband noticed that she was more quiet than usual but did not speak.

How did Mrs. Fernandez probably feel about the guests' delay?
She was probably disappointed and a little upset, since she waited all day and became quiet.

On Sundays, Selin's father cooked, and nobody was allowed in the kitchen. The family waited in the living room, sniffing the air and guessing the dish. This Sunday, a sharp smell of burning drifted out. Selin's brother stood up, but her mother put out a hand and shook her head. A little while later, her father came out with a tray: rice, plain yoghurt and a single, slightly blackened aubergine, split open. He announced the menu with a straight face. Everyone ate every bite and praised the aubergine. Her father went red with pleasure and sat down.

Why did Selin's mother stop her brother from going to the kitchen?
She wanted to protect her husband's pride and let him finish cooking without interference, even though something had burnt.

Baby Kabir cried at everyone except his great-aunt. When relatives came to visit, he screamed and hid his face in his mother's neck. But when great-aunt Bimla picked him up, he stared at her with round eyes and was quiet. She had a gentle way of humming under her breath, and she smelled of coconut oil. The relatives were astonished. They asked her what the secret was, and she said that babies like people who are not trying too hard. The relatives were silent for a moment, and then they all tried to act more casual.

What does great-aunt Bimla suggest about why Kabir liked her?
She suggests that he liked her because she was calm and did not try too hard to win him over.

The family's old dog, Bruno, could no longer climb the stairs, so Jaya's father moved his bed to the ground floor. At night, Jaya crept downstairs with a blanket and slept next to him on the tiles. Her mother found her there in the morning and did not wake her. She laid a pillow under her head and went to make tea. When Jaya woke, Bruno was resting his nose on her arm, and his tail gave two slow thumps. She did not tell anyone, but after that she slept downstairs every night until the winter ended.

Why did Jaya sleep downstairs every night?
She wanted to keep Bruno company, since he was old and could no longer climb the stairs.

Mrs. Joseph's children disliked bitter gourd, and each meal where it appeared was a battle. She stopped forcing them to eat it. One evening she served it fried in thin slices, crisp as chips, with a pinch of salt and lime. She put the plate in the middle of the table and said nothing about it. The children, busy talking, picked up the slices one by one without noticing. When the plate was empty, the youngest said, "More chips, please." Mrs. Joseph, turning away to hide her smile, said it would be on the table again next week.

Why did Mrs. Joseph turn away to hide her smile?
Her plan had worked, because the children ate the bitter gourd without realising it.

Reshma's grandmother had grown frail, and she now spent most of the day in bed. Every morning, Reshma carried a bucket of warm water to her. She poured it into a basin and helped her wash her face. Her mother said she did not need to do this every day, since the maid could do it. Reshma shook her head. She said it was not the work she liked but the time with her grandmother, who told her old stories while the water cooled. Her mother, after a pause, took the bucket from her hand and went to find a second basin so she could join them.

Why did Reshma want to carry the water herself?
She enjoyed the time with her grandmother and the stories, rather than the work.

Hira and her cousins spent every summer at their grandparents' farm in Punjab. The day began at sunrise, when the rooster crowed and the cows were milked. Breakfast was parathas with white butter, eaten on a cot in the courtyard. Then the children went to the fields to chase the water channel as it filled the rows. At noon, they napped under the neem tree while the elders rested indoors. In the afternoon, they climbed onto the tractor trailer, and the uncle drove them to the canal for a swim. When the sun set, they sat in the courtyard again for stories and sweet lassi.

Where did Hira and her cousins spend their summers?
They spent them at their grandparents' farm in Punjab.

Baby Anita's first Holi was spent mostly in her mother's arms, away from the water. Her mother wrapped her in a thick cotton sheet and sat on a chair in the shade. Anita watched the colours with wide eyes and did not make a sound. When her uncle came near with a pinch of pink powder, her mother let him touch it very lightly on the baby's forehead. Anita blinked, then scrunched her nose. A few seconds later, she sneezed three times, and everyone burst into laughter. Her mother wiped the powder away with a damp cloth.

Where did Anita's mother sit during Holi?
She sat on a chair in the shade.

When her mother-in-law visited, Mrs. Das wanted everything to be perfect. She polished the floors, aired the quilts and cooked her favourite fish. But at dinner, the older woman said nothing about the food. Mrs. Das watched her take every bite, hoping for a word. After the meal, her mother-in-law rose, walked to the kitchen and quietly washed her own plate. Then she turned and asked for the recipe. Mrs. Das's face lit up. She reached for the notebook. A moment later, the two women were sitting side by side, heads bent over a page.

What does the mother-in-law's request for the recipe tell us?
It tells us that she liked the fish very much, even though she did not say so in words.

A heavy fog covered the town on the morning of Grandpa's seventieth birthday. The visitors were due at eleven, but by ten-thirty nobody had come. Mum kept looking at the clock while she stirred the sweet pudding. Dad tried calling the cousins, but their phones were out of range. At last, a few minutes past noon, a line of headlights crawled up the road. The cousins climbed out, shivering and laughing, and said the drive had taken twice as long as usual. Grandpa met them at the gate with a blanket over his shoulders. He declared that fog was the best surprise guest he had ever had.

Why were the cousins late for the birthday?
The heavy fog slowed their drive so much that it took twice as long as usual.

Every night the Miller family's old dog, Tuck, barked at the back door at precisely ten. Nobody knew why. They stopped asking after a few months. One evening, Mr. Miller finally opened the door to see what the dog was looking at. A small hedgehog was sitting on the step, waiting for the saucer of milk that Mrs. Miller set out each night without telling anyone. Tuck wagged his tail and lay down beside it. Mr. Miller closed the door softly. He looked at his wife, who was suddenly very interested in her knitting.

Who had been putting out the milk for the hedgehog?
Mrs. Miller had been putting out the milk, and her interest in her knitting shows she was hiding it.

Mrs. Pillai lifts her granddaughter out of the cot each morning and carries her to the window. The baby, only four months old, stares at the leaves of the neem tree. Mrs. Pillai tells her the names of the birds that come: a crow, a mynah, a pair of green parrots. She says each name slowly and clearly. The baby's mother thinks it is too early for lessons, but Mrs. Pillai laughs and says that words must be sown early. After the bird names, she sings a short song, and the baby falls asleep against her shoulder.

How old is the baby?
She is four months old.

Every Sunday, Meera's grandfather walks to the corner bakery before anyone else wakes up. He buys six soft rolls and one small packet of jam, then carries them home in a cloth bag. By the time he returns, Meera's mother has already boiled the milk and set out the steel tumblers on the table. The whole family sits together on the floor mats, tearing the rolls and dipping them in warm tea. Meera's little brother always asks for the jam first. Her father reads the newspaper aloud, and her grandmother corrects his pronunciation with a smile. Meera thinks Sunday breakfast is the only time when nobody is in a hurry, and she hopes it never changes.

Where does Meera's grandfather buy the rolls?
He buys them at the corner bakery.

The Quraishi family's cat has one blue eye and one green. Her name is Neela, and she is quite proud of her looks. She sits on the arm of the sofa each evening, facing the door, as if she were the host. When visitors enter, she looks them over for a few seconds and then either walks away or settles on their lap. She is never wrong, the family says: those she chooses are always kind. The postman, who has never once been chosen, has begun to bring a small piece of fish every Friday.

What is unusual about Neela's eyes?
She has one blue eye and one green eye.

In the Verghese house, the three brothers sleep in the same room: Jacob in the bed, Ben on the floor mat and young Thomas on a folding cot. Each has a small shelf with his own things. Jacob keeps his books and trophies, Ben his cricket gear and Thomas his shells and stones. In the middle of the room, there is a large wooden trunk that serves as both a table and a seat. At night, the brothers talk until their mother knocks on the wall, and then they all go quiet at once.

Where does Ben sleep?
He sleeps on a floor mat.

Little Rhea has a special cloth rabbit that must be tucked in before she can sleep. Her mother says it has been through three washes and one trip to the dentist. Every night, Rhea carries it to bed under her arm and asks her father to say goodnight to it first. He bows slightly and says, "Goodnight, Mr. Hopper." Then Rhea says her own goodnight, and he turns out the light. If Mr. Hopper is missing, the whole house must search, and Rhea has been known to cry until he is found under a cushion.

What is the name of Rhea's rabbit?
Its name is Mr. Hopper.

Kiran's grandfather planted a neem sapling in the courtyard on the day Kiran was born. It was the size of a pencil. Now, twelve years later, the tree is taller than the house. Its branches shade the entire yard, and birds nest in the upper boughs. Every year on Kiran's birthday, his grandfather ties a red thread around the trunk and measures the width with his arms. This year the trunk was too wide for him to circle alone, so Kiran stepped forward and the two of them touched fingertips on the far side.

When did Kiran's grandfather plant the neem sapling?
He planted it on the day Kiran was born.

There is a guava tree behind Rahul's house, and every year the family argues about who owns the fruit. The tree stands exactly on the boundary between their yard and the neighbour's. The branches lean toward Mrs. Kapoor's side, so the best guavas fall into her garden. Rahul's father says the tree belongs to them because he planted it. Mrs. Kapoor says the fruit belongs to whoever catches it. In the end, the two families agreed on a rule: whatever falls on the ground is shared in equal baskets, and whatever hangs on the branch stays for the birds. Everyone has been friendly ever since.

What rule did the two families agree on?
Fallen guavas are shared in equal baskets, and fruit still on the branch is left for the birds.

On the way to the village, the car's engine started to smoke, and Mr. Khan pulled over to the side of the road. The family stood on the grass while he lifted the bonnet. It was midday, and the sun was fierce. The children were bored and hungry. Mrs. Khan took out a bottle of water and a bag of dried fruit and passed them round. She pointed to a banyan tree and said they could wait in its shade. After an hour, a passing truck driver stopped and helped Mr. Khan to fix the pipe. When they drove off, the children waved at him through the back window.

Why did Mrs. Khan take the children to the banyan tree?
She wanted them to rest in the shade and stay cool and calm during the long wait in the heat.

On the evening of Ganesh Chaturthi, the Joshi family welcomes a small clay idol into their living room. Mr. Joshi carries it in a cloth, walking very slowly through the front door as the neighbours watch. Mrs. Joshi waits with a tray holding a lamp, flowers and a bowl of modak. The children stand in a line and clap. The idol is placed on a decorated stool and covered with a red cloth, which is removed at the auspicious time. After the prayers, everyone eats modak, and the old people tell the story of how the elephant-headed god came to be.

What sweet is placed in a bowl on the tray?
The sweet is modak.

Hiroshi's job was to carry the water cans from the tap to the kitchen. The tap was at the end of the lane, and it ran for only one hour in the morning. He grumbled each day, but he did not skip the task. One day the tap did not run at all, and neighbours stood in a long, quiet queue with empty pots. Hiroshi waited too. When a truck finally arrived, he was at the front of the line. He filled three cans and carried them home carefully. His mother kissed his forehead, and he did not complain about water for a long time.

Why did Hiroshi stop complaining about water?
He learned how precious it was when the tap ran dry, and he saw his task was important.

Our dog, Sheru, is afraid of firecrackers, and every Diwali we make a safe corner for him. Father moves the old mattress to the storeroom and puts a bowl of water and his favourite blanket there. Mother closes the windows, and we turn on the radio loudly to cover the bangs. My sister sits with him for the first hour, stroking his back. By nine, most of the noise has stopped, and he comes out, shaking his ears. We give him a biscuit, and he sleeps at our feet.

Where does the family make a safe corner for Sheru?
They make it in the storeroom.

Hana's mother was famous in the neighbourhood for her rice balls, and every spring the school asked her to make them for the sports day. Hana always helped, and she knew the secret: wet hands and a pinch of salt. This year, her mother had a fever and could not stand for long. Hana sat her down and said she would do the work. She cooked the rice, wet her palms and shaped forty balls. They were slightly lopsided, but her mother, sitting on a stool, instructed her step by step. The teacher said the rice balls were the best in years. Hana did not say who had made them.

Why do you think Hana did not say who had made the rice balls?
She was modest, or she wanted the credit to go to her mother, who had taught her and guided her.

Kavya's mother makes lemon rice every Thursday because it is the quickest dish she knows. She heats oil in a small pan, adds mustard seeds, curry leaves and a handful of peanuts, and waits for the seeds to pop. Then she pours the mixture over cooked rice and squeezes in the juice of two lemons. Kavya packs the rice into her steel tiffin box, along with a slice of cucumber and a boiled egg. At school, her friends always gather around her desk at lunch to smell it. Today, her friend Rohan traded his sandwich for a spoonful of the rice and asked for the recipe.

Which day of the week does Kavya's mother make lemon rice?
She makes it every Thursday.

My aunt makes the best pickle in our family, and the recipe is a secret. Every summer she buys green mangoes in a large basket and cuts them into small pieces with a heavy knife. The pieces are rubbed with salt and turmeric and left in the sun for two days. Then she mixes the spice powder with mustard oil and pours it over the mango. The mixture goes into a glass jar and is covered with a muslin cloth. For two weeks, she moves it from the roof to the veranda and back to catch the sun. After that, the pickle is ready, and she hands each of us a small jar.

How long is the pickle left in the sun before the oil is added?
The pieces are left in the sun for two days.

When Uncle Farid arrived, the children ran to the door, but their mother stopped them. She had noticed that he was limping and carrying a heavy bag. She asked the children to take the bag, offer him a chair and bring water. They obeyed at once. Farid sat down, grateful, and rubbed his leg. In the evening, he told them that his bus had broken down, and he had walked the last three kilometres. The children made him a cushion from folded towels and put his feet up. He kept saying that he did not deserve so much attention, but he looked very happy.

Why did Farid look happy even while saying he did not deserve the attention?
He was touched by the children's care and welcome after a tiring journey.

Our family tried three times to keep a pet bird, but each one flew away when the cage was open. After the third, my mother said no more birds. My brother Vikram quietly began to leave a dish of seeds on the window ledge. Each morning, small sparrows came to eat. He counted them and drew them in a notebook, giving each a name. By the end of the month, twelve sparrows came every day, and one even perched on the window frame while he sat nearby. Our mother watched this from the kitchen and never said a word about the dish.

What does the mother's silence about the dish suggest?
It suggests she accepted the dish and was quietly pleased, because she watched the sparrows from the kitchen and never told him to stop.

When the bicycle's chain slipped, ten-year-old Arjun walked it home from the market, pushing it with one hand. His father was sitting on the veranda reading. He put down the paper, took a rag and showed Arjun how to lift the chain over the teeth of the gear. It took three tries before it sat properly. Then they turned the pedals by hand, listening to the soft whir. Arjun's father wiped his fingers and said that a bicycle was no more than a bundle of simple ideas. Arjun rode to the end of the lane and back, smiling.

How did Arjun get his bicycle home?
He walked it home, pushing it with one hand.

Marisol's family has no sofa. They sit on cushions on the floor around a low table, and when guests arrive, they bring out more cushions. Marisol was embarrassed about this when her new classmate came to visit. She kept saying that her father was planning to buy furniture soon. The classmate, Beth, looked around and asked if she could sit on the red cushion. She spent the afternoon cross-legged on the floor, eating peanuts and asking questions about everything. When she left, she said that Marisol's home was cosier than her own. Marisol closed the door and noticed that she was smiling.

Why was Marisol smiling when she closed the door?
Beth's kind words made her feel less embarrassed and proud of her home.

Amaya's brother had been born with a sickly cry, and the doctor kept him in the hospital for a week. When he finally came home, the family had decorated the house with balloons and a banner. Her father, who was usually serious, wore a paper crown. Her mother, thin and pale, smiled as she stepped through the door. Amaya, six years old, was the first to reach out. She laid her palm lightly on his small chest and whispered, "He is breathing!" Everyone in the room laughed, and some wiped their eyes. Her father picked her up and spun her round.

Why did some people wipe their eyes when Amaya said "He is breathing"?
They were moved with relief and joy that the baby was safe and healthy after the worry in the hospital.

In the Menon household, the first person up lights the lamp in the prayer corner. Usually that is Mr. Menon's mother, who rises at half past four. She bathes, tucks a flower behind her ear and walks quietly past the sleeping grandchildren. When the lamp is lit, a soft gold light spreads across the wall. Mr. Menon says he often wakes to the smell of the oil. His youngest daughter, Asha, has started getting up early too. She sits on the floor near her grandmother, but she is mostly asleep. Her grandmother does not wake her; she only places a shawl over her shoulders.

Who usually lights the lamp in the prayer corner?
Mr. Menon's mother usually lights it, because she is the first one up.

Dada always wakes at five and sits on the veranda with a steel glass of tea. He says the morning is the only time the world is quiet enough to think. When his grandson Karan was small, he began joining him. At first Karan just yawned and leaned against the railing. Now, at fourteen, he brings his own glass of milk and the two of them watch the street sweepers and the milkman on his cycle. They do not talk much. Dada sometimes points out a bird, and Karan names it. On the day Karan leaves for hostel next year, they have agreed to sit there once more.

How old is Karan now?
He is fourteen.

When Jun was nine, his father taught him to fold a paper crane. The first one came out lopsided, with a crumpled wing. His father said every crane needs a thousand tries before it flies. So Jun folded one each evening before bed and lined them up along the windowsill. His mother found them in the morning and moved them into a glass jar. By winter the jar was full, and Jun started a second one. His father had left for a job in another city by then, so Jun mailed him a small envelope of cranes every week. He wrote "Practise" on the back of each one.

What did Jun's mother do with the paper cranes?
She moved them from the windowsill into a glass jar.

The Alvarez family's rabbit, Nube, would not eat. She sat in the corner of her hutch with ears flat against her back. Seven-year-old Diego offered her carrot, lettuce and even a bit of apple, but she turned away from each one. He ran to find his mother. His mother listened, nodded and said they should take Nube to the animal clinic in the morning. Diego did not sleep well. At dawn, he put a soft cloth in a basket and carried the rabbit to the bus stop with both arms. His mother held the basket handle too, and neither of them said a word.

What does Diego's restless night show about how he felt?
It shows he was very worried about Nube.

The living room of the Kapadia family was always tidy because it was never used. The sofa had plastic over it, and the glass cabinet held the best cups, which no one drank from. Children were told not to touch. When Grandfather came to live with them, he sat on the sofa on his first day, plastic and all. He asked for tea in one of the best cups. Mrs. Kapadia opened her mouth to object but met his gentle eyes. She brought the cup. Within a week, the plastic had been taken off the sofa and the cabinet was open.

What does the change in the living room show about Mrs. Kapadia?
It shows that she cared more about Grandfather's comfort than her old rules, because after meeting his gentle eyes she brought the cup and let the room be used.

The Narayanan family always receives guests with a glass of buttermilk with a pinch of salt and crushed curry leaves. They believe that anyone coming in from the afternoon heat should cool down before speaking. The glasses are tall and steel, kept on a special shelf. Mrs. Narayanan carries them on a tray and bows slightly when she gives them. The guests drink in silence, and then the conversation begins. Even the plumber who comes to fix the pipes is given a glass. He usually says it is the best part of his visit.

What do the Narayanans give their guests first?
They give them a glass of buttermilk with salt and crushed curry leaves.

On her birthday, Anjali wanted only one thing for dinner: her grandmother's paneer curry. Her grandmother, who was visiting from Jaipur, rose early to grind the spices on a flat stone. She fried the paneer cubes until they turned golden and added tomatoes, cream and a pinch of dried fenugreek. The smell reached every corner of the flat. At seven, the family sat around the table, and Anjali's father brought a small cake with eight candles. After Anjali blew them out, she said the curry tasted better than any restaurant dish. Her grandmother laughed and told her that the secret was the stone.

Where had Anjali's grandmother come from to visit?
She had come from Jaipur.

Eight-year-old Imani refused to sleep without her bedroom door open a hand's width. Her father thought she was afraid of the dark and bought her a night light, but she kept asking for the door. One evening he sat on the edge of her bed and asked why. Imani said that she liked hearing him and Mum talk and wash the dishes downstairs. The sounds made the house feel safe. Her father smiled, switched off the night light and said he would make sure the dishes were always noisy at bedtime. Imani fell asleep before he reached the stairs.

Why did Imani want her door open?
She liked hearing her parents' voices and the dishes downstairs, because the sounds made her feel safe.

My grandmother's kitchen has a window that opens onto a courtyard. In the morning, the sun comes in at an angle and shines on a row of brass pots on the shelf. She says it is the best clock she has. The stove is a clay one with two openings, and she still lights it with dried twigs when the gas runs out. A string of garlic hangs from a hook beside the door, and a bunch of dried chillies is tied to the beam. When I visit, she gives me a tin cup of milk with a spoonful of jaggery, and I sit on a low wooden stool to drink it.

What does Grandmother's stove burn when the gas runs out?
It burns dried twigs.

The Fernandes family adopted a brown puppy named Biscuit last month. He sleeps in a cardboard box lined with an old shirt near the kitchen door. Every morning at six, Biscuit scratches at the door until Mr. Fernandes takes him for a walk around the building. His daughter Clara feeds him twice a day, once before school and once after, using a small blue bowl. Biscuit is not allowed on the sofa, but he tries to climb up whenever the adults look away. Clara's mother says he has already chewed three slippers. The family agreed that each person would hide their shoes on a high shelf.

How many slippers has Biscuit chewed so far?
He has chewed three slippers.

Lucas hated washing dishes. Each evening he would wait until his sister had gone upstairs, then stack the plates quickly and leave the pots soaking. One night his mother returned from work and found the sink full of cold, greasy water. She did not shout. She simply tied on an apron, rolled up her sleeves and began scrubbing the pots herself, though she looked very tired. Lucas stood in the doorway for a moment. Then he picked up a dish towel and started drying. Neither of them spoke. The next evening, the pots were clean before his mother had even taken off her shoes.

What does Lucas's change the next evening show?
It shows he felt sorry and wanted to help, because he saw his tired mother doing his work and then cleaned the pots himself.

When Mrs. Chaudhary fell and hurt her wrist, her family had to learn the work she did without being seen. Her husband found that the clothes did not wash themselves, and her son discovered that rice does not cook itself. For three days, the house was a mess. Nobody could find anything, and dinner was always late. On the fourth evening, her husband stood in the kitchen with a ladle in his hand and said quietly to the children that they had never thanked their mother enough. The three of them made a card that night and left it on her pillow.

Why did the family make a card for Mrs. Chaudhary?
They realised how much work she normally does for the family and wanted to thank her.

Nobody had told Faisal that the project was due on Friday. He found out on Thursday night, when his friend mentioned it on the phone. His heart sank. He had two blank sheets and a head full of nothing. His mother heard his groan and came to see. She did not scold him. She cleared the dining table, brought a pot of tea for herself and some milk for him and sat down with the newspaper. Faisal started to write. Around midnight, he put down his pen, rubbed his eyes and found his mother asleep beside him with the newspaper over her face.

What does the mother's behaviour show?
It shows that she supports him and stayed beside him to give comfort, even though it was late and she was tired.

Elena's balcony garden was her father's idea, but within a month it was her own. She named each of the plants after relatives: the tall cactus was Uncle Marco, the drooping fern was Aunt Rosa. When the cactus got a yellow flower, she announced it at dinner as news about Uncle Marco. When the fern lost a leaf, she wrapped it carefully in a tissue and put it in the bin with a short speech. Her father, watching, hid a smile behind his napkin. He noticed that his daughter, who had never been interested in anything but screens, now woke early each morning to check on her relatives.

What did the garden change in Elena?
It made her care about living things, so she woke early to look after the plants instead of staring at screens.

The baby of the house, little Veer, has a morning routine. At six, he wakes with a loud shout. His grandmother lifts him from the cot and carries him to the window, where he points at the crows. Then he is given a wet cloth to wipe his face, which he usually tries to eat. After his milk, he sits on a mat with his wooden blocks, and his sister builds towers for him to knock down. He does this for exactly twenty minutes and then falls asleep, with a block still in his fist.

What does Veer do at six every morning?
He wakes with a loud shout.

Wei's father owns a small repair shop on the ground floor of their building, and the family lives upstairs. On school days, Wei comes down for an hour each afternoon to sit at the back counter and do his homework. His father likes having him close. Customers sometimes bring broken radios, old clocks or torn umbrellas, and Wei watches how his father opens each one with a tiny screwdriver. Last week a woman brought in a clock that had belonged to her mother. His father worked on it for two evenings without charging extra. When she came back and heard it chime, she wiped her eyes and thanked him quietly.

Why did the woman wipe her eyes when she heard the clock chime?
The clock had belonged to her mother, so hearing it work again made her emotional.

Whenever Dipti's father returned from the night shift, he stepped through the door without a sound. He took off his shoes, carried them in his hand and walked on his toes past the children's room. In the kitchen, he warmed his own tea. The children, who were meant to be asleep, usually heard everything and pretended not to. One morning, Dipti got up before him and made the tea herself. She put it on the table with two biscuits. When her father came in and saw it steaming, he stood motionless for a long moment. Then he sat down and drank it slowly, looking at her.

Why did Dipti's father stand motionless when he saw the tea?
He was surprised and moved that his daughter had thought of him and made tea for him.

Our baby cousin Rohan came to stay for a week. He is nine months old and has two teeth. He loves to bang a steel spoon on the floor, and he laughs every time the sound rings. His mother brought a bag of toys, but he prefers the spoon and the empty plastic bottle. We made a mat out of a folded quilt and put him in the middle, surrounded by pillows. He rolled over, grabbed a cushion and tried to eat it. By the end of the week, he had learned to say "dada," though he used it for everyone.

How many teeth does baby Rohan have?
He has two teeth.

Shanti's dog, Moti, always knew when she was sad. When Shanti failed a maths test, she came home and sat on the back step without speaking. Moti walked over, lay down across her feet and rested his chin on her knee. He did not bark or wag his tail. Shanti stroked the soft fur behind his ears and felt the tightness in her chest loosen. After ten minutes, she said aloud that one test did not matter much. Moti raised his head and licked her hand. Shanti laughed, wiped her eyes and went inside to ask her father to help her with the next chapter.

Why did Shanti decide to ask her father for help?
Moti's comfort made her feel better and ready to face the problem, so she decided to work on the next chapter.

In Grandma Beth's house, everybody got a different portion of the pie. The largest went to whoever had worked hardest that week, and the smallest to whoever had been lazy. Children watched each other's work all week. When Billy cleaned the shed on Thursday, his sister Carol cleaned the stairs on Friday, each secretly aiming for the big slice. On Sunday, Grandma Beth cut the pie into four equal parts and handed them out without a word. The children stared. She smiled and said that it was too hot to judge fairly. The truth was that she had liked the extra work and wanted to reward both.

Why did Grandma Beth cut four equal slices?
She was pleased with both children's work and wanted to treat them equally, though she gave a different excuse.

For the first month, baby Leela slept in a small wooden cradle that her great-grandfather had made. The cradle had four tiny legs carved like lotus petals and a hood of white cotton. Leela's father sanded it down and painted it a soft green before she came home. Every night, her mother rocked it gently with one foot while reading a book. The baby's grandmother said the cradle had held eleven children in the family, and Leela was the twelfth. She added that every one of them had grown up strong. Leela, wrapped in a yellow blanket, yawned and curled her fist.

Who made the wooden cradle?
Leela's great-grandfather made it.

It was the hottest week of the year, and the fan in Zainab's bedroom had broken. Her father promised to fix it on Saturday, but until then the family slept on the roof. Zainab's mother spread cotton sheets over the concrete and her father brought up a jug of cold water. Lying on her back, Zainab could see more stars than she had ever seen from the window. Her little cousin counted them aloud until he fell asleep at forty-three. A light breeze moved across the roof near midnight, and the family pulled the sheets up to their shoulders.

Where did Zainab's family sleep during the hot week?
They slept on the roof.

The power cut came just as Mehdi's mother was reading him the last chapter of his book. The room went dark, and he gasped. His mother lit a candle, but the story was in tiny print, and she could not see it clearly. Mehdi said he would hold the candle, and she could read. He held it steady, though his arm shook after a few minutes. His mother finished the chapter, one eye on the small flame, and closed the book. Mehdi blew out the candle and said it was the best ending he had ever heard, even though he did not remember what happened.

Why did Mehdi say it was the best ending he had ever heard?
Reading by candlelight with his mother felt special, so he enjoyed the moment more than the story.

The old radio in the Murthy household had been silent for two years. One Sunday, nine-year-old Girish took it apart on the floor with a screwdriver, spreading the pieces on a newspaper. He found a wire that had come loose and twisted it back to the post. His grandfather, who was watching, held the torch. When Girish put the back cover on and turned the knob, a crackle came, then a song. His grandfather closed his eyes and swayed. He said it was the first song he had heard on that radio since his wife died.

What did Girish find inside the radio?
He found a loose wire.

Paulo's family rented the ground floor of a house with a leaking roof. Each time it rained, they placed pots and pans on the floor to catch the drips, and the sound filled the room: ting, tong, plop. Paulo, who was seven, thought it was a kind of music and arranged the pans from small to large. His mother, though, looked at the ceiling with worried eyes. That night she called the landlord and, speaking calmly but firmly, asked him to repair the roof before the next rain. The landlord promised to send a worker on Monday. Paulo was disappointed that his orchestra would soon end.

Why was Paulo's mother worried while Paulo enjoyed the sound?
She was worried because the leaking roof could damage the house, while Paulo only saw the dripping as music.

At our home, the guest room is also the storeroom. It has a bed in one corner and, along the wall, sacks of rice and lentils piled up to the shoulder. When guests arrive, my mother moves a few sacks and hangs a curtain. My cousin once slept there and complained in the morning about the smell of cumin. Since then, my mother has put a small bag of dried rose petals under the pillow. The guests have since said the room smells lovely, and she smiles and says nothing.

What does the guest room also serve as?
It also serves as the storeroom.

Four weeks before her exams, Salma stopped helping around the house. Her mother said nothing at first and washed the clothes herself, though her hands were sore. Salma's brother, who was twelve, began to carry the buckets and fold the laundry without being asked. When Salma noticed, she felt guilty and stood in the doorway. Her mother told her gently that studying was her work for now, and that the family would manage. Salma sat down to revise but could not concentrate. After a few minutes, she got up, took a dry sheet from the line and began to fold it. Her mother smiled but did not turn around.

Why could Salma not concentrate on revising?
She felt guilty that her mother and brother were doing all the housework while she studied.

Lakshmi's mother always packed two parathas in her lunch box, though Lakshmi said one was enough. In class, Lakshmi ate one quickly and kept the second wrapped in foil in her bag. After school, she walked past the bridge and handed it to an old man who sat there. He was the watchman of the empty godown, and he never asked for anything. He always said "Bless you, child." Lakshmi told no one. Her mother, who had noticed that the lunch box came back with a clean foil, only added a little extra butter to the second paratha each day.

Why did Lakshmi's mother add extra butter to the second paratha?
She knew Lakshmi was giving it to the old man and quietly wanted to make it better for him.

A sandstorm rolled into the town in the afternoon, turning the sky a muddy brown. Mrs. Ahmed shut every window and put wet towels along the sills. Her children came in from the lane, coughing, with dust in their hair. She sat them in the middle room and handed out wet cloths to hold over their faces. Her husband was still on his way back from the office. Every few minutes, Mrs. Ahmed went to the door and looked out through the narrow gap at the road. When she finally saw his scooter, she let out a long breath and opened the door wide.

Why did Mrs. Ahmed keep looking out at the road?
She was worried about her husband travelling home in the storm.

The summer holidays in the hills were always cool. In the morning, mist lay across the valley like a white sheet, and the sun took until nine to burn it away. Lina and her cousins woke early to sit in the porch wrapped in shawls. Her aunt boiled tea with tulsi leaves, and they drank it from big mugs, watching the mist thin out. By noon, the sun was bright, and the cousins played badminton in the yard. By four, clouds returned, and the cousins ran inside before the first drops fell.

When did the sun burn away the mist?
It burned the mist away by about nine in the morning.
