Nobody had told the new puppy that the sofa was off limits. Within the first hour in the Sengupta house, he jumped onto it, rolled over and fell asleep on a cushion with a loud sigh. The children, who had been told to be strict, looked at each other. Mr. Sengupta looked at the puppy. Then he looked at his wife. She raised an eyebrow, shrugged and went to make tea. Mr. Sengupta pulled up a small stool and sat beside the sofa. By evening, the rule about the sofa had quietly been forgotten.

What does the family's reaction suggest about the puppy?
It suggests that the puppy had already won their hearts, so they gave up the rule.

At first, Jamal thought his grandmother's old sewing machine was only a piece of furniture. It sat in the corner under a cloth, with a rusty wheel and a black iron base. Then one afternoon, his school uniform trousers ripped, and no one could stitch them before morning. His grandmother pulled off the cloth, oiled the wheel and placed the fabric under the needle. Her feet moved on the treadle, and the machine rattled loudly. In ten minutes, the trousers were mended, with a neat double seam. Jamal stared at the machine as if it were alive. After that, he dusted it every Sunday.

Why did Jamal begin to dust the machine every Sunday?
The machine saved his trousers, so he gained respect for it and wanted to look after it.

Mark's father believes every Saturday should begin with pancakes, and he takes the job seriously. He wears an apron that says "Chief Flipper" and sings while he stirs the batter. Mark's sisters stand at the counter, each holding a plate. The first pancake is always a failure, which his father calls the tester and feeds to the dog. The second is perfect. Mark likes his with sliced banana, while his sisters want honey. Last week the batter ran out too soon, and Mark gave his last pancake to his youngest sister without being asked. His father put an arm around him and said nothing, though he looked very pleased.

What does Mark's father do with the first pancake?
He feeds it to the dog, calling it the tester.

All morning, black clouds had gathered above the village, and Grandmother Lakshmi kept glancing at the sky. She told her grandsons to bring in the cow, the hens and the washing from the line. The boys complained that it was only drizzling. Grandmother said nothing and kept hurrying. An hour later, the wind came with a roar, and the rain drove sideways across the yard. The boys, dry inside the cowshed, listened to the water hammering on the roof. One of them looked at the other and said that Grandmother always knew. The other nodded and said they should listen to her next time.

What will the boys probably do the next time Grandmother warns them about the weather?
They will probably listen and act quickly, because her warning proved right this time.

Arjun's family wakes before sunrise on the morning of Diwali. His mother draws a rangoli at the front door using coloured powder, while his aunt arranges small clay lamps in a row along the steps. Arjun is in charge of the marigold garland, which he hangs across the doorframe. His cousins arrive at eight with boxes of sweets, and soon the room is crowded with relatives. The children are given new clothes to wear, and the elders hand out small envelopes. Arjun's grandfather lights the first lamp at dusk and says a short prayer. Then everyone steps outside to watch the sky.

What was Arjun in charge of on Diwali morning?
He was in charge of the marigold garland, which he hung across the doorframe.

The tortoise in the Rao family's garden is older than anyone in the house. Grandfather says it was already there when he bought the place forty years ago. Children name it Raju, though nobody knows whether it is male. Raju spends the day under the hibiscus bush, moving a few steps every hour. When it rains, he comes out into the open and sits still with his neck stretched. Nobody has ever seen him hurry. Last week a visiting boy tried to race him with a toy car, but Raju only blinked. The boy gave up and sat beside him, watching the clouds.

Where does Raju spend the day?
He spends the day under the hibiscus bush.

When our neighbour moved away, she left her old parrot with us. It was a green bird with a grey beak and a loud voice. For several days, it sat silently in its cage and would not eat. My mother talked to it gently and kept the cage near the window. On the fifth day, the parrot called out a name: "Meera, Meera." The whole family went quiet. My mother turned and said that Meera had been our neighbour's name. She picked up the phone and rang her, holding the phone toward the cage. The parrot began to eat that evening.

Why did the parrot start eating after the phone call?
It probably heard Meera's voice on the phone, and hearing its old owner comforted it enough to eat.

Nobody in the house could help with Zara's science project. It was about how plants drink water, and the family only knew that plants needed rain. So Zara cut a celery stalk, set it in a glass of red-coloured water and left it on the sill. In the morning, the leaves had faint red lines. She showed everyone at breakfast, and her brother whistled in surprise. Her grandfather took a magnifying glass and examined the tiny tubes in the stalk. He murmured that in seventy years he had never seen that. Zara wrote his remark under the photo for her project.

Why did Zara's grandfather say he had never seen that in seventy years?
He had never done or seen such an experiment, so the red lines in the celery surprised him.

A narrow lane in Pune leads to the Kulkarni house, which has a blue gate and a mango tree just inside it. Every afternoon, Mrs. Kulkarni sits under the tree to shell peas into a steel basin. Her neighbour, Mrs. Iyer, often joins her with a cup of tea. They talk about prices at the vegetable market, about the school exams and about whose cow has strayed. When the children come home, they drop their bags on the veranda and take mangoes from the low branches. Mrs. Kulkarni pretends not to see. By five o'clock the basin is full, and the two women carry it inside together.

What does Mrs. Kulkarni shell under the mango tree?
She shells peas.

The Bose family's Saturday begins with the bed linen. Mrs. Bose takes the sheets off each bed and counts them, and Shruti carries the pile to the tub. Her younger brother Tuhin brings the pillow covers, which he drops on the way. The tub holds twelve litres of soapy water, which Shruti measures with a mug. She scrubs, wrings and rinses, and Tuhin hangs everything on a rope across the terrace. The sheets flap like sails. When they are dry, Mrs. Bose irons them while listening to old film songs on the radio, humming along.

What does Mrs. Bose listen to while she irons?
She listens to old film songs on the radio.

On the first day of every month, Uncle Jamal brings home a whole watermelon from the wholesale market. He carries it on his shoulder and sets it on the kitchen floor with a thump. Aunt Reema cuts it into thick, wide slices on a wooden board. The children stand nearby with their hands behind their backs. When the first slice is handed out, there is a rush for the black seeds. The children have a spitting contest on the balcony, and Uncle Jamal measures the distance with a tape. Last month's winner shot a seed across the full width of the balcony.

Where does Uncle Jamal buy the watermelon?
He buys it from the wholesale market.

Whenever Max's mother turned off the light, he heard something under the bed. She looked every night and found nothing, but he remained unconvinced. One evening, his father suggested a different approach. He gave Max a torch and asked him to be the detective. Max crawled to the edge of the bed, held the torch under it and bravely looked. There was a lone sock, a marble and a very surprised spider. Max stared at them for a while and then said, "That is not very scary." He put the sock in the laundry basket and went to sleep without another word.

Why was Max not afraid after he looked under the bed?
He saw that there were only ordinary things, a sock, a marble and a small spider, and nothing scary.

Karim's family has lived on the fifth floor for twelve years, and the lift had been broken for three weeks. Karim's grandmother, who has bad knees, stopped going down to the market. His mother started carrying the heavy shopping bags alone. Other neighbours complained at the building meeting, but the secretary only said he had no money. On the fourth Sunday, Karim knocked on every door in the building. He collected a small amount from each flat and brought the money to the secretary in an envelope. Within a week, a mechanic arrived, and the lift hummed. Karim's grandmother called it a miracle and made him sweet rice.

Why did Karim's grandmother make him sweet rice?
She was thankful, because his collecting money got the lift repaired and let her go out again.

The day before Pongal, the Subramanian family cleans the house from top to bottom. Old newspapers are tied into bundles, and broken things are taken to the repair shop. The next morning, Mrs. Subramanian lights a fire in the courtyard and sets a clay pot on three stones. She pours in fresh milk, and when it boils over, the family shouts, "Pongalo Pongal!" The children toss rice into the pot, and the smell of jaggery fills the lane. Then the pot is placed before the sun as an offering of thanks for the harvest.

What do the children toss into the pot?
They toss rice into the pot.

Nani lives in a small flat on the third floor, and every holiday Priya takes the train to stay with her. The first thing Nani does is open the old wooden trunk under her bed. Inside are photographs wrapped in cloth, a silver bracelet and a bundle of letters tied with string. Priya loves hearing about each item. The bracelet was a wedding gift, Nani says, and the letters were written by her brother when he worked far away. Priya always asks to hold the bracelet, and Nani lets her wear it for the whole evening. Then they cook khichdi together on the single gas burner.

Who wrote the letters in the trunk?
Nani's brother wrote them, when he worked far away.

For the festival of Baisakhi, the Sidhu family goes to the fields before sunrise. The wheat has turned golden, and the air is cool. Mr. Sidhu cuts the first sheaf with a sickle and holds it up to the sky. The children collect the stalks in their arms. Later, the family takes a bath, puts on new clothes and walks to the village fair. There are swings and wrestlers, and the smell of fried jalebis hangs over everything. Grandfather buys a balloon for every child and a turban for himself.

What does Mr. Sidhu cut first in the field?
He cuts the first sheaf of wheat.

Beena's goat, Gauri, escaped through the gate every morning and trotted straight to the neighbour's vegetable patch. Mr. Sheikh, the neighbour, grumbled and drove her out, but Gauri would return again. One day, Beena tied a long rope to Gauri's neck and walked her to the neighbour's door. She apologised and offered to pay for the cabbage that had been eaten. Mr. Sheikh laughed and said that the goat had better taste than his own children, who would not touch cabbage. From then on, he put a small bunch of greens at his gate every morning for Gauri.

How did Mr. Sheikh feel about the goat by the end?
He had become fond of the goat and no longer minded, because he began to leave greens for her.

The kitchen tap at the Fonseca house dripped all night, and nobody could sleep. At seven, Mr. Fonseca took out a wrench and a roll of white tape. His daughter Marta handed him each tool and read the instructions from a booklet. He turned the tap off at the wall, unscrewed the top and pulled out a worn rubber ring. Marta ran to the toolbox for a spare. When he fitted it and turned the water on again, the tap was silent. Marta clapped. Her father held up the old ring between two fingers and said that this tiny circle had cost them a night's sleep.

What did Mr. Fonseca take out of the tap?
He took out a worn rubber ring.

After the earthquake, the Singhal family spent six nights outside. The house stayed standing but had deep cracks along the walls, and the engineer told them to wait before going in. They slept on mats under a blue plastic sheet in the neighbour's yard. Little Rohan asked every morning whether it was time to go home. His father always answered "soon," in a steady voice, though his hands were not steady. On the seventh day, the engineer finally said the house was safe. Rohan ran inside first, touched every wall and then sat in the middle of his room. His father stood in the doorway with a wet face.

Why did Rohan's father have a wet face?
He was relieved and emotional that the family could finally return to their home safely.

The Hussain family had no choice but to cook by candlelight when the power went out on Saturday evening. Nadia's father found two candles in the kitchen drawer and stood them in steel bowls so they would not tip over. Nadia, who was ten, held the torch while her mother chopped onions. Her brother Imran was told to keep the little ones busy, so he invented a shadow game against the wall. Soon the whole house was full of laughing and the smell of frying onions. When the lights flickered back on at nine, nobody cheered. The children asked if they could eat dinner by candlelight again next week.

Why did the children not cheer when the lights came back on?
They had enjoyed the candlelit evening so much that they wanted to do it again.

When baby Noor turned one, her family held a small party on the roof. Her uncle brought a cake with a single candle, and her aunt hung paper streamers from the water tank. Noor wore a white frock with tiny embroidered flowers. As the guests sang, she sat on her father's lap, clapping her hands at the wrong moments. When the cake arrived, she grabbed a fistful of cream and smeared it across her own face and her father's shirt. Everyone laughed so hard that the neighbour looked up from the street below. Noor's mother took a photo, and it later became the first picture on the fridge.

What did Noor's aunt hang from the water tank?
She hung paper streamers.

Olivia and her twin brother Jack argued about everything: who sat by the car window, who got the larger slice, who went first on the swing. Their grandmother listened to the squabbles for a week. Then she announced that on Saturday, the twins would bake a cake together, with one oven, one bowl and one spoon. The twins looked at each other with suspicion. By noon, they had flour on their noses and were fighting over the whisk. But when the cake came out golden and tall, both stared at it, forgetting everything. They ate the first slice at the same moment, grinning.

What did the twins forget when the cake came out?
They forgot their quarrel, because they were both proud and delighted with what they had made together.

My grandfather makes tea in a way no one else does. He boils the water first, then adds the tea leaves and lets them swirl for exactly one minute. Only after that does he pour in the milk. He drops in two cardamom pods and a small piece of ginger, crushed with the back of a spoon. Then he strains the tea through a steel sieve that has a bent handle. Everyone in the house says his tea is the best, though he claims it is just the water. He pours it into small glasses and carries them to the veranda on a tray.

What does the grandfather add after the milk?
He adds two cardamom pods and a small piece of crushed ginger.

By afternoon, snow had covered the road to the Larsen farmhouse, and the school bus could not get through. Mrs. Larsen telephoned the school and learned that classes were closed for two days. The children cheered, but their father looked at the pile of snow outside and sighed. He took two shovels from the shed and handed one to each child. Their cheering stopped. They spent the whole afternoon digging a path from the door to the gate, their faces red, their breath white. In the evening, they sat by the fire with hot chocolate, too tired even to argue.

Why were the children too tired to argue?
They had spent the whole afternoon shovelling snow, so they were exhausted.

In the room where I study, there is an old wooden table with a drawer that sticks. The table belonged to my father's teacher, who left it to him when he retired. It has ink stains on the left corner and a small carving of a bird near the edge. I keep my books in a neat pile on the right side and my lamp on the left. In the evening, the light falls on the polished wood, and I like to run my finger over the bird. I have never found out who carved it.

Whose teacher once owned the wooden table?
It belonged to the narrator's father's teacher.

Mrs. Dsouza was learning to knit so she could make a blanket for her first grandchild. Her fingers were stiff, and the first rows came out crooked, with holes where she had dropped stitches. Her daughter-in-law offered to help, but Mrs. Dsouza refused. She unpicked the whole thing three times. By the fourth attempt, the rows were nearly straight. She worked each evening after supper, humming softly, with the wool basket at her feet. The baby was due in March, and she had until then. When the blanket was finished, it was a little uneven at one corner, and she said that was her signature.

How did Mrs. Dsouza handle her mistakes while knitting?
She did not give up, and she unpicked her work three times and tried again until the rows were nearly straight.

The Gill sisters, Jasleen and Gurleen, are twins, but nobody can mistake one for the other. Jasleen speaks loudly and wears bright colours. Gurleen is quiet and prefers grey and blue. At school, their teachers know who is who by the way they enter the room: Jasleen bursts in, and Gurleen slips in. They share a bedroom, and Gurleen's half is tidy, while Jasleen's is a scatter of clothes and books. Their father says they are two halves of one good person, and the twins pretend to be offended.

What colours does Gurleen prefer?
She prefers grey and blue.

Dr. Rao's daughter has just started saying her first words, and the whole family keeps a notebook of them. The first was "ba," which might mean ball or bottle. The second, last Tuesday, was "amma," and her mother cried a little. Then came "no," said very firmly, whenever somebody tried to feed her carrots. The grandfather swears that last weekend she said his name, though it sounded like "doo-doo." Her father wrote it down anyway. The notebook now has seven entries, and each is marked with the date and the room where it happened.

What was the baby's second word?
Her second word was "amma."

The Kapoor family moved into the new flat in the rain. The movers dripped across the floor, and the boxes were damp. In the evening, a woman from the flat next door knocked on the door. She carried a covered plate. She said that nobody wants to cook on moving day, so she had made a little something. Under the cloth were hot parathas and a bowl of pickle. Mrs. Kapoor felt tears rise. She had been dreading the first night in a strange place. She invited the woman in, even though there were no chairs yet, and they sat on a carton.

How did Mrs. Kapoor feel when the neighbour brought food?
She felt touched and relieved, because she had been dreading the first night and she nearly cried.

Mrs. Banerjee had put out her best cups for the guests from the city. They arrived with a car full of gifts, and spent the evening admiring the hand-woven curtains and the polished brass lamp. When Mrs. Banerjee mentioned that she had made the curtains herself, one guest said, without looking, that they were very nice for a village house. Mrs. Banerjee's smile stayed, but the teapot she was holding trembled slightly. After the guests left, she took down the curtains and folded them into the chest. Her daughter watched in silence and knew the curtains would not go up again.

Why did Mrs. Banerjee take down the curtains?
The guest's remark hurt her pride, so she no longer wanted to display them.

Every Wednesday Ben rode his bike to his grandfather's house to help him with the crossword. His grandfather read the clues aloud while Ben wrote the answers in tiny letters. They argued about spelling and sometimes about facts. Grandfather kept a dictionary on the arm of his chair and thumped it whenever Ben was wrong. One week, Ben found a word that stumped them both: a seven-letter word for "patience." They looked through the dictionary for an hour. Finally they found "stamina" and shouted at the same time. Then they discovered that it did not fit the grid, and they laughed until Grandfather had to wipe his glasses.

On which day did Ben visit his grandfather?
He visited every Wednesday.

In the corner of the rooftop, Mr. Shah keeps a row of old paint tins full of soil. Each tin holds a different plant: chillies, marigolds, curry leaves. His neighbour once asked why he did not buy proper pots. He replied that the tins drain well and cost nothing. He also said that a plant does not care how it looks, only whether it has sun and water. The neighbour went home thoughtful. Two weeks later, the Shahs saw a line of cut plastic bottles on the neighbour's terrace, each with a small green seedling poking out of the top.

Why did the neighbour set up plastic bottle planters?
The neighbour was convinced by Mr. Shah's words that a plant needs only sun and water, not fancy pots.

On Raksha Bandhan, Neel always wakes his sister Pooja by pulling the blanket off her face. She does not mind, because she knows what he is up to: he wants his rakhi early. Pooja ties the thread around his wrist after her morning bath and applies a red mark on his forehead. In return, he hands her a small gift. This year it was a pair of silver earrings, bought with money he had saved from his pocket allowance for four months. Pooja asked how he had kept the secret so long, and Neel said it was easy because she never looks inside his cupboard.

How long did Neel save to buy the earrings?
He saved for four months.

Two weeks after the Dhillons got a hamster, they discovered that it was nocturnal. It slept all day curled in a ball of shredded paper and spent the night running on its wheel. The squeaking was loud enough to wake everyone. Mr. Dhillon moved the cage into the bathroom, where the sound was muffled by tiles and a closed door. The hamster seemed to enjoy the change and ran even faster. In the morning, the children peeked in to find it asleep again, one paw sticking out of the paper. They whispered "good night" before going to school.

Where did Mr. Dhillon move the hamster's cage?
He moved it into the bathroom.

When Leila's baby sister was born, their father took a week off from work. At first, Leila enjoyed having him home, but she soon noticed that he held the baby more than he held her. At dinner, he fed the baby first, then himself, and left Leila's questions unanswered. On the fifth night, Leila crawled into his lap with her blanket and said nothing. Her father looked at her, closed his book and put his arm around her. He said that he was sorry for being so busy. The baby was asleep, and he had all the time in the world for her.

Why did Leila crawl onto her father's lap without a word?
She felt ignored since the baby came and wanted her father's attention and comfort.

The wind blew hard on the day of the kite festival, and the sky above the town turned bright with paper birds. On the Rajput family's terrace, Dev held the spool, while his uncle guided the string. The kites dipped and rose like fish. Whenever an opponent's kite was cut loose, the children shouted and ran to the edge of the roof to see where it landed. By evening, Dev's fingers were red from the thread, and his uncle's kite had cut down four others. They ate sesame sweets and watched the last kites fade into the dusk.

How many kites did Dev's uncle cut down?
His kite cut down four others.

Gauri's father worked on a farm and did not read or write. Each evening, as she wrote the day's homework, he sat nearby with his tea. One night she asked him a spelling, and, unembarrassed, he said that he did not know. She looked at the page, then at him, and said that they could learn it together. She took a new sheet and wrote the alphabet in big letters. Her father traced them with a rough finger. By the next week, he could write his own name, and he signed it on the tea-stall bill with a flourish.

How did Gauri's father likely feel when he signed his name?
He was proud and happy, as he could write his own name for the first time.

The Sandhu family grows chillies in recycled tin cans along the balcony wall. Each can has a hole punched in the bottom and a layer of small stones. The seeds go in about a finger deep, and the cans are watered in the evening. After three weeks, small green shoots appear. After two months, white flowers open, then thin green chillies, which turn red as they ripen. The children pick them and put them in a plate in the kitchen. Their grandmother uses them to make pickle and chutney.

How deep are the seeds planted?
They are planted about a finger deep.

Christmas morning at the D'Souza house begins with the smell of plum cake. Grandma bakes it a month early and feeds it with a spoonful of rum-free syrup each week. The cake sits in a tin on top of the cupboard, out of the children's reach. On the morning itself, Grandma takes it down and cuts thin, even slices with a very sharp knife. Each grandchild is allowed two slices, no more. After church, the family sits in the garden and eats in silence, because the cake is too good to interrupt with talk.

How long before Christmas does Grandma bake the cake?
She bakes it a month early.

The best part of a visit to my grandmother's is the breakfast. She soaks lentils the night before and wakes before dawn, so the batter is ready for dosa. A big iron griddle sits on the gas stove, and she spreads each dosa in a perfect circle with the back of a ladle. We eat them straight from the pan, hot and crisp at the edges, with coconut chutney and a spicy powder mixed with sesame oil. She will not eat until all of us have had three. After the third, she smiles and finally turns the heat down for her own.

How many dosas must everyone eat before the grandmother eats?
Everyone must have three.

We went to my aunt's house for the wedding, and the whole family travelled by bus. It was a long journey, with the last hour spent on a dusty road through fields. My grandmother sat by the window and told us the names of the villages we passed. At one stop, a boy climbed on selling cucumbers cut in four, sprinkled with salt and chilli. My father bought one for each of us, and we ate them quickly. By the time we reached the gate, the sun was setting, and the whole sky was orange.

How did the family travel to the wedding?
They travelled by bus.

The Mehra children share a bicycle, and they use a notebook to keep track of whose turn it is. On weekdays, Nikhil gets it in the morning for school and Tanvi gets it in the evening for tuition. On Saturdays, they ride together, with Tanvi on the seat and Nikhil standing on the pedals. On Sundays, the bicycle stays in the shed. Their father oils the chain and checks the tyres on that day, whistling an old film tune as he works. The notebook sits on a nail by the shed door with a pencil tied to it by a string.

When does Tanvi use the bicycle on weekdays?
She uses it in the evening for tuition.

The old clock in the Das family's hallway has stopped working so many times that nobody trusts it. It shows ten past four, whatever the hour is, because the batteries have long since died. Mr. Das keeps promising to replace it. However, his children like it the way it is. When they were small, they used the broken clock as an excuse for coming late to the table: it was always ten past four somewhere. This year, Mr. Das bought a new battery and fixed the clock. For two days it kept perfect time. On the third morning, his daughter quietly moved the hands back to ten past four.

What time does the old clock show when it is broken?
It shows ten past four.

Priya's mother planted a row of sunflower seeds along the fence in April. Every morning, Priya measured the tallest stalk with a ruler and wrote the number in a notebook. By June, it was taller than she was. Her little brother, Dev, kept asking when the flowers would open, and Priya kept telling him to wait. One morning in July, a single yellow bloom appeared, facing the sun. Dev ran into the house shouting. Their mother put down her cup of tea and walked out barefoot onto the wet grass. The three of them stood in a line, looking up in silence.

What did Priya write in her notebook every morning?
She wrote the height of the tallest sunflower stalk.

Grandpa Oleg always predicted the weather from his knee. When it began to ache, he said, rain was on its way. His grandchildren laughed at him and checked the forecast on the phone. One Saturday, the phone said it would be sunny all day. Grandpa rubbed his knee and said they should not go on the picnic. The children went anyway, with sandwiches and a kite. By two o'clock, black clouds covered the sky, and a downpour drove them under a tree. They walked home soaked, giggling, and found Grandpa at the door with towels and a smile that said nothing.

Why was Grandpa waiting at the door with towels?
He had expected the rain from his aching knee and knew the children would get wet.

The Gupta children take turns to set the breakfast table, and the chart says Tuesday belongs to Mohan. He puts out five steel plates, five glasses and a jug of water. Then he goes to the cupboard and counts the spoons. His mother says he is the only one who counts, and so the only one who always has the right number. This Tuesday, however, he found only four spoons. He searched the drawer, the sink and even the flower pot on the table. At last he spotted the missing spoon in his baby sister's hand, held tight, dripping with porridge.

Where did Mohan find the missing spoon?
He found it in his baby sister's hand.

Sunil always took the last piece of every dish, and his sister Sudha always complained. One evening, there was a single laddoo left on the plate, and both of them glanced at it. Neither moved. Sunil, who was about to grab it, suddenly remembered the way Sudha had cried the week before when her kite was torn. He pushed the plate toward her. She looked at him in surprise, took the laddoo and broke it in two. She handed him the bigger half. Then they both ate in silence, smiling to themselves.

What do Sudha's actions at the end show?
They show that she is generous and was touched by her brother's kindness, so she shared the laddoo with him.

Chen's grandfather never learned to read, but he could tell any story from memory. Every evening, Chen sat beside him on the porch and asked for the one about the fisherman and the moon. The old man always told it a little differently. Sometimes the moon was a silver coin, sometimes a pearl. Chen once pointed out that he had changed the story. His grandfather winked and said that a story is like a river, never the same twice. Chen thought about it for days. When he began to write his own stories at school, he made sure that each new draft was slightly different.

What does Chen's grandfather think about stories?
He thinks stories change over time, like a river that is never the same twice.

At eight-thirty each night, the Wong children brush their teeth and climb into their bunk beds. Mei, the older girl, takes the top bunk, and her brother Ling takes the bottom. Their father comes in with a glass of warm milk for each, and they must finish it before the story. Tonight, he read a chapter about a fox in a snowy forest. Ling asked what the fox ate, and Mei said it ate mice. Their father turned off the lamp at the end of the chapter and told them that the fox would wait until tomorrow.

Which bunk does Mei take?
She takes the top bunk.

At Mrs. Reyes's house, everyone had to fold their own laundry. Her son Mateo used to throw his clean clothes into the drawer in a heap. His mother said nothing, but one day she took the pile out and shook it. A bad smell rose from a shirt that had been put away damp. Mateo looked at her, startled. She quietly handed him the shirt and a bar of soap. Mateo washed it by hand, dried it in the sun and folded it carefully. Afterwards, he checked each garment before putting it away.

What lesson did Mateo learn?
He learned to look after his clothes carefully and put them away properly, because a damp shirt began to smell.

Every afternoon, Grandmother Parvati sits at the door of her small house with a bundle of rice and a wide wicker tray. She picks out the stones and husks by hand, a handful at a time, and drops them into a bowl. A group of neighbourhood children sits nearby and watches. She tells them a story as she works, always different, always with a clever animal in it. When the tray is clean, she pours the rice into a jar. The children then run off to play, and she sits quietly, her hands still moving, as though picking out something invisible.

What does Grandmother Parvati pick out of the rice?
She picks out stones and husks.

The wooden gate of our house creaked for years, and everyone had a theory about how to fix it. My father said it needed oil. My uncle said it needed new hinges. My sister thought it was fine as it was. One afternoon, our neighbour, a retired carpenter, came by with a small tin of grease. He lifted the gate slightly, ran his finger along the hinge and applied a small drop to each. Then he swung the gate three times and it did not make a sound. He wiped his finger on a cloth and went back to his house without a word.

What did the neighbour use to fix the gate?
He used a small tin of grease on the hinges.

After the baby cried for most of the night, the whole Verma family woke up grumpy. Mr. Verma drank his coffee without a word, and Mrs. Verma sat with her head in her hands. Their five-year-old daughter, Sia, studied the scene for a moment. Then she got a small blanket, placed it carefully around her baby brother and sang a made-up song. Within a few minutes he was asleep in the cot. Mr. Verma stared at his daughter, and Mrs. Verma's tired eyes became wet. Sia only said that she was good at singing and the baby liked it.

What will the parents probably think of Sia after this?
They will probably feel proud and grateful, because Sia calmed the baby when they were too tired to do it.

Behind the Bhatia house there is a small patch of land where the family grows spinach, fenugreek and radishes. Mr. Bhatia digs the soil each autumn with a heavy hoe. His wife scatters the seeds in straight rows and covers them with a thin layer of earth. After ten days, small green leaves peek out, and the children are sent to count them. Within a month, the first spinach is ready, and Mrs. Bhatia cuts the leaves with kitchen scissors. They eat it the same night with chapatis and a spoonful of ghee.

What does Mrs. Bhatia use to cut the spinach?
She uses kitchen scissors.

Samira's family had always lived in the same house, but now they were going to leave. The new job was in a different city, and her father had already found a flat. The packing boxes were piled along the corridor. Samira walked from room to room, touching things: the mark on the wall where she had measured her height every birthday, the loose tile in the bathroom. On the last evening, she took a pen and wrote her name and the date on the inside of the cupboard door. She closed the door gently and said it was so the next child would know someone had been there.

Why did Samira write her name inside the cupboard?
She wanted the next child to know someone had been there, because she was sad to leave the only house she had lived in.

At the back of the Pinto house is a small kitchen garden with four beds. The first bed holds tomatoes, the second beans, the third spinach and the fourth only marigolds, which Mrs. Pinto says keep the insects away. Her husband brings a bucket of used tea leaves from the kitchen each evening and spreads them on the soil. Their son Neil is in charge of the watering can, which has a loose handle. He has hung a ribbon on the fence to mark where the garden ends. Visitors always stop to admire the marigolds before going inside.

Which vegetable grows in the third bed?
Spinach grows in the third bed.

The monsoon arrived suddenly on Tuesday afternoon, and Ritu's grandmother ran onto the terrace to pull in the clothes. By the time Ritu joined her, the shirts and bedsheets were already damp. They carried the whole heap downstairs and hung it across strings in the living room. For three days nothing dried. The room smelled of wet cotton, and Ritu's father complained that he could not find a single dry sock. On the fourth morning, the sun came out for an hour. Ritu's grandmother, who had been watching the sky, clapped her hands and said they should hurry. Within minutes, every piece was back on the terrace line.

What did Ritu's grandmother do when the sun came out?
She told everyone to hurry and put all the clothes back on the terrace line.

The garbage truck comes to our lane at seven on Mondays and Thursdays, and it is my job to carry the bin down. The bin has no lid and smells awful in summer, so I wear a cloth over my nose. The driver, Mr. Pillay, always sings loudly, and children come out of their houses to watch. He lets them ring the bell on the truck once each. After he leaves, I sweep the spot where the bin stood and carry the empty one back. Then I wash my hands for a full minute with soap before I have breakfast.

On which days does the garbage truck come?
It comes on Mondays and Thursdays.

Rita's family ate at a restaurant for the first time in a year, to mark her brother's graduation. The menu was long and had many prices. Her father studied it for a very long time. Then he said that he was not hungry and ordered only tea. Her mother, after a glance at him, did the same. Rita's brother, who was the guest of honour, ordered a plate of rice and dal. They ate quietly. Afterwards, Rita noticed that her father handed over all the notes in his wallet and counted the change twice. On the way home, he bought her brother an ice cream from a cart.

Why did Rita's parents order only tea?
They were worried about the cost and wanted to save money so that the graduation meal would not be too expensive.

Every evening at five, the dining table of the Thomas family becomes a classroom. Mrs. Thomas clears the fruit bowl, and Joshua and Jessica take out their notebooks. Joshua, who is in sixth grade, studies social science. Jessica, who is in third, practices her handwriting in a thick copybook. Mrs. Thomas sits at the head of the table and corrects both while she sorts the tea leaves. At six, she serves milk and a biscuit each. Then the children are allowed to go out and play in the lane for exactly one hour.

Which grade is Joshua in?
He is in sixth grade.

When snow fell in the village for the first time in ten years, Katya's grandmother brought out an old pair of wool mittens. The children had never seen so much white. Katya and her cousins rushed into the yard and began rolling a huge ball for a snowman. Her grandfather watched from the window with a cup of hot tea. After an hour, the snowman had a carrot nose, two coal eyes and a red scarf borrowed from the clothesline. That evening the children sat by the stove with pink cheeks and wet socks. Katya's grandmother hung the mittens on the rack and said they had waited a long time for this.

What did the snowman have for a nose?
It had a carrot nose.

Pepper is a black-and-white dog who belongs to the Hadley family, and she has one job: to meet the school bus. At three-thirty, she trots to the end of the lane and sits beside the mailbox. When the bus doors open, she barks twice, once for each child. The girl, Poppy, always has a biscuit for her in her pocket. The boy, Finn, sometimes forgets. Pepper does not seem to mind. She walks between them all the way home, her tail swinging like a metronome, and waits by the gate until both are inside.

What does Pepper do when the bus doors open?
She barks twice, once for each child.

The train was late by four hours, and the family waited on the cold station platform in the dark. Mrs. Nair took out a flask of tea and a packet of biscuits and divided them carefully. The children were tired and cross, and the youngest began to cry. Mr. Nair put him on his shoulders and walked him up and down the platform, pointing out the lights and signals. After ten minutes, the child was silent and wide-eyed. When the train finally arrived at last with its great horn, the little boy waved at it as though it were an old friend.

Why did the little boy stop crying on the platform?
His father put him on his shoulders and showed him the lights and signals, which interested him.

A surprise visitor knocked on the door at nine at night: Mrs. Nambiar's old classmate, who had come to the city for a wedding. Mrs. Nambiar had not seen her in thirty years. She pulled her inside, still in her nightdress, and called out to her husband to make tea. The two women sat on the sofa and talked until midnight, their heads close together, sometimes laughing so hard that the children peeped out of their room. At one point the guest took out an old black-and-white photograph from her bag. It showed six girls in school uniforms on a flight of steps.

How long had it been since Mrs. Nambiar had seen her classmate?
It had been thirty years.

Rhea and her older brother Abhay had not spoken for two days after a fight over a broken pencil box. Their mother tried to make peace and failed. On the third morning, Abhay found his shoes tied and placed neatly by the door, which was Rhea's silent way of saying sorry. He looked at them for a moment, then took a pencil box from his drawer, an almost new one, and set it on her plate at breakfast. She looked up, he looked away, and their mother turned back to the stove to hide her smile.

What did the new pencil box and the tied shoes mean?
They were silent apologies, showing that each wanted to make up after the fight.

The evening the cyclone warning came, the Pillai family stuffed rags in the cracks around the windows and tied the shutters with rope. Mr. Pillai filled six buckets with water and moved the gas cylinder to the safest corner. Mrs. Pillai packed rice, lentils and a small stove in a bag, in case they had to leave. The children sat on the bed with a torch and a radio. At ten, the first gust shook the whole house. By midnight, the wind was howling, and branches struck the roof. At dawn, the sky cleared, and the family stepped out to find only broken branches in the yard.

What did Mr. Pillai do with the gas cylinder?
He moved it to the safest corner.

Everyone in Arun's family was told that the new neighbours were vegetarians, so when they were invited for dinner, Arun's mother carefully planned a vegetable menu. She made dal, two vegetable dishes and rice pudding. At the table, one guest looked at the chicken curry placed in the centre and went still. Arun's mother had made it for her husband and had forgotten to remove it. Without a word, she picked up the dish and carried it to the kitchen. She came back with a fresh smile and told the guests that dinner was served, and nobody mentioned the dish again.

How did Arun's mother likely feel when she noticed the chicken curry on the table?
She was embarrassed, and she quickly removed the dish to be polite to her guests.

Grandfather Hasan's hands shook now, and he often spilled his tea. He grew very careful and soon stopped drinking tea in front of visitors. His granddaughter Safiya noticed that he sat out of the room whenever the family had company. One evening she brought him a heavy, wide-based mug and filled it only half way. She said it was a new design that she had found in the shop, and she wanted to know what he thought. Her grandfather held it with both hands and took a slow sip. Then he walked to the living room and sat with the guests.

Why did Grandfather Hasan join the guests in the living room?
The steady mug let him drink without spilling, so he no longer felt embarrassed.

At Holi, Sameer's family gathers in the courtyard of their building. The children fill buckets with coloured water and hide behind the pillars. The adults pretend to be annoyed, but they always bring out their oldest clothes. Sameer's grandmother stays on the balcony with a plate of gujiya and a small bag of dry colour. When a child runs past, she dabs a pink mark on the cheek. By noon everyone is a rainbow of red, green and yellow, and nobody can tell who is who. The water tank in the courtyard is empty by two o'clock, and the building's caretaker sighs and starts to sweep.

Where does Sameer's grandmother stay during Holi?
She stays on the balcony.

Mira's father had never gone beyond sixth class, yet every evening he sat beside her while she did her sums. He could not read the textbook, but he watched her pencil and asked her to explain each step. Often, in the middle of explaining, she found her own mistake. She would cry out, "Oh, I see," and he would nod as though he had known all along. When her teacher asked how she had become so careful, Mira said that her father helped her every day. The teacher was surprised, and then she understood.

Why did Mira find her own mistakes while explaining to her father?
Explaining each step aloud made her think carefully, so she noticed where she went wrong.

Our cat, Mishti, has a habit that confuses everyone. Every evening around seven she sits by the front door and stares at the handle. If someone opens it, she walks out, looks up and down the corridor, and comes right back in. She does not want to go anywhere. My brother thinks she is waiting for the neighbour's dog, who used to bark at the lift each night. But the dog moved away in May. Mishti still waits, tail curled around her feet. Last night my mother put a bowl of milk beside the door, and Mishti drank it and finally went to sleep.

Why might Mishti sit by the door every evening?
Her brother thinks she is waiting for the neighbour's dog, which used to bark at the lift each night but moved away in May.

On cold evenings my father makes hot chocolate in a heavy steel pot. He heats the milk slowly and breaks a bar of dark chocolate into it, stirring with a wooden spoon. He does not allow anyone to rush him. When it is ready, he pours it into five mugs and adds a pinch of cinnamon to each. We sit around the table with blankets over our knees. My little sister always drinks hers too fast and burns her tongue. Dad hands her a glass of cold water without a word and returns to the stove.

What does the father add to each mug?
He adds a pinch of cinnamon.

Little Aarav, who was only seven months old, had just learned to crawl, and now the family could not keep track of him. On Saturday he disappeared from the living room for five minutes. His mother searched under the sofa, behind the curtains and inside the laundry basket. Finally she heard a tiny giggle from the kitchen. Aarav had crawled in, opened the low cupboard and pulled out every steel lid. He sat in the middle of the floor banging two of them together like cymbals. His mother laughed with relief and took a photo before gathering up the lids. Then she tied the cupboard shut with a cloth.

Where was Aarav found?
He was found in the kitchen, sitting on the floor with the steel lids.

Before leaving for his first day at the new school, Armaan stood at the kitchen door with his bag already on his back. His mother was frying eggs, and she did not turn around. She slid one onto a plate and said quietly that it was the last warm breakfast before the big day. Armaan did not sit. He picked up the plate, ate standing, and then went to the sink to wash it himself. His father, reading in the hall, saw him straighten his collar twice in the mirror. Nobody said anything about the new school at all.

How was Armaan probably feeling that morning?
He was nervous about the new school, shown by the way he stood with his bag on, ate standing and kept straightening his collar.

The first time Dev made tea for his grandmother, he used too much sugar and almost no milk. He carried it in on a tray with great care and stood nervously beside the bed. His grandmother took a sip, paused and took another. Then she said it was exactly how her mother used to make it, a very long time ago. Dev knew she was only being kind, because her face had twitched. But he saw that her eyes were a little wet. He sat on the bed and drank his own cup, which was terrible, and she held his hand the whole time.

What does Dev's grandmother's reaction show?
It shows that she was being kind and that the tea reminded her of her mother, even though it did not taste good.

Sanjana is the youngest of four sisters, and she wears clothes that were once everyone else's. Her blue skirt belonged to Divya, her red kurta to Pooja, her sandals to Rekha. She did not mind until her birthday, when her parents gave her a brand new yellow dress with white buttons. She wore it to school, and several classmates complimented her. In the evening, she showed it to her sisters. They examined the stitching and fussed over the hem, as if it were a treasure. Sanjana laughed and said she might let them borrow it, but only on special days.

Which sister once owned Sanjana's blue skirt?
Divya once owned it.

Hannah's family celebrates Christmas in a small apartment, so there is no room for a tall tree. Every December her father brings home a potted pine barely knee-high. Hannah and her two brothers decorate it with paper stars, silver thread and tiny buttons. Nobody minds the size. On Christmas Eve, they gather around it and each person opens one present, saving the rest for morning. This year, Hannah's youngest brother gave her a bookmark he had made himself, with her name written in wobbly letters. She said it was the best gift she had ever received, and she used it that very night.

Why did Hannah say the bookmark was the best gift?
She valued it because her brother made it himself and wrote her name on it with care.

Every Friday, the Chopra household has a big cleaning hour. Mr. Chopra takes the broom and sweeps all the rooms, while his wife wipes the shelves with a damp cloth. Their daughter Sneha dusts the fan blades, standing on a plastic stool, and their son Rishi waters the plants. When the work is finished, they pull the curtains aside to let the afternoon sun in. Then everyone gets a glass of cold buttermilk. Sneha says the best part is the moment the floor is wet and shining. She stays quiet and looks at the room as though it were new.

What job does Sneha do during the cleaning hour?
She dusts the fan blades.

Sheela's family eats rice at least once a day, and it is her job to wash it. She pours two cups into a steel bowl and rinses it three times until the water runs clear. Her mother says that rice washed well always cooks fluffy. Sheela then soaks the grains for ten minutes, while her mother chops onions. A pinch of salt and a few drops of oil go into the water. When the pot starts to bubble, Sheela sets a plate on top and lowers the flame. She has learned to wait without lifting the lid, though she often wants to peek.

How many times does Sheela rinse the rice?
She rinses it three times.

Karthik has an arrangement with his younger sister: he helps her with reading, and she helps him with drawing. Every day after school, they spread their books on the floor of the hallway. Karthik listens while she reads a page aloud, and corrects her pronunciation of long words. Then she sits beside him and shows him how to shade a ball so it looks round. Last week, he drew an apple that his art teacher pinned on the class board. Karthik says he did it because of the lessons in the hallway.

What does Karthik's sister teach him?
She teaches him drawing, such as shading a ball so that it looks round.

The Joshi family has a rule that phones go into a basket during dinner. At first, sixteen-year-old Ketan complained loudly. He said he might miss important messages. His mother replied that the world had managed without them for a very long time. After a week, Ketan stopped arguing. He found that dinner was actually interesting. His sister told stories about her school trip, and his father described a funny customer. Last night, when the basket was passed round, Ketan put his phone in first and told everyone about a film he had watched. His parents exchanged a quick glance and said nothing, but they were smiling.

What did Ketan do last night when the basket was passed?
He put his phone in first and told everyone about a film he had watched.

In our town, the first rain of the year is always celebrated. Children run out of their houses without their slippers and jump in the puddles. My grandmother sits on the veranda with a plate of hot pakoras, watching them with half-closed eyes. My father holds out a bucket to catch the water for the plants. My mother turns on the radio to listen to the songs about monsoons. The smell of wet earth rises everywhere, and the sky turns a deep shade of grey. After half an hour, the shower thins, and the children go in for towels.

What do the children run out without?
They run out without their slippers.

Grandpa Walt used to be a carpenter, and his workshop in the backyard still smells of sawdust. When his granddaughter Lucy visits, he lets her choose a piece of scrap wood and hands her a small sanding block. She rubs it patiently until it is smooth as glass. Then he drills a tiny hole and threads a string through it, and it becomes a pendant. Lucy has made six so far, and each is a different shape. She keeps them in a tin on her shelf. Grandpa Walt says that when she has twelve, he will teach her to use the saw.

How many pendants has Lucy made so far?
She has made six pendants.

Pablo's grandmother lives in a village two hours from the city, and on the first Saturday of every month, the family goes to see her. Pablo's father hires an auto that smells of petrol and old seats. The road is bumpy, and the children hold on to the rail. At the village, they get down at the banyan tree and walk the rest of the way. Grandmother waits at the gate with a plate of sliced papaya. She has been waiting since morning. She says she can tell the time by her stomach, and that today it told her to wait at the gate.

How far is the village from the city?
It is two hours away.

In the Das family, the evening snack is always muri with sliced onion, green chilli and a splash of mustard oil. Mrs. Das mixes it in a steel bowl with her bare hands, because she says a spoon cannot reach the corners. The children are allowed one handful each, then another if they finish their homework. Mr. Das comes home at six, takes his bowl on the veranda and listens to the radio. On rainy days, Mrs. Das also makes onion fritters. The smell spreads down the lane, and sometimes the neighbour's children appear at the gate, politely pretending to be passing by.

What does Mrs. Das use to mix the muri?
She uses her bare hands.

Usha's older brother was supposed to check her essay, but he was busy with a video game. She stood at his shoulder for several minutes. He said, without looking up, that it was probably fine. Usha went back to her desk, read the essay aloud twice and found three mistakes on her own. She fixed them, copied the essay neatly and put it in her bag. The next day, the teacher gave her full marks. When her brother asked how she had done, she said "Fine," exactly as he had said it, and went off to the kitchen.

Why did Usha answer "Fine" in the same way her brother had?
She was gently teasing him, since he had not helped her and she had done well without him.

Mrs. Williams hands out cleaning jobs on a chart stuck to the fridge. Every child has a coloured magnet. The red one means kitchen duty, the blue one is for the garden and the green one is for the bathroom. At the end of each week, the magnets are moved one column to the right, so nobody keeps the same job for long. Seven-year-old Tim dislikes the green magnet, but he does not complain because his older brother has also taken a turn. The chart has worked for three years, and Mrs. Williams says it has saved her many arguments.

What does the blue magnet mean on the chart?
The blue magnet means garden duty.

For the Lantern Festival, Mr. Liu brings home a red paper lantern shaped like a rabbit. His daughter Mei writes a wish on a strip of paper and ties it to the handle. Her mother cooks sweet rice dumplings in a clay pot, and the family eats them while the lantern hangs outside the window. After supper, they walk to the park, where hundreds of lanterns have been hung on trees. Mei holds her father's hand and tilts her head back to look. She says it looks as though the stars have come down for a visit.

What shape is Mr. Liu's lantern?
It is shaped like a rabbit.

Old Mr. Banerjee had grown tomatoes on his balcony for twenty years. This summer, his granddaughter Tara came to stay and asked if she could water the plants for him. He agreed but warned her that tomato plants dislike too much water. Tara poured a full can on each pot every morning anyway, because she wanted the plants to grow fast. After a week the leaves turned yellow and began to droop. Mr. Banerjee did not scold her. He showed her how to push a finger into the soil to check if it felt dry before watering. The next week, Tara checked every pot first.

What will Tara probably do the next time she waters the plants?
She will probably check the soil with her finger first, because her grandfather taught her that and she did it the next week.

My father's brother, Uncle Raghu, drives a truck between Chennai and Delhi, and he visits us only twice a year. When he does, he brings a trunk full of presents from different cities: pickles from Andhra, bangles from Hyderabad, a wooden toy from Nagpur. He sleeps for the whole of the first day. On the second, he takes all the children to the fair in his dusty truck and lets them sound the horn. He leaves on the fourth morning, before dawn, and we find a small envelope of money under each child's pillow.

How often does Uncle Raghu visit the family?
He visits only twice a year.

Mrs. Okonkwo's yard was a small patch of cracked soil, and people said nothing would grow in it. She did not argue. Each morning, she carried compost from the kitchen scraps and spread it by hand, bit by bit. She planted spinach, chillies and a few stalks of maize in neat rows. By the rainy season, green leaves covered the whole patch. Her neighbours, who had laughed at first, came to the fence and asked what her secret was. She answered that the soil was not bad; it was only hungry. The next spring, three other yards on the street had little vegetable plots.

What does the change on the street show?
It shows that Mrs. Okonkwo's success inspired the neighbours, who copied her and started their own gardens.

When their mother was away, Nisha was in charge of the house, and she took the role very seriously. She woke her brother, packed his lunch and made sure he brushed his teeth. He grumbled that she was not the boss. In the evening, Nisha burned the rice. She stood at the stove, looking at the black pot, and her eyes filled with tears. Her brother looked at her for a moment and then ordered a plate of noodles from the stall at the corner with his own pocket money. He set it on the table and said, "Don't worry, I'll never tell Mum."

What does the brother's action show about him?
It shows that he is kind and loyal, since he used his own money to help his sister after he had grumbled.

At the Singh house, nobody is allowed to start eating until the oldest person has taken the first bite. Hardeep's great-grandmother is ninety-one, and she often takes a very long time to decide which dish to begin with. The children sit with their hands in their laps, trying not to stare at the hot rotis. Last Sunday, a visiting cousin reached for the butter, and Hardeep kicked him gently under the table. His great-grandmother saw this and laughed so hard that she coughed. She finally picked up a roti, folded it and said, "Now you may all begin." The children cheered quietly.

Who must take the first bite before the others eat?
The oldest person at the table, Hardeep's great-grandmother, must take the first bite.

For two years, Harpreet's family lived in a one-room flat in the city. They cooked, ate and slept in the same space. His mother hung a curtain to divide the room at night. There was no table, so Harpreet did his homework on a tray over his knees. He did not complain, but he often looked at the pictures of houses in magazines. The day his father signed the papers for a two-room flat, Harpreet walked slowly through the empty rooms and stopped at the small window in the second. He pressed his forehead against the glass and said, "This will be mine."

What does the way Harpreet walks through the new flat show?
It shows he is happy and moved about finally getting a space of his own.

When the monsoon ends, we put away the raincoats and umbrellas. My mother wipes each umbrella with a dry cloth and folds it tight. My father brings a stool and puts the umbrellas on the top shelf of the storeroom. The raincoats are washed first, with detergent and a soft brush, then dried in the sun for two days. My brother and I have to roll them up and put them in a plastic bag. Mother says that if they are put away wet, they will smell for the entire year.

Where does father put the umbrellas?
He puts them on the top shelf of the storeroom.

Our neighbours hold a small party in the compound on the last day of Navratri. The women wear their best silk saris, and the children are dressed as little gods and goddesses. A long table stands in the middle, covered with plates of sweets. Someone brings a tape player, and the garba begins. The circle grows wider and wider as more people join in. My grandmother sits on a chair at the edge and taps her foot to the rhythm. Near eleven, the music stops, and everyone sits on the ground to eat.

Where does the neighbours' party take place?
It takes place in the compound.

The house I grew up in had a red door and a tin roof that rang when it rained. There were three rooms in a row, and a kitchen at the end with a stone floor. At the back was a well with a rope and a bucket, and my mother drew water every morning before the sun was fully up. In the front, a mango tree cast shade over a rope cot where my father took his afternoon nap. I remember the smell of wet earth after the first rain, and the taste of cold water from the well on summer days.

What colour was the door of the house?
The door was red.

Every year, the Mukherjee family sets up the idol for Durga Puja in the lane outside the house. This year, the committee had less money, and the pandal was small and plain. Young Mitali was disappointed. She stared at the bare bamboo and said it was not like last year. Her grandfather asked her to help hang the lights. Together they wove tiny paper flowers into a long string and looped it across the roof. When the lamps were switched on that night, the pandal glowed, and strangers stopped to take pictures. Mitali stood below it, hands on her hips, and said it looked even better than before.

Why did Mitali change her mind about the pandal?
Her own paper flowers and the lights made it glow and look beautiful, so she took pride in it.

Ravi's grandmother told the same bedtime story every night: the one about the lion who lost his roar. Ravi knew it by heart and could correct her if she skipped a word. One night, she was so tired that she dozed off in the middle of a sentence, right where the lion was walking to the river. Ravi waited. Then, in a very soft voice, he finished the story himself, whispering the last lines into the dark. He pulled the quilt over his grandmother's feet, turned off the lamp and tiptoed to his own bed.

What does Ravi's action show about his feelings for his grandmother?
It shows that he cares for her and is considerate, because he finished the story quietly and covered her feet.

The Hoang family had to share one bathroom among seven people, so mornings were a battle. They solved it with a schedule written on a whiteboard hung on the door. Grandfather went first at five, then Father, then Mother, and the three children after that, in order of age. The youngest, Bao, complained that he was always last and often late for school. One day, his sister Linh quietly erased her own time slot and wrote Bao's name in its place. She said nothing about it and took the last slot herself. Bao arrived at school on time for the first time all week.

What does Linh's action show about her?
It shows she is kind and generous, because she gave up her time slot so her brother would not be late.

The Kimura family's cat, Mochi, was very old and slept most of the day. When the youngest son Sota began to get ready for school each morning, Mochi would follow him from room to room and sit by the door. Sota's mother thought the cat just wanted to be fed. But on the first day of the holidays, when Sota stayed in bed, Mochi curled up on his blanket and purred. He did not eat until Sota did. The family realised the cat did not want food at all. She simply wanted to be near the boy she loved.

What did the family finally understand about Mochi?
They understood that Mochi followed Sota because she loved him and wanted his company, not food.

We were short of rice that day, so Mother made upma from semolina. She roasted the grains in a dry pan until they smelled nutty, set them aside and fried mustard seeds, onion and a green chilli in oil. Then she poured in hot water and the roasted grains and stirred until the mixture thickened. A squeeze of lime finished it off. We ate it from small bowls with a spoonful of coconut chutney. Father said that he rarely eats upma at home, though he enjoyed it that morning. I had two helpings and was sleepy for the rest of the afternoon.

What did Mother squeeze on the upma at the end?
She squeezed lime on it.

Soon after the new baby came home, Ishaan started behaving strangely. He stopped finishing his dinner and followed his mother everywhere, even into the bathroom corridor. When his grandmother asked him to help fold the baby's tiny socks, he threw them on the floor and ran to his room. That night his father sat beside him on the bed. He said that all the visitors had been bringing gifts for the baby and nobody had asked Ishaan how he was. Ishaan's eyes filled with tears. His father promised that the two of them would go for ice cream on Sunday, just them.

Why did Ishaan act strangely after the baby came home?
He felt left out, because the visitors paid attention only to the baby and nobody asked how he was.

The new baby, Dara, did not like her bath. She screamed whenever the water touched her feet, and her mother had to hold her tightly. Her father wondered if the water was too hot or too cold and checked it with his elbow, again and again. One evening, the grandmother brought a small yellow rubber duck and floated it on the surface. Dara stopped screaming at once and stared at it. When it bobbed, she gurgled. After that, bath time was easier, and Dara splashed with both hands, trying to catch the duck.

Why did Dara stop screaming in the bath?
The floating yellow duck caught her attention and distracted her from the water.

Last winter the roof of the Joseph family's kitchen began to leak. Mr. Joseph climbed up with a bucket of tar and a sheet of tin. His son Eldho held the ladder at the bottom and passed up the tools in a basket tied to a rope. It took them most of the afternoon to cover the gap. Mrs. Joseph watched from the courtyard with her hand over her eyes, calling out warnings. When the work was done, Mr. Joseph slid down the ladder carefully, wiped his hands on a rag and asked for tea. The next rain left the kitchen dry.

What did Mr. Joseph use to cover the gap in the roof?
He used tar and a sheet of tin.

Whenever Sofia visited her grandmother in Lisbon, they baked custard tarts together. Her grandmother never used a recipe, only her hands and her memory. She would say, "A little more butter," and then, "No, that is too much." Sofia tried to write down the measurements, but they kept changing. After three visits, her notebook was a mess of crossed-out numbers. Then her grandmother took Sofia's hands in her own and pressed them into the dough. "Feel it," she said. Sofia closed her eyes. Back home that winter, she made the tarts without any notebook, and they tasted just like her grandmother's.

What did Sofia learn from her grandmother about baking?
She learned to judge by feel and practice rather than exact measurements, because she made the tarts correctly without her notebook.

Every Tuesday and Friday, Grandfather Karim goes to the market with a cloth bag and a list in his shirt pocket. He knows every vendor by name and bargains with a stern face that fools nobody. The vegetable woman gives him an extra bunch of coriander, and the fishmonger saves him the freshest pieces. On the way back, he stops at the tea shop for a glass of sweet chai and a biscuit. His grandson Ali sometimes joins him and carries the bag. Grandfather always insists on paying for Ali's biscuit and tells him not to mention it at home.

On which days does Grandfather Karim go to the market?
He goes on Tuesdays and Fridays.

When the lock on the cupboard jammed, nobody could open it, and the school uniforms were inside. It was seven in the morning. Mr. Fernandes tried pushing, then pulling, then kicking. His wife suggested calling the locksmith. His daughter Anita calmly slid a thin ruler into the gap near the lock and pressed gently downward. The door clicked open. Her father stood with his mouth slightly open. Anita put the ruler back in her pencil box and picked up her uniform. She said that she had seen it on a video, and walked off to school.

How did Mr. Fernandes feel when the door clicked open?
He felt surprised, and perhaps embarrassed, because his daughter solved the problem with a ruler after he had failed.

Mr. Thomas had lived alone since his wife died, and his grandchildren worried about him. They began calling in the evenings, taking turns. At first he answered shortly: "Yes, I have eaten. Yes, I am fine." Over time, the calls grew longer. He told them about the sparrow that nested in the balcony pot and about the new vegetable seller at the corner. One evening, twelve-year-old Anna rang and found the line busy. She tried again and again. Finally her grandfather answered, a little out of breath. He explained that he had been calling his old friend Jacob, whom he had not spoken to in years.

What does Mr. Thomas's call to Jacob suggest about how he is feeling?
It suggests he is less lonely and is reaching out to people again, after his grandchildren's calls helped him.

In Kerala, Onam is celebrated with a large flower carpet at the doorstep. Biju's family begins gathering petals nine days before the festival. His mother picks yellow ones from the garden, and his sister buys red and white ones from the market. On the last morning, Biju kneels to arrange them in circles, from the middle outward. His grandfather corrects the pattern whenever a petal is out of place. By noon, a lovely round carpet fills the entrance. Biju's grandfather stands back, nods and says it is the best one the family has ever made. Biju hides his grin behind his hand.

How did Biju feel about his grandfather's praise?
He felt proud and pleased, because he hid his grin behind his hand.

After the move, Nina's bedroom felt too big and too quiet. Her old room had been tiny, with a window that looked straight into a neighbour's kitchen, and she had always heard cutlery clinking and radios playing. Now she heard only the fridge humming down the hall. For the first week she slept with the light on. Her mother noticed and bought a small night lamp shaped like a moon. She also hung Nina's drawings along the wall above the bed. On the eighth night, Nina switched the lamp off herself. She said the drawings made the room feel like hers, and in the morning she asked if she could paint one wall yellow.

Why did Nina feel better in her new room after a few days?
Her mother gave her a night lamp and hung up her drawings, which made the room feel like her own.

Sunita's family drives to her uncle's village every winter. The road takes five hours, and they always stop at the same tea stall halfway. Her father buys four cups of tea and a packet of biscuits, and the owner, an old man with a white moustache, remembers every child's name. This year Sunita brought a sketchbook and drew the stall, the old man and the dog sleeping beneath the bench. When she showed him the picture, he held it for a long time. Then he asked if he might keep it. Sunita tore the page out carefully and handed it over. He pinned it above his counter.

What did Sunita draw at the tea stall?
She drew the stall, the old man and the dog sleeping under the bench.

My uncle's roof garden has a line of tomato plants in plastic buckets, and last year he put a net over them to keep the crows away. The crows sat on the water tank and watched the plants for days. One morning, a crow got in through a small gap at the corner and pecked at a red tomato. My uncle chased it away, waving a towel. The next day, he tied three old compact discs on strings above the plants. They shimmered in the sun and spun in the wind. The crows stayed on the tank, and uncle sat with his tea, looking pleased.

Why did the uncle tie the shiny discs above the plants?
He hoped that the flashing, spinning discs would scare the crows away from the tomatoes.

Felix wanted to grow a pumpkin big enough to win the school contest, so he put a single seed in a pot on the sunny balcony. He watered it, talked to it and checked it twice a day. Within two weeks, a green shoot appeared, but it stayed very small for a long time. Felix grew impatient and moved the pot to a different corner every day, hoping to find a better spot. By the third week, the shoot had stopped growing. His grandmother put it back on the sunny side and told him plants hate to be moved. Felix wrote the rule in his notebook and underlined it twice.

Why had the shoot stopped growing?
Felix kept moving the pot to a different corner, and plants do not do well when they are moved.

Mr. Wilson's parrot knows exactly three phrases: "Good morning," "Where are my keys?" and a loud laugh. Last week, Mr. Wilson's mother-in-law came to stay for the first time. The parrot greeted her cheerfully each morning, but at dinner, whenever she spoke, it let out the laugh. She went quiet and stared at her plate. Mr. Wilson hurried to cover the cage with a cloth, whispering that the bird did not mean anything by it. His wife covered her mouth to hide a grin. Later, even the mother-in-law was chuckling, and she asked if the parrot would learn her name.

How did the mother-in-law feel at first when the parrot laughed?
She felt uncomfortable and offended, because she went quiet and stared at her plate.

When baby Henry started teething, he cried at night and refused his food. His father, a night-shift worker, came home each morning exhausted but still offered to hold him. Henry's mother told him to go to bed, but he shook his head and walked the baby up and down the hall. After a week, he fell asleep standing against the wall with Henry in his arms. His wife took the baby gently and laid a blanket over him. Then she sat down in a chair and watched the two of them, her eyes soft.

Why did Henry's mother cover his father with a blanket?
She was grateful and caring, because he had exhausted himself looking after the baby.

The Bhargava sisters, Neha and Tara, run a small shop in their garage every summer. They sell lemonade for two rupees a glass and badges they have made out of cardboard. Neha handles the money, and Tara pours. A wooden sign hangs on a nail, painted in red letters. Customers are mostly the children from the lane and the occasional curious uncle. At the end of the week, the sisters count the coins and spend half of them on ice cream. The rest goes into a tin labelled "Next Summer."

Who handles the money in the sisters' shop?
Neha handles the money.

For Lohri, the neighbours of the Bedi family build a bonfire in the lane. Children carry sticks, and the women bring peanuts, sesame sweets and popcorn. Mr. Bedi's young nephew, Armaan, was nervous because he had never stood so close to a fire. His uncle took his hand and walked him to the edge of the circle, explaining how to throw popcorn into the flames. The heat warmed Armaan's face. After a moment, he threw a handful, and the kernels crackled. Then he turned and asked, in a loud voice, whether he could throw the next one too.

What does Armaan's loud question at the end show?
It shows he lost his fear and became confident and excited.

Saturday is laundry day at the Abraham house. Mrs. Abraham fills two big buckets with soapy water and sorts the clothes into whites and colours. Her son Joel brings the shirts from the bedroom, while her daughter Ruth carries the towels. They scrub the collars on a flat stone and wring each piece with both hands. The water in the first bucket turns grey by noon. Then they rinse everything three times and hang it across the terrace line. Mrs. Abraham says that the sun does the final washing. By evening, the terrace is a line of flapping colour, and the whole family has aching arms.

Into which two groups does Mrs. Abraham sort the clothes?
She sorts them into whites and colours.

A rainbow appeared over the hill town of Kodaikanal at five in the afternoon, just after a short shower. The arch stretched from the pine forest on one side to the lake on the other. Children ran out of their homes, pointing and shouting. A photographer standing at the viewpoint took several pictures, and a group of tourists applauded. An old shopkeeper stood in his doorway, watching with folded arms, and told a small girl that the rainbow has seven colours: violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange and red. She counted them out loud on her fingers as the colours slowly faded.

How many colours did the shopkeeper say a rainbow has?
He said it has seven colours.

The old farmer, Mr. Mwangi, always threw a handful of the first harvest into the field before he cut a single stalk. His grandson Joseph asked him one day whether it was a waste. Mr. Mwangi said it was a way of saying thank you to the land. Joseph laughed, but when he took over the farm after his grandfather's death, he found himself standing at the edge of the field with a handful of the new millet in his palm. He hesitated, felt the grain between his fingers, and tossed it gently into the soil. Then, without a word, he lifted the sickle and began to cut.

What does Joseph's action show about how he felt about his grandfather's habit?
It shows he had come to respect the tradition and wanted to honour his grandfather, because he tossed the first millet into the soil just as his grandfather used to.

When the sun finally came out after a week of rain, the children of Jorhat ran out into the street, shouting. Their mothers rushed to hang out every bit of washing they owned. The vegetable seller took the tarpaulin off his cart and spread out his bright produce. The cats came out from under the porches and sat in the warm patches on the steps.
