Even the old man who usually sat by the window with a stern face went out and stood with his face turned up, eyes closed. Someone started a song, and soon half the lane had joined in.

Why was everyone in such a good mood?
The sun had come out after a week of rain, and people were glad to have dry, bright weather again.

One morning in the village of Hosur, Reshma saw hundreds of butterflies sitting on a wet patch of ground by the stream. They had folded wings, which showed a plain brown colour, but when one flew up, the sunlit wings were bright orange. Reshma waited and watched. She noticed that the butterflies were not drinking water; they seemed to be sipping the damp mud. She asked her teacher, who explained that the butterflies were gathering salts from the soil, which they needed. Reshma wrote it down and decided to study butterflies more closely. The next Saturday, she brought a small notebook and a magnifying glass.

What does Reshma's decision to bring a notebook and magnifying glass show?
It shows that she became very curious and wanted to study butterflies carefully.

The ferry man in the town of Pandharpur is known by everyone as Kaka. He is almost eighty, but he still rows the boat across the river twice a day, once in the morning and once in the evening. His boat is painted bright blue and has a small bell at the front, which he rings as he leaves each bank. Passengers pay what they can, and children travel free. He keeps a spare pair of spectacles, a tin of snuff and a cloth bag of peppermints under the seat. Every child who crosses is offered a peppermint, and the line to the boat is always longest on Saturdays.

What does Kaka offer every child who crosses?
He offers every child a peppermint.

Nadia's village had a custom: whoever caught the first fish of the season would share it with a neighbour. This year, Nadia's brother Sameer caught a large silver fish. He proudly carried it home and showed it to his mother, and she began to scale it for dinner. Then the old man from next door, who had a broken hip, stopped by with his stick. Sameer looked at the fish, then at the man. Without a word, he took a banana leaf, wrapped half the fish and handed it over. The old man's eyes crinkled, and he said he had not eaten fresh fish in months.

Why did Sameer give half the fish to the old man?
Because it was the village custom to share the first fish, and the old man next door had a broken hip and walked with a stick.

The village well of Kherwadi had always been shared by two communities, but a dispute over who could use it first had left them unwilling to speak. For months, the women of each side fetched water at different times. One scorching May day, the well-rope snapped, and the bucket fell deep. Neither group could reach it alone. Sulochana, the oldest woman from one side, looked at the faces on the other side, and then called out for help. Within minutes, women from both communities were lowering a long pole with a hook, taking turns, until the bucket came up. They all burst out laughing, then argued about whose turn it was to fetch water.

What changed between the two communities that day?
They had to work together to recover the bucket, and began speaking and laughing together again.

On the longest day of the year, the town of Tromso in Norway sees the sun for twenty-four hours. It never sets. People sleep with heavy curtains drawn, and children play football in the street at midnight. Shops stay open late, and cafes put chairs outside. In the winter the opposite happens: the sun does not rise for two months, and the town is lit by lamps and by the green curtains of the northern lights. Tourists come in both seasons to see something different. The locals, used to the changes, say you learn to rest when your body asks, not when the clock says.

How long does the sun stay visible on the longest day?
It stays visible for twenty-four hours.

Last Sunday, Karan's family went for a walk in the forest near Dehradun. They started at seven in the morning, carrying water bottles, a few bananas and a small first-aid box. A narrow trail led through tall sal trees and over two wooden bridges. Karan spotted a deer drinking at a stream, and his little sister Tanvi found a feather as long as her arm. At the top of a small hill, they sat on a rock and ate the bananas. The walk took about three hours, and they were back at the car by ten, tired but very happy.

What did Tanvi find on the trail?
She found a feather as long as her arm.

Mr. Verghese had the habit of tapping the barometer in his hall every morning. For months it showed the same steady line, and his children teased him for checking something that never changed. One August morning, when he tapped the glass, the needle dropped sharply. He stood very still for a moment, then walked through the house, closing all the windows and tying down the shutters. He asked his wife to fill the water buckets and charge all the torches. By the afternoon, the sky was black, and a powerful gale struck the village. When it was over, the children looked at their father and said nothing at all about the barometer ever again.

Why did the children stop teasing their father?
The barometer had correctly warned of the storm, proving it was useful.

An old stone well in the garden of Mrs. Perera has become a home for frogs. Each evening after rain, their croaking rises from it in a loud chorus. The frogs are small and green, and they hide under the damp stones during the day. Mrs. Perera's grandson Dilan once counted seventeen of them in a single evening. He keeps a notebook where he lists dates, the number of frogs and the weather. His grandmother says he should become a scientist, but Dilan only shrugs and says he would rather work at a zoo.

How many frogs did Dilan count one evening?
He counted seventeen.

The captain of the village football team, Emeka, looked at the weather forecast on his phone and frowned. Saturday's final would be played on a field that had been soaked all week. At practice on Thursday, he told the team to wear their old boots and to forget about fancy passing. "Keep it simple, pass short, and stay on your feet," he said. During the match, the ball skidded through puddles, and the other team, who tried long kicks, kept losing it in the mud. Emeka's players kept the ball low and scored twice before half-time. The cup went to Emeka's team for the first time in six years.

Why did Emeka's team win?
They changed their style to suit the wet pitch, keeping passes short and low, while the other team lost the ball in mud.

Every Friday afternoon, the women of the village of Kaladi gather in the courtyard of the community hall to weave baskets. They use dried palm leaves that have been soaked overnight to make them soft. Jaya, the oldest of the weavers, teaches the younger ones how to braid the edges so the basket will not come undone. They talk about their children, recipes and the price of rice while their fingers move quickly. A van collects the finished baskets once a month and takes them to a shop in the town. The money is shared equally among all the women, and Jaya keeps the accounts in a green notebook.

On which day of the week do the women gather to weave?
They gather on Fridays, in the afternoon.

The kitten appeared in the farmyard one rainy night and has not left since. It is small, grey and thin, with big green eyes. Joseph's mother said they could not keep another animal, because the farm was already full of dogs and hens. But every evening, a small saucer of milk appeared beside the kitchen door, and somebody had left a folded sack in the corner of the shed. Nobody admitted putting them there, and the kitten grew rounder by the week. When Joseph's mother found the sack, she looked at her husband and at the children, and sighed. Then she put a second saucer next to the first.

What can we guess about Joseph's mother at the end?
She has decided to let the kitten stay and care for it, because she put a second saucer of milk next to the first.

At the village meeting in Pipli, the headman asked for volunteers to look after the new community garden. No one spoke. The hall was silent, and people looked at their feet. Then a small voice from the back said, "I will." Everyone turned to see Anita, a nine-year-old girl who had come with her father. The headman smiled kindly and asked if she was sure. She nodded firmly. Her father, who had been staring at the floor, cleared his throat and said he would help her. Then another woman stood up, and then two men. By the end of the meeting, a rota of twelve names was written on the board.

What does this passage suggest about Anita's courage?
It shows her courage inspired others: after she said 'I will', her father, a woman and two men also volunteered.

For the whole of January, the town of Leh lay under a deep layer of snow. The pipes froze, so the women melted snow on stoves to cook and wash. The school stayed shut, and the children learned their lessons sitting around the kitchen stove while a grandfather read aloud from a worn book. When February came, the sun grew stronger, and at noon, drops of water began to fall from the roof edges. Children rushed outside to see the thin streams. One old woman put her hand over her eyes, looked at the bright white mountains and said, "It is almost over," with a long breath.

What do the dripping roof edges tell us?
They show that winter is ending, because the sun is melting the snow.

Little Dev stood at the village gate on the first day of school, holding the rope of his goat, Chinku. His mother said that goats could not come to school. Dev's lip trembled, but he tied the rope to the fence and walked slowly in. During the first lesson, the class heard a loud bleating at the window. Chinku had slipped his rope and had come to find his friend, looking in with his head on one side. The teacher, Mrs. Iyer, tried to look cross but burst out laughing. She let the goat stay in the yard for the day, tied to the guava tree, and Dev learned his letters with a wide smile.

How did Dev feel about the goat staying in the yard?
He was happy and comforted, because he stayed close to his friend and enjoyed the lesson with a wide smile.

During the festival of Pongal, Meenakshi's family cooks the first rice of the season in a clay pot on an open fire in the courtyard. Everyone watches the pot closely. When the milk and rice bubble over the rim, they shout together, and the children clap. This year, the pot overflowed very early, and Meenakshi's grandfather smiled for the first time in weeks. The previous year's harvest had been poor, and money had been tight. He said that an early overflow was a sign of a good year to come. Her mother wiped her eyes with the end of her sari, and the family sat down to eat, more cheerful than they had been for a long time.

Why did Meenakshi's grandfather smile when the pot overflowed early?
He took it as a sign that the new year would bring a good harvest after a poor one.

Two brothers, Tariq and Jamal, inherited their father's orchard. The old man had always said it would be best if they shared the work equally. In the first year, Tariq picked the fruit, and Jamal sold it. At the end of the season, Jamal brought a bag of money and said he had sold the fruit for a high price. Tariq was suspicious and walked to the market the next Saturday to check the prices himself. He found that the price was exactly what Jamal had said. Embarrassed, he went home and handed his brother a basket of the best apples as an apology without saying why.

Why did Tariq give his brother a basket of apples?
He felt ashamed for doubting Jamal and wanted to apologise.

Our school's flower garden has a winding path of red bricks and a small bench under a gulmohar tree. Each class plants and looks after one flower bed. Class six has marigolds, class seven has zinnias, and class eight has petunias in many colours. A gardener named Mr. Mahato visits twice a week to check on the soil and mend the fence. In April, the gulmohar tree drops red petals across the bench, and the children sit there to read at lunchtime. The headmaster says that the most visited spot in the school is not the library or the playground, but this bench.

Which class looks after the zinnias?
Class seven looks after them.

The old temple in the village of Halebidu is carved from soft stone, and each pillar shows scenes of dancers, musicians and elephants. Visitors come from far away to look at the carvings. A local guide, Mr. Hegde, leads groups on Saturday mornings and tells stories of the kings who built it nine hundred years ago. He asks visitors to look for a tiny carving of a monkey hidden near the base of one column. Whoever finds it receives a sweet from his pocket. The temple is open from eight to six, and entry for children is free.

Who receives a sweet from Mr. Hegde?
Whoever finds the tiny monkey carving receives a sweet.

April in the village of Sonbarsa brings dust storms. They come in the late afternoon without warning. A brown cloud rises on the horizon, grows quickly, and then the wind throws sand against walls and windows. People hurry indoors and shut the shutters. Mothers call their children home, and shopkeepers drop the curtains over their stalls. The storm usually lasts about half an hour. When it ends, a fine layer of dust covers everything: the beds, the cooking pots and even the food that was left uncovered. Women spend the evening sweeping and washing, and say the same words each year: "Next time, we will cover everything first."

How long does the storm usually last?
It usually lasts about half an hour.

The first snow of the year fell on the town of Manali on a Thursday night. By morning, the roofs were white, and the deodar trees wore thick coats of powder on their branches. Children came out with woollen caps and made snowmen in front of their houses. Tenzin, aged nine, rolled the biggest ball and used two apples for eyes and a carrot for the nose. The school was closed for the day because the road was blocked by a drift. Shopkeepers cleared the steps with wide wooden shovels and served hot butter tea to anyone who walked past.

How old is Tenzin?
Tenzin is nine years old.

The village school in Hilltop Lane has only two rooms and one teacher, Miss Joseph. In the first room, the younger children sit on a mat and learn letters from a painted board. In the second, older students study maths and reading at wooden desks. Miss Joseph arrives by bicycle at half past eight and rings a small brass bell to start the day. At noon, the children eat lunch under a guava tree, and afterwards they play kabaddi in the dusty yard. Last year, the villagers collected money to buy twelve new books, and they kept them in a green steel cupboard that Miss Joseph keeps locked.

How does Miss Joseph travel to school?
She comes by bicycle.

The path from the village of Nako to the high pastures is narrow and steep. Every summer, shepherds take their sheep and goats up to graze, and they stay for three months in small stone huts. They carry flour, salt, tea and blankets on the backs of mules. Their wives remain in the village and work on barley fields. At night, the shepherds light a fire, cook flat bread on a hot stone and sing old songs. Their dogs, large and white, sleep around the flock and protect it from wolves. When winter approaches, the herds return, and the village holds a feast to welcome them.

How long do the shepherds stay in the high pastures?
They stay for three months.

On the outskirts of Tilonia, a group of women runs a solar workshop. They learned to make small lamps and chargers from a trainer who came for six months from the city. Now they make about fifty lamps every month and sell them in neighbouring villages. The lamps have a panel on top and a switch at the side. Customers can charge their phones in the evening using a socket on the base. The women meet in a mud-brick room painted yellow, where a small chart on the wall shows their orders. The earnings are shared equally, and part of the money goes to the school.

How many lamps do the women make each month?
They make about fifty lamps a month.

Fog is common in the plains of Punjab during December and January. In the early morning, it settles over the wheat fields like a white blanket, and a person can hardly see ten steps ahead. Trains run late, and buses crawl along the road with their lights on. Farmers wrap themselves in thick shawls called chadars and light small fires of straw near their fields to keep warm. The fog usually clears around ten, when the sun rises higher, and then the golden light spreads across the green wheat. Schoolchildren like the fog because it sometimes delays the first period.

When does the fog usually clear?
It usually clears around ten o'clock, when the sun rises higher.

A day on a tea estate in Assam begins at six o'clock, when the bell rings. Workers collect their baskets from the shed and walk to their assigned rows of tea bushes. They pick for four hours, and then bring their baskets to the weighing shed. At midday, there is a meal of rice, lentils and vegetables, served in a large open hall. The afternoon shift sorts and carries the leaves to the factory. There, the leaves are dried, rolled and heated until they turn dark. At dusk, the workers go home to their small houses beside the estate, where their children wait.

What time does the bell ring on the tea estate?
It rings at six o'clock.

Hira's family had just moved to the village from a big city. On the first morning, she woke to the sound of a rooster and looked out at a muddy lane with no pavements and no shops. She felt very small and homesick, and she asked her mother when they were going back. Her mother only smiled and told her to go and see the pond at the end of the lane. Hira went reluctantly. At the pond, three girls her age were sitting on stones and tossing flat pebbles across the water. One of them waved and called, "Come and try!" Hira's frown slowly softened, and she walked over.

How did Hira's feelings change in the passage?
She began feeling homesick and unhappy but became friendlier and more hopeful when the girls invited her.

Every year in March, people in the village of Mayapur wait for the first mango blossom and the first warm wind. The days grow longer, and the cold of winter slips away. Women pack away the heavy quilts and hang them in the sun to air. Men repair the cattle sheds and sweep the dust from their porches. Children spend hours in the field flying kites, and the evenings are filled with the sound of crickets. It is the time when everybody feels new energy and begins small jobs left undone all winter. Later in the month, the festival of colours takes place.

In which month is the festival of colours held?
It is held in March.

There was once a tall tree on the hill above a village near Almora where an eagle had made its nest. Every morning, the villagers saw it soar above their fields. When a drought came, the streams dried up, and the villagers began to worry. One day, a boy noticed the eagle circling in a wide, slow spiral over a certain hollow in the hills and returning to it again and again. He told the elders, who followed the bird the next day and found a hidden spring behind a rock. Within a week, they had dug a channel from it to the village, and water flowed again.

How did the eagle help the villagers, without meaning to?
Its circling led the boy and the elders to a hidden spring, which gave the village water.

Mr. Achebe's radio announced that the harmattan wind would blow strongly for the next three days. This dry wind comes from the desert each year between December and February. It carries fine dust that settles on every surface, turning the sky into a pale brown haze. Doors and windows are kept shut, and women wrap their faces with cloth when walking in the open. Lips and hands become dry and cracked, so people rub them with shea butter. Children are told to drink plenty of water. When the wind stops, the sky turns blue again, and the rains seem not far behind.

What do people rub on dry lips and hands?
They rub shea butter on them.

The sky was blue and without clouds on the morning of the school sports day. The children of Tarapur arrived at eight o'clock in white shirts and shorts, waving flags that their mothers had stitched. First, there was a march past the headmaster, followed by a lemon-and-spoon race and a sack race. A hot wind began blowing at eleven, and the teachers set up a canopy of cloth for the little ones. The relay was run at noon, and the winning team from the red house received a silver cup. The headmaster gave everyone cold lemonade, and the day ended with songs.

Which house won the silver cup?
The red house won it.

Every night for a week, something had been eating the groundnuts in Nasir's field. He found small holes in the soil and torn plants in the morning. His wife suggested sitting up and waiting. On the eighth night, Nasir wrapped himself in a blanket and hid behind a haystack with a torch. A little after midnight, he heard a soft scratching, and the torch beam showed three wild boars rooting among the plants. Nasir did not shout or run. He quietly backed away, walked to the neighbour's house and woke up the farmers who shared the field. "We need to build a fence together," he whispered.

Why did Nasir go to wake his neighbours instead of chasing the boars?
The field was shared, so he wanted all the farmers to deal with the boars together; he whispered that they needed to build a fence together.

In a small village in Japan, an old woman named Mrs. Tanaka looks after the community's rice shrine. Each morning, she sweeps the path leading to it and places a fresh bowl of water on the stone altar. The village celebrates the planting of rice in May, when young and old stand in a line in the flooded paddy and push seedlings into the mud by hand. A drummer keeps time, and the women sing a slow song. When the work is done, they eat rice balls wrapped in seaweed. The festival ends when the last seedling is planted, usually just after sunset.

In which month does the village celebrate rice planting?
They celebrate it in May.

In a coastal village near Puri, a cyclone warning came on Tuesday evening. The fishermen dragged their boats far up the beach and tied them to coconut palms with thick ropes. Teachers closed the school, and the local officer announced on a loudspeaker that families living near the shore should move to the concrete shelter by the main road. Volunteers handed out blankets, rice and drinking water. By midnight, the wind howled, and branches crashed on the roofs. In the morning, the storm had moved inland, and people returned to find their houses wet but standing. No one had been hurt.

Where were families near the shore told to go?
They were told to go to the concrete shelter by the main road.

Kofi checked the sky for the third time that morning. The wheat in his field was golden and dry, and the stalks bent in the wind. His neighbour had already hired the harvesting machine, and it was due to arrive by noon. Far in the west, dark clouds were piling up like heaps of ash. Kofi called his sons and told them to leave their breakfast and bring the sickles. "We cut as much as we can before the first drop falls," he said. The boys ran to the field without a word, and the three of them worked side by side until their shirts were soaked with sweat, glancing up at the clouds now and then.

Why did Kofi tell his sons to leave their breakfast?
He was worried the dark clouds meant rain, so he wanted to cut as much wheat as possible before it fell.

The old woman who sold roasted peanuts near the station had not come to her spot for three days. The vendors on either side noticed her empty place, and Raju, the boy who sold newspapers, asked the tea seller if he knew where she lived. Nobody did. On the fourth day, Raju walked along the railway track to the small colony where the labourers lived and began asking at every door. At last, a woman in a blue sari pointed to a hut at the end. Inside, the peanut seller lay on a cot with a fever, and her cooking pot stood cold. Raju ran to fetch the others.

Why did Raju go looking for the old woman?
He was worried because she had been absent for three days, and he wanted to find out whether she was all right.

Every evening, as the sun set behind the paddy fields, the herd of water buffaloes was led to the pond. Little Linh, only seven, had been given the job of leading them for the first time. She held a thin bamboo stick and walked in front, trying to look brave. The biggest buffalo, which was almost three times her size, followed calmly behind. When they came to the narrow bank near the pond, Linh's foot slipped, and she nearly fell. The big buffalo stopped at once and stood quite still until she regained her balance. Linh patted its nose and said quietly, "Thank you."

What does the buffalo's behaviour on the bank suggest?
It suggests the buffalo was gentle and careful, and waited so Linh would not be hurt.

Ten children from Anand's school camped overnight at the edge of a forest. The guide, Mr. Thomas, showed them how to pitch the tents, light a fire with dry sticks and cook rice in a tin pot. After dinner, he told ghost stories, but the children only laughed. At ten, they crawled into their sleeping bags and listened to crickets. Early in the morning, a cuckoo called from the trees, and Anand woke first. He tiptoed out of the tent and saw mist rising from the grass. For a long while he stood there in his socks, watching the light grow between the trunks.

What woke Anand first in the morning?
A cuckoo calling from the trees woke him.

Mr. Rahim, the village tailor, had always worked alone in his small shop, bent over a sewing machine from morning until night. One day, a young girl named Sumi came to the door and asked if she could watch. He shrugged. She watched the next day too, and the day after. Soon she was threading needles and sorting buttons. After three months, he handed her a piece of cloth and told her to try a simple shirt for her brother. She stitched it slowly, tongue between her teeth, and when it was done, Mr. Rahim examined every seam. "Not bad," he said, but his moustache moved in a way that showed he was smiling.

How did Mr. Rahim feel about Sumi's shirt?
He was pleased, because although he said only 'Not bad', his moustache showed he was smiling.

Soon after dawn, the village of Chitkul is already awake. Women carry buckets of milk to the dairy, and men load apples into a truck headed for the plains. The village lies high in the mountains, and winters are so cold that most families store enough food in September to last till April. Houses are built of stone and wood with slate roofs. In the middle stands a small temple with a carved wooden door. The only shop sells matches, soap, biscuits and warm socks. Children walk two kilometres to school on a stony path, and in winter, they carry their lunch inside their coats to keep it from freezing.

How do children keep their lunch from freezing in winter?
They carry it inside their coats.

Late in the afternoon, the farmer Tendai noticed that the sky above the maize field was turning an unusual yellow-green. The air smelled metallic, and the birds had gone silent. He called his wife and daughters from the house and told them to bring everything they could carry into the storage hut. Then he checked that the cattle gate was closed. A few minutes later, the wind roared across the field, bending the maize stalks flat, and hail the size of eggs fell. The family huddled in the hut, listening to the pounding on the roof, and Tendai held his youngest daughter close, relieved that everyone was together.

Why did Tendai bring his family and belongings to the hut?
He saw the strange sky and silent birds as signs of a dangerous storm and wanted everyone to be safe.

Fishermen's wives in a coastal village near Malvan dry their husbands' catch on long bamboo racks beside the road. Slender fish called bombil are tied in pairs and hung on ropes like laundry. The smell is strong, but the villagers hardly notice it. Visiting traders come on Thursday mornings and bargain for the best. Children chase the crows that try to steal the fish and wave plastic bags to scare them. The dried fish is sold in sacks and sent to the town, and the women keep a few for their own kitchens to make a spicy curry with coconut.

On which day do the traders come?
They come on Thursday mornings.

The cooperative dairy in a village near Anand opens its doors at five thirty each morning. Farmers line up with steel cans of milk, and a clerk named Mr. Joshi tests each can for thickness and fat. He writes the figures on a slip, which the farmer carries to the window to collect payment at the end of the week. Women wait with their children on a long bench, while men chat near the gate. By seven, the milk is poured into a large tank, and a tanker truck takes it to the city. Mr. Joshi has worked at the dairy for eighteen years and knows the farmers' cows by name.

How long has Mr. Joshi worked at the dairy?
He has worked there for eighteen years.

Along the shore of Lake Naivasha in Kenya, hippos spend the day in the water and come out at night to graze. Local rangers warn visitors never to walk near the shore after dark. In the morning, the guides take tourists out in small boats to watch the animals from a safe distance. The hippos blink and flick their ears, with only their eyes and noses above the surface. Pelicans glide overhead, and fish eagles sit on the dead trees along the bank. The tour lasts two hours, and visitors are given binoculars and a cup of tea halfway through.

When do the hippos come out to graze?
They come out at night.

The fishermen of a village near Karwar sat on the sand and watched the horizon. The sky was clear, the sea calm, and yet none of them pushed their boats into the water. A newcomer asked why. An old fisherman pointed to a faint line of white cloud far off. "That is no ordinary cloud," he said. "It looks like a wall, and the waves are slowly getting bigger." A few hours later, the wind rose, and the waves crashed against the rocks. The newcomer watched from the safety of the beach and said that he would never again question an old fisherman's eyes.

What does the newcomer's final remark show?
It shows he now trusts the old fisherman's experience, since the storm proved him right.

Before lunch on Wednesday, the air in Chennai felt thick and still. Leaves on the coconut trees hung motionless, and the sky had turned a heavy grey. Kavya wiped her forehead with her hand and noticed that the ceiling fan was doing very little. Her mother quickly took the washing off the line and carried it inside. In the street, a boy ran past, shouting to his friends to hurry home. A few minutes later, big warm drops began to fall, hitting the dust and leaving round dark marks. Within a minute, the rain was pouring so hard that the road looked like a river.

Why did Kavya's mother take the washing off the line?
She sensed that rain was coming, because the sky was grey and the air was still, so she wanted to keep the clothes dry.

Each morning, the buffalo named Kali walked from the cowshed to the pond without being led. Ashok never had to guide her. One day, a new gate was fixed across the usual path. Kali stopped and stared at it. Then she turned to the left and walked slowly around the shed, crossed the dry field, and reached the pond from the other side. Ashok, who was watching from the doorway, laughed in surprise. "She found another way," he told his wife. That evening, he noticed that Kali had left a clear trail of hoof prints along her new route, as if she meant to use it again.

What does the story show about Kali?
It shows that Kali is clever and can find a new way when her usual path is blocked.

A group of children from Arun's school went to plant seeds on a hillside that had been burned by a forest fire. Each child carried a small cloth bag of seeds from native trees: neem, jamun and amla. The forest officer, Mr. Pillai, showed them how to push each seed a finger's depth into the ground, and how to place a flat stone next to it to hold moisture. By lunchtime, they had planted four hundred seeds. After the meal of rice and curd, the children returned to school, singing and tired. Mr. Pillai promised to bring them back in the monsoon to see which seeds had sprouted.

How many seeds did the children plant by lunchtime?
They planted four hundred seeds.

An old banyan tree stands in the middle of Kalyan's village, and its branches reach so wide that the tree seems like a small forest. Many creatures live there. Birds build nests in the high branches, bats sleep upside down in the dark hollows, and lizards sun themselves on the roots. In the afternoon heat, farmers rest beneath it, and old men play cards on a flat stone. Last year, the district office suggested cutting the tree to widen the road. Every person in the village went to the office together and asked them to build the road around it instead. The tree is still standing today.

Why did the villagers go to the office?
They valued the tree and wanted to save it, so they asked the office to build the road around it instead of cutting it down.

Esther's vegetable patch behind the farmhouse is divided into four parts. The first has onions and garlic, the second has carrots and radishes, the third grows beans on bamboo poles, and the last is for pumpkins that spread across the ground. Every morning before school, Esther waters the beds with a green can. On Saturdays, she pulls the weeds and feeds the soil with leftover tea leaves and eggshells. Her mother cooks whatever is ready, and extra vegetables go to the neighbour, Mrs. Dsouza, who has a bad knee. Esther is saving the biggest pumpkin for the village fair.

What is grown on the bamboo poles?
Beans are grown on them.

In a village near Pune, a young woman named Sunita started a small library in a bullock-cart shed. She collected old books from the town and from friends, wrapped them in plastic covers and arranged them on shelves made from wooden crates. Every afternoon, the children gather there to read or listen to stories. On Saturdays, Sunita holds a reading hour for adults who never learned to read well. At first, only three people came, but now there are sixteen. She keeps a record book where each person signs a name when borrowing, and the oldest member of the class is seventy-two.

How old is the oldest member of the adult reading class?
The oldest member is seventy-two.

The old tractor on Mr. Lopez's farm had broken down in the middle of the harvest. He lifted the bonnet, looked inside and sighed. His neighbour, a young woman named Ines, walked over and offered her own tractor for the afternoon. Mr. Lopez hesitated, then said he could not repay her. Ines shrugged and said that last spring, he had lent her his seed drill when she needed it. By evening, both fields had been cut, and the two of them sat on the tractor's mudguard, sharing sandwiches and talking about the price of fuel. Mr. Lopez said he would help her again with whatever she needed next year.

Why did Ines lend her tractor to Mr. Lopez?
Because Mr. Lopez had lent her his seed drill last spring, and she wanted to return the kindness.

Kiran's back ached at the end of a long day in the paddy field, and his hands were cracked from the cold water. His younger brother, Anil, who had just come from the city for a holiday, had lasted an hour before declaring that farming was too hard and sitting on the bank with his phone. In the evening, Kiran placed a bowl of rice and lentils in front of Anil and said, "This is the rice you were complaining about." Anil looked at the steaming bowl for a moment, then at his brother's hands, and ate quietly. The next morning, he was the first one out in the field.

Why was Anil the first one in the field the next morning?
He had seen how hard his brother worked for the food, and felt ashamed and wanted to help.

Salma climbed the guava tree behind her house every afternoon after school. The tree was old, with a thick trunk and a low fork where she could sit. From there, she could see the whole lane, the temple roof and the distant railway line. She took a book, a small steel box of puffed rice and a flask of water. Sometimes a squirrel came and sat on a nearby branch, watching her eat. Her mother, who did not like her climbing, finally gave up complaining and tied a small cloth cushion to the fork. Salma used it every day until the monsoon rotted it.

What did Salma's mother tie to the fork of the tree?
She tied a small cloth cushion to it.

Early on Sunday, Oscar and his father took a rowing boat onto the lake near their cottage in Scotland. The water was flat and grey, and a pale mist hung over the far shore. They brought a flask of hot chocolate, a small net and a notebook for counting birds. In two hours they saw four swans, a pair of ducks and one grey heron standing on a rock. Oscar wrote each sighting in the notebook with a tiny drawing. When the sun came out, his father let him hold the oars for ten minutes. They reached the jetty at noon, with cold hands and warm hearts.

What did Oscar and his father bring in the boat to count birds?
They brought a notebook for counting birds.

A whole colony of weaver birds has built nests in the tall palm tree beside Gopi's house. Each nest hangs like a small woven basket from the end of a branch and has a narrow entrance pointing down. The male birds do the weaving, using long strips of grass that they pull with their beaks and tie with knots. Female birds inspect the finished nests and choose the one they like. Gopi watches them from his window with a pair of old field glasses. He has counted thirty-two nests and is trying to find out how many birds actually live in them.

How many nests has Gopi counted?
He has counted thirty-two nests.

The cowherd boy Gopal takes the village cattle to the hills every morning at seven. He carries a stick, a cloth bundle of roti and a flute that he made himself from bamboo. The cows know his flute, and when he plays a certain tune, they raise their heads and walk toward him. At noon, he finds a shady rock and eats lunch while the herd grazes on the slope. He returns at five, and the village women wait at their doors to take back their own cows. Gopal says that the favourite cow in the herd is a small brown one named Lakshmi.

What did Gopal make from bamboo?
He made a flute.

A boy named Chidi arrived at the village school with no shoes and a torn bag. The other children noticed, and some began to whisper. The teacher, Mrs. Eze, said nothing. The next morning, she brought a spare pair of shoes that had belonged to her own son and left them on a bench outside the class, with no note. After the lesson, Chidi found them and stared. He looked round, but nobody was watching. He slipped them on, and they fit. The following day, he walked into class holding his head high, and when Mrs. Eze looked at him, they both pretended that nothing had happened.

Why did Mrs. Eze leave the shoes without a note?
She wanted to help Chidi without embarrassing him, which is why she left the shoes quietly and later pretended nothing had happened.

A thin boy sat on a rock near the village river, watching the water. His kite lay torn in his lap. He had spent the whole week making it from thin paper and bamboo sticks, and the first strong wind had ripped it. His older sister, passing with a pot of water, stopped and put it down. She did not say anything. She sat beside him and began to turn over the torn pieces. Then she took out a small pot of rice paste from her bag and started gluing. By the time the sun was low, the two of them were running along the bank, the repaired kite rising above their heads.

How did the boy's mood change by the end?
He was sad at first when the kite was torn, but became happy once his sister helped him repair it and fly it.

In Orchha, a man named Devi Singh has been the night watchman for thirty years. He wears a thick brown blanket, carries a long bamboo stick and a lantern and walks through every lane after ten. At each crossing, he taps his stick on the ground three times and calls out, "All is well!" The villagers, lying in their beds, hear him and fall asleep. During festivals, he joins the dancing, and at weddings he watches the sweets table. Once, when a fire broke out in a straw shed, he woke the whole lane in minutes and the fire was put out with buckets of water.

What does Devi Singh call out at each crossing?
He calls out, 'All is well!'

Hamid's cattle shed had a leaking roof, and every monsoon his cows stood in damp straw. He had no money for tin sheets. His neighbour Farida suggested that they mend the roof together by gathering coconut leaves from the trees behind their houses. Hamid had never worked with coconut thatching, but Farida showed him how to braid the leaves into mats. For two weekends, they sat in the yard weaving, and then climbed up the ladder to tie the mats to the frame. When the next storm came, Hamid stood inside the dry shed with a cup of tea, listening to the rain with a very pleased look on his face.

How did Hamid feel when he stood in the dry shed?
He felt pleased and relieved, because the roof no longer leaked.

A heat wave struck a village near Barmer in the middle of May. For six days, the temperature stayed above forty-five degrees. Schools shortened their hours, and the village council arranged for water tankers to visit every lane. Shops opened only early in the morning and again after sunset. Grandmothers advised families to drink buttermilk and cover their heads when walking outside. Tarun, who is eleven, spent each afternoon lying on the cool floor of his room, reading comics with a wet towel on his forehead. On the seventh day, a light breeze finally arrived from the north, and everyone opened their windows.

How many days did the temperature stay above forty-five degrees?
It stayed that high for six days.

Ibrahim's tea stall stands at the crossing of two lanes in the village of Tanda. He sells tea in small glass cups, along with plain biscuits and fried snacks wrapped in newspaper. In the morning, farmers stop for a quick cup before heading to the fields. At noon, drivers of tractors and carts rest on his bench. In the evening, the old men come to talk about prices and politics for hours. Ibrahim keeps a small radio on the shelf and turns it on for the cricket scores. On the wall hangs a calendar with a picture of a mountain, which his daughter brought him from the city.

What does Ibrahim keep on the shelf?
He keeps a small radio on it.

The shepherd's dog, Tiger, had been the best sheepdog in the valley for ten years. Now he walked slowly, and his muzzle was grey. The shepherd, Mr. Raza, noticed that Tiger no longer ran to the farthest edge of the flock but stayed near the middle. A young black-and-white pup named Bolt had joined the farm. Mr. Raza began taking both dogs out together. Tiger sat at the top of the hill and watched while Bolt did the running. The old dog looked at the pup, then at the shepherd, and wagged his tail slowly. When they came home, Mr. Raza gave Tiger the first bowl of food.

Why did Mr. Raza give Tiger the first bowl of food?
He respected and loved the old dog for his years of service, even though Bolt now did the running.

Pablo's village in the Andes sits so high that clouds sometimes drift between the houses. The families keep llamas and grow potatoes in terraces cut into the slopes. On Sundays, everyone walks to the small chapel at the centre, where the bell is rung by whichever child arrives first. After the service, there is a market on the square, with piles of purple and yellow potatoes, wool hats and hot corn soup. Pablo's mother sells scarves that she weaves herself. When the market closes, the children play a game with a ball made of rolled-up socks, and the youngest one always has the first kick.

What do the families grow on the terraces?
They grow potatoes on the terraces.

The hailstorm hit the village of Narayangaon at two o'clock on Monday afternoon. Round white balls, some as big as marbles, rattled down on the tin roofs with a deafening sound. People ran to the nearest doorway. Children stuck out their hands to catch the ice and laughed as it stung their palms. Within ten minutes, the road was white, and the temperature dropped sharply. The storm destroyed part of the tomato crop, and farmers walked around their fields afterwards, counting the broken plants. The village leader said he would write to the district office to ask about help.

What size were some of the hailstones?
Some were as big as marbles.

Granny Rose ran the village library from a corner of her front room. She had only about two hundred books, but she knew each one by heart and could name a story for every child who walked in. When a shy boy named Peter began coming every Saturday, she noticed that he always picked books about trains. The next week she borrowed a new train book from the town library and left it on the top shelf. Peter found it before he had even taken off his cap. He read it standing up, right there by the door, and when he finished he looked at Granny Rose and gave her a big grin.

Why did Granny Rose borrow a book about trains?
She had noticed that Peter liked train books and wanted him to have a new one to read.

Jorge was proud of his new scarecrow. He had dressed it in an old red shirt, a straw hat and a pair of faded trousers, and he fixed it in the middle of the maize field. For two days, no bird came near the crop. On the third morning, Jorge went to check and found a small sparrow sitting calmly on the scarecrow's hat. Several others hopped between the maize plants, pecking at the grains that had fallen. Jorge stood with his hands on his hips for a moment. Then he laughed, took a tin plate and a stick from his bag, and began walking the field himself, banging the plate loudly.

What does the sparrow on the hat show?
It shows the birds had stopped being afraid of the scarecrow, so it no longer protected the field.

Anil's father had told him to bring the buffalo back by sunset, but the afternoon was so pleasant that Anil fell asleep under a tree. When he woke, the sky was orange, and the buffalo was nowhere to be seen. His heart began to pound. He ran along the dusty track, calling out and checking behind every bush. At last, he found the animal standing in the shallow pond with half her body underwater, quite happy. Anil sat on the bank, breathing hard, and laughed with relief. On the way home, he decided that he would not tell his father about the nap, and he walked behind the buffalo with a slight frown.

How did Anil feel when he found the buffalo?
He felt relieved, and he laughed once he saw it was safe.

For the Brown family, the pumpkin competition at the village fair was the highlight of the year. Mr. Brown's pumpkin was huge, but it had a soft patch on one side, and he feared the judges would notice. That morning, he turned the bad side toward the wall and stood in front of it. His daughter, Chloe, watched him and raised an eyebrow. "Dad," she said, "the judges will walk all the way around." Mr. Brown sighed and moved aside. When the judges did notice the patch, they remarked that it was a fine pumpkin all the same. He won the third prize and told Chloe she had been right.

Why did Mr. Brown move away from the pumpkin?
Chloe reminded him that the judges would see the whole pumpkin anyway, so hiding the patch would not work.

The Western Ghats are home to a plant called the Neelakurinji, which blooms only once every twelve years. When it does, whole hillsides turn a soft shade of blue-purple. Thousands of tourists travel to the town of Munnar to see it. The last big bloom took place in 2018, and the next will not come until 2030. Local guides lead visitors along marked paths so they do not trample the flowers. Bees and butterflies fill the air during the weeks of bloom, and the honey that local farmers collect that season is considered special.

How often does the Neelakurinji bloom?
It blooms once every twelve years.

Reena's school in the hills was closed for two days because of heavy snow. On the first day, she built a small igloo in the garden with her brother and sat inside it with a flask of hot tea. On the second day, she found herself looking out of the window and sighing. All her friends lived on the other side of the hill, and the road was blocked by snow. She took out her notebook and wrote a long letter to her best friend Chitra, describing the igloo and the quiet. When the road opened on the third day, she handed the letter to the postman herself.

Why did Reena write a long letter to Chitra?
She was missing her friend, who lived on the other side of the hill, and could not visit because of the snow.

When the monsoon comes to Kerala, it arrives on the first of June, or close to it. Thick grey clouds roll in from the Arabian Sea, and the sky stays dark for days. School children are given umbrellas and rubber slippers, and the coconut palms bend in the wind. Streets turn into streams, and the women hang washing indoors on long lines tied between pillars. Fishermen do not take their boats out for weeks. Raju's grandfather says that nothing smells better than the first rain on the dry earth, and he sits on the veranda every evening listening to it on the roof.

When does the monsoon usually arrive in Kerala?
It arrives on or about the first of June.

When the dry months came, the farmers of the village used to take their goats to the riverbank to graze. This year, however, the bank was bare. The village elder, Mr. Biswas, called a meeting and announced that every family would have to send its goats in turns to the greener hill pastures, but the hills were a full day's walk away. Some families protested that they could not spare a child for so long. Then fourteen-year-old Karan stood up and said that he would take all the village goats himself if each family gave him a little food. A murmur of agreement went around the room.

What does Karan's offer show about him?
It shows he is responsible and generous, because he offered to take all the village goats himself so that families would not have to spare a child.

Ravi's grandfather was famous for finding water. Whenever a family wanted to dig a well, he would walk across the field with a forked stick of guava wood and wait for it to twitch. But Ravi, who studied science at school, doubted that it worked. He decided to test it. He asked his grandfather to try the stick in three places, while he marked where the soil was dampest after rain. At the end, the stick had twitched in places that matched none of his marks. But Ravi noticed something else: his grandfather always walked first to low ground near tall green trees, where water was likely to collect. That evening, he sat next to his grandfather on the porch and asked him to teach him how to read the land.

Why did Ravi ask his grandfather to teach him?
Because he saw that his grandfather really knew where water collects, always choosing low ground near green trees, even though the stick showed no pattern.

The lamplighter of Old Haven, Mr. Gupta, walks the length of the village every evening at dusk. He carries a ladder on one shoulder and a can of oil in his hand. At each post he climbs up, fills the lamp, trims the wick and lights it with a long taper. The lamps in the main street come first, and those near the pond come last. By seven, the whole village glows with a soft yellow light, and children are allowed to play outside until the church bell rings. Mr. Gupta is paid by the village council, and he has done this job since he was nineteen.

What does Mr. Gupta carry on his shoulder?
He carries a ladder.

When Sunil returned to the beach after the storm, the sand was covered in seaweed, broken shells and bits of driftwood. He walked slowly along the waterline with a plastic bag, picking up everything that did not belong there. By the time he had walked half a kilometre, the bag was heavy with bottles and old fishing line. A small boy from the nearby hut came and watched, then silently picked up a bag of his own. Later, a few other children joined in, and soon more than ten were scattered along the shore. Sunil only smiled and kept walking, a little straighter than before.

Why did the children begin picking up rubbish?
They saw Sunil doing it and followed his example.

Every harvest, the tractor driver Mr. Dubey drove through the village with a loudspeaker announcing the price of wheat at the nearest market. This year, however, he drove past without a word. A farmer named Gopal called to him over the fence, and Mr. Dubey slowed. He explained, with a lowered voice, that the price had fallen. Gopal said nothing, but he looked across his field of heavy golden wheat. Then he straightened his shoulders and told Mr. Dubey that he would wait until the price improved. The driver nodded and drove on, and Gopal went back to stacking sheaves, humming under his breath, as though the news had not troubled him at all.

What do Gopal's actions suggest about how he really felt?
He may have been worried about the price, but he tried to stay calm and hopeful and chose to wait.

Yesterday, Leila and her brother Sami planted a sapling in the school garden as part of a tree-planting day. Their teacher gave each pair of students a small neem plant, a spade and a can of water. Leila dug a hole about as deep as her arm, and Sami set the plant carefully into it. Then they filled the hole with soil and pressed it down with their hands. Finally they tied a small label with their names to a branch. The teacher told them to water it twice a week. Leila promised to bring a bottle from home every Monday and Thursday.

What did Leila and Sami plant?
They planted a neem sapling.

Anwar's aunt always claimed that she could feel the weather in her bones, but nobody believed her. One evening, while the family was getting ready for a cousin's outdoor wedding, she announced that rain was coming before midnight. The sky was starry and calm. The family laughed, and the groom's father said she was spoiling the mood. But the aunt asked quietly that a tent be kept ready. The men put up a large canvas awning over the dining area, mostly to please her. At eleven, a heavy shower came, and the guests, crowded under the awning with their plates of food, looked at the aunt with respect.

Why did the guests look at the aunt with respect?
Her forecast of rain was proved right, and the awning she asked for kept them dry.

Nizam's sheep farm lies in a high valley of Kashmir. Each spring, he and his brothers shear the animals with long metal clippers. The wool is washed in the river, spread on rocks to dry and then packed in sacks. His mother and sisters spin it into thread using wooden wheels, and the thread is later woven into shawls and blankets. A trader from Srinagar visits every autumn to buy what the family has made. Nizam's youngest brother, Imtiyaz, helps by keeping the flock together with the help of two sheepdogs named Bholu and Sheru.

Who buys the shawls and blankets every autumn?
A trader from Srinagar buys them.

Every Tuesday, the weekly market sets up under the big banyan tree in Rampur. Farmers from nearby hamlets arrive before sunrise with baskets of brinjal, spinach and green chillies. Old Salma sells hand-woven mats near the water tank, and her grandson Imran helps her tie the bundles with jute string. By eight o'clock the lane is so crowded that cycles must be pushed instead of ridden. The sweet seller, Mr. Pillai, fries hot jalebis in a wide iron pan, and children gather around to watch the orange spirals float in the oil. When the sun gets hot, most of the stalls pack up and the banyan tree is quiet again.

Where is the weekly market held in Rampur?
It is held under the big banyan tree.

Nobody on the farm remembered who had planted the lone fig tree in the corner of the field. It was gnarled and low, and for years it had given only a few small fruits. The farmer's wife, Mrs. Ndlovu, was about to cut it down to make room for beans when her small grandson ran up and begged her to wait. He had found a nest of tiny blue eggs among the leaves. Mrs. Ndlovu put down her axe, looked at the eggs for a moment, and went inside. The next spring, the tree was loaded with figs, and the bean rows were planted around it.

Why did Mrs. Ndlovu put down her axe?
She saw the bird's nest and did not want to destroy it, so she spared the tree.

At the fish farm beside Kolleru Lake, there are twelve ponds, each about the size of a football field. Workers rise early to feed the fish with pellets thrown by hand from a boat. Every week, they check the water, testing it for oxygen with a small kit. Large fans on floats churn the surface and add air during the hot months. In winter, the fish are netted and counted. A refrigerated truck takes them to the city market the same night. The farm owner, Mr. Raju, has planted coconut trees around the ponds to give shade and keep the water cooler.

How many ponds are there at the fish farm?
There are twelve ponds.

Savita works as the village's only electrician. She learned the trade from her uncle, and now she carries a leather bag with pliers, wire and a screwdriver. Her phone number is written on the wall of the tea stall. Last week, she repaired the street light at the crossing, fixed a fan in the school and wired a new lamp in the temple. Her fee is small, and she often takes payment in vegetables or eggs. The villagers say she is more reliable than any electrician from the town. Savita is training two young girls to help her, and they follow her on foot.

What does Savita carry in her leather bag?
She carries pliers, wire and a screwdriver.

Washing day in the village of Ghat takes place every Monday at the river. Women arrive after breakfast with heavy bundles of clothes, carrying them in baskets on their heads. They scrub the garments on flat stones using blocks of soap and beat them with wooden paddles. The wet clothes are spread on the grass and on bushes to dry in the sun. While they wait, the women gossip, sing and share boiled sweet corn. Children swim and splash nearby under their watchful eyes. By two o'clock, everything is folded and packed again, and the women walk home in a long line.

On which day does washing day take place?
It takes place every Monday.

Thunder woke Tomas at two in the morning on Saturday. Rain was drumming on the tin roof so hard that he could not hear his own voice. He crept to the window and watched silver lines of lightning run across the sky. The street lamp flickered and then went out, leaving the whole lane dark. His mother came into his room with a candle and a blanket, and they sat together on the bed. After half an hour, the rain became softer, and by dawn it had stopped completely. In the morning, Tomas found two broken branches and a flooded yard.

What did Tomas find in the morning?
He found two broken branches and a flooded yard.

When the teacher announced that the school picnic might be cancelled due to the weather, a groan went through the class. Aarti, who had been looking forward to it for weeks, watched the clouds from the window all morning. At lunchtime, a thin ray of sun broke through, and she silently crossed her fingers. By two o'clock, the clouds had thinned, and the headmaster declared that the picnic would go ahead. Cheers rang from every classroom. Aarti grabbed her bag and ran to the bus, her braid flying behind her, and sat in the front seat, waving to everyone she knew.

How did Aarti feel when the picnic was confirmed?
She was excited and delighted, because she ran to the bus and waved to everyone.

Sofia had been given a small plot of land at the corner of her father's farm to grow whatever she liked. She chose strawberries. Every day after school she watered them, plucked off dead leaves and chased away the sparrows. Weeks went by, and the plants flowered, but the berries stayed pale green. Her brother teased her, saying she had wasted her effort. Sofia said nothing, but she kept watering. In early summer, one morning, she walked out and found the whole bed dotted with red. She picked one, wiped it on her sleeve and ate it while her brother stood watching with his mouth slightly open.

What does Sofia's silence in the face of teasing show about her?
It shows she was patient and determined, and did not give up because of his words.

The lamb born in the cold night was weaker than the others and could barely stand. The shepherd, Mr. Ahmed, wrapped it in a sack and carried it to his own kitchen, where it lay near the warm stove. For three days, he fed it milk from a bottle every two hours, even during the night. His wife watched him sit up on the second night, yawning, with the lamb in his lap. "It is only a lamb," she said gently. "I know," he said, and went on feeding it. On the fourth day, the little animal stood up and wobbled across the floor to his boots.

What does Mr. Ahmed's behaviour show about him?
It shows he is caring and patient, and works hard to keep even a weak lamb alive.

A thick cloud of locusts was spotted over the next district, and the farmers in Rampura were told to expect them within a day. Mr. Ghosh did not sleep that night. At dawn, he called all the neighbours, and they gathered at the edge of the largest field with drums, metal plates and bundles of smoking straw. When the swarm arrived at noon, darkening the sky, the farmers beat their plates and drums as loudly as they could. The smoke rose, the noise rolled over the field, and the locusts, confused, moved on toward the river. Most of the crop was saved, and the farmers sat down in the dust, too tired to speak.

Why did the farmers make so much noise?
They were trying to scare the locusts away from the crop.

In the forest near the village of Sasan, a pride of lions rests under the trees during the afternoon. The forest guard, Mr. Jadeja, drives slowly along the sandy track in an open jeep. He raises his hand, and the jeep stops. Without a word, he points to a bush where two cubs are playing. The tourists in the back seat hold their breath, and a woman reaches for her camera, then thinks better of it and puts it down. For a minute or two, the only sound is the soft huff of the cubs tumbling over one another, and a bird calling far off.

Why did the tourists hold their breath?
They were enchanted by the cubs and did not want to disturb them; one woman even put her camera down.

A small stream runs behind Meera's school, and in the month of July it fills up with brown water. Her science teacher took the class there last week to look for life near the bank. They found three kinds of dragonflies, a green frog sitting on a flat stone, and a line of red ants carrying a dead beetle. Meera drew the frog in her notebook and wrote down its colour and size. A boy named Tarun found a snail shell and wanted to keep it, but the teacher asked him to put it back where it was. The class returned to school at eleven with muddy shoes and full notebooks.

What did Meera draw in her notebook?
She drew the green frog.

On Tuesday morning, a truck from the agriculture department arrived at Karthik's farm with sacks of seeds. They were a new variety of millet that needed less water than the old kind. The officer, Ms. Menon, showed the farmers how to plant them in shallow furrows spaced a hand apart. Twelve farmers had gathered under the tamarind tree to listen. She also left a small booklet in simple language with pictures of each step. Karthik planted his portion that same afternoon, using a string to keep the rows straight. He marked the date on the wall of his shed with a piece of charcoal.

What did the truck bring to Karthik's farm?
It brought sacks of a new variety of millet seeds.

The path through the forest behind Mira's school had been closed by a fallen tree. For two days the older students stepped over the trunk, but the little ones had to take the long way around the road. On the third morning, Mira arrived early with a saw she had borrowed from her uncle. She looked at the thick trunk and then at the small saw in her hand. She laughed, put the saw down, and ran back to the school. Ten minutes later, she was back with the caretaker and four tall boys, who lifted the smaller branches away and rolled the log to the side of the path.

Why did Mira laugh and put the saw down?
She realised the saw was too small for such a thick trunk, so she needed help.

Priya's school has a rule that nobody may pick flowers or break branches in the forest next to the playground. One Friday, a new boy, Arman, broke a small branch of the flowering tree to make a sword. Priya saw it and felt her stomach tighten. She did not shout or tell the teacher. Instead she walked over to him quietly and showed him the sticky white sap oozing from the broken place. "That's like a cut," she said. Arman looked at the branch, then at the tree, and put the stick down. The next day, he brought a small bottle of water and sprinkled it near the roots.

Why did Arman bring a bottle of water the next day?
He felt sorry for hurting the tree after Priya showed him the sap and said it was like a cut, so he wanted to help it.

One of the strongest winds ever recorded in the village of Gulmarg blew on a night in January. Residents say that the sound was like a long train passing overhead. Several tin roofs lifted, and a few tall trees fell across the road. In the morning, the army sent a team with saws to clear the paths. Children were not allowed outside until the road was open, and they watched the work from the windows. By noon, the sun was shining as if nothing had happened, and a few boys rushed out with sledges. The village repaired its roofs by the end of the week.

What did the army send to clear the paths?
The army sent a team with saws.

Mr. Okoro had grown cassava for thirty years, and he had always planted it in March. This year, a young agriculture officer visited and suggested planting in April, after the first rains had settled. Mr. Okoro folded his arms. "My father planted in March, and so did his father," he said. The officer did not argue; he only asked whether Mr. Okoro would try one small plot. After a pause, the farmer agreed, grumbling that he would still be right. At harvest time, the April plot gave larger roots than the others. Mr. Okoro said nothing at the market, but he quietly marked the new date in his calendar.

What does Mr. Okoro marking the new date show?
It shows he accepted the officer's advice and planned to plant in April in future, though he did not say so.

When Bela the cow went missing, the whole family searched for two days. On the third morning, Mohan, the youngest son, noticed that his grandfather's old dog, Moti, had not come for his breakfast. He followed the dog's paw prints through the grass, down to the hollow beyond the mango grove. There stood Bela, her leg tangled in a rope, with Moti lying calmly beside her. The dog wagged his tail when he saw Mohan. The boy untied the rope, patted the dog and led the cow home. Moti walked behind them, looking pleased with himself, and was given a bowl of milk.

What had Moti been doing while he was away?
He had stayed beside Bela to guard her, because Mohan found him lying calmly next to the trapped cow.

Maria noticed that the spider in the corner of the garden shed had built a new web every morning for a week. Each time, the web was in a slightly different spot. On the first day, it hung between the shelf and the window. On the second, it stretched from the hoe to the wall. Maria asked her uncle why the spider kept moving. He told her that a spider chooses its place where insects are most likely to fly. Maria placed a small jar of overripe banana near the window, and by evening a swarm of tiny flies had gathered there. The next morning the new web hung right above the jar.

Why did the spider put its web above the jar?
Many flies gathered around the jar, so it was a good place to catch food.

The summer heat in Jodhpur is strong from April to June. Temperatures often climb above forty degrees by noon, and the hot wind called loo blows across the streets. Shops close for a few hours in the afternoon, and people rest indoors behind thick curtains. Dinesh's grandmother makes a cool drink from raw mango, called aam panna, and she keeps a clay pot of water covered with a wet cloth near the door. Children are told not to play outside until five o'clock. In the evening, families sit on their rooftops, where a light breeze blows and the sky turns orange.

What cool drink does Dinesh's grandmother make?
She makes aam panna from raw mango.

After the long dry months, the pond behind the temple had shrunk to a tiny puddle. The fish, which usually swam in schools, huddled together in the last patch of water. Eight-year-old Varun saw them when he went to fetch his lost ball. He watched them for a while, then ran to his father and said, "They need help." His father found a big bucket, and together they scooped up the fish and carried them to the river half a kilometre away. Varun poured them in gently and stood watching until the last silver tail disappeared. He walked home slowly, smiling and quiet.

Why did Varun and his father carry the fish to the river?
The pond was almost dry, so the fish would not survive there.

A clock tower that has not worked for ten years stands at the corner of the village square. Its hands point to a quarter to four, and nobody has fixed them. Pigeons live inside its tiny windows, and the old iron door at the bottom is rusted shut. Once a year, on the village festival day, the children decorate the tower with paper flowers and strings of lights. The headmaster, Mr. Verma, tells them stories of how the tower's bell rang the hour in his youth. Though the clock is broken, villagers still say "Meet me at the tower" when they want to arrange a meeting.

Who decorates the tower on festival day?
The children decorate it.

Raj's family grows sweet potatoes on a small patch of sandy land. He plants the cuttings in ridges after the rains and covers them with soil. By autumn, thick vines have spread across the whole field. His mother digs the potatoes with a flat spade, shaking off the sand and putting them in a basket. Some are boiled and eaten with salt, others are baked in the ashes of the cooking fire. A neighbour buys the extra ones for her tea stall. This year, the biggest potato Raj dug weighed almost two kilos, and he showed it to everyone in the lane before his mother took it to the kitchen.

How much did the biggest potato weigh?
It weighed almost two kilos.

There is a saying in a village near Hardoi that mist in the morning means a hot day ahead. Farmers rely on it to decide when to sow and when to rest. They note that when mist fades by eight, the day is usually dry. If mist lingers till noon, rain may fall in the evening. Their children, who have never read a weather book, can often predict the day by looking at the sky from the doorstep. A visiting scientist, on hearing this, spent a week with the farmers and wrote down every saying in a notebook. He said that many of them matched what scientists had found.

What does mist in the morning mean, according to the saying?
It means a hot day is ahead.

Sara's family keeps twelve hens, and each one has a name. The big white hen is called Cloud, and the speckled one is Pepper. Every morning Sara scatters a handful of rice and broken wheat on the ground, and the hens run up in a noisy crowd. Then she carries a wicker basket to the little wooden coop to collect eggs. Usually there are eight or nine. She keeps the eggs in a bowl on the kitchen shelf, and her mother uses them for breakfast. On Sundays, Sara cleans the coop and puts fresh straw inside, so the hens have a soft place to lay.

How many hens does Sara's family keep?
They keep twelve hens.

Rice was drying in the courtyard of Priyanka's house when the clouds gathered. Her grandmother, who was sitting at the doorway shelling peas, looked at the sky and stood up quickly. "Everyone out!" she called. Priyanka's brothers dropped their game of marbles, and her mother ran out of the kitchen with a broom. Together, they swept the spread grain into heaps and pulled a heavy tarpaulin over it. Hardly had they finished tying the last corner when the first heavy drops fell. Priyanka's grandmother sat down again and picked up her peas, as calm as before, and nobody lost a single grain.

What would probably have happened if the family had been slow?
The rain would have soaked the rice and some of the grain would probably have been lost.

For several years, a pair of storks had nested on the roof of the old school in the village. When the school was repaired, workers removed the old nest, and the storks flew away. The children were upset. They collected twigs and straw and asked the headmaster for permission to build a new nest platform on the roof. With the help of the carpenter, they tied a wooden wheel to a pole and covered it with soft grass. For weeks nothing happened. Then one March morning, a stork appeared and circled twice. By the end of the week, there were two birds on the wheel, rearranging the twigs with their beaks.

What did the storks' return show about the children's work?
It showed that their nest platform worked, because a pair of storks came back and began using it.

Dadi's village has only one well that never dries up, and every woman in the lane knows its story. Her great-grandfather dug it with six other men during a hot summer long ago. They struck water after twenty days, and the whole village gathered to celebrate with sweet rice. Since then the well has been repaired twice. The stone wall around it is covered in green moss, and a rope with a steel bucket hangs from a wooden beam. In the evenings, girls come with brass pots, share news and laugh. Dadi says the well is the heart of the village because everyone meets there at least once a day.

How many days did the men take to reach water?
They took twenty days.

The whole village of Chandpur turned out to repair the road after the floods. Men carried stones in wheelbarrows, women mixed cement in large pans, and teenagers filled the potholes with gravel. Mrs. Dhillon brought tea and biscuits for the workers, and the shopkeeper sent a crate of oranges. Nobody was paid, and no officer was there to give orders. By evening, the muddy track had become a firm road again, and the school bus could pass. Grandfather Harpal leaned on his stick and looked at the work with pride. "In this village," he said, "when something breaks, we fix it together."

What does this passage show about the people of Chandpur?
It shows they cooperate and help each other, repairing the road together without being paid.

Everyone at the bus stop was wearing a thick coat except Rafael, who had left his at home. He stood with his arms wrapped around himself, his teeth chattering, pretending not to feel cold. His friend, Pedro, glanced at him and said nothing, but pulled off his woollen scarf and held it out. Rafael hesitated. Then he took it and wound it twice around his neck. The bus came ten minutes later, and when they climbed aboard, Rafael looked at his friend with a shy smile. At the next stop, he offered to hold both their bags as a way of saying thanks.

Why did Rafael offer to hold both the bags?
He wanted to thank Pedro for lending him the scarf.

The village of Pochampally was famous for its silk saris, but fewer young people were learning to weave. The old weaver, Mr. Reddy, noticed that the second loom had stood silent for weeks, ever since his apprentice had left to work in a city shop. He sat at the loom each morning anyway, and the clacking sound still came from his open window. One day, a girl from the neighbouring house knocked on the door and asked if she could try. Mr. Reddy looked at her for a long time. Then he moved over on the bench and handed her the shuttle. "Watch my hands first," he said, and the clacking resumed.

What does Mr. Reddy's action at the end suggest?
He was glad someone wanted to learn and was ready to pass on his skill, because he moved over and handed her the shuttle.

In the evenings, the village of Kunnur comes alive with the sound of drums. A group of young men practise outside the temple for the upcoming festival. They sit in a half circle, each holding a long drum on his lap, and a leader keeps the beat with a pair of brass cymbals. Children watch from the steps, clapping along. The older people sit on benches and nod their heads. The practice lasts an hour, and when it ends, the leader gives a short speech about the next day's rehearsal. The festival is only twelve days away, and the drummers hope to be perfect.

How many days are left before the festival?
There are twelve days left.

Mrs. Pereira's cow gave birth to a calf on the night of the village feast, and the whole neighbourhood came to see it in the morning. The calf was wobbly, with long legs and a white star on its forehead. Children stood in a row at the fence, whispering. Mrs. Pereira's husband had said they could not afford another animal, and he stood with his arms folded at the back of the group. But when the calf stumbled and fell, he stepped forward without thinking and helped it up, and then he stayed beside it, stroking its neck, for a long while. Nobody in the crowd said a word.

What do we learn about Mr. Pereira's feelings by the end?
He had grown fond of the calf, in spite of his earlier worry about money, because he helped it and stayed with it.

At the edge of the Western Ghats, a path leads up to a waterfall known as Silver Thread. The walk takes about forty minutes through thick forest. Visitors must start before ten, because the rangers close the gate at noon for safety. Along the way, one can see hornbills in the tall trees and giant squirrels leaping between branches. The path is slippery near the top, so the guide, Mr. Nair, always carries a long stick and asks everyone to hold the rope. At the end there is a clear pool, cold and green, where the water falls from a height of about thirty metres. Nobody is allowed to swim.

At what time do the rangers close the gate?
They close it at noon.

The sunflower field outside the town of Gadag stretches farther than the eye can see. In August, the flower heads, as large as dinner plates, all face the east, towards the morning sun. Bees fill the field with a steady hum. A photographer who visited last year said that standing among the plants made him feel like a small child among tall friendly giants. Farmers harvest the seeds in September and press them for oil. Children are allowed to take a few flower heads home, and they hang them from their roofs to dry and attract birds.

Which direction do the flower heads face?
They face the east, towards the morning sun.

The announcement at the village school was short: because of the heat wave, classes would end at ten o'clock until further notice. A cheer went up among the older boys, but the teachers did not smile. Mrs. Das reminded the class to drink water and wear caps on the way home. At the gate, Faisal noticed a little girl in the first grade standing with no hat, and he pulled his own cap from his bag and handed it to her. She looked up in surprise. He shrugged, waved and walked off bareheaded, squinting at the bright sun, whistling a tune.
