What does Faisal's action show about his character?
It shows he is thoughtful and generous, because he gave his own cap to a first-grade girl and walked home bareheaded in the sun.

In the first week of December, the rice in Anjali's village was ready to cut. Neighbours helped each other in turns, so each family's field was cleared in a single day. When Anjali's family's turn came, forty people arrived at dawn with sickles and baskets. The work went quickly, with songs and jokes passing along the lines. At midday, Anjali's mother served hot rice and dal on banana leaves to everyone seated in the field. By sunset, only stubble remained, and the sheaves stood tied in neat bundles. Anjali's father bowed to the group with folded hands, and he was already planning how to repay the favour next week at the neighbour's field.

What does this passage show about the neighbours?
It shows that they work together and help one another, so each field is harvested quickly.

Every year, on the first day of spring, the people of Kalimpong gather at the old stone bridge to release paper boats into the stream. Each boat carries a small wish, written by a child in coloured pencils. Teachers help the younger ones with spelling, and grandparents hold the hands of the toddlers at the edge of the water. A drummer plays slow beats as the boats float away. Some of them sink at once, while others travel as far as the bend before they disappear. Afterwards, everyone eats sweet rice cooked in milk, served on leaf plates, in the schoolyard.

What is released into the stream on the first day of spring?
Paper boats with small wishes written on them are released.

Neha's grandmother grows roses, marigolds and jasmine in pots on the balcony of their flat. She wakes at six, picks the dry leaves off every plant and sprinkles water with her fingers. The marigolds are for the prayer room, and the jasmine is tied into small strings and given to her granddaughters. A single red rose, the tallest one, belongs to Neha, who is allowed to cut it on her birthday. This year, the rose bloomed two days early, and Neha wore it in her hair to school. Her friends asked where she got it, and she said proudly that her grandmother had grown it.

Which flower is Neha allowed to cut on her birthday?
She is allowed to cut the tall red rose.

On the Walker family farm, apple picking starts in the first week of October. Everyone helps, even the youngest children. Mr. Walker puts up tall wooden ladders under the trees, and his daughter Emma holds each one steady while her brother climbs. The ripe apples go gently into canvas bags so that they do not bruise. Full bags are emptied into big crates, which are loaded onto a trailer pulled by a green tractor. Mrs. Walker serves lunch under the oldest tree: cheese sandwiches, boiled eggs and a jug of fresh juice. The family usually finishes picking about the end of the second week.

What is put on the trailer pulled by the tractor?
The crates full of apples are put on it.

Nobody had ever seen a tiger in the forest near the village of Bandipur, but everybody knew they lived there. One morning, a farmer noticed a heavy paw print in the soft soil near the stream. He called his neighbours, and they stood in a circle looking down at it. A small boy asked if they should be afraid. The farmer rubbed his chin and said that the tiger had passed by and gone on, and it was probably as shy of them as they were of it. From that day, the villagers did not walk alone at dusk, and they left the forest edge in peace.

What did the villagers do after seeing the paw print?
They stopped walking alone at dusk and kept away from the forest edge.

Whenever a stranger enters the town of Sirsi, the tea seller is the first to speak to him. He offers a seat, a glass of hot tea and a few words about the weather. He asks where the stranger is going, and where he is from, and he nods as though the answers matter. One day, a young man arrived with a heavy bag and a map he could not read. The tea seller listened to his story, then called the shopkeeper's son, who knew the road. Within minutes, the young man was on his way, with directions, a packet of biscuits and a surprising feeling that he had friends in a place he had never visited.

What does this passage show about the people of Sirsi?
It shows they are welcoming and helpful to strangers, like the tea seller who gave the young man tea and found someone to show him the road.

When Amina woke on Friday, her window was white with frost, and the water in the bucket outside had a thin skin of ice. She remembered her mother saying that the rice seedlings in the nursery bed were very young and tender. Without finishing her tea, Amina pulled on a sweater and ran to the field with an old plastic sheet. Her cousin Farid joined her, and together they covered the seedlings and held the corners down with stones. In the afternoon, when the sun came out, they uncovered the bed and found every tiny green plant standing straight. Amina sat on the bank and finally had her cold tea.

Why did Amina run to the field with a plastic sheet?
The frost could damage the young rice seedlings, so she wanted to protect them from the cold.

On harvest day in Kuttanad, the paddy fields stretch like a golden carpet below the level of the sea. Farmers wade through soft, wet mud to cut the heavy stalks with sickles. The sheaves are loaded onto long wooden boats and rowed to the threshing yard. Women sing as they work, and children ride on top of the piled bundles. At sunset, the boats glide home, low in the water. In the evening, the families gather at the farmhouse for a meal of rice, fish curry and boiled tapioca. The whole harvest takes about ten days, if the weather holds.

How are the sheaves carried to the threshing yard?
They are carried in long wooden boats.

The weather in the hills changed fast on the day of the school trip. At eight, the sky was blue, and the class set out with light bags and thin jackets. By eleven, clouds began to roll in from behind the peak, and a cold wind blew. Mr. Rao stopped the group on the path and looked up. "Everyone, put on your sweaters, and keep together," he said. The children, who had been running ahead, came back and stood close. Within twenty minutes, they were walking in a light drizzle, following the teacher in a line, back down to the bus.

Why did Mr. Rao ask the children to keep together and wear sweaters?
The weather turned cold and wet, so he wanted them warm and safe.

The hill station of Munnar is covered by mist for much of the monsoon. Tourists come to walk through it, wrapped in raincoats, and photograph tea bushes dripping with water. Vendors sell hot corn and spicy fritters from small wooden stalls. At night, the temperature drops to about fifteen degrees, and hotels light fires in their lounges. The roads become slippery, and drivers move slowly with their headlights on in broad daylight. Even so, the town is lively, because many people love the sound of rain on tin roofs and the smell of wet earth. The season lasts till the end of September.

Till when does the rainy season last in Munnar?
It lasts till the end of September.

When the tide goes out near Bhitarkanika, the mud flats are covered with thousands of tiny holes. Each belongs to a small crab, which scuttles out to look for food in the soft mud. Birds gather in great numbers: sandpipers, curlews and godwits, all probing with long beaks. Local children walk barefoot along the edge, collecting shells in plastic buckets. A teacher, Mr. Dash, takes his class there every month to count the species of birds they see. Last month they counted twenty-three kinds, including one that Mr. Dash had never seen before and had to look up in a book.

What do the birds use to probe the mud?
They use their long beaks.

Mangroves line the banks of the river near a village in the Sundarbans. Their roots rise from the mud like crooked fingers, and at high tide, only the tops of the trees can be seen. Honey collectors enter the forest in April, travelling in boats with a guard at the front, because tigers live nearby. They wear masks on the back of their heads, believing that a tiger will not attack a person who seems to be watching it. They collect honey from wild hives hanging among the branches and return after about a week, with large tin drums full.

In which month do the honey collectors enter the forest?
They enter the forest in April.

Everybody on the farm called Mr. Abebe's mule stubborn. When it did not want to carry a load, it simply stopped in the road and no amount of pulling could make it move. One day, while taking sacks to the market, the mule stopped halfway up a hill. Mr. Abebe sighed, sat down beside the animal and took out his lunch. He ate slowly, then broke off a piece of bread and held it out. The mule looked at him, took the bread and, after a few minutes, started walking again. Mr. Abebe followed with the empty bag, smiling to himself, and said nothing about it to anyone.

What did Mr. Abebe learn about handling the mule?
He learned that patience and a small treat worked better than pulling.

Two boys, Vikram and Ali, stood at the edge of the river and argued about whether it was safe to cross on the old log that lay across the water. Vikram, who was braver, put one foot on it and said it was dry and strong. Ali pointed to the green slime along the middle and shook his head. They stood there for a moment, then Vikram stepped back and picked up a stone. He threw it onto the log, and it slid straight off into the water. Without another word, the two boys turned and walked upstream to the bridge.

Why did Vikram change his mind about crossing?
The stone slid off the slimy log, showing him it was slippery and unsafe.

When Samuel opened the barn door, the cows did not move toward their feed as usual. They huddled together in the corner, looking at the roof. A few seconds later, he heard it too: a low rumble in the distance, like a train. He had lived on the farm for forty years and knew that sound. He quickly opened the gate to the high pasture, called the dog, and drove the cattle uphill, away from the river. His wife stuffed blankets and bread into a bag. By the time the water rose over the lower field, every animal was safe on the hill.

What was the rumble that Samuel heard?
It was probably a flood coming down the river, which is why he moved the cattle uphill.

Grandfather Joseph kept a small tin cup out on the garden wall. Each time it rained, he measured the water in the cup with a ruler and wrote the number in a notebook. His granddaughter Tina thought it was strange and asked him why. He opened the notebook and showed her pages filled with numbers going back thirty years. "This tells me when the monsoon comes early and when it comes late," he said. "A farmer who remembers the rain can plan his sowing." Tina picked up the pencil and asked if she could write the next number. From then on, the notebook had two handwritings.

What does the notebook teach Tina about her grandfather?
It shows he is careful and patient and that he values keeping records to help farmers plan.

The mango tree in front of Rohan's house is more than fifty years old. Each March it fills with tiny cream-coloured flowers, and bees buzz around it from dawn until dusk. By May the branches hang low with green mangoes, and by June the fruits turn golden and sweet. Rohan's grandmother makes pickle from the raw ones and keeps the ripe ones in a basket for guests. Squirrels and parrots also love the tree, so Rohan's job is to scare them away in the afternoons with a clapping stick. He does not mind much, because the tree gives him shade for his homework.

What does Rohan's grandmother make from the raw mangoes?
She makes pickle.

Maya's grandfather keeps bees in six wooden boxes at the edge of his orchard. In spring, he wears a hat with a net and uses a metal tool with a smoking cloth to calm the bees. Gently, he lifts out the frames and checks that the queen is laying eggs. Honey is collected only twice a year, in June and in November. He pours it through a clean cloth into glass jars and sticks a handwritten label on each one. Maya's job is to carry the jars to a shelf in the cool storeroom. She is not allowed near the boxes unless her grandfather is beside her.

How many wooden bee boxes does Maya's grandfather have?
He has six boxes.

Laila's grandmother lives in a village in Morocco where the houses are painted blue and white. Each morning, she goes to the communal bakery with a tray of dough, which the baker places in a big wood-fired oven. The tray returns an hour later with round loaves, still hot. Laila and her cousins collect the bread for the whole street, running from door to door. In the afternoon, they sit in the courtyard with a glass of mint tea. The village's oldest man, Si Ahmed, tells them stories about desert travellers and lost caravans, and no one is allowed to talk until he has finished.

What colour are the houses in Laila's grandmother's village?
They are painted blue and white.

Tashi's grandmother kept a yak herd in the high pastures above the monastery. Over the years she had noticed that when the herd came down from the pastures earlier than usual, the weather turned cold within a week. This year, in late August, the yaks started coming down, even though the grass up high was still green. Tashi's grandmother did not ask why. She pulled out the winter blankets from the chest and told Tashi to bring in extra firewood. When the first snow fell eight days later, the family had everything they needed, and the neighbours came to ask how she had known.

How did Tashi's grandmother know winter would come early?
She had seen the yaks come down from the high pastures earlier than usual, which in past years had meant cold weather soon.

The new bridge over the canal near Sundarpur was finished in March. Before, villagers had to cross on a narrow plank, and many people slipped in the water, especially during the monsoon. Mothers carrying babies held their breath on the crossing, and the school bus had to take a long detour of nearly eight kilometres. Now the bridge is wide enough for two carts to pass. On the first morning after the opening, seventy-year-old Ramdas walked from one side to the other three times, tapping the railing with his stick. "I did not think I would live to see it," he told the children.

Why did Ramdas walk across the bridge three times?
He was delighted and amazed that the bridge existed, since he had long wished for it.

The bus to the town leaves the village of Kotli only twice a day, at seven and at three. Mrs. Kaur missed the morning bus because her goat had wandered off, and she walked to the gate just as the dust was settling behind it. She stood there for a moment with her bag on her arm. Then she turned around and walked back, muttering. She spent the day mending a fence and baking bread, and at three o'clock, she sat on the doorstep and watched the afternoon bus pass without stopping. Her appointment in town would have to wait for another day.

How did Mrs. Kaur probably feel as she watched the bus go?
She felt annoyed and disappointed, since she muttered and had missed her trip.

The fisherman Domingo set out before dawn every morning in his small wooden boat. For a week, he had returned with only a handful of tiny fish, hardly enough to feed his family. On Sunday, instead of casting his nets in the usual spot, he rowed up the river toward a bend where the water ran deeper and darker. His wife watched him go from the bank with her hand on her forehead. That evening, he came back with a boat so full that he had to call his son to help him carry the load. Domingo said nothing, but he grinned as he tied up the boat.

Why did Domingo grin as he tied up the boat?
He had caught plenty of fish after a week of poor luck, so his move to the deeper water at the bend had worked.

When the monsoon floods came early to a village near Sitamarhi, Rekha's family had little time to move. The water rose over the road at midnight, and by dawn it was knee-deep in the courtyard. Her father lifted the youngest child on his shoulders and told everyone to hold hands. They waded to the high school building, where the village had agreed to meet in a flood. Other families were already there, sharing mats and food. Rekha noticed that nobody asked who had more or less. A woman handed her a cup of hot tea, and she realised with a small shock that she was not afraid any more.

Why was Rekha no longer afraid at the end?
She felt safe and supported, because the families at the school shared mats and food, and a woman gave her hot tea.

The farmers of Dharwad knew what the clouds meant when they saw them gather in the west on a hot afternoon in June. But this year, the clouds had passed three times without a single drop of rain. When the fourth set of clouds came, Mr. Patil did not look up. He sat at the edge of his field with a handful of dry seeds, rolling them between his fingers. His wife came and sat beside him, and neither of them spoke. After a while, she said they could wait one more week before sowing. He nodded slowly, put the seeds back in the cloth bag and tied the knot.

How was Mr. Patil feeling, and what shows it?
He was worried and discouraged; he did not look up at the clouds, and sat silently with dry seeds.

A gentle rain was falling on the tea garden of Darjeeling on Thursday morning. Pickers in plastic aprons moved along the rows, plucking two leaves and a bud from each bush and tossing them into baskets on their backs. The rain stopped around ten, and shafts of sunlight lit up the wet leaves. Down the slope, the factory chimney sent up thin white smoke. At noon, the workers sat on their baskets and drank sweet tea from steel mugs. The supervisor, Mr. Lepcha, walked among them with a notebook, weighing each basket and writing down the numbers.

What do the pickers pluck from each bush?
They pluck two leaves and a bud.

Lucia runs the only bakery in the village of San Telmo, and she begins work at three in the morning. First she lights the stone oven with dry olive wood. Then she kneads the dough on a long table, adding a pinch of salt and a spoon of olive oil. By six o'clock, the first loaves are ready, and the smell travels down the hill to wake the sleeping houses. Farmers stop by on their way to the fields to buy warm rolls. Lucia's niece, Carmen, delivers the bread to the old people who cannot walk to the shop, riding a small blue bicycle with a basket on the front.

Who delivers bread to the old people?
Lucia's niece, Carmen, delivers it.

Anya found a baby bird on the ground beneath the tree in her garden. It was small and pink, with a few feathers, and it was making a thin squeaking sound. She looked up and saw a nest high on a branch. She ran to get her mother, who told her that the bird's parents would not abandon it just because a human had touched it. Anya found a small ladder, climbed up carefully, and put the chick back in the nest. Then she went inside and watched from the window. A few minutes later, two adult birds returned with food in their beaks, and she let out a long breath.

How did Anya feel when the parent birds returned?
She felt relieved and happy, because her rescue had worked and the chick would be fed.

A snake slid out from the woodpile in Zainab's yard one evening. She saw it first, a dark thin shape moving between the logs, and stood very still. Her younger cousin Ali, who was playing nearby, started to run toward it with a stick. "Stop!" Zainab said sharply, grabbing his shirt. The snake paused, then continued into the tall grass at the edge of the yard. Zainab told Ali that snakes only bite when frightened or cornered. That night, she called the forest office, and a man came the next day to explain which snakes were harmless and which were not. Ali sat very quiet and listened to every word.

Why did Zainab grab Ali's shirt?
She wanted to stop him from frightening the snake and getting bitten, since she knew snakes bite when frightened or cornered.

Everyone in a village near Palampur woke up to a silent morning. The wind that usually rattled the shutters had vanished, and the air was strangely warm for winter. Birds did not sing, and the dogs lay flat on the ground. Old Mr. Thakur, sitting on his porch, rubbed his chin and said that a storm was coming. Nobody listened until noon, when a thick blue-black cloud covered the whole sky. By the time the thunder started, the shops had already closed, the cows were in their sheds, and families were sitting together indoors, thanks to the old man's warning.

What clues did Mr. Thakur use to predict the storm?
He noticed the sudden stillness, the unusual warmth, and the quiet birds and dogs.

On the third morning of the monsoon, Salim's father took his tools to the roof and checked every corner for leaks. He found a crack above the kitchen and filled it with tar. Salim, holding the ladder below, asked why his father was working so hard when the rain had already started. His father told him that the first week of heavy rain was always the worst, and a dry kitchen was worth more than a rested back. That night, the storm lashed the roof, and water poured off the edges in thick sheets. Inside, Salim's mother cooked dinner, and the kitchen floor was perfectly dry.

Why had Salim's father repaired the roof?
He knew heavy rain would come and wanted to stop the kitchen from leaking.

The morning in Shimla began with a thin white mist that covered the hills. By ten o'clock the mist had thickened so much that Aarav could not see the house across the road. The school bus driver switched on his yellow lights and drove very slowly. Shopkeepers lit small lamps outside their doors, and a man selling roasted corn pulled a thick shawl around his shoulders. Even the dogs stayed under the tea stall bench and did not bark. At noon, a gentle wind pushed the mist up the valley, and the sun came out, bright and warm, as if nothing had happened.

Why did the bus driver switch on his yellow lights?
The mist was so thick that it was hard to see, so he used the lights to be seen and to drive safely.

Noor's father owned the only radio in the lane, and every evening at seven, neighbours came to listen to the news. They sat on the veranda steps, passing around a flask of tea. One evening in August, the radio would not work. Noor's father opened the back, shook it, tapped it and finally put it aside with a sigh. The neighbours left slowly, each saying a polite goodnight. The next morning, before school, Noor saw old Mr. Banerjee standing at the door with a small toolbox in his hand. "I used to mend these," he said, smiling. By evening the radio was playing again, and the veranda was full.

Why did Mr. Banerjee come to Noor's door with a toolbox?
He had heard the radio was broken and, since he used to repair radios, he wanted to fix it.

The village well at Sonepur has dried up, so women now walk to the river with pots on their heads. The path leads through a field of sunflowers, past a small shrine and down a flight of twenty mud steps. At the river, they fill their pots and rest for a few minutes in the shade of a peepal tree. Teenage girls often bring their younger brothers along, and the boys splash in the shallow water while their sisters wait. The return walk is uphill, so the women go slowly, balancing the heavy pots and chatting. Each family needs about four trips a day.

How many mud steps lead down to the river?
There are twenty mud steps.

The village dog, Raja, belongs to nobody and everybody. He sleeps in the shade of the bus shelter during the day and walks the streets at night as though he were the watchman. The tea stall owner gives him a biscuit each morning, and the school children save pieces of their lunch for him. In the monsoon, a woman from the lane puts out an old gunny sack for him to lie on. Last year, he followed the postman for a whole week, but then he came back to his place at the bus shelter. Everyone was happy to see him, and the tea stall owner gave him two biscuits.

Where does Raja sleep during the day?
He sleeps in the shade of the bus shelter.

The old schoolhouse at Nandgaon had only one door, and the children had to bend their heads to go through it. When the new government school was built next to the road, with wide corridors and big windows, everyone expected the old building to be pulled down. Instead, the villagers voted to keep it. They painted its walls white, repaired the roof and put a board outside that read "Our First School." On the first day of the new year, the oldest villagers gathered in its dusty room, sitting on small benches that were too low for them, and spent the morning laughing about their childhood.

Why did the villagers decide to keep the old schoolhouse?
It held happy memories for them, and they valued it as the place where they first studied.

Tomorrow is the day when a village in the Nilgiri hills chooses its best vegetable. All the farmers bring their finest produce to the village hall: cabbages as big as footballs, carrots as long as a ruler and glossy purple brinjals. Three judges walk slowly along the tables, writing notes on small cards. They look at colour, size and freshness. At noon, a bell rings, and the winners are called to the front. The first prize is a silver cup and a bag of seeds. Last year, the cup was won by Mr. Kutty for a pumpkin that took four men to lift.

How many men were needed to lift last year's winning pumpkin?
It took four men to lift it.

Every evening at sunset, hundreds of crows gather on the neem tree outside Ishaan's window. They arrive in small groups, calling loudly, and settle on the branches one by one. For an hour the tree is full of noise and flapping wings. Then, as if someone has given a signal, all the birds go quiet at the same moment. Ishaan has watched this for years, and he has noticed that when it is going to rain, the crows come earlier and sit lower on the tree. Yesterday they arrived before five, and Ishaan took an umbrella to school this morning. By noon, the sky was dark with clouds.

Why did Ishaan take an umbrella to school?
The crows arrived early the day before, which he knows is a sign that rain is coming.

A small boat called a shikara glides across Dal Lake every morning, carrying vegetables from the floating gardens to the market. The boatman, Abdul, stands at the back and pushes it forward with a long paddle shaped like a heart. In his boat today are bright red tomatoes, green gourds, lotus stems and bunches of mint. Other boats come alongside, and the sellers call out prices in rhythmic voices. The whole market floats on the water. By nine, most of the produce is sold, and Abdul returns home with a handful of coins and a loaf of bread from the baker's boat.

What shape is Abdul's paddle?
It is shaped like a heart.

A pair of kingfishers has built a nest in the bank of the stream behind Isha's school. Their bright blue backs flash against the green leaves when they dive for small fish. Isha's class has been told to watch from a distance and not to throw stones or make loud noises. Each lunch break, a few students sit on the grass about twenty steps away with a notebook and write what they see. So far, they have counted nine dives in one hour. Their science teacher says the chicks will hatch in about three weeks, and she plans to bring a pair of binoculars for the whole class.

Why do the students sit twenty steps away from the nest?
They have been told to watch from a distance so they do not disturb the birds.

At Mudumalai, Hira and her cousins watched the elephants bathe in the river. A keeper, called a mahout, sat on the neck of the largest elephant and scrubbed its back with a coconut husk. The elephant filled its trunk with water and sprayed it over its own head, splashing the children on the bank. A calf played in the shallows nearby, rolling and squeaking. The bath lasted nearly an hour. Afterwards, the elephants were led back to the camp to be fed with balls of rice and jaggery wrapped in grass. The cousins stayed for the feeding and were allowed to give one ball to the calf.

What did the mahout use to scrub the elephant's back?
The mahout used a coconut husk.

Last month, Priti's class went on a field trip to a mangrove swamp. They wore rubber boots because the mud was deep and sticky. Their guide, Dr. Hassan, showed them the breathing roots of the trees, which stick up from the mud like pencils. He explained that these roots help the trees get air when the tide covers the ground. Tiny crabs scuttled over the mud, and mudskipper fish hopped away as the children approached. Priti took twenty photographs, and when she got home, she printed her favourite and stuck it above her desk. Her little brother asked if mudskippers could be kept as pets, but Priti said no.

What did Dr. Hassan show the children?
He showed them the breathing roots of the mangrove trees.

Ants have been marching along the kitchen wall of Pooja's house for two days. They come in a neat brown line from a crack near the window and go straight to the sugar jar. Her mother tried wiping the wall twice, but the line came back each time. Then Pooja remembered that their science teacher had said ants leave a scent trail for others to follow. She took a wet cloth with a little vinegar and scrubbed the whole path from the crack to the shelf. The next morning, the ants were wandering about the wall in confusion, and there was no line at all.

Why did the ants wander in confusion the next morning?
Pooja cleaned away their scent trail with vinegar, so they could no longer follow it.

Mei's tomato plant had grown tall and strong, but it had no tomatoes. Day after day, she looked at the yellow flowers and wondered. Her neighbour, an old man named Mr. Chan, saw her frowning and came over with a small paintbrush. He gently touched the brush inside one flower, then another, and another. "No bees came, so we must be the bees," he said. Mei laughed and took the brush from him to try. A week later, she called him over, holding up a small green ball no bigger than a marble. They both stood and looked at it for a long time without speaking.

What was Mr. Chan doing with the paintbrush?
He was moving pollen from flower to flower, since no bees had visited the plant.

The sun rises early in the village of Kausani, and Anil has made a habit of watching it from the roof of his house. He climbs the narrow stairs at five, wraps himself in a blanket and sits facing the east. First, the snowy peaks in the far distance turn a pale pink. Then the colour grows deeper, turning orange and finally a bright gold. A few birds call from the pine trees, and smoke rises from the kitchen chimneys below. Anil's mother brings him a cup of hot milk, and they sit together without saying much until the sun is completely above the hills.

What does Anil's mother bring him on the roof?
She brings him a cup of hot milk.

Rain makes the soil of the hills near Cherrapunji so soft that roots wash out and stones tumble down. The people who live there have found a clever way to build bridges. They take the roots of the rubber fig tree and guide them across a stream with bamboo poles. Over many years, the roots grow thick and strong and weave together into a living bridge. Some of these bridges are more than a hundred years old and can carry fifty people at once. Each generation looks after the bridges its grandparents began, and trains the young trees for those who will follow.

What kind of tree roots are used to build the bridges?
The roots of the rubber fig tree are used.

All of Adoor agreed that the new teacher, Mr. Das, was too strict. He insisted that students arrive by eight and wear polished shoes. He assigned homework every day, including Saturdays. Parents grumbled at the tea stall, and children rolled their eyes. But when the board results came out in May, every one of his twenty students had passed, and three of them had scored the highest marks the school had ever seen. At the next meeting of the village council, the same parents stood up one by one and thanked him. Mr. Das only nodded and said that the children had done the work.

How did the parents' opinion of Mr. Das change?
They first thought he was too strict, but after the excellent results they thanked him.

Roshni's father keeps bees as well as growing mustard, and the two jobs help each other. The bees pollinate the mustard flowers, so the crop is richer, and the mustard flowers give nectar for the bees. In February, when the yellow fields are in full bloom, the boxes are placed along the edge of the field. Roshni's job is to carry water in a small can to a shallow dish so that the bees can drink. In March, the honey is thick and golden with a mild mustard flavour. Her father sells it in glass jars at the Sunday market in the town.

When is the honey thick and golden?
It is thick and golden in March.

Ellen noticed that the sunflowers on the south side of the farm were all drooping, while those near the river stood proud and green. She walked along the row, touching the soil. It was dry and crumbly near the road, but damp close to the river. She ran home and told her father, who said that he had been too busy to check. Together they pulled a long hose from the tank and watered each plant. The next morning, Ellen got up early and went to see. The flowers had not straightened yet, but they looked less sad. She nodded to herself, and decided to water them again that evening.

Why were the sunflowers by the road drooping?
The soil near the road was dry, so the plants needed water.

The cyclone shelter in a village near Konark is a two-storey concrete building painted bright yellow. It stands on high ground, a short walk from the beach. The ground floor holds a store of rice, blankets, candles and first-aid boxes. The upper floor is a large hall where families can sleep. A committee of villagers keeps the shelter clean and holds a practice drill every year before the storm season. During the drill, children take their school bags and walk quickly, in pairs, with a teacher at the front. A siren on the roof can be heard from two kilometres away.

What colour is the cyclone shelter painted?
It is painted bright yellow.

When the sun goes down over the lake at Pushkar, hundreds of birds fly home in long straight lines. First come the cormorants, black and quick. Then come the egrets, white and slow. The last to arrive are the herons, which land on a single leg in the shallow water and stand still for a long time. Tourists gather on the stone steps with cameras, but the local boys, who have seen it all their lives, only keep an eye on the clock for their evening tea. The lake is calm and gold, and the whole scene seems like a painting that moves.

Which birds arrive last at the lake?
The herons arrive last.

Fireflies gather in the forests around Bhandardara in the weeks just before the monsoon. At dusk, the trees at the edge of the village begin to blink with thousands of tiny lights, flashing on and off among the leaves. Visitors come in the evenings with their families and stand silently along the forest path. Local children have been taught not to catch the insects, because adult fireflies live only a few weeks. A guide, Mr. Sawant, tells the visitors that the lights are signals the fireflies use to find a mate. The show lasts about a month and is best on a night without a moon.

How long does the firefly show last?
It lasts about a month.

Holi morning dawned clear and warm in the village of Barsana. By nine o'clock, the streets were full of people carrying bags of powder in red, yellow, green and pink. They threw colour in the air and on each other, laughing and shouting. Drummers marched along the lane, and a group of women sang folk songs from a balcony. Children ran with water guns, while elders sat on benches in clean white clothes, trying to stay dry, though they usually failed. By noon, everyone was covered in bright dust, and the lanes were stained in all colours.

What time did the streets fill with people carrying powder?
They filled up by nine o'clock.

For months, the villagers of Anantapur had prayed for rain, and finally, in July, it came. The first night, nobody slept. They sat in doorways and listened to the steady sound on the roofs. In the morning, the lanes were rivers of red mud, and the cattle stood with their faces turned up. A farmer named Venkat stood in his dry field with his boots off, letting the water run over his feet. He bent and picked up a handful of wet soil, which smelled rich and cool. "Now," he said softly, and began to walk toward the shed for his seed bags.

What did Venkat plan to do after the rain?
He planned to begin sowing seed, since he went to fetch his seed bags.

Every year in January, the village of Wadgaon holds a kite festival on the dry riverbed. Boys and girls bring kites made of coloured paper and bamboo sticks,, and older cousins help the little ones tie the strings. A man named Prakash sells fresh sesame sweets from a cart. Shouts of laughter fill the air whenever a kite dips and tumbles. The festival lasts the whole day, and prizes are given at five in the evening for the highest kite and the neatest design. This year, twelve-year-old Zoya won the prize for the highest kite.

Who won the prize for the highest kite this year?
Twelve-year-old Zoya won it.

Early one morning, Ravi saw a peacock dancing on the roof of the village temple. Its blue neck shone in the sunlight, and the long green tail was spread like a giant fan. A few smaller peahens walked near the wall below, pretending not to look. Ravi stood very still, holding his breath so as not to frighten it. The dance lasted nearly five minutes, and then the bird gave a loud cry and flew down into the neem grove. Ravi ran home and told his sister, but she did not believe him until she saw a fallen feather by the steps.

What did Ravi see on the temple roof?
He saw a peacock dancing.

Greta's farm in Germany sits at the foot of a gentle hill. She keeps forty pigs, ten cows and a donkey named Hugo. Each morning, she mixes feed in large metal buckets and carries them to the troughs. In the afternoon, she cleans the stable with a long broom and sprays the floor with water. On Fridays, a veterinary student named Paul comes to check the animals and weigh the piglets. Hugo, the donkey, has no real job, but he is the farm's favourite. He follows Greta around the yard and nudges her pocket whenever he thinks she has a carrot.

What is the donkey's name?
The donkey's name is Hugo.

The mountains of Ladakh are home to a rare animal called the snow leopard. Few people have ever seen one, because it is quiet, shy and the colour of rock. Local guides say the best months to look for it are January and February, when snow forces the leopard down to lower slopes. Visitors wake at four, drive in the dark, and wait for hours with telescopes in the freezing air. Many return without seeing anything, but they do not seem to mind. They tell stories of fresh paw prints in the snow and the long, strange calls echoing off the cliffs.

In which months do guides say it is best to look for the snow leopard?
They say the best months are January and February.

At sunset on the hill above Ooty, a girl named Divya noticed that the grass was moving even though there was no wind. She bent down and looked closely. Hundreds of small insects were crawling slowly up the stalks all together, as though following a signal. She had seen this once before, on the day before a storm, and she felt a small chill. She took her little brother's hand and walked home quickly. Her mother, who was lighting the lamp, was surprised to see them back so early. That night, a heavy rain washed the road, and Divya did not tell anyone about the grass, but she was glad.

Why did Divya hurry home?
She thought the moving insects meant a storm was coming and wanted to get home before it started.

Daniel stood at the fence of his orchard and counted the cherry trees. Three of them were bare, even though the rest were covered in blossoms. His brother Lars, who had come to help for the week, bent down and picked up a handful of soil near the first bare tree. He rubbed it between his fingers and sniffed. "Too wet," he said. "Water stays here after rain." Daniel looked at the slope of the ground and saw, for the first time, that the three trees stood in a shallow dip. Without saying more, he went to the shed, brought out two shovels and handed one to his brother.

What did Daniel realise by looking at the slope of the ground?
He realised the three bare trees stood in a dip where water collected, which probably damaged them.

In the vineyards of northern Italy, grape picking begins in the middle of September. Whole families arrive at dawn, wearing hats and carrying small curved knives. Each picker walks along a row, cutting the bunches and dropping them into plastic crates. When a crate is full, a worker carries it to the trailer at the end of the row. By eleven, the sun is warm, and the pickers stop for a long break with bread, cheese and olives. In the afternoon, the trailers go to the cellar, where the grapes are crushed. The smell of sweet juice fills the whole valley for weeks.

When does grape picking begin in the vineyards?
It begins in the middle of September.

A tall stranger came to the village of Hampi and asked for work. He said little, but carried sacks, mended walls and cleaned the well without any complaint. The headman gave him a place to sleep in the grain store. Some villagers whispered that he must be hiding something. One evening, a boy fell from a tree and cut his leg badly. The stranger lifted him gently, washed the wound with clean water and wrapped it in a strip of cloth torn from his own shirt. The next morning, the whispers had stopped, and an old woman came to his door with a bowl of hot rice.

Why did the whispering stop?
The stranger's kindness to the injured boy showed the villagers that he was a good man.

The giant bamboo grove at the edge of the village grows so fast that it can be seen getting taller from one day to the next. The villagers cut the stalks to make fences, ladders, baskets and the frames of their houses. The young shoots, soft and pale, are cooked in curries. Children are told that the bamboo flowers only once in about fifty years, and then dies. The oldest woman in the village remembers one such flowering, when she was a girl, and says that thousands of rats came out of the forest to eat the seeds, and then went on to eat the grain in the village stores.

What do villagers make from bamboo stalks?
They make fences, ladders, baskets and house frames.

The cowshed of the Sharma family is cleaned twice a day, once at dawn and once at dusk. The dung is carried to a pit behind the shed, where it is mixed with straw and left for several weeks to rot. This becomes compost, which the family spreads on their vegetable garden. Part of the dung is shaped into round cakes and dried in the sun to be used as fuel for the cooking stove. The family also has a small biogas plant, which makes gas for the kitchen from the waste. Mrs. Sharma says that nothing from the cows is wasted.

What is the dung mixed with in the pit?
It is mixed with straw.

The goat shed on Aisha's farm holds eleven goats and four kids. Each morning, Aisha lets them out onto the hillside to graze, and each evening, she calls them back with a long, high whistle. The white goat with a black ear is always first to come running. In winter, Aisha covers the shed floor with dry straw and hangs an old blanket over the door to keep out the wind. Last month, one of the goats had twin kids at midnight. Aisha stayed in the shed until dawn and then gave the mother goat warm water with a little jaggery.

What did Aisha give the mother goat after the twins were born?
She gave her warm water with a little jaggery.

It had not rained in a village near Phalodi for fourteen months. The ponds had turned to cracked clay, and the farmers had sold most of their cattle. In the village square, the elders gathered to perform a prayer for rain. They sat in a circle, beating a slow rhythm on small drums. Children stood along the edge and watched in silence. The prayer lasted until sunset, and then everyone went home to eat a simple meal of millet bread and chutney. That night, a distant roll of thunder was heard, and two days later, the first rain fell. The village celebrated for a whole week.

How long had it been since the last rain in the village?
It had been fourteen months.

In the high apple villages above Kullu, the first snow usually comes after the apples have been picked. This year, however, it came early. On the morning of October fifth, Mr. Kapoor opened his front door and found that the whole hillside was white. The apple orchards on the opposite slope, still full of unpicked fruit, looked as if they had been dusted with sugar. Pickers rushed to collect the apples before the weight of the snow broke the branches. Within two hours, the whole village was in the orchards, laughing and shouting, filling baskets and warming their hands over small fires.

What date did Mr. Kapoor find the valley white?
It was the morning of October fifth.

At seven every evening, the village of Khajuri gathers in the open ground beside the school for a volleyball game. A net is stretched between two wooden poles, and the line is drawn with white powder. Teams are chosen quickly, and anyone may join, from the schoolboys to the bank clerk. The shopkeeper, Mr. Nayak, acts as referee, calling points loudly and keeping the score on a slate. The game stops when it gets too dark to see the ball. Afterwards, players share a tin of roasted groundnuts and talk about the match as they walk home together.

Who is the referee in the evening game?
Mr. Nayak, the shopkeeper, is the referee.

Pradeep planted tomato seedlings in neat rows and watered them every evening. After two weeks, he noticed that the leaves on the left side of the field were curling and turning yellow, while the right side stayed green. He walked along the rows, looking at the soil. The ground on the left was hard and pale, and water seemed to run off it instead of sinking in. On the right, the soil was dark and crumbly. Pradeep scratched his head, then went to the shed and came back with two sacks of compost and a spade. He began mixing the compost into the left side, row by row, until the sun went down.

Why did Pradeep begin adding compost to the left side of the field?
The soil there was hard and pale and the plants were turning yellow, so he wanted to improve it.

Cotton picking in the fields near Nagpur starts in October and goes on until January. Women walk along the rows with long cloth bags tied across their shoulders. They pull the white fluffy bolls from the dry brown plants, taking care not to prick their fingers on the sharp husks. At the end of each day, the bags are weighed at a small shed, and the workers are paid by the kilogram. A good picker can gather more than fifty kilos in a day. The cotton is then loaded onto trucks and taken to a mill in the town, where it is cleaned and spun into thread.

How are the workers paid?
They are paid by the kilogram of cotton they pick.

A boy named Mateo lives in a village beside a wide rainforest river. Each morning, he paddles a small wooden canoe to school, taking about forty minutes. On the way, he sees pink river dolphins surfacing and sometimes a sloth hanging from a branch. Parrots shriek in the trees, and the air smells of wet leaves. At school, there are twelve children, one teacher and no electricity. They learn to read by the light from the open windows. In the afternoon, Mateo paddles back home, usually with a couple of fish that he has caught on the way, wrapped in a banana leaf for his mother.

How long does Mateo take to reach school?
He takes about forty minutes.

During the dry season, forest fires are a danger in the hills near Almora. The forest department has built watchtowers, and guards take turns to watch from them with binoculars. If they see smoke, they call the village heads by phone, and each village sends a team with branches and buckets. The villagers know that a fire spreads fastest uphill, so they work from above. School children are taught how to make a firebreak by clearing dry leaves in a strip. Last year, thanks to a quick alert, a fire that began at noon was put out before sunset.

What do guards use to watch for fires?
They use binoculars from watchtowers.

Rani sells flower garlands at the gate of the village temple. On most days, she is cheerful and greets every visitor by name. Last Thursday, however, she sat with her head down and her hands in her lap, and several garlands lay unsold in the basket. The tea stall owner noticed it and sent his son over with a hot glass of tea. When she did not drink it, the boy ran back and told his father. That evening, three neighbours came to her house with sweets and asked what was wrong. Rani wiped her eyes and said her mother had been ill in a faraway town.

How did Rani feel last Thursday, and how can you tell?
She felt sad and worried; she sat with her head down and left garlands unsold.

A loud rooster crows at the farm of the Kapoor family every morning at half past four. Mr. Kapoor gets up first and heats water for his wife's tea. By five, the whole family is awake. The sons feed the poultry, the daughters take the cows to the shed and Mr. Kapoor opens the tube-well. Mrs. Kapoor makes rotis on a clay stove in the open courtyard, and the smell drifts across the yard. By seven, everyone has had breakfast, and the school bag rack by the door is filled with satchels. The bus honks outside, and the children run out, tying their shoelaces on the way.

At what time does the rooster crow?
It crows at half past four every morning.

In the village of Dhampur, a boy named Suraj always came last in the school race. The others teased him, and he took it quietly. One day, the sports teacher, Mr. Khan, noticed that Suraj walked three kilometres to school every day, along a rough path, carrying two buckets of water for his mother. Mr. Khan took him aside and spoke to him for a while. The next month, a district race was announced. Suraj was entered. On the day, he ran with his lips pressed tight, and he finished fourth out of thirty. His friends, who had teased him before, cheered as loudly as anyone, and Mr. Khan wrote his name on the board.

Why could Suraj do well in the district race even though he came last at school?
Walking three kilometres daily while carrying water had made him strong and gave him a lot of practice.

Mr. Hussain's garden was famous for its roses, so the neighbours were surprised when he began digging up half of them. He replaced the flower beds with rows of onions, tomatoes and beans. People shook their heads. When asked why, he only said that the price of vegetables had gone up. Only his wife knew that their daughter had lost her job in the city and had come home with her two small children. In the evenings, the neighbours saw all five of them kneeling in the vegetable beds together, laughing and getting muddy. After a while, they stopped asking questions.

Why did Mr. Hussain dig up the roses?
He wanted to grow food for his family, as his daughter and grandchildren had come home without a job.

The grain store of Kottur village is the biggest building in the village. It is made of mud bricks with a thatched roof and stands on stilts to keep out rats and damp. Each family stores a portion of its harvest there, to be shared in bad years. The keeper of the store, an old man named Muniswamy, keeps a ledger in which he writes the amount given by each household. Twice a year, he opens the store for a public count, and the villagers gather to watch. During the famine of three years ago, the store fed the whole village for four months.

Why is the grain store built on stilts?
It is built on stilts to keep out rats and damp.

At Brook Farm in Wales, lambing season begins in March. Farmer Gwen walks through the fields at night with a torch, checking each ewe. When a lamb is born, she weighs it and marks it with a coloured dot of paint, so that it can be matched with its mother. Weak lambs are brought to the kitchen, where they lie in a box beside the stove. Gwen's two children feed them warm milk from small bottles. When the lambs are strong enough, they are returned to the field. By May, the hillside is filled with white bouncing shapes, and the children name their favourites.

Where are the weak lambs brought?
They are brought to the kitchen and kept in a box beside the stove.

The village of Pattadakal holds a market every Wednesday on the dry bed of the stream. Sellers spread cloth on the ground and set out pots, onions, plastic buckets, bangles and second-hand clothes. Bullock carts bring in sacks of grain from distant farms. A man with a loudspeaker advertises a medicine for coughs, while a boy beside him sells roasted gram in paper cones. The air is full of dust, shouting and the smell of frying. At four o'clock, when the sun is lower, the sellers fold up their cloths, and the stream bed becomes an empty stretch of sand again, with a few stray dogs sniffing around.

On which day is the market held?
It is held every Wednesday.

Boats in the delta village of Kainat are not only used for fishing. A boat carries children to school in the morning and comes back to collect them in the afternoon. Another carries a doctor on Wednesdays, and a post boat brings letters and parcels. At weddings, a decorated boat takes the bride and groom around the village while friends follow in smaller craft playing drums. Even the temple festival involves a float, lit with lamps and slowly paddled across the river at night. Houses stand on poles, and ladders hang from their doors to reach the water. People say that a boat is as important as a bicycle.

What day does the doctor's boat visit?
It visits on Wednesdays.

During the winter break, Sana travelled to the Rann of Kutch with her uncle. The land there is flat and white, covered with salt that glitters in the sun. At night, under a clear sky, the stars looked so thick that Sana could not count them. Her uncle pointed out the Great Bear and the Pole Star, and told her that camel drivers once used the stars to find their way. Sana wrote the names in her diary and drew a sketch of the pattern. In the morning, they watched a flock of pink flamingos wading in a shallow pool far off.

What did Sana's uncle point out in the night sky?
He pointed out the Great Bear and the Pole Star.

When the monsoon ended, Tara walked to the hill behind her village and found it covered with wildflowers. Purple, yellow and white blossoms filled every slope, and the air smelled sweet. She took a few photographs and then sat down in the grass. A boy from the next village came by with his goats, and he told her that these flowers appeared once every year, only for two weeks, and then disappeared. "If you come next week, they will be gone," he said. Tara stood up at once, brushed the grass from her clothes and ran to fetch her friends so that they would not miss the sight.

Why did Tara run to fetch her friends?
The flowers would only last about two weeks, so she wanted them to see them before they vanished.

Along the beach near Kovalam, Hari found a large turtle shell lying half buried in the sand. It was dry and light, and a few barnacles still clung to its edge. He ran to his uncle, a fisherman who had lived by the sea all his life. The uncle turned the shell over, tapped it and shook his head. "This turtle was very old," he said quietly. "See how big the shell is? Sea turtles grow slowly, so a shell this size took many years." Hari wanted to take it home, but his uncle suggested leaving it near the dunes where the next tide could not carry it away. Hari nodded and carefully placed it on a dry mound.

Why did the uncle say the turtle was very old?
Because the shell was so big, and he said sea turtles grow slowly, so a shell that size took many years.

A strange thing happened at the pond near Meena's house. Every evening, for a week, a single white egret stood in the same place, even though the water was shrinking. On the eighth day, Meena saw that the egret had gone, and in its place, a large number of tiny fish lay gasping in the mud. She ran inside, filled two buckets with water from the tap and poured them into the pond. Then she called her friends. Together, they carried more water until the fish were swimming again. Later, Meena wondered if the egret had known all along that the fish would soon be stranded, and had been waiting.

Why had the egret been waiting by the pond?
It was probably waiting for the fish to be left in the shallows, so it could eat them.

A strong wind blew across the plains all afternoon in the village of Dhanora. By four o'clock, it was lifting sand from the road and carrying dry leaves high into the air. Women gathered their washing from the roofs, and men tied down the tarpaulin over the grain stack. Little Bilal's kite pulled so hard that the string cut his finger, so he let it go, and it drifted far over the fields. The wind finally calmed at dusk, and the village was quiet again, except for the sound of a loose tin sheet clapping against a wall.

What happened to Bilal's kite?
He let go of it and it drifted far over the fields.

Ahmed fished from the same rock on the river every morning for thirty years. When a new dam was built upstream, the water level dropped, and his rock stood high and dry. He climbed on it anyway, holding his rod, and looked down at a muddy strip. His grandson, who had come to keep him company, asked what he would do. Ahmed was silent. Then he picked up his bucket and walked down the bank to the new edge of the water. He found a flat stone there, brushed off the mud with his sleeve, sat and cast his line. "The river moves," he said. "A fisherman moves with it."

What does Ahmed's last remark mean?
It means a person must adapt when things change, just as he moved to the new edge of the river.

The goats on Karim's farm had been bleating all afternoon, and he could not understand why. Their water trough was full, and the grass in the pen was green. He walked around the fence three times. Finally, he knelt down and saw that a section of the wire at the bottom was loose and bent upward. On the other side, a few steps away, a patch of fresh clover grew in the shade of a wall. Karim chuckled, fetched a hammer and nails and repaired the fence. Then, taking a basket, he cut a large armful of clover and carried it into the pen, where the goats gathered round him.

Why were the goats bleating?
They could smell and see the fresh clover on the other side of the fence and wanted it.

The match was supposed to start at four, but a thin grey drizzle had been falling since lunch. The boys of Tilak Nagar stood in a line along the edge of the muddy cricket field, their white shirts clean and their bats ready. Captain Rahul checked the wicket with his foot and shook his head. A few of the younger boys groaned loudly. Rahul called a quick huddle and said they would play at the same time on Sunday. Nobody argued, but one boy kicked a stone across the grass. They picked up the stumps and walked home together under the rain, planning how to dry the pitch.

Why did Rahul decide to postpone the match?
The drizzle had made the pitch wet and muddy, so it was not suitable for playing.

Nobody in the village of Alipur could understand why the temple bell had stopped ringing. Every morning for forty years, old Pandit Sharma had rung it at six o'clock. This week, the bell stayed silent, and people kept looking at their clocks and shaking their heads. On the third morning, a group of children walked to the pandit's small house at the end of the lane. They found him sitting in a chair with a bandaged foot, grumbling about a slip on the wet steps. The children looked at each other. Then the eldest, Divya, picked up the temple keys and said she would ring it herself until he was better.

Why had the temple bell stopped ringing?
Pandit Sharma had hurt his foot after slipping on the wet steps, so he could not ring it.

Mrs. Fernandes keeps the village post office, a small yellow building next to the bus stop. She opens the door at nine and closes at four, except on Sundays. People come to her for stamps, money orders and sometimes just advice. Her biggest job is sorting the letters that arrive each afternoon by van. She puts them in wooden boxes marked with house names, because most lanes in the village have no numbers. When the postman, Kishore, returns from his round, she gives him a glass of lemon water. Last week, a letter reached an old farmer from his son abroad, and the whole lane gathered to hear it read aloud.

What time does Mrs. Fernandes open the post office?
She opens it at nine.

Majuli is a river island in the Brahmaputra, one of the widest rivers in India, and the water around it changes colour with the seasons. In the rainy months, it is brown and fast, and it floods the low land around the houses. Villagers build their homes on high bamboo stilts to stay dry. Children travel to school by boat, and the teacher waits at the bank with a big umbrella. When the water goes down in October, the fields are covered with new soft silt, and farmers plant mustard and vegetables. Fishermen put out nets at dusk and pull them in at dawn, singing as they work.

How do children travel to school during the floods?
They travel by boat.

The sky over the salt pans of a village near Mithapur turned grey in the early afternoon. Workers had spent weeks raking the salt into long white heaps, ready for the trucks that would arrive the next morning. The foreman, Mr. Solanki, climbed on a stack and watched the clouds. He blew his whistle three times, and all the workers dropped their rakes and ran to fetch black plastic sheets from the store. They spread them over the salt and weighted them with stones. Within the hour, rain fell in sheets, and the workers stood together, soaked but smiling, looking at their covered piles.

Why did the workers cover the salt with plastic?
They wanted to keep the salt from dissolving in the rain.

At dawn on a cool winter morning, Yusuf's father drove the buffalo cart to the sugarcane field. Stalks as tall as a man stood in thick green rows, and the ground was still wet with dew. Together they cut the canes with sharp curved knives, stripped off the leaves and tied them in bundles of ten. By nine o'clock, the cart was piled high. They took the load to a small mill on the main road, where the cane was crushed to make juice. At the mill, Yusuf drank a glass of the sweet juice with a slice of lime. Then he rode home sitting on top of the bundles.

What did Yusuf drink at the mill?
He drank a glass of sweet sugarcane juice with a slice of lime.

A full moon rose over the village of Kasol on Friday night, silver against the black outline of the mountains. The river below shone like a ribbon, and the pine trees stood still. Families sat outside after dinner, wrapped in blankets, drinking warm milk with turmeric. A grandfather explained that the moon was about three hundred and eighty thousand kilometres away. His grandson, who was seven, asked if anybody had ever walked on it. The old man said yes, and told him that astronauts had done so more than fifty years ago. The boy fell asleep on his lap, still looking up.

What did the grandfather drink with his family?
They drank warm milk with turmeric.

The village midwife, Mrs. Lobo, lives in a small house at the bottom of the hill. Her bicycle has a basket, a bell and a torch tied to the handlebar with string. Day or night, when someone knocks at her door, she puts on her sandals and goes. She has visited nearly every home in the village, carrying clean cloth, soap and a notebook. Children she helped to bring into the world now have children of their own. At the village fair each year, mothers and grandmothers seat her in the front row and applaud when she arrives. Mrs. Lobo says she has never needed a prize.

What is tied to the handlebar of Mrs. Lobo's bicycle?
A torch is tied to it with string.

Near the last house in the village of Khavda lives a potter named Karim, who makes water pots, lamps and toy animals. He starts work at dawn at a wooden wheel turned by his foot. His hands, wet with clay, lift the shape up slowly from a lump on the wheel. Once the pots are dried in the sun, he bakes them in a kiln of dung cakes. Children love to visit on Saturdays, when he lets them shape a small ball of clay. Karim's wife paints the finished pots with red and white patterns, and sells them to visitors from the city.

What does Karim's wife do with the finished pots?
She paints them with red and white patterns and sells them.

Fatima's grandfather had always said that a good farmer listens to the soil. One evening, after a long hot week, she watched him kneel in the field and press his palm against the earth. He stayed there for half a minute with his eyes closed. Then he stood up and told her they would water the beans after dark, not before. Fatima, who would have sprayed the plants right away, asked why. He explained that water poured in the heat of the evening would evaporate quickly, while night water sinks deep. She nodded slowly and went to fetch the hose after supper, thinking that his hands knew things her books did not.

What does Fatima think about her grandfather at the end?
She respects him and thinks his experience teaches him things that her books do not.

At the village fair of Kalpa, the biggest crowd gathers around the wrestling ring. Two strong men, covered in dust and oil, circle each other while the audience claps in a steady beat. Beyond the ring, there are stalls selling bangles, steel utensils and hot samosas. A puppeteer with painted string puppets entertains children, who throw coins into his tin. In the evening, folk singers perform on a raised wooden stage, and the fair ends at ten with a display of fireworks. Families travel from five neighbouring villages to attend, and many of them stay overnight in tents.

How many neighbouring villages do families come from?
They come from five neighbouring villages.

The Millers hold a supper in the barn on the last day of the corn harvest in Ohio. Everyone who helped with the cutting is invited, along with their families. Tables are made from planks and bales of straw, and the women bring pies, stew and cornbread from their own kitchens. Mr. Miller thanks the helpers, and the youngest worker receives a small wooden whistle as a prize. After the meal, an old fiddler plays folk tunes, and the children dance on the straw. By ten o'clock, the last guest has gone home, and the family sweeps the barn floor.

What does the youngest worker receive as a prize?
The youngest worker receives a small wooden whistle.

No one in Ratnagiri could explain why the mangoes on old Mr. Phadke's tree were always the sweetest. He did not use any special fertiliser, and he watered it no more than anyone else. Some people suspected that he had a secret. One evening, a curious boy hid behind a wall and watched. Mr. Phadke came out at dusk, sat beneath the tree, and quietly talked to it, telling it about his day. The boy went home puzzled, and did not tell anyone what he saw. But the next morning, he stood in front of his own family's tree and, feeling slightly foolish, said good morning.

What did the boy do after watching Mr. Phadke?
He tried talking to his own family's mango tree, copying the old man.

Hannah woke up at five to milk the cows, as she did every day. Today, though, Bessie, the brown cow, did not come to the gate when called. She stood at the far end of the shed, shifting her feet, and did not touch her hay. Hannah put her hand on Bessie's neck and noticed that the cow's side was warm and her breathing was fast. Instead of milking, Hannah ran to the house and woke her father. "Please call the animal doctor," she said. While they waited, Hannah sat beside Bessie and gently stroked her head, speaking softly until the cow stopped shifting.

What does Hannah's behaviour show about how she feels toward Bessie?
It shows she cares about Bessie; she noticed the problem, got help and stayed to comfort her.

Mr. Basu's roof was made of tin sheets, and when the first hailstones fell, the noise was like a thousand drums. His daughter Piya clapped her hands over her ears and ran to hide under the bed. Mr. Basu laughed and called her out, saying that the hail would not hurt them, and sat down with her at the door to watch. He picked up a hailstone, held it in her palm and told her to look at the layers inside. Piya, forgetting her fear, held it up to the light and squinted. The storm passed in ten minutes, and she asked her father to show her another one.

How did Piya's feelings change?
She was afraid at first, but became curious and interested once her father showed her a hailstone.

Four-year-old Lily was given the job of feeding the chickens for the first time. She held the little bowl of grain carefully in both hands and walked toward the coop. The hens came running, flapping their wings and clucking, and Lily stopped in her tracks. She looked at her grandfather, who was standing by the fence, and her eyes were wide. Then she dropped the bowl, grain flying everywhere, and ran straight into his legs, hiding her face in his trousers. The hens quickly ate everything on the ground. Her grandfather laughed gently, picked her up and promised they would try again together tomorrow.

How did Lily feel when the hens ran toward her?
She felt scared, because she stopped, dropped the bowl and hid her face.

Hot winds had been blowing for days, and the haystacks in the village of Ladwa were as dry as paper. One afternoon, Mr. Gill saw a thin curl of smoke rising from the far end of the field. He did not wait to find out what it was. He rang the bell at the gurdwara, and within minutes, dozens of people appeared with buckets and wet sacks. They formed a line from the pond to the fire and passed the buckets quickly. The flames were beaten out before they could reach the houses. Afterwards, Mr. Gill suggested that they should keep a barrel of water at each corner of the village during summer.

Why did Mr. Gill suggest keeping water barrels at the corners of the village?
The dry, hot weather made fires likely, and having water ready would help put them out faster.

The river near Gautam's village changes through the year. During the monsoon months, it is wide and brown, and it roars loudly over the stones. In winter, the water becomes clear and slow, and one can see small silver fish swimming near the bank. By May it shrinks to a narrow channel, and children can walk across it. Fishermen use round boats made of bamboo and tar, which they carry on their heads when the river is low. Gautam likes the river best in October, when the rains have ended and white egrets stand in the shallow water looking for fish.

In which month does Gautam like the river best?
He likes it best in October.

Dew forms on the grass of a village in Sikkim every night during autumn. At first light, each blade glitters with tiny drops, and the spider webs on the fences look like silver nets. Children walk barefoot across the meadow because they believe the cold water is good for the eyes. Their grandmothers watch from the doorstep, wrapped in shawls. By eight o'clock, the sun dries the dew, and the grass turns plain green again. Cows go out to graze right after, and the farmers call their dogs to the fields. Anyone who wishes to see the dew at its best must wake before six.

What do the children believe about walking barefoot on the dew?
They believe the cold water is good for the eyes.

One year, the plum trees on the Kowalski farm flowered unusually early in the warm spell of February. Mr. Kowalski watched them with a worried face. He knew a frost could still come, and he had heard on the radio that the night would be clear. After dinner, he went out with his sons, carrying a roll of old sacking, lanterns and buckets of straw. They lit small smoky fires in the orchard rows and hung lanterns in the lowest branches. The family took turns guarding the fires until dawn. When the sun rose over the white frost on the grass, the blossoms were still white and whole.

Why did Mr. Kowalski light fires in the orchard?
He wanted to keep the blossoms warm and protect them from the frost.

A long dry spell had made the fields of a village near Rajkot hard and pale. When the rain finally came, it fell so gently that nobody noticed at first. Then Chanda, hanging washing on the roof, felt a drop on her arm and looked up. She dropped the clothes and ran down the stairs, calling to her sisters. All three stood in the courtyard, faces tilted back, eyes shut, letting the rain run down their cheeks. Their mother came out of the kitchen with a ladle in her hand, started to scold them for getting wet, and then stopped and joined them, laughing.

Why did Chanda's mother stop scolding the girls?
She felt as happy about the rain as they did after the dry spell, so she joined them instead.

In Jamila's coastal village, the mornings in May are still and very hot. By noon, the lane is empty, and even the goats lie in the shade. Then, at about two o'clock, the curtains in Jamila's room begin to move. A cool breeze blows in from the sea, smelling of salt, and the whole house seems to breathe out. Jamila's teacher once explained that land heats up faster than water in the sun, so the warm air over the land rises and cooler air from the sea moves in to take its place. Jamila's mother does not need the explanation. Every day at two, she opens all the windows and sets the water pot where the breeze will cool it.

Why does a cool breeze come in from the sea in the afternoon?
Because land heats up faster than water, the warm air over the land rises, and cooler air from the sea moves in to take its place.

Last winter, a heron stood in the pond behind the Rao house for many days, perfectly still on one leg. Rohit, who was nine, watched it from the kitchen window as he ate his cereal. For a long time nothing happened. Then, in one sudden movement, the heron's neck shot forward, and when it lifted its beak, a small fish wriggled in it. Rohit nearly dropped his spoon. He went to school and told the whole class about it, and the teacher asked him to draw a picture. He drew the heron from memory and wrote underneath: "Patience."

Why did Rohit write 'Patience' under his drawing?
He saw that the heron waited quietly for a long time before catching the fish.

The apple harvest in the town of Sopore begins in late August. Pickers wear cloth bags tied around their waists and climb wooden ladders to reach the high branches. They sort the apples by size and colour into three grades. The best ones, bright red and perfectly round, are wrapped in paper and packed in wooden boxes for export. The second grade goes to the local market, and the smallest fruits are sent to a factory that makes juice and jam. Pickers earn more if they pick carefully, because bruised fruit is returned. Many of the pickers are students working during their holidays.

Where do the best apples go?
They are wrapped, packed in wooden boxes and sent for export.

On the roof of a school in Kolkata, there is a garden tended by the students of class seven. They grow chillies, spinach, coriander and a few brinjal plants in old paint tins and plastic tubs. Each group of four children is responsible for one corner. Every morning before the first bell, they water the plants with a hose that stretches from the tank. A small notice board records each week's harvest. Last month, they gathered two kilos of spinach, which went to the school kitchen. The headmistress hopes that every class will have its own corner by next year.

Who tends the rooftop garden at the school?
The students of class seven tend it.

When the first potatoes were dug out of the ground at the Murphy farm, they were as small as walnuts. Mr. Murphy turned over a second plant, then a third, and the potatoes were the same. His eldest daughter, Aoife, watched his face grow longer. The summer had been so dry that the plants had barely grown. That night, the family sat around the kitchen table and Mr. Murphy did not eat much. Aoife quietly brought out her savings tin and put it in front of him. "For the seed next year," she said. He looked at the tin, and then at her, and for a while he could not speak.

How did Mr. Murphy feel when Aoife put down her savings tin?
He felt deeply moved and grateful, because he could not speak.

At dusk, the little ferry across the river stopped running because of the strong current. A group of villagers who had come from the market were left on the far bank. They looked at the water, which was brown and fast, and at the sky, which was growing darker. A woman among them sat down and began to cry softly. An elderly man took out his lantern, lit it and tied it to a pole. "Someone on the other side will see it," he said. After half an hour, a small boat came across, and the boatman called out that he had spotted the light and come at once.

Why did the old man light his lantern and tie it to a pole?
He wanted to signal to the people on the other side that they were stranded and needed help.

Every May, before the monsoon reaches the coast, the people of a village near Kundapur clean out their old pond. The water is low by then, and thick black silt has settled on the bottom. Men dig it out with spades, women carry it away in shallow pans on their heads, and the children pick out plastic and broken glass. The silt is rich, so farmers spread it on their fields as manure. Old Mr. Gowda keeps count of the cartloads in a notebook; this year there were sixty-three. When the rains arrive in June, the cleaned pond holds much more water, and the wells around it stay full well into the dry months.

Why do the wells near the pond stay full for longer after the cleaning?
Because the cleaned pond holds much more water when the rains come, and that water keeps the nearby wells full well into the dry months.

Rukmini noticed that the birds had stopped coming to the feeder she had set up on her window ledge. For weeks, sparrows and bulbuls had fought noisily over the grain. Now the ledge was empty, and the grain lay untouched. She looked out and saw a large grey cat sitting on the garden wall, perfectly still, watching the window. Rukmini opened the window and clapped her hands. The cat jumped down and slipped away. She moved the feeder to a hanging hook in the middle of the garden, where no cat could reach it. By evening, three sparrows had already returned, and a bulbul was perched on the rim.

Why had the birds stopped coming to the feeder?
A cat was sitting near the window, and the birds were afraid of it.

For three summers, the village of Rasulpur had asked the council for a hand pump near the school. For three summers, nothing happened. This year, the schoolchildren decided to write letters, each in their own words, and sign them with their names. Forty-two letters were tied in a bundle with red ribbon and carried to the council office by the headmaster. One week later, a truck arrived at the school gate carrying pipes, a pump and four workers. Nobody had expected such a quick reply. The children crowded around, and the youngest ones clapped as the first bucket of cool water came out.
