What probably made the council act so quickly?
The forty-two letters from the children probably made the council take the request seriously.

The river ferry at the village of Devghat carries thirty people at a time, and the boatman, Bikram, never starts until every passenger is seated. One afternoon, a woman arrived at the bank out of breath, carrying a basket of eggs and a small child. The boat was already a few metres from the shore. Bikram looked at her, then at the other passengers, and steered the ferry back. A man grumbled about being late, but Bikram only said, "A few minutes is not long." When she stepped on, she thanked him twice and held her child tightly. Nobody grumbled again after that.

What does Bikram's choice to go back for the woman show about him?
It shows he is kind and patient, because he steered back for a woman carrying eggs and a child and said a few minutes is not long.

The first cold wave arrived in the town of Kotagiri in the last week of November. Thick mist covered the tea slopes until noon, and the air smelled of woodsmoke. In every home, shawls and sweaters were taken out of trunks. Parents wrapped their children in woollen caps and scarves before sending them to school. At the bus stand, the vendor began selling roasted peanuts in paper cones, which sold out in an hour. Old men gathered around small fires in front of the shops and told stories of colder winters. By evening, the temperature had dropped to six degrees.

What did the vendor at the bus stand begin selling?
The vendor began selling roasted peanuts in paper cones.

The village of Chand Bagh did not have a single tree in its main square. Summer afternoons were unbearably hot, and old people sat in doorways with wet cloths on their heads. A schoolteacher, Ms. Fonseca, brought a basket of saplings one morning and asked her students to plant them along the edge of the square. Some villagers laughed. Others said the saplings would never survive the dry months. But the children watered them every morning, and the old people took turns guarding them from goats. Six years later, children study in the shade of the tallest tree, and nobody laughs.

What made the saplings survive?
The children watered them every day and the old people protected them from goats.

Mustard flowers cover the fields around Mohan's village in January, turning the whole valley yellow. Mohan's family grows mustard on two acres, and each plant is about as tall as his shoulder. When the flowers fade, the green pods fill with tiny black seeds. In March, the family cuts the plants and spreads them on a large cloth in the yard to dry. Then Mohan and his brothers beat them with sticks until the seeds fall out. The seeds are taken to the oil press, and the thick golden oil is brought home in tin cans. His mother says nothing tastes like the first fried bread made with new oil.

How tall is each mustard plant?
Each plant is about as tall as Mohan's shoulder.

Mrs. Obi was hanging out the washing when she saw a flash of lightning far beyond the hills. She began to count slowly, and she had reached twelve when the thunder rolled in. Her grandson Chike asked why she was counting. She told him that sound travels much more slowly than light, so every three seconds between the flash and the thunder means the storm is about one kilometre away. "Twelve seconds," she said, "so it is about four kilometres off." At the next flash, she counted only to six. She called the children in from the yard, and they sat on the veranda to watch. Soon the rain was drumming on the roof, and nobody was outside.

How far away did Mrs. Obi say the storm was when she counted to twelve?
She said it was about four kilometres away.

Wei had always grown rice the old way, planting seedlings by hand in flooded fields. This year, his daughter Mei came home from agriculture college with a new idea. She suggested letting ducks swim among the rice plants. Wei laughed at first. "Ducks will eat the crop," he said. But Mei explained that they would eat the insects and weeds instead, and their droppings would feed the plants. Wei crossed his arms and thought about it for a long time. Then he walked to the market, bought twenty ducklings and carried them home in a bamboo basket. Mei smiled and began building a small shelter at the edge of the field.

What can we tell about Wei's feelings by the end of the passage?
He had changed his mind and was willing to try the idea, since he bought the ducklings himself.

When Anika stepped outside on Monday, the pond near her home was covered with a thin skin of ice. Her breath came out as white smoke, and the grass crunched under her boots. She had to scrape frost off the windows of her father's car with an old ruler. At the bus stop, the other children stood close together, hopping from one foot to the other and rubbing their gloved hands. The milk delivery man wore two sweaters and a woollen cap that covered his ears. Anika thought about the hot soup waiting at lunchtime and walked a little faster.

What was the weather like that Monday, and what is the clue?
It was very cold; there was ice on the pond, frost on the windows, and everyone wore warm clothes.

At the Lakshmi dairy farm, each cow has a number tag on her ear and a card on the wall of the shed. The card shows her name, her birthday, the dates of her check-ups and the amount of milk she gives each day. Mrs. Lakshmi checks the cards every Sunday evening, and if a cow gives less than usual, she calls the vet. The cows are milked by machine at half past five in the morning and half past four in the afternoon. After milking, they are let out to a wide pasture with a pond. In the evening, they walk back by themselves, in a line, with the same leader each time.

What is written on each cow's card?
It shows her name, birthday, check-up dates and daily milk.

The bullock cart creaked slowly toward the market with twelve sacks of lentils. Kamal sat at the front, holding the rope lightly. Behind him, his young son Rafi watched the road pass by. At the river crossing, the water was higher than usual, and Kamal stopped the cart and stepped down to look. He tested the depth with a long bamboo pole and shook his head. Then he turned the bullocks around and drove toward the upper ford, a longer road but with a stone bottom. "Better late than lose the lentils," he said to Rafi, who nodded as if he understood.

Why did Kamal take the longer road?
The river was too high to cross safely at the usual place, and he did not want to lose the lentils.

In Muthur, a barber named Selvam sets up his chair under the shade of a tamarind tree every morning. He carries a small tin box with scissors, a razor, a comb and a mirror. Customers sit on a wooden stool, and Selvam covers their shoulders with a clean cotton cloth. Men talk with him about crops, cricket and school fees while he works. A haircut costs very little, and old people often pay with rice or vegetables instead of money. He has done this work for twenty-five years and knows every family in the village by name.

Where does Selvam set up his chair?
He sets it up under a tamarind tree.

A wooden bridge crosses the narrow river that divides the villages of Upper Brook and Lower Brook. The two villages share a market every second Saturday, held on the Upper Brook side. Farmers from Lower Brook walk across with carts of potatoes and cabbages, and Upper Brook's weavers bring colourful scarves. The bridge was built by the grandfathers of the present villagers, using oak planks and iron nails. Each spring, the council paints it green, and children carry the buckets. Near the middle, a small sign carved into the rail says: Walk slowly, this bridge is old.

How often is the market held?
It is held every second Saturday.

The old pipal tree in the centre of the village was dropping its leaves in March, and the children were sad to see it bare. Their grandmother told them to wait. Each morning, they ran to look at the branches, and each morning there was nothing but grey twigs. Then, one day in April, a boy shouted from the school gate. Everyone rushed out. Along every twig, tiny copper-coloured leaves had appeared, shining in the sunlight. Within a week, the whole tree was a soft green cloud. The grandmother, sitting beneath it with her knitting, said that she had never doubted it and that patience was the best friend of a gardener.

What does the story teach about the tree's bare branches?
They were only a stage in the tree's yearly cycle, and new leaves came after waiting.

On the Singh farm, the day begins with the sound of the tube-well engine starting at five o'clock. Water gushes into the channels, and Mr. Singh opens the little mud gates one by one to let it flow into each field. His wife, Gurmeet, milks the cows and fills the steel cans for the dairy truck. Their son Harjit takes the buffalo to the pond, and their daughter Simran sweeps the courtyard. After breakfast of paratha and curd, the children leave for school, and the parents go to weed the sugarcane. At noon, the whole family rests under a large neem tree with a pitcher of cold lassi.

What do the family members drink under the neem tree at noon?
They drink cold lassi.

A narrow stone path connects the two halves of the village of Goa Velha. On one side is the church with a white spire and a small square where women sell fish. On the other side is the school, painted pale blue, and a playground with two goalposts and no grass. The path crosses a stream, and a plank has been laid over it. At the end of the school day, children run across in twos and threes, and the plank shakes beneath their feet. The priest, Father Mathew, stands at the church gate each evening and waves to every child as they pass.

What colour is the school painted?
It is painted pale blue.

Hari ran a fruit cart near the university gate in Kozhikode. He weighed everything carefully, and students trusted him. One day a student named Shiva came by with a worried face. He had lost his wallet and had not eaten since morning. Hari gave him a banana and said to pay when he could. A month later, Shiva returned with the money and a large paper bag. Inside were notes from fifteen other students, each saying thank you for the fruit he had sold them over the year. Hari read them at his cart and said nothing for a while.

What was inside the paper bag that Shiva brought?
It held notes from fifteen students thanking Hari for the fruit.

The online test for the job application closed at midnight, and Preeti began it at eleven forty. The internet at her hostel was slow, and the page kept freezing. She tried again, her heart beating loudly. Finally, at eleven fifty-five, the questions appeared. She answered as fast as she could and pressed submit with seconds to spare. A green tick appeared on the screen. She leaned back and laughed in the dark room. In the morning, she told her roommate that she would never leave an application for the last twenty minutes again, and she meant it.

What does Preeti plan to do in future about deadlines?
She plans to start applications well before the last minutes, since she said she would never leave them that late again.

When Zara heard that her friend Lena had been promoted, her stomach tightened. They had joined the company on the same day, and Zara had worked equally hard. She smiled and said congratulations, then went to the stairwell and stood alone for a minute. Back at her desk, she wrote a list of what she could improve: learning the new software, speaking up in meetings, asking for feedback. She booked a meeting with her manager for the next week. By evening, the knot in her stomach had eased. She texted Lena, "Dinner on me," and Lena replied with a row of smiling faces.

How did Zara feel at first about Lena's promotion, and what shows it?
She felt jealous and disappointed. Her stomach tightened and she went to the stairwell to be alone.

Siva has delivered newspapers in Madurai since he was twelve. Now he is twenty-two and studies in the evening college. His day begins at four thirty, when the bundles arrive at the shop. He sorts them by street, tucks each into a plastic cover on rainy days, and cycles through quiet lanes. By seven, he has delivered a hundred and forty papers and is back home for a bath and breakfast. He says the best moment is the first hour, when the streets are empty and only dogs and milkmen are about. The money pays his college fees, and he has never been late for class.

How many newspapers does Siva deliver each morning?
He delivers a hundred and forty papers.

Aman wrote poems on the back of his bus tickets and left them on the seat when he got off. He never signed them. One day he found a reply on the seat of the same bus, written in blue ink on a ticket: "Thank you for the one about the rain." Aman read it twice and grinned all the way to the office. For weeks they exchanged tiny poems without ever meeting. Aman never learned who it was, and the thought did not bother him. He said the secret was half the pleasure.

How did Aman feel about not knowing who his reader was?
He did not mind. He said the secret was half the pleasure.

The cost of living in a big city surprised Rhea. In her small town, a plate of lunch cost forty rupees, and here it cost one hundred and fifty. She had thought her stipend would stretch, but after rent and travel, little remained. She began carrying lunch from home and found a cheaper shop for vegetables. A senior at work, Mr. D'Souza, showed her how to use the monthly bus pass rather than paying each day. By the third month, Rhea had saved enough to buy a small gift for her mother and felt, for the first time, that she could manage on her own.

What helped Rhea save money?
She carried lunch from home, bought vegetables from a cheaper shop and used a monthly bus pass.

Latha woke at three on the day of her first marathon in Chennai. She ate a banana, tied her shoes twice, and took a rickshaw to the starting line. Crowds were already stretching and jogging in place. The starting horn sounded at five. For the first ten kilometres she felt strong. By the thirtieth, her legs ached. She slowed but never stopped. At the finishing line, volunteers handed her a medal and a cold towel. She did not run fast, but she crossed the line in five hours and twelve minutes, and she sat on the kerb with the medal in her hand.

At what time did the race start?
The race started at five in the morning.

In a small park near Shivaji Nagar, a bench carries a brass plate that reads, "For anyone who needs to sit." It was placed by a retired teacher, Mr. Kulkarni, in memory of his wife. Every morning, he sits on the bench's left side and leaves the right side open. Young office workers often stop for a few minutes to eat sandwiches. Some talk to him, some do not. One girl asked him why he left the space. He answered that a seat is nicer when it can be shared, and that his wife had always liked company.

What does the brass plate on the bench say?
It says, "For anyone who needs to sit."

Every office has a person who keeps things running, and in ours it is Bhaiya, the chai man. He arrives at nine with a steel kettle and a basket of glasses, and by ten he has served every floor. He remembers who likes less sugar and who needs extra ginger. During a long night of work, someone only has to wave and a glass appears. Bhaiya never writes anything down, yet at month end his accounts match the diary exactly. When a young engineer asked how he did it, he tapped his forehead and said that remembering people is easier than remembering numbers.

What time does Bhaiya arrive at the office?
He arrives at the office at nine.

Zeynep got a place at a university in Ankara but could not afford the first term's books. She walked into the library on the first day and found that the books she needed were all there. She visited every evening until closing, taking notes by hand and borrowing one volume at a time. A librarian noticed and quietly began setting aside the next book for her. On the last day of term, Zeynep left a small card on the desk saying thank you. The librarian pinned it above her computer, where it stayed for years.

What shows that the librarian was touched by Zeynep's card?
She pinned it above her computer, where it stayed for years.

Tomas joined a gym near his office in Prague. His last checkup had shown nothing alarming, but he knew he sat too much. For the first week, he arrived at six in the morning, did ten minutes on a treadmill and left. The trainer, a patient man called Pavel, suggested a plan with three short sessions a week. Tomas followed it. After two months, he could run for twenty minutes without stopping and climbed the office stairs without losing his breath. He kept a small chart on his fridge with green ticks for each completed session, and he enjoyed ticking more than anything.

What did Tomas keep on his fridge?
He kept a chart with green ticks for each completed session.

Esra and her sister rented a flat in Istanbul. After a month, the landlord raised the rent without warning, saying prices were rising everywhere. Esra felt angry but kept calm. She wrote a polite letter asking if the increase could start after the agreed period ended. She attached a copy of their agreement and asked for a reply in writing. The landlord called the next day and said she was right. He apologised and promised to keep the old rent until the end of the contract. Esra thanked him and noted the date in her diary, just in case.

What did Esra's calm letter achieve?
It made the landlord agree to keep the old rent until the contract ended, because she politely pointed to their written agreement.

The Mumbai local was packed, and Aman stood near the door with his bag hugged to his chest. At Dadar, a woman with two shopping bags tried to get in and was pushed back. A young man shifted aside, pulled her in by the elbow and held her bags until she found space. Nobody spoke, yet three people moved closer together to make room. At the next stop, the woman stepped out, smiled and called over her shoulder, "Thank you, bhaiya!" The young man, who was already looking out of the window, gave a small wave without turning around.

At which station did the woman have trouble getting into the train?
She had trouble at Dadar.

The new metro line opened last Monday, and Tanya decided to try it instead of her usual bus. The station was clean and bright, with signs in two languages and a lift for wheelchairs. She bought a card at the counter, loaded two hundred rupees and tapped it at the gate. The train arrived in three minutes, quiet and cool. Her journey to work, which usually took an hour in traffic, took twenty-five minutes. She sat near a window and watched rooftops pass. At her stop, she walked to the street smiling, thinking she might never take the bus to work again.

How long did Tanya's metro trip to work take?
Her trip took twenty-five minutes.

Saturday is cooking day in the flat where Rukmini lives with three friends. They take turns, and this week it was Rukmini's. She made lemon rice with roasted peanuts, a recipe from her grandmother in Mysuru. While the rice cooled, she tempered mustard seeds, curry leaves and dried chillies in hot oil. The smell reached the other rooms, and one by one her flatmates drifted into the kitchen. Gabriel, who had never eaten it, asked for a second plate. Rukmini smiled and wrote down the steps on a scrap of paper for him to keep, adding in the corner, "Don't skip the curry leaves."

What did Rukmini write on the scrap of paper?
She wrote down the steps of the recipe and a note not to skip the curry leaves.

The truck delivering Anita's furniture arrived two hours late, and by then the rain had started. Two workers carried the sofa into her new flat on the third floor, leaving wet footprints on the stairs. Anita, tired and anxious, almost scolded them. Instead, she noticed that one of the men was limping. She gave him a towel and a glass of water and asked him to sit for a minute. He protested, but she insisted. They finished the work in silence, and when they left, the older worker said that in twenty years, no one had offered him a towel.

What did Anita give the limping worker?
She gave him a towel and a glass of water.

Ten years ago, the tram in Kolkata was Basu's favourite way to travel. Now he is a young engineer, and he still takes it once a week, even though the bus is faster. He sits near the open window, watching the slow streets pass. He says the tram teaches him patience. On one ride, a boy sat across from him and asked why he smiled at the empty tracks. Basu said he was remembering his school days. The boy nodded as if he understood and waved when Basu got off at Esplanade, though he had known him for only twenty minutes.

What does Basu say the tram teaches him?
He says it teaches him patience.

When Anjum's younger sister Rubina started college in Aligarh, she called home every evening. Her voice sounded tired and thin. Anjum, who lived two hours away, took a morning bus to visit her. She found Rubina sitting in a narrow room, staring at a pile of unfinished notes. Anjum did not lecture her. She simply made two cups of tea, sat beside her and began to sort the notes into piles. By evening, the piles were neat, and Rubina's eyes had lost their shadows. Anjum stayed the night, and in the morning Rubina walked her to the bus stand and said she felt ready.

Why did Rubina feel ready the next morning?
Because her sister had come to help and sort her notes, which eased her stress and made her feel supported.

During the first week at a new company, Ayan ate lunch at his desk to look busy. On Thursday, a colleague named Rita tapped on his monitor and said, "We eat in the pantry, and you are coming." Ayan blushed but followed. Around the long table, six people shared their lunches and swapped stories about weekend trips. They asked him where he came from and promised to try his mother's pickle if he brought it. Ayan carried a small jar the following Monday, and it disappeared in minutes. From then on, he never ate alone at his desk.

Why did Ayan eat at his desk during the first week?
He wanted to look busy, probably because he felt new and unsure about joining the others.

Pooja was ten minutes late to her new job because the bus had stalled. Her supervisor, Mr. Kapoor, noticed but said nothing. At the end of the day, he called her aside. Pooja prepared an excuse. Instead, he asked whether the bus route was always unreliable. She said yes. He suggested that she start work at nine thirty rather than nine, as other staff did, and make up the time in the evening. Pooja felt a rush of gratitude. The next morning, she arrived on time, calm, and with a small notebook where she planned to write down everything she learned.

What did Mr. Kapoor suggest to Pooja?
He suggested she start at nine thirty and make up the time in the evening.

In the quiet hours before dawn in Chennai, the temple bell rings at five and the milk van rattles along the street. By five thirty, women are drawing white kolam patterns outside their doors with rice flour. Karthik, who has just started a job as a trainee in a bank, wakes with the sound and boils water for coffee. He sits on the balcony with his cup and watches the street come alive. At six, he leaves for the bus stop, where the same old man sells jasmine strings. Karthik buys one every Friday and takes it to his mother.

On which day does Karthik buy jasmine strings?
He buys one every Friday.

Hassan's editor needed the article by evening, and Hassan had written only the first paragraph. He opened the window, listened to the traffic and tried to write again. Words refused to come. After an hour, he closed the laptop and walked to the corner shop for a cold drink. On the way, he overheard two women arguing kindly about the best way to cook fish. Their lively talk gave him an idea: he would write about how ordinary people on the street explain their daily lives. He rushed home and wrote the rest in ninety minutes, sending it to his editor just before six.

What gave Hassan the idea for his article?
Overhearing two women arguing kindly about cooking fish gave him the idea.

The college student council election was announced on Monday, and Shreya decided to stand for the post of secretary. She did not print big posters. Instead, she walked into every classroom during break and asked students one question: what one thing would they like to change? She wrote the answers in a notebook. Many mentioned the broken water cooler and the lack of seating in the garden. On the day of the speeches, she held up the notebook and read out five of the answers, then promised a plan for each. The hall went silent, then applauded. She won by a large margin the next afternoon.

Why did Shreya win by a large margin?
Because she listened to students first and promised plans for their real concerns. She asked what they wanted changed and read their answers aloud.

Nisha started as a receptionist at a city hospital in Chennai. On her first morning, she watched a nurse calm a crying child with a paper boat. She noticed that people arrived with worry on their faces and left with small relief when someone spoke gently. Her job was to enter names, give tokens and point people to the right floor. She learned to say each instruction slowly and to repeat the room number. Whenever someone seemed lost, she walked them to the lift instead of just pointing. By the end of the week, the senior staff were asking her to train the next new person.

What did Nisha do when someone seemed lost?
She walked them to the lift instead of only pointing.

On Wednesday evening, the sky turned dark over Bengaluru and the first drops fell as Tessa left the office. She did not have an umbrella. At the bus stop, a stranger held out half of his and said, "Share?" She hesitated, then stepped under it. They did not speak much. When her bus came, she said thank you and climbed in. Through the window, she saw him still standing there, waiting for his own, with his shoulder wet from where he had kept the umbrella tilted toward her.

What did the stranger do for Tessa at the bus stop?
He shared his umbrella with her.

Vinod borrowed two thousand rupees from his friend Salim in the first week of the month and promised to pay it back on the fifth. On the fifth, his salary had not arrived. Vinod sent Salim a message, explaining honestly that he would pay on the tenth. Salim replied with a thumbs-up and a short line saying thank you for telling him. On the tenth, Vinod paid back the full amount, plus a packet of samosas. Salim said the samosas were unnecessary but ate them all, and the friendship felt a little stronger than before.

Why did Salim thank Vinod for his message?
Because Vinod told him honestly about the delay instead of staying silent.

When Aarav learned that he had won a scholarship to study in Bengaluru, he could not speak for a full minute. He read the letter twice, then walked to the kitchen where his mother was cooking and handed it to her without a word. She wiped her hands, read it slowly, and sat down on a stool. Her eyes filled, but she was smiling. His father, who drove an auto, came home late that night and listened to the news standing in the doorway. Then he took out his small box of savings, counted it quietly, and said that Aarav should buy a good bag for the journey.

What did Aarav's father do after hearing the news?
He took out his small box of savings, counted it quietly and said Aarav should buy a good bag.

Heavy rain flooded the road outside the college in Chennai, and exams had to be postponed. Students stood at the gate watching the water rise to the bus tyres. Vijay, a second-year student, noticed that an old man with a cart of bananas was stuck in the middle of the road. Vijay and three friends waded in, pushed the cart to dry ground and helped him pile the fruit back. The old man thanked them in Tamil and handed each a banana. They ate them standing under a shop awning, soaked and laughing, while the water slowly began to drain away.

What did the old man give the students as thanks?
He gave each of them a banana.

Under the arches near the station in London, a young man named Idris played the violin every evening. Commuters hurried past with their eyes on their phones, and most dropped nothing in his case. One rainy night, an old man stopped and listened to the whole piece. When it ended, he said that it was the tune his late wife used to hum. He pulled out a coin, placed it in the case and walked on slowly. Idris did not count the coin until much later. He kept it in his pocket, and for weeks afterwards, he played that tune first, slowing the pace for the tired travellers.

What did the old man say about the tune?
He said it was the tune his late wife used to hum.

Parul had one hour before her last paper, and instead of reading, she walked around the college garden. Her friends were frantically turning pages near the gate. She did not join them. She sat under a mango tree and ate an orange slowly, watching ants carry crumbs. When the bell rang, she walked to the hall calmly. During the exam, she remembered one question she had not studied, and she stayed relaxed enough to think it through. Afterwards, her friends asked how she remained so calm, and she told them that her mind needed rest as much as practice.

Why did Parul stay relaxed during the exam?
Because she had rested her mind in the garden instead of panicking over books.

When the storm warning came, the students in the hostel in Kochi were told to stay indoors. By evening, wind bent the coconut trees, and power cut out. The girls gathered in the common room with candles and a small radio. Somebody started a game of antakshari, and the room filled with songs. When the lights failed to return by midnight, Fathima made tea on a camping stove. They sat wrapped in blankets, sharing biscuits. In the morning, trees lay across the road, but everyone said that the night had been the best they had spent in college.

How did the girls pass the time during the power cut?
They played antakshari, drank tea and shared biscuits by candlelight.

In the apartment block where Fatima lives, there is a single dusty pot on the stairs that nobody remembered to water. Fatima looked at it every day. One day she brought a cup of water and poured it in. The next week, the plant had a new green shoot. Soon a neighbour left a small can near the pot, and another brought a bag of soil. By the end of the month, the stairs held four pots in a neat row, and someone had hung a little sign saying, "Please water me." Nobody knew who painted it, but everyone seemed to be smiling.

What did Fatima's small act lead to?
It led neighbours to join in, adding soil, a can and more pots, so the stairs became greener and friendlier.

Arif came to Kolkata for a job interview and got lost in the lanes near College Street. His phone had no signal, and the street names were written in a script he could barely read. He stopped a young woman carrying a pile of books and asked for directions. She smiled and, instead of explaining, said, "Come, I'm going that way." They walked together for ten minutes, talking about books. At the corner of the interview building, she pointed and wished him luck. Arif arrived a few minutes early and told the panel later that he had already met the kindest person in the city.

How did the young woman help Arif?
She walked with him to the building instead of only giving directions.

The college quiz team, called the Brain Boxes, had never won a round. Before the inter-college contest, their captain, Ritu, changed the practice. Instead of everyone reading all subjects, each member took one area: Nikhil took history, Sara took science, and Ritu took current events. During the contest, a question about ancient trade routes came up and Nikhil answered before the host had finished reading. The crowd cheered. They ended in second place, their best result so far. On the bus home, nobody talked about the loss. They were busy listing the areas where they could improve, and Ritu wrote them down on the back of her ticket.

Why did the team do better in this contest?
Because each member specialised in one subject. Ritu changed practice so Nikhil took history, Sara science and Ritu current events.

On Saturday mornings, a group of young volunteers meets at the beach in Chennai to collect plastic. They carry gloves and sacks. Most are students, but some are office workers who have never done anything like this before. Last Saturday, a girl found a toy car half buried in the sand. She washed it in a bucket and gave it to a small boy watching from the road. The boy held it tight and ran away calling to his mother. The girl smiled as she watched him go, and then she went back to the sacks with new energy.

Why did the girl return to the sacks with new energy?
Because seeing the boy's joy at the toy made her feel her work was worthwhile.

Bilal's laptop crashed three days before his final project was due. The screen turned blue, and a small message said the system could not start. He felt a hot wave of panic, because the only copy of his report was inside. He called his friend Chen, who studied computer science, and Chen asked him to bring the machine over. Chen opened it, plugged the drive into another computer, and copied everything out in twenty minutes. Bilal almost hugged him. From that day, he saved every file to a pen drive each night and kept a second copy with his sister, just in case.

What will Bilal probably do with his files from now on?
He will keep backups. After the crash, he started saving to a pen drive each night and giving a copy to his sister.

Rohan missed the 7:40 bus again. He had stayed up late finishing a presentation, and his alarm rang twice before he heard it. By the time he reached the stop, only the dust from the bus was left. His manager had asked everyone to be early for the client visit, so Rohan could not just wait for the next one. He walked fast to the main road, waved down an auto, and promised the driver an extra twenty rupees if he went quickly. He reached the office at 8:55, sweating and breathless, but he still had five minutes to open his slides and check the projector.

Why did Rohan take an auto instead of waiting for the next bus?
Because his manager had asked everyone to be early for the client visit, so he could not wait for the next bus. That is why he promised the driver extra money to go quickly.

The shared kitchen in Sahil's hostel had one stove for forty boys. During dinner hour, a long queue formed with pots and bowls. To avoid fights, the students made a timetable: each floor had a slot of thirty minutes. The first week, there were complaints that the fourth floor always overran. So Sahil, who was floor representative, brought a small kitchen timer and set it on the shelf. When it rang, the cook had to finish and clean the burner for the next person. The queue shortened. By the third week, boys from other floors asked if they could copy the timer idea.

Why did boys from other floors want to copy the timer idea?
Because it made the cooking turns fair and shortened the queue. It had solved the problem of one floor overrunning its slot.

Along the pavement outside the railway station in Patna, a cobbler named Ramdeen has sat for thirty years under a faded blue umbrella. He mends sandals, polishes shoes and stitches bags. His tools lie in a tin box: needles, thread, a small hammer and a worn brush. He charges ten rupees for a polish and twenty for a stitch, and many customers pay him with a coin and a word of thanks. When it rains, he covers his tools and shares his umbrella with whoever stands nearby. Several people remember the day he fixed a student's shoe for free before an entrance exam.

Where has Ramdeen sat for thirty years?
He has sat on the pavement outside the railway station in Patna.

At the airport in Dubai, Karim worked as a baggage handler. His shift began at four in the afternoon, when most flights from India and Europe arrived. The conveyor belts hummed all night, and the bags came in all shapes: pink suitcases, cardboard boxes tied with rope, golf bags. Karim's job was to load them on trolleys according to flight numbers. He had learned to read a tag in two seconds. One night he found a small stuffed rabbit lying next to a trolley, and he tied it to a handle at the lost property counter with a note. The next day a girl's mother came to collect it, crying with relief.

Where did Karim take the stuffed rabbit?
He took it to the lost property counter.

Mohit had never cooked anything except instant noodles. When his mother fell ill for a week, he decided to make dinner for the family. He chose a simple dal and rice. The dal was salty, and the rice was slightly burnt at the bottom. His sister took one bite and tried to hide a grin. His father ate the whole plate, saying nothing, and then asked for more. Mohit felt a lump in his throat. The next day, he asked his mother for the recipe, wrote it on a card and practised until the dal tasted right.

Why did Mohit feel a lump in his throat when his father asked for more?
Because his father's quiet kindness touched him, even though the food was not good.

Lakshya's first week as a software trainee did not go well. He fixed a bug and, in doing so, created two more. His team lead, Mrs. Verma, called him to her desk. Lakshya expected a scolding. Instead she opened the code and walked through it line by line, asking him what each part did. He explained, stumbled, and then found the faulty line himself. She nodded and said that mistakes found early cost less than mistakes found late. Lakshya went back to his seat, wrote the fix and added a short comment so anyone could understand it later. He felt like he had learned more in an hour than in a month at college.

Why did Lakshya feel he learned a lot in an hour?
Because his team lead patiently guided him through the code instead of scolding him, and he found the mistake himself.

Two roommates in Singapore, Bao and Jae, stopped talking after a quarrel over the air conditioner. For three days they passed each other in silence. On the fourth day, Bao came home with a small fan and placed it on Jae's desk without a word. Jae looked at it, then at Bao, and burst out laughing. They sat down and agreed to set the air conditioner at twenty-four degrees from ten to six. The quarrel had lasted three days but the new rule lasted all year, and Jae used the fan on the days when he wanted it cooler.

How long did the quarrel between Bao and Jae last?
The quarrel lasted three days.

In December, the mornings in Delhi are cold and grey with fog. Rohit leaves for work wrapped in a shawl, his breath a pale cloud. On the metro he sits next to a man who sells roasted peanuts, and sometimes buys a small paper cone. The office heater is broken, so everyone keeps gloves on while typing. At lunchtime they gather in the sun on the terrace, eating sweet potatoes from a street cart. Rohit says winter makes the whole city slower and kinder. People hold doors open, share blankets at bus stops, and talk to strangers about the weather.

What does Rohit think winter does to the city?
He thinks it makes the city slower and kinder, with people holding doors and talking to strangers.

When Anika moved out of her rented room in Gurgaon, the owner refused to return her deposit, saying the walls were dirty. Anika remembered that she had taken photographs on the day she moved in, and again on the day she left. She showed them to the owner, who looked closely and admitted that the marks had been there before. He returned the full amount within an hour. Anika thanked him, and on the way out she told the next tenant, a nervous young man, to take pictures of everything on his first day, in every corner of the room.

Why did the owner return the deposit?
Because Anika's photographs proved that the marks on the walls had been there before she moved in.

The conductor on the 21 bus in Kochi, Mr. Joseph, knows each regular by face and stop. One morning, a young woman got on and gave him a ten-rupee note for a seven-rupee ticket. He pretended to forget the change. She waited a moment, then asked politely for her three rupees. He laughed and put them in her hand, saying he had been testing if she was a careful girl. The next day, she gave him exact change with a smile. The whole bus chuckled. Mr. Joseph laughed again and went back to ringing the bell.

Why did Mr. Joseph say he had been testing the young woman?
It was a joke to cover the change he had kept back. The clue is that he laughed as he put the three rupees in her hand.

The auto driver quoted two hundred rupees for a ride that usually cost ninety. Riya, who had just arrived in Bhubaneswar, did not argue. She smiled and said she would check the fare in the app that the hostel had recommended. The driver hesitated and lowered the price to one hundred and twenty. She asked politely for the meter. He grumbled, switched it on, and the fare came to ninety-five. Riya paid one hundred, thanked him, and walked into the hostel. She later told her roommate that staying calm and asking for the meter had worked better than any argument.

How much did Riya finally pay the driver?
She paid one hundred rupees.

Elena works part time at a small cafe near the university in Madrid. She starts at four in the afternoon, when students come in to study. Her tasks are simple: wipe tables, take orders and refill sugar jars. The owner, Mr. Alvarez, insists that every customer be greeted within a minute, even when the cafe is full. On a slow Tuesday, Elena noticed a boy sitting alone for two hours with only a glass of water. Instead of hinting that he should leave, she brought him a small plate of bread and said it was extra. The boy blushed, thanked her, and returned the next week with a friend.

Why did the boy return to the cafe the next week with a friend?
Because Elena had made him feel welcome. She gave him free bread instead of hinting that he should leave.

Mehul was offered two jobs on the same day. One paid more money, but the office was far away in another city. The other paid less, but it was ten minutes from his parents' home and let him join a music class on weekends. He asked his father for advice, but his father only said, "Think about where you will smile more." Mehul walked around the block three times. He imagined the long train rides and the small flat he would have to rent. He imagined his mother's dal and the Saturday music room. By evening, he had written an acceptance email to the closer job.

Which job did Mehul choose, and what clue shows his reasoning?
He chose the closer, lower-paying job. He imagined the long train rides and lonely flat against his mother's cooking and his music class.

Every Sunday, a flea market takes over the old parking lot behind the cinema in Bandra. Sellers spread out blankets with secondhand books, records, lamps and jackets. Early shoppers get the best bargains, so the crowd begins at eight. Tania, who studies design, goes every week to find old buttons and ribbons. She uses them in her projects. Last week she found a tin full of brass buttons for fifty rupees and carried it home like treasure. She sewed them onto a plain jacket and wore it to class, where three people asked her where she had bought it.

How much did Tania pay for the tin of brass buttons?
She paid fifty rupees for the tin.

The project was due at noon, and at ten the team still had three slides missing. Sofia glanced at the clock and felt her stomach tighten. Instead of panicking, she split the work: Joel wrote the summary, Preeti made the charts, and she finished the introduction. They did not talk except to ask for small things. At 11:40, they merged the pieces and found two mismatched fonts. Joel fixed it in two minutes. Sofia sent the file at 11:55 and leaned back, exhausted but relieved. Their professor replied with a single word, "Received," and the team burst out laughing at the lack of drama.

At what time did Sofia send the file?
She sent it at 11:55.

Sana stood in the office lift on the twelfth floor, watching the numbers go down. At the sixth floor, the lift shuddered and stopped. The light flickered. Three others stood with her: a courier, an old accountant and a young intern holding a stack of files. The intern's hands were shaking, and Sana noticed she was breathing fast. Sana smiled and began asking her about the files, where she studied, and what she wanted to do next. The intern answered slowly at first, then more freely. When the lift finally moved after eight minutes, the girl whispered a thank you, and her hands were steady again.

Why did Sana start asking the intern questions?
To calm her down. The intern's hands were shaking and she was breathing fast, so Sana kept her talking until the lift moved.

The lane behind our office in Pune is lined with small food stalls. At lunch, the air smells of frying onions and sweet jalebis. We usually go to the same stall, run by a man called Ganpat, who serves misal in steel bowls with a slice of lemon on the side. He knows who likes it mild and who likes it hot. He tells jokes in Marathi that I only half understand, but I laugh anyway. It costs sixty rupees, and we often stand in the sun because the benches are full. I have never had a better lunch.

What does Ganpat serve in steel bowls?
He serves misal with a slice of lemon on the side.

Maya had promised to help her friend Dhruv move to his new flat on Saturday. On Friday night, she went to a party and slept through her alarm. She woke at noon to six missed calls. She felt sick with guilt. She called Dhruv, who did not answer. She went to his flat anyway, carrying a box of pastries. Dhruv, dusty and tired, opened the door but said nothing. Maya said she had no excuse and that she would help carry whatever remained. He sighed, pointed to the heavy bookcase, and said, "Start there." By evening, they were laughing over tea and the small dents in the wall.

What does Dhruv's pointing to the bookcase show?
It shows he accepted her apology and was giving her a chance to make up for it by helping.

Behind the old cinema in Lucknow, a tailor named Ashfaq stitches shirts for college students. He charges two hundred rupees for a plain shirt and says he can finish it in three days. A boy from the engineering college once ordered a shirt for an interview and needed it in one day. Ashfaq looked at the cloth, then at the boy's face, and sat at his machine without a word. He worked through the afternoon. At six, he handed over the pressed shirt wrapped in brown paper and refused extra money. The boy got the job and still wears the shirt to important meetings.

How much does Ashfaq charge for a plain shirt?
He charges two hundred rupees for a plain shirt.

At the mill canteen, Rajesh opened his tiffin and found a small note inside, written in his daughter's round handwriting: "Papa, eat everything." He had left the house early and had not seen her that morning. He laughed quietly and showed it to the man beside him. Then he ate every bit of the roti and sabzi, scraping the corners. In the evening, when he returned home, his daughter was already at the door. He handed her the empty tiffin and said that the note had worked, and she giggled and hid behind her mother.

What did the note in the tiffin say?
It said, "Papa, eat everything."

Dr. Shah's clinic in Surat opens at five in the evening, after he finishes his hospital rounds. Patients wait on wooden benches under a ceiling fan, reading old magazines. The receptionist, Kusum, writes each name in a notebook and calls them in order. On busy days she brings a jug of water and small paper cups. A boy of about ten once waited quietly for an hour, holding his mother's hand. Kusum gave him a picture book from her drawer. When his turn came, he did not want to put the book down. Dr. Shah smiled and told him to take it home and return it next week.

What did Kusum give the boy while he waited?
She gave him a picture book.

The flight to Singapore was delayed by five hours, and the departure lounge was full of tired faces. Kavya, travelling alone for a conference, sat on the floor near a charging point. A mother with a crying baby sat beside her. Kavya offered to hold the baby while the mother ate. The baby stopped crying, stared at her bracelet and fell asleep. When the mother returned, she thanked Kavya warmly and said that she had been awake for twenty hours. Kavya smiled, though her own eyes were heavy, and said the time had gone faster with a baby to hold.

Why did the baby stop crying?
The baby became interested in Kavya's bracelet and then fell asleep in her arms.

Ten years after leaving school, forty classmates met in a hotel hall in Nagpur. Some had become engineers, others teachers, and one had opened a bakery. Nandini arrived early and stood near the entrance, watching faces. A tall man walked up and said her name. She did not recognise him until he smiled and she saw the gap between his front teeth. It was Sandeep, who had once shared his lunch with her every day for a year. They laughed and remembered the old teacher who had punished them for giggling. Before the evening ended, they exchanged numbers and promised to meet more often.

How did Nandini recognise Sandeep?
She recognised him by the gap between his front teeth when he smiled.

A heatwave struck Ahmedabad in May, and the temperature rose far above what anyone could remember. The office air conditioner stopped working at noon. Employees wrapped wet cloths around their necks and drank water every ten minutes. The manager sent everyone home early, which brought loud cheers. On the way out, Kiran saw an old rickshaw puller resting under a tree with no water. He ran back, filled his bottle at the office cooler and handed it over. The man drank it in one go and thanked him in Gujarati, and Kiran walked on feeling the heat a little less.

What did the manager do when the air conditioner stopped working?
He sent everyone home early.

Our college club ordered pizza for the meeting, and the delivery boy arrived dripping from the rain. Anil, our secretary, took the boxes and asked him to wait. He ran inside, got a towel from his room and gave it to the boy along with a glass of hot milk. The boy hesitated, then accepted. When he left, he said he would remember our college every time it rained. We all watched the scooter's red light vanish into the rain, and later we agreed that the moment had stayed with us longer than the taste of the pizza.

What did Anil bring for the delivery boy?
He brought a towel and a glass of hot milk.

On a rainy afternoon in Darjeeling, Amit stepped into a small tea shop to wait out the downpour. The owner, a quiet woman named Pema, set a cup of steaming tea before him without being asked. He sipped it and felt warmth spread through him. He asked about the leaves, and she described how they were picked, rolled and dried on the slopes behind the shop. By the time the rain stopped, Amit had bought two packets and learned how to tell good tea by its smell. He walked out into the wet street carrying the packets close to his chest like gifts.

How many packets of tea did Amit buy?
He bought two packets of tea.

Rahul and his friends studied at a tiny tea stall near the college gate every evening before the exams. The owner, a woman called Amma, let them sit as long as they wished. She even lowered the radio volume without being asked. On the night before the last paper, they stayed until ten. When they stood up to pay, Amma pushed the money back and said, "Pay me with good marks." Rahul looked at his friends, and each of them nodded silently. When the results came, they all passed, and the first thing they did was visit the stall with a box of sweets.

Why did they take a box of sweets to the stall?
To thank Amma, since she had let them study there and told them to pay her with good marks.

The first week of college can be confusing, and Ananya felt it in her bones. Every corridor looked the same, and she was late to her first class because she went into the wrong block. Seniors in colourful scarves called out to her and asked her to sing, but she only smiled and moved on. At lunch, she sat alone with her tiffin. A girl from her class, Joanna, asked if she could join. They compared timetables and discovered that they shared four subjects. Joanna drew a rough map of the campus on a napkin and wrote the names of the canteen and the library in capital letters.

Why did Joanna draw a map for Ananya?
Because Ananya was lost and new to the campus. Joanna wanted to help her find places like the canteen and the library.

Kiran waited outside the interview room with his certificates in a plastic folder. He had practised answers all night, but now his mind seemed blank. The receptionist offered him water and said the panel was running late. Beside him sat a woman in a grey suit, reading something on her phone and tapping her foot. Kiran closed his eyes, took three slow breaths and silently repeated his name and the first line of his introduction. When the door opened and his name was called, he stood up straight and walked in. The panel's first question was easy, and he began to relax almost immediately.

What did Kiran do to calm himself before the interview?
He took three slow breaths and silently repeated his name and the first line of his introduction.

Aarti and Jeevan had a chemistry practical exam the next morning, but neither of them had written the lab record. At nine in the evening, they sat in the hostel corridor with two notebooks, a ruler and a cup of coffee each. They copied nothing. Instead, they re-did each experiment in their heads and wrote down the steps in their own words, one by one. By midnight, they had finished half the record. They slept for five hours and ran to the lab at seven. The examiner flipped through their notebooks and asked them three questions. Both answered each one without a pause.

Why could Aarti and Jeevan answer the examiner's questions so easily?
Because they had written the record in their own words after thinking through each experiment, so they understood it.

The rooftop of an old building in Kolkata has become a garden. Tenants planted tomatoes, chillies and marigolds in old paint buckets. A retired teacher, Mrs. Sen, watches over the watering rota, which hangs on the wall. Last summer, a heatwave nearly killed the plants. The young residents carried water in jugs every evening and hung old bedsheets for shade. When the first tomatoes ripened, Mrs. Sen cut them into slices and served them with salt on a steel plate. Everyone ate on the roof in silence, and that was when a tenant said the building finally felt like a family.

What does the silence while eating tomatoes suggest?
It suggests that they were content and moved, sharing a simple reward for their hard work together.

When the month began, Pradeep checked his bank balance three times. His salary had arrived, and he felt rich for about an hour. Then he thought about the rent, the electricity bill and the loan he had promised to repay his brother. He took a notebook and wrote three columns: needs, savings and fun. He put money in each column and smiled when he saw that fun had a small but real share. At the end of the month, he still had two hundred rupees in the fun column and spent it on a book that he had been wanting for weeks.

What did Pradeep do with the leftover fun money?
He spent it on a book he had wanted for weeks.

Tanvir earned twenty-two thousand rupees a month at his first job and spent it all within three weeks. He ate out, bought clothes online and paid for a gym he rarely visited. His father suggested writing down every expense for a month. Tanvir hesitated but tried it. At the end of the month, he saw that food orders and small purchases were taking nearly half his pay. He cancelled the gym, cooked dinner twice a week, and moved the savings into a separate account that he could not touch easily. By the third month, he still had a little money left on the last day, which had never happened before.

What took up nearly half of Tanvir's pay?
Food orders and small purchases took nearly half of his pay.

Lena had a history test on Friday and a bad habit of reading her notes without remembering them. On Wednesday evening, her friend Omar showed her a trick. Instead of rereading, she closed the book, and spoke aloud everything she could remember about each chapter. Then she opened the book and checked what she had missed. At first she remembered very little. By the third chapter she remembered nearly half. Lena kept going until ten at night, then slept without worrying. On Friday she found that many answers came to her easily, and she even recalled a date she had forgotten earlier.

What did Lena do instead of simply rereading her notes?
She closed the book and spoke aloud what she remembered, then checked the book for what she had missed.

Miguel got a job at a hotel in Cancun as a night receptionist. His first night, a guest arrived at three in the morning, upset because his luggage was lost. Miguel did not know what to do, but he listened and wrote down every detail. He phoned the airport three times until he found the bag. The guest, who had been shouting, grew quiet and said it was the first time anyone had listened to him on the whole trip. In the morning, the manager called Miguel and said the guest had written a letter of praise for the hotel.

How did the guest change after Miguel listened to him?
He became calm and grateful. He stopped shouting and later wrote a letter of praise.

Under a bright blue tarpaulin at the weekend market, Shobha sells hand-woven baskets. She learned the craft from her grandmother in a village near Cuttack. The baskets come in four sizes, and the smallest is used for keeping fruits. Many city customers admire them but find the price high. Shobha explains that each basket takes two full days. A young woman once asked her to teach a class. Shobha agreed, and now she holds a free workshop on the first Sunday of each month, where students bring their own palm leaves and sit on mats beside her stall.

How many days does each basket take Shobha to make?
Each basket takes two full days.

The college athletics meet begins at seven in the morning with the hundred-metre race. Runners gather at the starting line in spiked shoes, stretching and shaking their arms. A teacher with a whistle sits on a high stool, holding a stopwatch. When the starter's pistol cracks, the crowd on the benches leaps up. Last year's champion, a girl named Harpreet, was considered the favourite. This year she ran second, and a first-year student named Leela won by a fraction of a second. Harpreet walked across the line and hugged Leela before the cameras could reach them.

What does Harpreet's hug show about her?
It shows she is a good sport who can accept losing gracefully and congratulate the winner.

Hemant spent three months looking for a job and began to lose hope. One afternoon, a friend sent him an advert for a junior librarian at a school. He had never thought of working in a library, but he liked books. He wrote a short letter and went for the interview wearing a borrowed shirt. The principal asked him what he would do if a child lost a book. He said he would first ask the child how they felt. The principal laughed and offered him the job. Hemant ran all the way to the bus stop with the letter in his hand.

What does Hemant's answer about the lost book show about him?
It shows he is kind and understanding with children, thinking first about feelings.

Mahesh set three alarms for the morning of his exam, but a power cut drained his phone overnight. He woke to bright sunlight, panic and silence. The exam was at nine, and it was already eight fifteen. He pulled on yesterday's shirt, grabbed his hall ticket and ran to the bus stop. The bus was late, so he flagged down a stranger on a scooter, who agreed to take him to the college gate. They reached with four minutes to spare. Mahesh thanked him and sprinted up the stairs. In the hall, he sat down breathless, wrote his number and took one deep breath before opening the paper.

How did Mahesh reach the college in time?
A stranger on a scooter gave him a ride to the college gate.

Shanti's mock interview at the placement cell went badly. She talked too fast and forgot her own project name. The trainer, Mr. Ghosh, did not scold her. He asked her to step outside, take three breaths and come back as if it were a new interview. The second time, she spoke slowly and described her project clearly. Mr. Ghosh then gave her a list of five questions to practise aloud, one a day. In the real interview a month later, Shanti heard the first question and smiled, because it was almost the same as one on the list.

Why did Shanti smile at the first question in the real interview?
Because it was almost the same as one she had practised from Mr. Ghosh's list, so she felt prepared.

In the flat above the library lives a retired engineer, Mr. Nair, and his cat, Biscuit. Biscuit sits on the window sill every afternoon and watches students walk by. A group of girls started to stop and wave at the cat. Mr. Nair noticed and began placing a small bowl of water on the sill for stray birds. The girls started to bring seeds. Soon the windowsill was a small gathering place. On Sundays, Mr. Nair brought down a tray of tea for them. He told his daughter on the phone that his lonely flat had become the friendliest corner of the street.

What did the girls bring for the birds?
The girls brought seeds for the birds.

The construction site beside Leena's office made so much noise that she could hardly hear her own phone calls. For three weeks she wore earplugs and kept the windows closed in the August heat. Her colleagues grumbled but did nothing. Leena wrote down the hours when drilling was loudest and found that it began at seven in the morning. She shared this with the building manager, who spoke to the contractor. The next week, drilling started at nine, and the loudest machines worked only after lunch. Leena removed her earplugs for the first time in a month and opened a window, smiling at the fresh air.

What did Leena find out by writing down the noise hours?
She found that the loudest drilling began at seven in the morning.

After losing his job at a printing press in Bhopal, Waheed felt lost for several weeks. His wife suggested he try repairing mobile phones, since many people nearby needed that. He joined a six-week course at a training centre and spent each evening practising on old phones. A shopkeeper, Mr. Sethi, gave him a small corner of his store to work from. In the first month, Waheed fixed only eleven phones. By the fourth month, there was a line outside his desk every Saturday. He hung a small sign above it, painted by his son, that read "Waheed Mobile Care," and he looked at it each morning with pride.

How many phones did Waheed fix in his first month?
He fixed only eleven phones that month.

Before joining the company, Hana went through a three-day trial period in the Seoul office. On the second day, a senior engineer asked her to find the fault in a piece of code. After an hour, she told him honestly that she could not find it. He nodded and asked her to explain what she had tried. She listed the steps, one by one. Halfway through, the senior engineer pointed to a line she had checked twice and said, "There." He said that her calm explanation was why he wanted her on the team, though she had not solved the problem.

Why did the senior engineer want Hana on his team?
Because she was honest and explained her steps calmly, even though she had not solved the problem.

Vikram had worked in the accounts department for six years, and he knew everyone's name. When a new manager joined, many staff were uneasy about changes. Vikram quietly took the new manager through the filing system and explained why certain forms were kept in red folders. He did not ask for credit. A month later, the manager announced that Vikram would lead a small team handling year-end reports. Vikram was surprised. At home that evening, he told his wife that he would need to learn more about spreadsheets and promised to start practising the next morning at six before leaving for the bus.

Why was Vikram chosen to lead the team?
Because he helped the new manager understand the department. He explained the filing system and worked quietly without asking for credit.

After the flood, Nalini's flat was knee deep in mud. She stood in the doorway, near tears. Then she heard footsteps. Four students from the college next door had arrived with buckets, brooms and old shirts to use as rags. They did not say much. They carried furniture to the landing, scrubbed the floor and wiped the walls. By evening the flat smelled of soap, not mud. Nalini offered them tea in plastic cups. A girl said that they had done the same for six other flats that day, and that they would be back tomorrow.

What does the students' plan to return tomorrow show?
It shows that they are committed helpers who wanted to keep helping more flats after the flood.

Jonah noticed that his friend Asha had stopped coming to the college canteen. She sat alone in the library and answered messages with a single word. He did not push her. One afternoon he left a cup of her favourite masala tea on her table with a note that said only, "No need to talk. I'm here." Asha looked up, her eyes wet, and nodded. A week later, she sat with him in the canteen and told him that her grandfather had been ill. Jonah listened without giving advice and walked with her to the bus stop when she was ready to go.

What does Jonah's note show about the kind of friend he is?
It shows he is caring and respectful. He did not push her to talk but let her know he was there.

Meera takes the metro to her office in Hyderabad every weekday. She boards at Ameerpet at 8:15, when the platform is already packed with students and clerks. Most mornings she stands near the door, holding a steel rod and reading a paperback. Last Tuesday the train stopped between two stations for ten minutes because of a signal fault. Nobody panicked. A man beside her offered his seat to an elderly woman, and a teenager shared her water bottle with a boy who felt dizzy. When the doors finally opened at Hitec City, Meera ran to the lift and reached her desk just as the meeting began.

At which station does Meera board the metro?
She boards at Ameerpet.

When Jasmine's friend Kofi moved away from London, they promised to stay in touch. Weeks became months. Jasmine noticed that her messages to him were replied to more slowly each time. Rather than feeling hurt, she sent him a small parcel with a packet of his favourite biscuits and a note: "No reply needed. Just thinking of you." Three days later, a long voice message arrived, warm and apologetic. Kofi said that he had been struggling to settle in and had felt too embarrassed to say so. Jasmine listened twice, then replied with a joke about the biscuits.

Why had Kofi been replying slowly?
Because he was struggling to settle into his new place and felt embarrassed to say so.

On the metro in Delhi, a man took the reserved seat for women and refused to move. A young woman standing near him, Aisha, did not argue. She asked politely if he had noticed the sign. He pretended not to hear. Then a passenger beside her pointed at the sign and said it aloud, and soon two others joined in. The man looked around, flushed and stood up without a word. Aisha thanked the passengers with a nod and sat down. She said later that she had expected to fight alone, but kindness had turned out to be catching.

Why did the man finally stand up?
Because several passengers backed Aisha and pointed out the sign, which embarrassed him.

Dhanya looked for a gift for her colleague who was leaving the company. She wanted something useful but not expensive. At a stall in the Chennai market, she found a small brass bell with a deep sound. She remembered that the colleague, Mr. Sundaram, had a habit of ringing a desk bell whenever the team finished a project. She bought it, wrapped it in newspaper and tied it with a green ribbon. On his last day, he unwrapped it and rang it softly. The whole floor stopped working, listened and smiled. Mr. Sundaram thanked her and said he would hang it in his new office.

What was the gift Dhanya chose?
She chose a small brass bell.

Carmen's group project in the university in Bogota was stuck. Two members were not replying to messages, and the deadline was close. Instead of complaining, she called each of them by phone. One said he had a family emergency and was too embarrassed to tell anyone. The other had misread the date. Carmen redistributed the work, giving smaller tasks to the person in trouble. The group met on a video call that evening and finished on time. Their professor praised the project. Carmen later said that a call had worked better than ten messages, since it let her hear the problem in people's voices.

What did Carmen learn from the experience?
She learned that talking by phone can solve problems better than many messages, because she could hear what was wrong.

Farhan works the night shift at a call centre in Gurgaon. His day begins at six in the evening, when he eats dinner and rides to work in a shared cab. By midnight the office is quiet, and the only sounds are keyboards and soft voices. Farhan likes the extra pay but misses family dinners. On weekends he tries to sleep until noon, yet his mother keeps the television on low in the next room, and her footsteps wake him. Last month he asked her to keep the television off until noon on weekends. She agreed and even put a thick curtain over his door.

What does Farhan like and dislike about his job?
He likes the extra pay but misses family dinners.

A senior named Varun walked up to a nervous group of first-years on the first day of classes and asked if they knew where the physics lab was. They did not. He grinned and said he did not either, and that he had been lost on his first day too. They searched the corridors together and found it behind the library. Varun showed them the way to the canteen, the printing shop and the cheapest tea stall. By the end of the afternoon, the first-years were laughing, and one of them said that he was the kindest senior they could have met.

How did Varun make the first-years feel comfortable?
By admitting he had been lost on his first day too and walking with them to find places.

Nadeem was learning to drive in the crowded streets of Lahore. His instructor, Mr. Hussain, sat beside him with one foot near the second brake. At a busy junction, Nadeem stalled the car twice. Horns blared. His hands grew slippery on the wheel. Mr. Hussain said calmly, "Breathe. The horns are not for you. They are for the road." Nadeem took a breath, restarted the car and moved forward with the traffic. By the end of the lesson, he had stalled only once more. He parked the car, wiped his palms and thanked the instructor with a shaky smile.

Why did Nadeem's hands grow slippery on the wheel?
Because he was nervous, since he had stalled twice with horns blaring around him.

Roshan found an envelope with three thousand rupees lying beside the ATM near his office. He looked around, but nobody was there. He could have kept it, as money was tight that month. Instead, he took it to the bank manager, who wrote down the details. The next afternoon, the manager called Roshan to say a retired schoolteacher had come back looking for it, as it was her medicine money. Roshan felt an enormous relief. He had not slept well the night before, and he walked home lighter than he had in weeks, humming softly.

Why did Roshan walk home feeling lighter?
Because returning the money to its owner relieved his worry, and he knew he had done the right thing.

After midnight, the corner pharmacy in the lane behind Rohan's building is the only shop still lit. The pharmacist, Mr. Alvi, sits behind a glass counter with a small lamp and a thick book. People arrive at all hours: a mother with a feverish child, a taxi driver with a headache, a student after a late study session. Mr. Alvi never seems surprised. He greets each one by name and listens carefully. If something is serious, he gently tells them to see a doctor. Rohan once asked why he stays open so late. He said someone must be awake for those who are not.

Why does Mr. Alvi keep his shop open late into the night?
Because he believes someone should be awake and available for people who need help at odd hours.

Arjun and Mei climbed a hill outside Pune at four in the morning to watch the sunrise before their exams. They carried a torch, a flask of tea and their notes. At the top, the sky was still dark, and the city glowed far below like scattered coins. They sat on a rock and read aloud in whispers. When the first line of orange appeared, they stopped. Neither said anything. After the sun cleared the horizon, Mei closed her notebook and said she felt calm for the first time in days. Arjun agreed, and they walked down together, talking about nothing important.

Why did Mei close her notebook?
Because the sunrise made her feel calm for the first time in days, and she wanted to enjoy that moment instead of studying.

The hostel mess at Anjali's college serves breakfast from seven to nine. On Mondays there is poha with peanuts, on Tuesdays idli and sambar, and on Wednesdays paratha with curd. Students line up with steel plates and chat while the cooks fill each one. A board near the door shows the menu in chalk, and a small box beside it collects complaints and suggestions. Last week the warden added a fruit counter after several girls asked for it. Anjali usually takes a banana and a glass of milk, then hurries off to her first lecture in the science block.

What is served on Tuesdays for breakfast?
Idli and sambar are served on Tuesdays.

The 6:10 express to Delhi was already crowded when Vishal found his seat. Next to him sat a young woman reading a thick book with a worn cover. After an hour, she closed it and sighed. Vishal asked if it was a sad story. She said it was not sad but so good that she did not want it to end. They talked about books for the next two hours. When the train neared the station, she took a pencil, wrote a title on the corner of his newspaper and said he would like it. Vishal folded the page carefully and put it in his pocket.

Why did the woman sigh when she closed her book?
Because she liked the story so much that she did not want it to end.

Every evening after work, Gita practises the harmonium for an hour in her small Chennai apartment. Her neighbours do not mind, because the music is soft. At first she could play only two songs, and her fingers kept hitting the wrong keys. Her teacher, Mr. Subbu, told her to play slowly and listen carefully to each note. After six months, she could play a full raga with only a few mistakes. On the day of her first small concert at a neighbourhood hall, her hands shook, but when the first note came out clear and warm, she knew that every evening of practice had been worth it.

Why did Gita feel her practice was worth it?
Because the first note at her concert came out clear and warm, showing that her slow, careful practice had worked.

Noor's first night shift as a nurse in a Karachi hospital felt endless. At two in the morning the corridor was quiet except for the squeak of a trolley. A patient called out from room six, and she went in to find an old man restless and unable to sleep. She sat beside him and listened as he talked about his farm and his grandchildren. After twenty minutes, his eyes grew heavy. Noor tucked the blanket around his shoulders and dimmed the light. When she returned to the desk, a senior nurse looked at her, nodded and said, "That is the part of the job nobody can teach."

What did the senior nurse mean when she said, "That is the part of the job nobody can teach"?
She meant that caring for people kindly, like listening to the old man, comes from the heart and cannot be taught from a book.

Malika learned to type fast on an old computer in her aunt's shop in Tashkent. At sixteen, she could type faster than anyone in the neighbourhood. She began typing documents for neighbours at a few coins a page. Her aunt encouraged her to save the coins in a jar. At twenty, she used the money to join a computer course at the technical college. She says the jar of coins taught her more than any lecture: that small things add up if you keep doing them. She now teaches typing to other girls in the evening.

What does Malika believe about small things?
She believes small things add up if you keep doing them, as the jar of coins taught her.

At five in the morning, the bakery lane in Pune smells of warm bread. Sameer, the baker's son, stirs a huge tub of dough while his father shapes buns. By six, the first tray goes into the oven. Customers begin to arrive before seven: schoolboys, cyclists and a man who buys four pav every day for his tiffin. Sameer wants to study business, but he wakes up early to help his father until the shop is steady. He says he enjoys watching the lane wake up. By nine, the trays are empty and the two of them sit down with tea and a plain bun.

Who shapes the buns at the bakery?
Sameer's father shapes the buns.

As the interview ended, the manager asked Rekha if she had any questions. She had prepared one about the salary, but she noticed on the wall a framed photo of employees planting trees. She asked instead about the photo. The manager's face lit up, and he spent several minutes describing the company's yearly tree drive. Rekha listened and said she would like to volunteer. When she left, she felt she had done something right. Two days later, she got a call offering her the job, and the manager added that the tree question was the one he had been hoping someone would ask.

Why was the manager pleased with Rekha's question?
Because it showed she was interested in the company's values, not only in pay, and it touched something he cared about.

Joaquin had wanted a camera since he was fifteen. At twenty-two, with his first job in a bank in Mexico City, he finally had an income. But the camera he wanted cost nearly two months of salary. Instead of borrowing, he set aside a fixed amount each week and kept it in an envelope. His friends invited him out almost every Friday, and he sometimes joined them, but he stopped buying new shoes. After seven months, the envelope was full. He walked into the shop on a rainy Saturday, paid in cash and carried the box out with both hands as if it held glass.

What does Joaquin's carrying the box with both hands show?
It shows how much the camera meant to him. He had saved for months, so he handled it with great care.

Ravi's flight to Delhi was delayed by three hours, so he found a seat near gate 14 and opened his laptop. The airport was loud with announcements and children running between the rows. Across from him sat an elderly man holding a small cloth bag and looking at the board anxiously. Ravi noticed the man's ticket was for a flight that had already been called. He walked over, pointed to the screen, and showed him that the gate had changed to 22. The man thanked him in Tamil and hurried away with surprising speed. Ravi went back to his emails, feeling oddly pleased with himself.

Which gate was the elderly man's flight moved to?
His flight was moved to gate 22.
