Priyanka's cousin got married in a banquet hall in Lucknow on a warm evening in February. The ceremony began at seven with music from a small band, and guests arrived in bright silk. Priyanka had volunteered to manage the gift table, so she wore comfortable shoes and kept a notebook for the names. By ten, the table was covered with boxes. At dinner, she finally sat and ate rice with paneer, her feet aching but her mind happy. Her aunt came by and squeezed her shoulder, saying that nobody else in the family would have kept such a tidy list.

In which city did the wedding take place?
It took place in Lucknow.

Three college friends bought tickets for the Saturday night show at a cinema in Chennai. They arrived early and joined the line, chatting about the film's reviews. At the counter, the clerk said that one of their tickets had been sold twice by mistake. Another family already held seat F12. Rather than argue, the friends accepted a refund for that ticket and chose another show on Sunday for all three. They went to a nearby restaurant instead and shared a plate of dosas. Afterwards, one of them, Latha, joked that the evening had become better than the film could ever have been.

Why did the friends decide to see the film on Sunday?
Because one of their tickets had been sold twice, so they could not all sit together on Saturday. They took a refund and chose a new show for all three.

When Marcus opened a small bakery in Lyon, he expected quick success. Instead, the first month brought only a trickle of customers. He stood at the counter, watching rain, feeling foolish. Then a woman came in, bought a plain loaf and said it was the best she had tasted in years. She returned the next day with a friend. Within a week, a queue began forming at seven each morning. Marcus did not change a single recipe. He understood that people had simply needed time to find him, and he decided that patience was an ingredient too.

What did Marcus understand about his early weeks?
He understood that his bread was good and people just needed time to discover the bakery.

Dev was frightened of speaking in English because he feared people would laugh at his accent. At his first job in Pune, he stayed silent in meetings. His manager, Mrs. Hegde, noticed and asked him to send his ideas by email. His emails were clear and smart. Over several months, she asked him to read one of them aloud, and then another. Dev's voice shook at first, but nobody laughed. By the end of the year, he was presenting a small project to the whole team. Afterwards, Mrs. Hegde said she had never doubted him; she had only waited until he believed in himself.

What did Mrs. Hegde do that helped Dev gain confidence?
She let him share ideas in writing first and then gradually asked him to read them aloud, giving him time.

Sunita runs a small vegetable stall near the railway bridge in Kolkata. She wakes at four to buy fresh produce from the wholesale market and sets up her baskets by six. Her customers are mostly office workers and housewives who pass on their way to the station. When a new supermarket opened across the road, she feared her sales would fall. Instead of lowering her prices, she began to chop vegetables for soup and sell small ready packets. Within two weeks, the packets sold out before nine every morning. She now hires a helper, a boy named Biju, to cut onions and carrots while she talks to customers.

Why did Sunita start selling chopped vegetable packets?
She wanted to keep her customers after the supermarket opened. The text says she feared her sales would fall, so she tried something new instead of cutting prices.

Valentina had five minutes to pitch her app idea to a panel of investors in Milan. She wore her best jacket and practised in the mirror until her voice sounded steady. When she entered the room, one of the judges was checking his watch and another was whispering. Valentina paused, took a breath and began with a story about her grandmother, who could never find the bus timetable. The room fell quiet. She showed a simple screen on her laptop and explained how it would help older people. After the pitch, two judges asked for her number. She walked out calmly and only then felt her knees tremble.

How did Valentina begin her pitch?
She began with a story about her grandmother, who could never find the bus timetable.

On the corner outside the engineering block, a young man sells hot noodles from a small cart. His name is Pankaj, and he started the cart after his father fell ill. Students line up from noon until three. He has a rule that anyone who is short of money can pay later. A first-year boy once ate three days of lunches before paying. Pankaj never reminded him. On the fourth day, the boy came back with the full amount and a handful of coins as a tip, and Pankaj tied a small note to his cart that said, "Trust is also on the menu."

What rule does Pankaj have about money?
Anyone who is short of money can pay later.

Priya found a small flat in Pune near her new job. The rent was fourteen thousand rupees a month, and the owner, Mr. Deshpande, asked for a deposit of two months. The flat had one bedroom, a tiny balcony and a kitchen with a window facing a neem tree. Priya liked that the bus stop was only five minutes away. Before signing the agreement, she asked a friend to read it with her. They checked the dates, the notice period and the list of repairs the owner would handle. Two days later she moved in with three suitcases and a folding table.

Who owns the flat that Priya rented?
Mr. Deshpande owns it.

Arun had applied to nine companies and heard back from only two. His cousin suggested he improve his resume, so Arun spent a weekend reading sample ones and cutting his down to a single page. He wrote short lines about his projects and numbers where he could, such as the website he built that handled two hundred visitors a day. He also asked a former teacher to read it. The teacher fixed three spelling mistakes and told him to remove the long hobby list. On Monday Arun sent the new resume to five more companies. By Friday, three of them had called him for an interview.

Who read Arun's resume and fixed the spelling mistakes?
A former teacher of his did.

A dripping tap in Joel's flat in Bristol had kept him awake for two nights. He decided not to call the landlord but to fix it himself. He watched a short video, bought a small washer from the hardware shop for one pound, and spent Saturday morning with a wrench and a towel. The first try leaked more. On the second try, he tightened the nut carefully, and the dripping stopped. He stood in the kitchen, listening to the silence, feeling like he had won a small war. He told three friends about it that evening, even though they did not ask.

How much did the washer cost?
The washer cost one pound.

Noah's sister Eva called him from Sydney every Sunday at ten at night, his time, no matter how busy she was. They talked about small things: the weather, a bus she had missed, a funny cat. When Noah began working long hours in Berlin, he sometimes did not answer. Eva did not complain. She only sent a voice message saying that she would call again next Sunday. Noah realised how much he depended on those calls. The following week, he cleared his schedule and waited for her call with a cup of tea, and he answered on the first ring.

Why did Noah answer on the first ring?
Because he realised how much those calls meant to him and was eager to talk to his sister.

In a night class on photography at a community centre in Birmingham, the teacher, Mrs. Clarke, gave each student a task: take a picture of something ordinary that looks special. Dev photographed a row of steel tiffin boxes drying on a rack after being washed. The light from the window made them gleam like a line of mirrors. When Mrs. Clarke saw the picture, she asked him to explain it. He said his mother washed those boxes every evening, and he had never noticed how they shone. She told the class that was the secret: seeing things you pass every day.

What did Dev photograph for the task?
He photographed a row of steel tiffin boxes drying on a rack.

Ola's first week as a trainee teacher in Lagos was exhausting. Forty children shouted and ran around. On Friday, she tried something different: she knelt down and whispered the instructions. The room quieted so that the children could hear. Whispering became her method. When the headmistress visited, she saw a class of forty bending forward to listen and nodded thoughtfully. Afterwards, she asked Ola to share the trick with the staff meeting. Ola felt her cheeks warm, since she had only been trying to survive.

Why did Ola feel her cheeks warm?
She was surprised and a little shy that her survival trick was being praised by the headmistress.

Three friends from college, Isha, Tom and Waseem, meet at the same tea stall every Sunday evening. The stall is behind the bus depot, and the owner knows their orders: strong ginger tea for Isha, sweet tea for Tom and a plain glass of water for Waseem, who dislikes tea. They sit on a low bench and talk about jobs, family and cricket. When one of them has a bad week, the others listen first and give advice later. Last Sunday, Tom arrived with news that he had been offered a job in Singapore, and the other two clapped louder than the crowd near the radio.

What does Waseem order at the stall?
He orders a plain glass of water.

Lalit could not stand mornings. He pressed snooze three times and arrived at work with his shirt untucked. His manager joked about it, but one day mentioned that mornings were the only quiet time in the office. Lalit decided to test this. The next day he arrived at eight instead of nine thirty. It was true: the office was still, and he finished a task in one hour that usually took three. Over time, he began to wake up earlier, not because he enjoyed it, but because he enjoyed the feeling of having a finished day by lunch.

Why did Lalit begin to wake up earlier?
Because he found that working in the quiet morning helped him finish tasks faster.

In the college debate on whether cities are better than villages, Harini was asked to speak for villages, though she had lived in a city all her life. She spent the week reading and talking to her grandfather, who still lived on a farm near Tirunelveli. In her speech, she described how neighbours brought food when someone was ill. The audience sat very still. The judges gave her the first prize, but afterwards she told her friend that she had learned more from preparing than from winning. She added that she planned to visit her grandfather during the next holiday.

What will Harini probably do in the next holiday?
She will probably visit her grandfather on his farm, since she said she planned to.

On graduation day, Naveen wore a rented black gown that was a little too long. His parents had travelled eleven hours by train and sat in the third row. When his name was called, he walked across the stage, shook hands with the dean and accepted a rolled certificate tied with a red ribbon. He looked into the crowd and saw his mother wiping her face with the end of her sari. His father held up a phone to take a photo, but his hand shook so much the picture was blurry. Afterwards, Naveen insisted that the blurry one was the best picture ever taken.

Why did Naveen say the blurry photo was the best?
Because it showed how emotional and proud his father was. The photo was blurry since his father's hand shook with feeling.

Fiona taught English to adults at a night school in Glasgow. One of her students was Mr. Okonkwo, a driver who had recently moved from Nigeria. He was shy about speaking and often waited until the end of class to ask questions. Fiona began to give him a short sentence every day to practise on his driving route. After two weeks, he came to class and said the sentence perfectly, and added another that he had made himself. The other students clapped. Mr. Okonkwo sat taller in his chair, and from then on, he was the first to raise his hand.

What does Mr. Okonkwo's sitting taller show?
It shows his growing confidence and pride after the class applauded him.

Yuki works as a cashier at a neighbourhood grocery store in Osaka. Her shift starts at nine, and the first customers are usually older residents who buy fresh tofu and vegetables. She has learned each regular's habits. Mr. Tanaka takes exactly two bananas, and Mrs. Sato always forgets her bag and apologises. Yuki keeps spare cloth bags under the counter for her. One morning, Mrs. Sato did not come. Yuki worried through the day. The next morning, Mrs. Sato appeared, explaining that she had a cold. Yuki handed her a small bag and said the shop felt strangely quiet without her.

What does Mrs. Sato often forget to bring?
She often forgets her shopping bag.

Mateo owns a tiny coffee cart outside the Santa Clara train station. He opens at six, before the first commuters arrive, and serves fifty cups before eight. His speciality is a cinnamon latte, listed as number three on his menu board. One rainy morning, a young woman hurried past without an umbrella. Mateo handed her a spare one from under the cart and told her to return it later. She came back the next day with the umbrella, a box of cookies and a polite smile. They talked for ten minutes while he made her drink, and she now stops at his cart every morning on her way to the bank.

What is the cinnamon latte's number on Mateo's menu?
It is number three.

The red double-decker bus in Hong Kong climbs a hill so steep that Mei Ling always holds the rail on the upper deck. She rides it to work at a trading office every morning. At one stop, a street seller boards with a basket of egg tarts and sells them for a few coins. Mei Ling buys one every day and shares half with her friend Jun, who works at the same office. They eat them on the stairs outside before going in. Jun says the tart is the best part of the commute, and Mei Ling thinks he might be right.

What does Mei Ling share with Jun every day?
She shares half of an egg tart with him.

Zubair's first order as a food delivery rider was a bag of hot biryani for a customer on the ninth floor. The lift was broken. He climbed all nine floors, knocked, and found the customer, an old man, waiting at the door with a worried face. The man said his daughter had ordered it for him from another city. He took the bag with trembling hands and asked Zubair to wait. Then he brought out a glass of cold water. Zubair drank it in one go. On the stairs going down, he felt tired but strangely happy, as if he had delivered more than food.

On which floor did the customer live?
He lived on the ninth floor.

Hamid went to a bank in the city to open his first savings account. A clerk handed him a form with many boxes, and he filled them slowly, double-checking his father's name and his address. When he reached the signature box, his hand trembled. The clerk noticed and said that everybody feels that way the first time. She explained the passbook, the debit card and the rule about keeping a minimum balance. Hamid asked two questions and wrote the answers in the margin of the form. He left the bank holding his new passbook like something fragile, and he placed it carefully inside the zip pocket of his bag.

What did the clerk explain to Hamid?
She explained the passbook, the debit card and the rule about keeping a minimum balance.

Fatima opened her letter from the university with trembling fingers. She read the first line twice, then covered her mouth. Her hostel roommate, Linda, who had been pretending to read, looked up. "Well?" she asked. Fatima turned the letter around so Linda could see it. It was an offer of a scholarship for her second year. Linda jumped out of her chair and hugged her so tightly that the letter fell to the floor. They danced around the small room and finally collapsed on the bed laughing. Later, Fatima called her father, and he said nothing for a long moment, then wept softly.

What was in Fatima's letter?
It was an offer of a scholarship for her second year.

On weekends, Arjun volunteers at a small shelter that teaches street children to read. The first Saturday, he brought a bag of storybooks, but the children seemed shy. A boy named Pintu sat in the corner and refused to open a book. Arjun did not push him. He read aloud a story about a lion who lost his roar, doing voices and growling. Halfway through, Pintu moved closer. When Arjun paused, Pintu asked quietly what happened next. The following week, Pintu arrived early and picked out the same book, tracing the words with his finger. Arjun said nothing but smiled, and quickly turned away so Pintu would not see his eyes shine.

What does Arjun's turning away at the end show?
It shows he was deeply moved and happy. His eyes shone, and he did not want Pintu to notice.

Prakruti worked at a small publishing house in Ahmedabad. One Monday, she found that the printer had sent five hundred copies of a book with a blank page in the middle. Her stomach dropped. She told her editor immediately instead of hiding it. Together they called the printer, who agreed to reprint the faulty copies at his own cost. The delay was only four days. Her editor said later that the mistake had not been Prakruti's fault, but speaking up quickly had saved the company a great deal of embarrassment, and it was exactly what he wanted from his team.

What did Prakruti's editor value most in how she acted?
He valued that she spoke up quickly instead of hiding the problem.

Opposite the bus stand in Madurai, there is a tiny stationery shop run by two sisters, Valli and Kala. They sell notebooks, pens, glue sticks and, hidden under the counter, hand-painted bookmarks. A girl once came in and said she needed a gift for a teacher who was retiring. Valli showed her a bookmark with a small peacock. The girl paid and left. A week later, she returned with five friends, each wanting one. Kala looked at Valli and grinned. They quietly brought out more bookmarks and began to lay them out on the counter instead of hiding them.

Why did the sisters start laying the bookmarks out on the counter?
Because customers loved them and wanted more, so there was no reason to keep them hidden.

Our college hackathon started on Friday evening and lasted twenty-four hours. Teams of four sat in the computer lab with pizza boxes, laptops and a whiteboard. My team's idea was an app that helps older people find nearby clinics. At three in the morning, our program crashed, and the whole team stared at the screen in silence. Shreya found a missing bracket in the code. We cheered so loudly that the guard looked in. By noon on Saturday, we had a working demo. We did not win, but the judges said our idea was the most useful one in the room.

What was the narrator's team's app meant to do?
It was meant to help older people find nearby clinics.

Gautam never took notes in class. He believed he could remember everything. When the mid-term exam came, he found he could recall the lecture jokes but not the formulas. His classmate Zoe lent him her notebook, which had neat headings and small coloured boxes around key ideas. Gautam copied them out and tried to understand each one. He passed the exam with an average score. He then started taking short notes in every class, even if they were only five lines. By the final exam, he scored higher than Zoe in one subject, and he returned her notebook with a bar of chocolate tucked inside the cover.

What did Gautam put inside Zoe's notebook when he returned it?
He put a bar of chocolate inside the cover.

The entrance test for the management course in Ahmedabad lasts three hours. Candidates arrive at eight, show their identity cards at the gate and are seated in a large hall. Mobile phones must be switched off and left with the staff. The paper has three sections: English, reasoning and numbers. Each section is timed separately, and a bell rings when it is time to move on. Candidates are allowed a short break after the second section. Water is provided in the corridor. The results are announced on the college website within ten days, and shortlisted students receive a message for an interview.

How many sections does the paper have?
The paper has three sections.

Maria moved from Brazil to Bangalore for work and knew no Kannada. On her first trip to the vegetable market, she pointed at tomatoes and held up fingers for the quantity. The seller laughed kindly and said the word for tomato slowly. Maria repeated it and he beamed. She began writing new words in her phone each evening: onion, water, how much, thank you. A month later, she could bargain in simple Kannada, and the seller gave her a free bunch of coriander every time. She says the market has been her best classroom, because people there want to be understood as much as she does.

Why does Maria call the market her best classroom?
Because people there help her practise and want to understand her. The seller taught her words and rewarded her efforts with free coriander.

Deepa's family expected her to become a doctor, but she loved drawing buildings. During her twelfth year she hid her sketchbook beneath her textbooks. One evening, her uncle, an engineer, found it by accident and spent a long time turning the pages. He told her parents quietly that the drawings showed real skill. Her father was silent for a day. Then he asked her to explain one of the sketches. Deepa described every window and balcony with shining eyes, and her mother, who had been listening in the doorway, said they should find out about colleges that teach architecture. Deepa cried a little and laughed at the same time.

How did Deepa feel when her mother mentioned architecture colleges?
She felt happy and relieved. She cried and laughed at the same time.

The college canteen is busiest at one o'clock, when three classes finish together. Raju, who runs the counter, has worked there for eleven years and knows most students by name. He sells samosas, bread omelettes, tea and cold lemon soda. On Fridays he also makes a big pot of rajma chawal, which sells out within half an hour. Last month a group of students asked him to keep a vegetarian shelf separate from the egg dishes, and he did it the next day. The students now tie a small paper flag on that shelf so new visitors can find it easily.

How long has Raju worked at the canteen?
He has worked there for eleven years.

The night bus from Pune to Mumbai leaves at ten, and Swati takes it twice a month to visit her parents. She carries a small pillow, a shawl and a packet of roasted chana. The conductor, a cheerful man called Sunil, knows her by now and always keeps the window seat on the left. Around midnight, the bus stops at a roadside dhaba where passengers drink tea and stretch their legs. Swati usually sits on a plastic chair and listens to the truckers argue about cricket. The bus reaches Dadar at about four, when the city is still sleeping and the streets are washed clean by the dark.

Where does the bus stop around midnight?
It stops at a roadside dhaba.

Divya had been at an advertising firm in Mumbai for a month, and she felt that nothing she had done was good enough. Her ideas were often changed, and she spent hours on slides that were thrown away. One evening, an older colleague, Mr. Chopra, stopped by her desk and said that every strong idea in the firm had been rewritten at least five times. He pointed to a famous poster on the wall and told her it began as a messy sketch on a napkin. Divya looked at it for a long time, then smiled for the first time that week.

Why did Divya smile after hearing Mr. Chopra?
Because she learned that rewriting is normal even for great ideas, which made her feel less discouraged.

On Sunday afternoons, a quiet bookshop near Marine Drive welcomes a small group of readers. They sit on cushions and read for an hour without talking. Afterwards, they share one line they liked. Rashmi, a shy accountant, had come for months and never spoken. Last Sunday she stood up and read a sentence about the sea at night. Her voice shook a little. Afterwards, the others clapped softly. A student, Amit, said that the line reminded him of his grandfather's village. Rashmi sat down, smiling, and for the first time, she stayed after the session to drink tea with the group.

How did Rashmi feel after reading her line?
She felt happy and more comfortable with the group. She smiled and stayed for tea for the first time.

"The geyser is making a strange noise again," said Ishaan, standing at the bathroom door with a towel over his shoulder. His flatmate Callum looked up from the sofa and sighed. They had told the landlord twice already, and both times he had promised to send a plumber "by the weekend." This time Callum took a photograph of the pipe, wrote a short message with the date of the earlier complaints, and sent it to the landlord. Then he called the building's caretaker, who agreed to look at it that very afternoon. By evening, a man with a toolbox had tightened a loose valve, and the noise stopped.

Who agreed to look at the geyser that afternoon?
The building's caretaker agreed to look at it.

Sahana had been working late for weeks, and her colleagues could see it. She stopped joining lunch, forgot small details and snapped at a coworker over a missing file. One evening, her manager, Mr. Das, stopped by her desk and said, "Go home. The report can wait until tomorrow." Sahana started to argue but then felt her shoulders loosen. She closed her laptop and took the earlier bus. At home, she slept for ten hours. The next day, she finished the report in two hours and apologised to her coworker. She realised that rest had done more for her work than another night of overtime.

Why did Sahana finish the report so quickly the next day?
Because she was well rested after sleeping ten hours. Being tired had been slowing her work.

Rajat sent an email to the whole company instead of just his team. It contained his rough notes about a client, including a few careless remarks. When he saw the error, his stomach dropped. He sat quite still for a minute, then walked straight to his manager's desk and explained exactly what had happened. The manager asked him to send a short, polite correction to everyone and to call the client personally. Rajat did both before lunch. Though the client was mildly annoyed, he thanked Rajat for the call. In the evening, the manager told Rajat that how he handled the mistake mattered more than the mistake.

What did Rajat do right after he realised his mistake?
He told his manager exactly what happened and then sent a correction and called the client.

Naresh bought his first scooter with his own savings after two years of work in a bakery. It was second-hand, dark blue with a small dent on the left side. He washed it every Sunday and checked the tyres each Monday. When his friend Rafi asked to borrow it, Naresh hesitated for a long minute. Then he said yes, but asked him to be careful on the corners. Rafi returned it that evening with a full tank of petrol and the dent still intact. Naresh smiled, shook his hand and said he would lend it again any time.

What did Rafi do to the scooter before returning it?
He filled the tank with petrol.

The night before the final exam, the whole floor of the dormitory was awake. Some students studied in the corridor, sitting on the floor with their notes; others made tea in the common kitchen. Priti knocked on every door and offered to quiz anyone who wanted it. She had topped the previous exam and everyone trusted her memory. Around two in the morning, the warden, Mrs. Nair, appeared with a tray of biscuits and a flask of hot milk. She did not tell anyone to go to bed. She simply said that tomorrow would be easier if they ate something, and the students thanked her with tired smiles.

What did Mrs. Nair bring to the students at two in the morning?
She brought a tray of biscuits and a flask of hot milk.

Siddharth turned twenty-three alone in his rented room. His friends lived in other cities and his family was far away. He decided to treat himself and bought a small chocolate cake from the corner shop, with one candle. Just as he lit it, the door buzzed. His neighbour, Mrs. Fonseca, stood outside with a plate of homemade biscuits. She had heard him humming the birthday song on the stairs the previous night. They shared the cake and biscuits at his small table and talked about her years in Goa. When she left, Siddharth realised that the room no longer felt empty.

What clue shows Mrs. Fonseca knew it was his birthday?
She had heard him humming the birthday song on the stairs the night before.

The central library in Jaipur opens at nine, but a small group of students waits outside from half past eight. Most of them are preparing for entrance exams and want the long tables near the windows. Inside, a sign asks everyone to keep phones on silent. The librarian, Mrs. Kapoor, keeps a register for reserved books and a shelf for newspapers in three languages. On the second floor there is a quiet room with only twelve seats. Students who want it must put their names on a list at the desk. The room closes at eight in the evening, and Mrs. Kapoor rings a small bell five minutes before.

How many seats are there in the quiet room?
There are twelve seats.

Sandeep and his mother ran a tea stall at the bus stop in Ranchi. Every morning, the first customer was a postman, who drank his tea standing and read each letter's address under his breath. One day Sandeep saw him smile at a particular envelope. The postman told him it was addressed to a woman in the next lane, from her son abroad. He said that delivering such letters was the best part of the job. After that, Sandeep began to see the postman as more than a customer, and always gave him a second biscuit for free.

What did the postman say was the best part of his job?
He said delivering letters like the one from a son abroad was the best part.

In the university cafeteria in Seoul, Min-jun noticed that a classmate, Hana, ate lunch alone every day. He decided to sit across from her one afternoon with his tray. She looked surprised, then pleased. They spoke about the difficult statistics class. Hana admitted she did not understand the last chapter. Min-jun said he could explain it, and drew a small diagram on a napkin. She studied it for a minute and said it finally made sense. The next day, three other students joined their table, asking if they could look at the napkin diagram.

What did Min-jun draw on the napkin?
He drew a small diagram to explain the statistics chapter.

Carlos packed his whole life into four boxes and a backpack before moving to Toronto for work. At the airport, his younger sister hugged him so hard that his bag fell. He promised to call every Sunday. The first month in the new city was lonely. He ate cereal for dinner and watched videos of his family's village festival on his laptop. Then a colleague, Grace, invited him to a weekend hike. He nearly refused, but something in him wanted to see the trees. Standing on a cold hilltop beside strangers, he realised that the city might become home after all, one small step at a time.

What changed Carlos's mind about the city on the hilltop?
Being outdoors among the trees with new people gave him hope. On the hilltop he realised the city might become home one step at a time.

On weekday evenings, a group of young office workers plays cricket in a small lane behind a Hyderabad market. The pitch is just a strip of cement, and the wicket is three bricks stacked beside a wall. They play with a tennis ball wrapped in tape. Neighbours watch from balconies and occasionally throw the ball back when it lands on a roof. One evening, a tall bowler named Mukesh hit a shot over the wall and into a flowerpot. The owner, an old woman, came out frowning. Mukesh walked over, apologised, and offered to replace the pot. She laughed and told them to play, but away from the tulsi plant.

How did the old woman react after Mukesh apologised?
She laughed and let them keep playing, asking only that they stay away from her tulsi plant. The apology and offer to replace the pot softened her.

Karan stared at the question paper and felt his hands go cold. He had revised the first four chapters carefully, but the paper began with questions from the last two. He read the first one three times. Around him, other students were already writing. Then he remembered something his senior had said: begin with what you know. He skipped ahead, found a question on the water cycle, and wrote a full answer with a neat diagram. His breathing slowed. By the time he returned to the harder questions, his hands were steady again, and he even finished with ten minutes to check his work.

What did Karan write after he skipped ahead?
He wrote a full answer with a neat diagram on the water cycle.

Marta rents a desk in a shared workspace in Lisbon. The place is full of people with laptops: designers, translators and a man who builds drones. At eleven there is a coffee break, and everyone gathers around a long wooden table. Marta, who works alone as a copywriter, enjoys these ten minutes more than she expected. Someone always asks what she is working on, and the answers sometimes lead to new clients. Last month a translator mentioned that his cousin needed website text. Marta handed over her card, and by the next week she had a new job from a company she had never heard of before.

Why does Marta enjoy the coffee break at the workspace?
Because it lets her meet people and talk, and it sometimes brings new work. A conversation with a translator led to a new client.

The college fest, called Spandan, begins on the fourteenth of March and lasts three days. The first day has music and dance competitions in the open-air theatre. On the second day, there are stalls selling snacks, handmade jewellery and secondhand books. Students from nearby colleges are allowed to enter with a pass that costs fifty rupees. The final day ends with a concert, and the college gates stay open until ten. Volunteers wear yellow T-shirts, and anyone who needs help can find them near the main stage. The organising committee has also set up a first-aid tent beside the principal's office.

On which date does the fest begin?
It begins on the fourteenth of March.

The first monsoon shower arrived in Mumbai just as Pooja was leaving her office. Within minutes the road became a shallow river, and auto-rickshaws vanished. She stood under a tea stall's tin roof beside a group of strangers, each holding a bag over their head. A boy sold paper cups of hot tea and fried onion pakoras. Pooja bought both and ate while watching cars crawl through the water. Someone began humming an old film song, and two others joined in. When the rain eased after forty minutes, she realised she did not mind the wait at all.

Where did Pooja wait out the rain?
She waited under a tea stall's tin roof.

The restaurant in Colombo where Dilani worked as a waitress had one rule: serve the old customers first. On a busy night, a young couple came in with an old man in a wheelchair. The waiters were busy with a big group, but Dilani cleared a table by the window, moved a chair aside so the wheelchair would fit, and served the old man's tea before anything else. The couple whispered thanks. Later, the old man called her over and said the soup reminded him of his wife's cooking. Dilani carried the bowl back to the kitchen to tell the cook the compliment.

Who served the old man's tea first?
Dilani served the old man's tea first.

Kamini had a stammer, and she dreaded oral exams. Her teacher, Mr. Joseph, told her that she could take as long as she needed. During the exam, she stumbled over the first word, then paused and began again. The examiners waited patiently. By the end of the exam, her answers were full and clear, though slow. Mr. Joseph handed her the marks sheet afterwards. She had scored higher than half her class. She did not say a word. She simply held the paper to her chest for a moment and then folded it neatly into her bag.

What does Kamini's silence and folding the paper show?
It shows she was deeply moved and proud, and wanted to keep the moment private.

Aditi and her roommate Sana agreed on a simple rule: whoever cooks does not wash the dishes. For two weeks it worked well. Then Sana began cooking only noodles, which took five minutes and made almost no mess. Aditi, who cooked rice, dal and vegetables, ended up washing a mountain of pots. One evening she did not complain. She simply made a chart on the fridge showing how many dishes each person's meal had used. Sana read it, laughed, and said she would try making a proper dinner on Saturday. The following weekend, the kitchen smelled of onions and curry, and the dish chart had a small smiley on it.

Why did Aditi make a chart on the fridge?
She wanted to show that the rule was unfair in practice, since her meals made far more dishes. The chart showed how many dishes each person's meal used.

Sunil's roommate snored so loudly that the whole corridor could hear it. For two weeks, Sunil lay awake and grew grumpy in classes. He thought about asking for a room change but did not want to hurt his friend's feelings. One afternoon, he mentioned the problem to a senior, who suggested earplugs and a soft talk. That evening, Sunil told his roommate gently, "I think I sleep badly because of the noise. Could you try sleeping on your side?" The roommate was embarrassed but agreed. He also bought a second pillow. After a few nights, the snoring dropped to a gentle hum, and the two remained friends.

What did the senior suggest Sunil do?
The senior suggested earplugs and talking gently to his roommate.

Dhruv's grandfather ran a small electronics repair shop in Lajpat Nagar for forty years. When Dhruv finished his degree, he was expected to find a corporate job, but he surprised everyone by asking to learn the trade. His grandfather shook his head at first, saying the work was dirty and the pay small. Still, he handed Dhruv a screwdriver and an old radio. For a week, Dhruv opened it, labelled every part on a sheet and put it back together. When it finally played a song, his grandfather laughed and clapped his shoulder. "Come tomorrow at nine," he said, "and bring your own tea."

How long did Dhruv's grandfather run the shop?
He ran it for forty years.

On a Sunday morning in Pune, Aditya's friends planned a cycling trip to a lake thirty kilometres away. Aditya had not ridden in two years and borrowed a bicycle from his cousin. The first ten kilometres felt fine. After that, his legs burned and he fell behind. His friend Meghna slowed to ride beside him. They stopped at a roadside stall to drink coconut water. When they reached the lake, Aditya lay on the grass, panting and grinning. He said he could not move, but he wanted to do it again next week. Meghna laughed and promised to bring a proper helmet for him.

How far was the lake from where they started?
The lake was thirty kilometres away.

Ayesha rented a room in a house in Lahore, and the landlady, Mrs. Qureshi, was strict. She did not like noise, late nights or shoes inside the house. At first, Ayesha found the rules tiring. But slowly she saw that the house was always clean and calm, and she could study well. When she came down with a fever, Mrs. Qureshi brought her soup and sat beside her bed without saying much. Ayesha began to see the rules as a form of care. When the year ended, she hugged Mrs. Qureshi and promised to visit.

How did Ayesha's view of the landlady's rules change?
She began to see the rules as a form of care. The calm house and the soup she brought during Ayesha's fever changed her mind.

Every day at one o'clock, the office on the fifth floor turns into a small dining hall. People push desks together and open their steel tiffins. Rekha brings parathas, Daniel brings pasta, and Mr. Joshi brings only boiled vegetables because of his doctor's advice. The group has a habit of tasting one thing from each other's box. Last week, Daniel tried Rekha's mango pickle and coughed for a full minute while the others laughed. Since then, he asks for only a tiny bit. The lunch hour is the one time when nobody mentions deadlines, and even the busiest manager tends to wander by and listen.

What does Mr. Joshi bring for lunch, and why?
He brings boiled vegetables because of his doctor's advice.

Zainab's phone slipped from her hand on the escalator at the mall and landed on the step below with a loud crack. A teenager picked it up and held it out. The screen had a long split down the middle, but it still worked. Zainab thanked the boy, put it in her bag and went on shopping. In the evening, she found that the repair would cost almost half the price of a new one. She decided to use the phone as it was for a month, since she could still make calls and send messages. She stuck a clear tape over the crack and carried on.

Why did Zainab use the cracked phone for a month?
Because the repair cost nearly half the price of a new phone, and the phone still worked for calls and messages.

The campus of the engineering college in Coimbatore covers sixty acres, and a free shuttle carries students between the main gate and the hostels. The shuttle runs every fifteen minutes from seven in the morning to nine at night. A small notice in the library reminds students that the last bus on Sundays leaves at six. Most first-years miss it at least once and end up walking back along the dim road beside the playground. Some seniors have started a habit of waiting at the library steps and walking in groups. They call it the "lamp walk" because someone always carries a small torch.

When does the last shuttle on Sundays leave?
The last shuttle leaves at six.

The canteen at Reema's office served the same rice every day, and it was often cold. People muttered, but nobody did anything. Reema asked a few colleagues to join her and they wrote a short note with suggestions: serve hot food at one, add a vegetable option, and take feedback once a month. They handed it to the HR manager politely. A week later, the canteen began using steam trays, and a feedback box appeared on the wall. Reema watched people line up for hot dal that day, and she felt that a small effort by a few had changed the daily lives of many.

What does Reema's story show about speaking up?
It shows that a polite, organised suggestion can bring real change, since the canteen began serving hot food after the note.

Every morning, Hari crosses a long iron bridge on his way to the printing office in Howrah. The bridge shakes slightly when trucks pass, and some commuters hold their breath. Hari does not mind. He stops halfway to look at the river, where boats move slowly and gulls glide near the water. He says the view gives him one calm minute before the busy day. A coworker once asked if he was late because of it. Hari answered that he left home five minutes early just to afford that moment, and the coworker started to leave earlier too.

Why does Hari leave home five minutes early?
So he can stop on the bridge and enjoy the river view for a calm minute without being late.

Day twelve at my new internship. I made three mistakes in a spreadsheet today, and my supervisor, Mr. Iyer, noticed all of them. I felt my face grow hot. But he did not scold me. He pulled up a chair and showed me how to use a simple check formula that finds mistakes automatically. I spent the rest of the afternoon trying it. By evening, my sheet was clean. On the bus home I thought about how he had said, "Everyone starts like this." I think I will remember that sentence longer than the formula.

Why will the writer remember Mr. Iyer's sentence longer than the formula?
Because it comforted and encouraged the writer, who had felt embarrassed about the mistakes.

The lift in the old building in Kolkata where Rahul works is slow, so most people use the stairs. On each landing, someone has painted a small flower, one on the first floor, two on the second and so on up to six. Rahul asked a janitor about it. The man said that years ago, a child had been scared of the stairs, so a worker painted flowers to help him count. The child grew up and left, but the flowers stayed. Now every new employee climbs and counts them without knowing why.

How many flowers are painted on the sixth landing?
There are six flowers on the sixth landing.

Sophia was always late. Her colleagues teased her, and her manager frowned. She decided to find out why. For a week, she wrote down everything she did in the morning. She discovered that she spent twenty minutes choosing clothes and another ten looking for her keys. That evening she laid out her clothes, put the keys in a dish by the door and packed her bag. The next morning, she reached the office ten minutes early, a first for her. Her manager looked at his watch twice, and Sophia hid a proud smile behind her coffee cup.

What did Sophia discover when she wrote down her morning routine?
She discovered that she lost time choosing clothes and looking for her keys.

Dr. Fischer's seminar on climate and cities began at ten in the auditorium on the first floor. About ninety students attended, mostly from the engineering and design departments. Dr. Fischer showed a chart of temperatures in different parts of a city and pointed out that areas with more trees were cooler by several degrees. A student at the back raised his hand and asked whether painting roofs white would help. She replied that it could, but trees also gave shade and cleaned the air. At the end, she asked everyone to look at their own street on the way home and count how many trees it had.

What did Dr. Fischer ask students to do on the way home?
She asked them to look at their own street and count how many trees it had.

Working at a mobile shop in Jaipur, Kavita met a customer who shouted that his new phone was useless. She did not shout back. She asked him to sit, offered water, and then asked what exactly was not working. It turned out that he had never turned on the data setting. She showed him how, and he stood silent. He then apologised, saying that he had been rude. Kavita replied that a phone can be confusing when one is new to it. The man bought a case and a charger before he left, and two weeks later he sent his wife to the shop.

Why did the customer send his wife to the shop later?
Because Kavita had treated him patiently and helped him, so he trusted the shop.

Admissions at the polytechnic in Nashik close on the thirtieth of June. Students must bring their tenth mark sheet, a school leaving certificate and four passport photographs. The fee can be paid in two parts: half at admission and half before the first term exam. The hostel has only sixty beds, so applicants who live more than twenty kilometres away get priority. Classes begin on the first of August. A small helpdesk near the main gate answers questions from nine to five, and there is a notice board with the list of documents beside it. Late forms will not be accepted after the closing date.

On which date do admissions close?
Admissions close on the thirtieth of June.

Iqbal had always been the quiet one in the group. At the college annual day, a teacher asked for volunteers to host the programme. Nobody raised a hand. Iqbal felt his heart pound, then lifted his arm slowly. His friends stared. Backstage, his hands were cold. When he walked to the microphone, he forgot his first line. The audience waited. He smiled, took a breath and said, "I forgot my line, but I remembered your faces." People laughed warmly. The rest of the show passed easily. Afterwards, his friends surrounded him, and one of them said he should host every year.

What does the audience's laughter suggest about how they felt?
It suggests they were warm and supportive, and liked his honest, humorous way of handling his mistake.

Every Sunday, a cycle ride begins at the India Gate lawns in Delhi at six in the morning. About forty people meet there every week, from schoolboys to a retired colonel. Their leader, Anita, checks every bike for air in the tyres and brakes that work. The route is twelve kilometres and ends at a small tea shop where everyone gets a glass of hot milk. Last Sunday, a new rider fell behind on the slope. Anita slowed down and rode beside him, talking about her first ride years ago. When he reached the tea shop, the others cheered, and he laughed, too tired to speak.

How long is the cycle route?
It is twelve kilometres.

Gopal has driven a taxi in Kolkata for twenty years. He keeps a small notebook on the dashboard in which passengers write their names and one word about the ride. Some write "calm," others write "fast," and a child once drew a tiny cow. Gopal says the notebook reminds him that every trip is different. Last winter an old woman asked him to drive past her childhood home before taking her to the hospital for a routine visit. He took the longer road without increasing the fare. She wrote only one word that day: "Thank you." Gopal kept that page folded in the corner of the book.

What does Gopal keep on his dashboard?
He keeps a small notebook where passengers write their names and one word about the ride.

On Saturday, Beena went to the supermarket with a short list and came out with a full cart. She had forgotten her glasses and could not read the labels. A teenage worker named Imran noticed her squinting and asked if she needed help. He read each label aloud and found the cheapest brand of rice. Later, at the billing counter, she realised she had bought two bags of sugar. She laughed and said her tea would be sweet for months. Imran carried her bags to the auto stand. Beena tipped him, but he refused and said it was part of his job.

Why did Imran refuse the tip?
He considered helping customers part of his job and did not want extra money for it.

Two hours before closing, the night market near the harbour in Cape Town fills with music. Vendors light small lamps over their tables of spices, scarves and grilled corn. Thando has a stall of beaded bracelets. A man bargained with her for ten minutes over a bracelet that cost fifty rand, then offered thirty. Thando shook her head and smiled. She said each bead was sewn by her mother. The man looked at the small stitches, was silent for a moment and handed over the full amount. Thando wrapped the bracelet in a bit of cloth and added a second tiny one for his daughter.

Why did the man pay the full price?
Because Thando explained that her mother sewed each bead, and he saw the careful stitches and respected the work.

Kunal lost his wallet on the train to Pune. It held his identity card, a few notes and a photo of his grandmother. He felt a sinking feeling and asked other passengers if they had seen it. Nobody had. At the next station, he went to the railway office and filled out a form. Three days later, his phone rang. A man on the line said he had found the wallet under a seat and had posted it to the address on the card. Kunal received it the next morning. Every item was there, including the photo. He wrote a thank-you letter and mailed it to the man.

How did Kunal get his wallet back?
A man found it under a seat on the train and posted it to the address on the card.

On Sunday evenings, Esha cooks a big dinner for her flatmates in Edinburgh. This week, she planned a South Indian meal with lemon rice, sambar and fried papad. She spent the afternoon buying curry leaves and tamarind at a small Asian grocery. Her flatmate Rory, who had never tasted this kind of food, hovered near the stove, asking questions. Esha let him stir the sambar. When they sat down to eat, Rory took a bite, blinked, and asked for water, but then he took a second helping. "It is hot," he said, "but it is also the best thing I have had all month."

What did Rory do after he first tasted the food?
He asked for water, but then took a second helping.

The night guard of the office building in Gurgaon, Mr. Bisht, has worked from eight in the evening to six in the morning for twelve years. He sits at a small desk with a flask of tea and a radio turned low. Late workers wave to him when they leave, and he waves back. On the night of the big storm, the power went out, and he used his torch to lead six people down the stairs. Nobody was hurt. The next week, the company manager gave him a certificate and a new torch. Mr. Bisht put the certificate in his drawer and kept the torch on his desk.

What did the manager give Mr. Bisht after the storm?
He gave him a certificate and a new torch.

During his first winter in Berlin, Tarun missed the noise of home. The streets were quiet, and everyone seemed busy. He called his mother, but the time difference meant she was usually asleep. One Sunday, he found an Indian grocery shop and bought a packet of tea and some spices. In his tiny kitchen, he boiled tea the way his mother did, with ginger and too much milk. The smell filled the room. Tarun sat on the floor with his cup and closed his eyes. For a few minutes, he was back in his mother's kitchen, and when he opened his eyes, the room felt a little warmer.

Why did the room feel warmer to Tarun?
Because the smell and taste of his mother's style of tea reminded him of home and comforted him.

Ivan told his grandmother in Kyiv's suburbs that he would call every evening once he left for his job in Warsaw. In the first month, he called daily. Then work became heavy, and sometimes he forgot. One night he realised it was past ten and he had not called. He rang her anyway. She answered cheerfully and said she had been waiting but was not worried. Ivan felt a pinch in his chest. He set a daily reminder on his phone that rang at seven, and from then on he never missed a call.

What does the pinch Ivan felt in his chest show?
It shows he felt guilty and sad for making his grandmother wait.

A short walk from the main road in Ahmedabad, a lane of old shops sells kites before Uttarayan. The shopkeepers start preparing in December, stacking paper kites in red, yellow and blue. Children press their noses to the windows and count their pocket money. Hamid, a young kite maker, shapes each frame from thin bamboo and glues colourful paper on it, finishing about forty a day. He says the best kite is not the prettiest but the one that flies straight. He tests every new design on the rooftop behind his shop, running along the edge with the string wrapped around his hand.

How many kites does Hamid finish in a day?
He finishes about forty a day.

Farah lived in a hostel where the hot water ran out by six in the morning. For weeks, girls grumbled in the corridor but did nothing. Farah decided to write a short letter to the warden. She did not use angry words. She listed dates when the water had stopped early, and she suggested that the heater timer might be set wrongly. Twelve girls signed it. The warden read it the same day and called the maintenance man, who found that the timer had indeed been set an hour early. By the next morning, the water stayed hot until eight, and several girls thanked Farah at breakfast.

Why was Farah's letter successful?
It was polite and specific. She listed dates and suggested a likely cause, and many girls signed it.

Rishi was too shy to ask a girl in his class, Mehak, for her notes. For three days, he looked at her from a distance, rehearsing his sentence. On the fourth, she walked up to him and said she had noticed he missed a lecture and offered her notes. Rishi stammered a thank you and took them. He copied them at once and returned them with a small chocolate bar. Mehak smiled and said that the next time he could simply ask. Rishi walked home feeling light and a little foolish, thinking about all the wasted days.

How did Rishi feel as he walked home?
He felt light and happy, but also a little foolish for waiting so long to speak.

Vivek failed his driving test twice because he got nervous when the examiner sat beside him. For the third attempt, he practised with his sister sitting silently in the back seat holding a clipboard, pretending to be the examiner. At first, he was tense. After the fifth time, he stopped noticing her. On the test day, he drove the route smoothly, signalled early and parked in a single move. The examiner nodded and stamped his form. Vivek came out of the office, handed the paper to his sister and said she could be the one to drive them home.

How did Vivek's sister help him pass?
She sat in the back seat with a clipboard, pretending to be the examiner, so he got used to being watched.

At the entrance of the hostel, a new notice says that the study room will stay open until midnight during exam week. Students must carry their identity cards and sign a register at the door. Food is not allowed inside, but water bottles are. The night watchman will check the room every hour. If anyone wishes to request extra tables, they can write their names on the list kept with the warden. The notice also reminds students that the gate will be locked at half past midnight, and anyone staying out later will need the warden's written permission.

Until what time will the study room stay open during exam week?
It will stay open until midnight.

Dev noticed that the printer on the third floor jammed every Monday. People wasted time pulling out crumpled paper and arguing about whose turn it was to fix it. Instead of complaining, Dev spent his lunch break reading the manual. He learned that the tray was too full and the paper was damp. He asked the stationery clerk for a fresh pack, stored it in a drawer, and put a small note on the machine saying to load no more than a hundred sheets. The next Monday nothing jammed. Colleagues stopped to thank him, and his manager mentioned his name in the weekly meeting.

What did Dev read during his lunch break?
He read the printer's manual.

Sumit joined a rock climbing club at college, even though he was afraid of heights. For his first climb, the instructor, Ms. Alvarez, let him try the lowest wall. Halfway up, he froze and refused to look down. Ms. Alvarez spoke calmly from below, telling him to look only at the next handhold. He found it, moved, and found the next one. At the top, he looked out over the campus and laughed in amazement. Back on the ground, his hands were scratched and his knees were shaking, but he asked to climb again right away, this time on a slightly higher wall.

What does Sumit's wish to climb again show?
It shows that he overcame his fear and enjoyed the challenge.

A group of college friends on their way to a trek in the hills near Manali stopped for tea at a roadside stall. An old woman served them with thick, sweet tea and told them the path ahead was steep after the second bridge. Rakesh, the group's leader, thanked her and bought a bag of dried apricots. Beyond the second bridge, the path did turn steep. The friends found themselves resting more often, passing the apricots around. At the top, they remembered the woman's warning and the sweet tea, and Rakesh said they should visit her again on the way down.

What did Rakesh buy from the old woman?
He bought a bag of dried apricots.

Everyone in Mahi's family expected her to study engineering. She had the marks, and her cousin was already at a famous college. But Mahi liked history and spent weekends in a small museum in Delhi. When it was time to fill the forms, she sat at the table with two papers in front of her. Her grandmother, who was peeling peas nearby, said that people do their best work where their curiosity lives. Mahi looked at her for a long moment. Then she took the pen and ticked the box for history. Her mother sighed, but she also put an arm around her.

What clue shows that Mahi's mother accepted her choice?
She sighed, but she also put an arm around her daughter.

Nikhil rides a bicycle to work in Amsterdam, even in rain. He keeps a yellow raincoat folded under the seat and a spare scarf in his bag. The ride takes twenty minutes along a path beside a canal. On the way he passes a bakery, and on Fridays he buys a warm roll and eats it at the first red light. Colleagues sometimes tease him for not owning a car, but he says he has never been stuck in a traffic jam. At the office, a small room is set aside for bicycles, and Nikhil's is always the cleanest one because he wipes it every evening.

How long is Nikhil's ride to work?
It takes twenty minutes.

Once work ends each day, Anil and his wife Deepti walk around the lake in Bhopal. They talk about small things: a rude customer, a colleague's wedding, whether to buy a new fridge. Anil likes the part when the sun is low and the water looks like a sheet of copper. Deepti likes to stop near the old banyan tree and listen to the birds settle. On the way back, they buy roasted corn from a woman who knows them by name. They have done this for six years, and they say it is how they keep their marriage calm.

Where do Anil and Deepti walk every evening?
They walk around the lake in Bhopal.

On a quiet Sunday, Teodor walked from his flat in Bucharest to the old market. He bought a loaf of bread, a bag of walnuts and a small bunch of wildflowers. On the way back, he met his neighbour, Mrs. Popescu, carrying a heavy basket. He took the basket from her and carried it to her door. She insisted that he come in for tea. He stayed for two hours, listening to her stories of the city fifty years ago. When he finally left, he found that the flowers had begun to droop, and he put them in water at once.

What did Teodor buy at the market?
He bought a loaf of bread, a bag of walnuts and a small bunch of wildflowers.

It was nine at night, and the third floor was empty except for Ruchi and the cleaner, Mrs. Dsouza. Ruchi was finishing a report. Mrs. Dsouza set a small cup of tea beside her without saying a word. Ruchi looked up, surprised, and said she had not expected it. Mrs. Dsouza replied that she had seen Ruchi eating a biscuit for dinner twice that week. Ruchi laughed and took the cup. She told the cleaner she would leave soon, and half an hour later she did. On her way out, she left a note on the cleaner's trolley, thanking her for the tea.

Why did Mrs. Dsouza bring Ruchi tea?
Because she had noticed that Ruchi was working late and eating only a biscuit for dinner, and she wanted to look after her.

Ellie was a designer at a small agency in Manchester. On Friday afternoon, the client changed everything and wanted a new logo by Monday. The team groaned. Ellie said she would take the weekend to work on it, but she asked her manager for Monday morning off in return. The manager agreed. On Saturday, she sketched ten ideas on paper and picked the best one. On Sunday, she made it digital and sent it to the client before midnight. The client replied with a single line: "Perfect." On Monday, instead of going to the office, Ellie slept until noon and had a long, quiet breakfast.

What did Ellie ask her manager for in return for working the weekend?
She asked for Monday morning off.

Mr. Pinto, a retired engineer, volunteers every Saturday at the youth centre to guide young job seekers. He does not give speeches. He asks each person to describe a problem they once solved. When Neha said she had once fixed a leaking tap in her hostel, he asked her to explain how. She described each step. He said that was exactly the way to answer interview questions: calmly, in order, with the result. Two weeks later, Neha got her first job offer. She brought Mr. Pinto a small box of sweets and said she had used the tap story in every interview.

What did Neha use in her interviews?
She used the story about fixing the leaking tap.

Devika quit her job as an accountant to start a plant nursery in Coimbatore. Her friends thought it was risky. She rented a small plot near a highway and began with fifty pots of herbs. During the first monsoon, half of them rotted. She nearly gave up. But a local farmer, Mr. Murugan, stopped by and showed her how to improve drainage. The following season, her herbs thrived. Within a year, she was supplying three restaurants. She says she still uses her accountant skills to track every pot, and she has never regretted leaving the office.

What helped Devika's herbs survive the second season?
Mr. Murugan showed her how to improve drainage, so the plants stopped rotting.

Mumbai never sleeps, people say. At two in the morning, Chetan walks past a tea stall where taxi drivers sit on plastic stools and compare fares. A paper boy cycles by with a stack of newspapers tied to his back. Under a streetlight, a woman sells flower garlands to anyone heading to the early temple. Chetan, who has just finished a night shift at the printing press, buys a cup of tea and stands with the drivers for a few minutes. They do not know his name, but they nod to him as if he were one of them.

What does Chetan do at the tea stall?
He buys a cup of tea and stands with the drivers for a few minutes.

Ritika earns pocket money by teaching two children in her neighbourhood after college. Her student Aman, aged ten, struggles with fractions. At first she explained them with numbers, and he stared blankly at the page. Then she cut a roti into quarters and asked him to eat three. He laughed and said, "Three out of four!" From then on, Ritika used food for every lesson: slices of apple, pieces of chocolate and cups of milk. After two weeks, Aman's test score rose from four to eight out of ten. His mother, who had been worried, sent a box of laddoos to Ritika's house.

How did Ritika make fractions clear to Aman?
She cut a roti into quarters and used food examples.

Dear diary, today I started my job at the bookshop on Park Street. The owner, Mr. Banerjee, gave me an apron and a list of rules: smile at everyone, never let a book touch the floor, and always ask a customer what they last enjoyed reading. At first I felt shy, but a girl came in looking for a gift for her brother and I suggested a detective novel. She bought two copies, one for him and one for herself. Mr. Banerjee watched from behind the counter and said nothing, but he winked. I walked home humming, even though my feet hurt from standing for eight hours.

What did Mr. Banerjee give the narrator on the first day?
He gave the narrator an apron and a list of rules.

Professor Menon always begins his lecture with a question instead of a definition. Today he asked the class, "Why does a bridge not fall down?" Students offered guesses: strong steel, good cement, luck. He wrote each answer on the board and then drew two arrows showing how weight spreads along a curve. The room became quiet as the idea sank in. At the end he asked them to bring a small paper bridge to the next class and test how many coins it could hold. A girl in the back row grinned, because she had already started thinking about how to fold the paper.

What homework did Professor Menon give?
He asked them to bring a small paper bridge and test how many coins it could hold.

At her friend's wedding in Udaipur, Sonal was asked to hold the bride's bouquet during the vows. She was so busy watching that she almost forgot it was in her hand. The groom's father leaned over and whispered that she should keep it steady, because it was going to be thrown at the end. When the moment came, Sonal handed it to the bride, who turned and threw it straight at her. She caught it with both hands, and the crowd cheered. Sonal blushed and hid her face behind the flowers, and her friends teased her all evening.

What did Sonal do after she caught the bouquet?
She blushed and hid her face behind the flowers.

On the fourth floor of a Mumbai building, an old lift often broke down, and residents had to climb the stairs with heavy bags. One evening a young tenant named Jaspreet saw an elderly neighbour, Mr. Pillai, sitting on the second landing with a bag of groceries, too tired to continue. Jaspreet took the bag in one hand and offered his arm with the other. They went up slowly, stopping on each landing. Mr. Pillai talked about the days when the building was new and the lift worked perfectly. At his door, he insisted that Jaspreet take two oranges as a thank you, and Jaspreet accepted them with a smile.

What did Mr. Pillai give Jaspreet as thanks?
He gave Jaspreet two oranges.

A group of friends from the college in Rishikesh planned a rafting trip on the Ganga. Before the trip, the guide, Bunty, gave them a talk about safety. He told them to listen to his shout, hold the rope and never stand up in the raft. The water was cold and loud. When they reached the first rapid, two of the friends laughed out loud and one closed her eyes. Bunty shouted, and everyone paddled together. The raft dipped, rose and slid out into calm water. Afterwards, Bunty told them that the river is easy to respect when you listen to it.

What did the guide tell the friends not to do in the raft?
He told them never to stand up in the raft.

The lane behind Anwar's flat in Hyderabad begins to buzz at six in the morning. A milkman rings his bicycle bell, a woman sweeps the doorstep, and a street dog yawns on the corner. Anwar, a young nurse, walks to the bus stop with her shoes in her hand because the road is wet from water poured on the ground. A fruit seller gives her a single guava and tells her to eat it later. She slides it into her bag. During her long shift, in the hospital canteen, she finds the guava and eats it, and thinks of the lane.

What did the fruit seller give Anwar?
He gave her a single guava.

Dinesh opened a small noodle stall in a lane near a college in Guwahati. In the first week, he sold fewer than twenty plates a day. He noticed that students liked spicy food and hated waiting. So he began to prepare sauce in advance, added a chilli level from one to five on a hand-painted board, and promised any plate in seven minutes. Customers started coming in groups. After a month, he was selling over a hundred plates daily and had hired a boy to wash dishes. He kept the old wooden spoon he used on his first day, tied to the stall with a red thread.

What did Dinesh add to the board to attract students?
He added a chilli level from one to five.

On the first night in the hostel, Divya lay awake listening to the ceiling fan. Her roommate, Kavitha, was asleep, and the corridor was full of footsteps and laughter that did not belong to her. She missed her mother's cooking and her own bed. In the morning, Kavitha offered her half of a mango and asked about her hometown. Divya talked about the lake near her house, and Kavitha said her village had one too. They discovered they both hated early mornings and loved old film songs. By evening, Divya had stopped counting the days until the holidays and had hummed a tune while arranging her books.

What did Kavitha offer Divya in the morning?
She offered her half of a mango.

The local train from Churchgate to Virar leaves every four minutes at peak hour. Manoj, a clerk, has learned exactly where to stand on the platform to get a seat near the window. He keeps his lunch in a small bag on his lap and listens to old songs through one earphone, keeping the other ear free for station announcements. On some days the coach is so crowded that he cannot move his arms. Still, the ride has become his quiet time. He gets down at Borivali, walks to a small tea shop, and takes ten minutes to finish the crossword before climbing the stairs to the office.

At which station does Manoj get down?
He gets down at Borivali.

When Sneha became a team manager at twenty-six, she was the youngest on the floor. Several older colleagues treated her with polite distance. In her first week, she made a point to ask each person about their work, and she wrote down their suggestions. She noticed that Mr. Rao, who had been there for twenty years, never spoke in meetings. She asked him privately what he thought of a new plan. He gave a surprisingly good idea about reducing paperwork. In the next meeting, Sneha mentioned it and gave him credit. Mr. Rao sat a little straighter, and from that day, he began to speak.

Why did Mr. Rao begin to speak in meetings?
Because Sneha asked for his opinion and gave him credit in front of others. That made him feel respected and confident.

Subject: Change of room for Thursday's review. Hello team, the review meeting will now be held in Room 204 instead of the main hall, because the projector in the hall is being repaired. We will start at 2:30 as planned. Please bring your printed progress sheets and a pen. Anyone who cannot attend should tell Nalini by Wednesday evening so she can adjust the seating. Tea and biscuits will be arranged in the corridor outside the room. Thank you for your understanding, and apologies for the late notice. Regards, Sunita from the admin office.

Why was the meeting moved to Room 204?
Because the projector in the main hall is being repaired.

Early each morning, a group of older residents does laughing yoga in Cubbon Park. Among them is a young woman named Prerna, who joined to ease her stress after a hard month at work. At first she felt silly making forced laughs, and she stood at the back. But the sound of fifteen people laughing at nothing was so absurd that she began to giggle for real. Soon she was in the front row. After the session, one of the members, Mr. Gowda, shared his flask of ginger tea with her. She now arrives at six every morning, even on Sundays, and says the laughter makes the office feel lighter.

Why did Prerna join the laughing group?
She joined to ease her stress after a hard month at work.

Our college cricket team had lost four matches in a row. Before the fifth, the captain, Yash, gathered everyone under a banyan tree. He did not give a speech. He asked each player to name one thing they liked about the person to their left. At first, it felt awkward. Then people began to laugh. Aryan said that Samir always saved the ball with his bare hands. Samir blushed. On the field, the team seemed different: they cheered each catch and patted each other's backs. They won the match by twelve runs, and no one was sure whether it was the cricket or the tree.

What did Yash ask each player to do under the banyan tree?
He asked each player to name one thing they liked about the person to their left.

At 10 p.m., the girls' hostel gates close. One evening, Pallavi came back from the library twelve minutes late, and the guard, Mr. Raman, was already holding the lock. She apologised and said the library had stayed open for an exam week. Mr. Raman looked at her, then at the clock, and opened the gate with a grunt. He asked her to write her name in the late register. Pallavi did so carefully. The next morning, the warden told the girls that the register was meant for safety, so someone would always know who was inside and who was not.

What was the late register meant for, according to the warden?
It was meant for safety, so that someone would always know who was inside the hostel and who was not.

The economics lecture in Hall B starts at nine, but students begin to arrive at ten to. Professor Rao uses a long stick to point at a chart that fills the entire wall. Today the chart showed how the price of tomatoes changed through the year. A student asked why prices went up in the rainy season, and the professor explained that rain made roads bad and slowed down the trucks. Then he asked the class to guess what would happen to prices if a new road was built. After a moment, a girl said they would probably fall, and he nodded and wrote her answer on the board.

What did the girl guess would happen to prices if a new road was built?
She guessed that the prices would probably fall.

Professor Lim's class on public speaking has a rule: no slides. Each student stands before the group for two minutes and talks about an everyday object. Neel chose a spoon. He began by holding it up and saying that his grandmother stirred tea with the same kind of spoon for fifty years. The class smiled. He talked about the shape, the sound it made against a glass, and the way it reminded him of home. When the two minutes ended, Professor Lim said nothing but wrote one word on the board: "Memorable." Neel sat down, his ears red, and he did not stop smiling for the rest of the lesson.

Why were Neel's ears red when he sat down?
Because he felt shy and pleased at the praise. The professor wrote the word memorable, and Neel kept smiling.

Ignacio found a flatmate through a notice at the university in Seville. The first evening, the new flatmate, a quiet student named Pablo, set a pot of lentils on the stove and asked if Ignacio wanted some. They ate at the small table, talking about football and exams. Pablo explained that he had grown up in a village, where the dinner table was always crowded. Ignacio admitted that he missed his family too. They agreed to cook together every Sunday, taking turns choosing the menu. The following Sunday, Ignacio made rice with peppers, and Pablo cleaned the whole kitchen without being asked.

What did Pablo cook on the first evening?
He cooked a pot of lentils.

Nikhat's day in Delhi begins at five thirty. She boils water, packs her tiffin and wakes her younger brother for school. At six forty, she walks to the bus stop, where she meets two women from her building who work at the same hospital. They talk about the price of onions and the latest TV serial. The bus takes forty minutes. At work, Nikhat arranges files and answers calls at the front desk. She eats lunch at one with a woman who sells bangles outside the gate. By seven in the evening, she is back home, making dinner and checking her brother's homework.

At what time does Nikhat walk to the bus stop?
She walks to the bus stop at six forty.

The hostel curfew was ten o'clock, but Neelam had a train to catch at eleven to visit her sick grandmother. She went to the warden, Mrs. Thomas, and explained. Mrs. Thomas asked for a letter from her parents. Neelam called her mother, who promptly sent a photo of a signed note. The warden read it, nodded, and wrote a pass. She also asked the guard to keep the gate open until Neelam's auto arrived. As Neelam climbed in, she looked back and saw Mrs. Thomas standing at the gate, one hand raised in a small wave.

What did Mrs. Thomas ask Neelam for before giving the pass?
She asked for a letter from her parents.

On his first day as an intern, Samir arrived thirty minutes early and waited in the lobby. The receptionist smiled and gave him a visitor card. His supervisor, Ms. Fernandes, took him around the floor and introduced him to the design team. She gave him a laptop and a simple task: sort two hundred customer photos into folders by product. Samir worked quietly until lunch. When Ms. Fernandes checked his folders, she nodded and said the labels were very clear. She then asked whether he would like to sit in on the afternoon meeting. Samir said yes, and he took a notebook along.

Why did Ms. Fernandes invite Samir to the afternoon meeting?
She was pleased with his work. She said his labels were very clear, and then she asked if he wanted to join.

My cousin Arun lives in a tiny room in Mumbai, with a window that looks at a brick wall. When I visited, he cooked eggs on a one-ring stove and apologised for having only one chair. I sat on the bed. He said that he was saving every rupee to bring his parents to the city next year. His room was not much, but he had pinned a calendar on the wall with a circle around a date in March. He tapped it and said, "That is when my mother sees the sea."

What is circled on Arun's calendar?
A date in March, when his mother will come to see the sea.
