Kabir's friends laughed when he joined a pottery class. They thought it was a hobby for retired people. But after a hard week of coding at his job in Bengaluru, he found that shaping wet clay on a wheel emptied his mind. The first bowls he made were lopsided and thick. His teacher, Mrs. Iyer, told him to stop trying to force the clay and to feel it. By the fifth class, he made a small cup that stood straight. He carried it home on his lap in the bus, steering carefully around every bump, and placed it on his desk next to his keyboard.

How did Kabir feel about the pottery cup he made?
He felt proud of it. He carried it home carefully on his lap and put it on his desk.

At the college canteen, a poster on the wall announces a new rule: students must return their trays to the counter. Before the rule, tables were often cluttered, and workers spent half the lunch hour clearing. On the first day, a few students forgot, and a volunteer reminded them politely. By the third day, almost everyone did it without being asked. The head cook, Mrs. Lobo, said that the canteen felt calmer and her team had time to serve hot food. A new line of students now forms at the dosa counter at the back, where the oil is still fresh.

Why does the canteen feel calmer now?
Because students return their trays, so workers no longer spend most of the lunch hour clearing tables.

Every year before Diwali, the apartment block where Harsh lives decorates its courtyard with marigolds and small clay lamps. This year, the young residents offered to paint rangoli at the entrance. Harsh and four friends worked from five in the afternoon until dark, arguing mildly about colours. Mrs. Rao, who lives on the ground floor, brought them tea and sweets. When the design was finished, a gentle wind blew a little coloured powder out of place near the edge. Harsh did not sigh. He bent down and quietly patted it back, and Mrs. Rao smiled and said the rangoli looked better because it was made with care.

Who brought the young people tea and sweets while they worked?
Mrs. Rao brought them tea and sweets.

Aisha spent two days trying to find an error in her program. It printed the wrong answer, but she could not see why. She asked her friend Ben to look at it. Ben read it silently for a few minutes and then asked her to explain the code aloud, line by line. Halfway through, Aisha stopped and said, "Oh. I never reset the counter." She laughed and changed one line. The program ran correctly. Ben said that explaining a problem to someone else often reveals the answer. From then on, Aisha kept a small rubber duck on her desk and talked to it whenever she got stuck.

What was the error in Aisha's program?
She had never reset the counter.

The library at Rhea's college is a place of strict silence, so when her phone rang loudly one afternoon, every head turned. She fumbled and switched it off, her face burning. A boy at the next table whispered that it happens to everyone and slid her a small slip of paper. It said, "I once sneezed in the exam hall and the invigilator laughed." Rhea stifled a giggle into her sleeve. She wrote a thank you on the same slip, passed it back and returned to her reading, her face slowly cooling to its usual colour.

What did the boy write on the slip of paper?
He wrote about the time he sneezed in the exam hall and the invigilator laughed.

The gym at the university in Delhi opens at six and closes at nine. Nitin goes at seven, before his first class. He has a simple routine: ten minutes on the cycle, three rounds of weights and five minutes of stretching. The instructor, Mr. Bhatia, writes each member's plan on a small card and keeps the cards in a wooden box near the door. Nitin's card says he should add one kilo every two weeks. On Fridays, the gym is nearly empty, and Nitin enjoys having the whole floor to himself. He wipes the equipment with a towel and returns the card to the box before he leaves.

Where does Mr. Bhatia keep the members' plan cards?
He keeps them in a wooden box near the door.

The flat above Camila's in Buenos Aires hosted a party every Friday night. For several weeks, she lay in bed and put a pillow over her head. One Friday, she went upstairs, not angry but tired. A young man opened the door with a friendly face. Camila explained that she had a baby sister who visited on weekends and needed sleep. The man looked ashamed and promised to lower the music after eleven. He kept his word. A month later, he invited Camila and her sister to a quiet Sunday lunch to say sorry again. Camila accepted and brought a cake.

Why did the man look ashamed?
Because he realised that his loud parties were keeping a baby from sleeping.

Louise drove a ride-share car at night in Montreal to pay for her studies. One cold evening, a young man got in carrying a pot plant wrapped in newspaper. He kept it safe on his lap and asked her to avoid the bumps. On the way, he explained it was a gift for his grandmother, whose garden had been lost when she moved to a small flat. Louise drove slowly the whole way. When he got out, he left a generous tip and a small note saying thank you. Louise kept the note in her glove box and read it again whenever her shifts felt very long.

Why did Louise drive slowly?
Because the passenger asked her to avoid bumps to protect the plant meant as a gift for his grandmother.

Mira promised her roommate she would be home by nine to help prepare for an exam. Then her office manager asked her to stay and finish a report. Mira checked the clock again and again. At eight thirty, she took her bag, walked into the manager's room and said, politely, that she had a promise to keep and could complete the report first thing in the morning. The manager frowned but agreed. Mira ran to the bus, reached home at five to nine and found her roommate pacing with her notes. They studied until midnight, and Mira felt good about keeping both responsibilities in order.

What does Mira's decision to leave show about her?
It shows that she takes promises seriously and can speak up politely. She kept her word to her roommate and offered to finish the report in the morning.

On a crowded bus in Chennai, a young man named Prakash sat by the window, half asleep after a night shift. At the next stop, an elderly woman got on, holding the rail with both hands. Nobody offered her a seat. Prakash noticed her trembling arm and stood up at once, waking himself with a jolt. She thanked him and sat down. At the next stop, a student who had been watching offered to carry her bag. By the end of the route, three people had begun a small conversation with her. Prakash stayed standing, holding the rail, feeling warmer than he had all day.

Why did Prakash feel warm at the end of the ride?
Because helping the woman made him feel good, and it led others to be kind too.

Whenever Pranav came home late from work, his younger sister Tara left a plate of food on the table and a light on in the hall. She never mentioned it. One night he arrived at midnight, drained from a long deadline, and found a note beside the plate: "Eat. Sleep. No emails." He laughed, sat down, and ate the cold rice with relish. Then he switched off his phone. The next morning he knocked on her door and said he would take her to her favourite ice-cream shop on Sunday. She pretended not to care but smiled into her pillow.

What does the note from Tara show about her?
It shows she cares about her brother and wants him to rest, even if she does not say so openly.

On the final night of the college fest, the open-air theatre was packed. A band of first-year students was supposed to perform third, but their drummer was stuck in traffic. The host announced a ten-minute break. The band's singer, Ira, looked at her friends and said they would go on without him. She taught the guitarist a simple beat on the edge of the stage with her hands. The audience clapped along. Halfway through the second song, the drummer ran in, panting, and slid onto his seat. The crowd roared. At the end, Ira bowed first to the drummer, then to everyone else.

Why was there a ten-minute break?
The band's drummer was stuck in traffic.

Neha's scooter broke down on the flyover during the evening rush. Cars slowed behind her, and a few drivers honked impatiently. She pushed the scooter to the edge, switched on the hazard lights and took out her phone. The battery showed two percent. She quickly called her brother and told him the exact spot, then the phone went dark. Ten minutes later, a delivery rider stopped and asked if she needed help. He checked the petrol and found the tank empty. He rode to a nearby pump, filled a bottle and returned. Neha thanked him twice and promised herself she would never ignore the fuel light again.

What did the delivery rider find when he checked the scooter?
He found that the petrol tank was empty.

Hira read the message from her manager three times. It said only, "Call me when you are free." She could think of nothing but trouble. She stared at her phone for ten minutes, then walked to a quiet corner and dialled. The manager answered in a cheerful voice and said the client had loved her presentation and wanted her to lead the next one. Hira put her hand on her chest and breathed out slowly. She realised she had spent ten minutes imagining the worst, and she promised herself to wait for facts before worrying, though she knew it would not be easy.

Why did Hira put her hand on her chest and breathe out slowly?
She felt great relief, because the call was good news and not the trouble she had feared.

Sanjay drives an auto-rickshaw in Bhopal. He starts at six, takes a break at noon and works again until eight. He says the best passengers are children going to school, because they tell him jokes. The worst, he says, are people who argue about the fare. On most days he earns enough for fuel, food and a small saving. His daughter is in the ninth class and wants to become a pilot. Every month, Sanjay puts aside five hundred rupees in a tin box labelled with her name. When he passes the small airport, he slows down for a few seconds and looks at the planes.

What does Sanjay's slowing down near the airport show?
It shows he is thinking about his daughter's dream of becoming a pilot and hoping to help her reach it.

The inter-hostel football final was played under floodlights on Saturday night. Both teams had unbeaten records, and the stands were packed with students waving scarves. In the final minute, with the score level, a young defender named Ayaan misjudged a pass and the ball rolled to the other team's striker. Everyone held their breath. The striker shot, and the goalkeeper dived and tipped it round the post. Ayaan dropped to his knees, covering his face. His captain ran over, pulled him up and shouted that the match was not over. The game went to a penalty shoot-out, which Ayaan's team won, and he sobbed openly on the shoulder of his goalkeeper.

Why did Ayaan sob at the end of the match?
He was overwhelmed with relief after his mistake nearly cost the game. His team won on penalties, so the tension he felt after the error finally broke.

Lucia took her first job as a barista in a cafe in Rome. She learned to steam milk and draw a heart on the foam. On her second day, she spilled an entire jug on the counter, and the owner, Signor Rossi, did not scold her. He handed her a cloth and said everyone spills in the first week. By Friday, her hearts looked like hearts, and a regular customer remarked that her cappuccino was almost as good as the owner's. Signor Rossi pretended to look offended and then added, "Almost," with a grin that made everyone in the cafe laugh.

What did Signor Rossi do when Lucia spilled the jug?
He handed her a cloth and said everyone spills in the first week.

Every morning at six, the bus to the hill station leaves Dehradun and takes five hours. Passengers carry woollen caps, flasks and bags of oranges. Gopal, the driver, begins every trip by touching the steering wheel and whispering something. A girl at the front asked him once what it was. He said it was a small thank you to the road for letting him pass. The girl laughed, then went quiet and watched the pine trees slide by. On the next trip, she touched the rail beside her window as the bus started, and she whispered the same.

What does the girl's touching the rail suggest?
It suggests she liked Gopal's habit and wanted to copy it as her own way of thanking the road.

The results were to be posted on the department notice board at four. By three thirty, nearly sixty students stood in the corridor, pushing gently and checking their phones. Rina stood near the wall, her arms crossed. She had studied hard but could not tell whether the paper had gone well. At four sharp, a clerk pinned the sheets. A cheer broke out near the front. Rina waited until the crowd thinned, then walked up and ran her finger down the list. She found her roll number and stopped. She had passed with distinction. She turned around and walked out quietly, then ran down the stairs two at a time.

At what time were the results posted?
They were posted at four.

Maya was asked to design a poster for the college blood donation camp. She sat in the library and drew a red drop with two hands holding it. Her first draft had so many words that nobody would read them. A friend, Joseph, looked at it and said, "If I were walking past, I would read three words, no more." Maya erased half of the text and kept the date, the place and one line: "Give an hour, save a life." The camp organisers loved it. On the day of the camp, the queue stretched past the notice board, and Maya stood at the back, quietly checking her poster.

Which line did Maya keep on the poster along with the date and place?
She kept the line: Give an hour, save a life.

Three students started a small business from their dorm room selling hand-stitched cloth bags. At first they sold ten bags a week to friends. Then one of them, Zoya, suggested they put a photo of each bag on a notice board near the canteen with a price. Orders began to arrive from other departments. The trio bought a second sewing machine from savings and split the work: Zoya cut the cloth, Peter stitched, and Hari handled orders and deliveries. They kept a small notebook for expenses, since they had agreed never to spend more than they earned. After three months, the bags had earned back the cost of the second machine.

What did Zoya suggest that helped sales grow?
Putting a photo of each bag with its price on a notice board near the canteen.

The traffic signal at Brigade Road had been dead for two days, and the city looked angry. Cars crept forward from all four sides, and a bus stood sideways across the junction. Constable Lakshmi stepped into the middle with a whistle and a white glove. She held up one hand to stop the buses, waved the cars from the left, and let a line of schoolchildren cross. At first drivers ignored her, but her calm voice and steady hands soon won them over. In half an hour the jam shrank to a short queue. A shopkeeper brought her a cup of water, and she accepted it with a small nod.

Why did the drivers finally listen to Constable Lakshmi?
Because she stayed calm and gave clear signals. The text says her calm voice and steady hands won them over.

Winston began painting small pictures of Mumbai's trains on postcards. He sold them at a stall outside the station for fifty rupees each. At first, few people stopped. Then a tourist bought three and posted one to her mother. A week later, the tourist emailed him a photo of the card pinned on her mother's fridge. Winston printed the photo and fixed it to his stall. People began to ask where the card had travelled. He kept painting every evening after his job at the courier company and found that each postcard felt like sending a bit of the city abroad.

Why did Winston fix the photo on his stall?
To show that his cards had travelled and been loved, which made more people curious and interested.

The new neighbour in 3B played the guitar every night at eleven. For a week Tara said nothing, though she had an early shift at the clinic. On the eighth night, she knocked on the door holding a plate of biscuits. The young man, Luis, opened it with a puzzled look. Tara said she loved the music but needed to sleep by ten thirty on weekdays. He apologised at once, said he had not known the walls were so thin, and offered to practise at six in the evening instead. They shook hands in the doorway, and from then on, she could hear soft tunes drifting through her wall in the early evening.

Why did Tara bring biscuits when she knocked on Luis's door?
She wanted to ask him politely without causing a quarrel. The biscuits were a friendly gesture while she explained that she needed to sleep early.

The warehouse in Noida runs two shifts, and Imran works the morning one, from six to two. His job is to scan boxes and load them onto trolleys for the delivery vans. The work is noisy and the floor is cold in winter. His supervisor, Mr. Thapa, hands out gloves at the start and asks everyone to stretch for two minutes. Imran has noticed that the days feel shorter when the group sings a line of a film song while sorting. Last Thursday they did it for an entire hour, and the trolleys moved faster than usual. Even Mr. Thapa tapped his foot near the gate.

What time does Imran's shift end?
It ends at two in the afternoon.

The team meeting had been going for an hour, and nothing was decided. Karthik, a junior designer, had an idea but felt too nervous to say it. He doodled on his notebook and watched the senior members argue about colours. Finally, the manager, Mrs. George, asked if anyone from the back wanted to add something. Karthik's heart pounded. He raised his hand slightly and explained a simple layout he had sketched. The room went silent, and then the manager said, "Show me." He passed the sketch forward. By the end of the meeting, the team had chosen his layout, and Karthik was careful not to grin too widely.

Why was Karthik careful not to grin too widely?
He was pleased but did not want to look boastful. His idea had just been chosen in front of senior colleagues.

Four colleagues in Gurgaon share a car to work, taking turns to drive. On Mondays it is Ria's turn, on Tuesdays Faiz's, and so on. They agreed on one rule: the driver chooses the music. Faiz picks old Hindi songs, Ria prefers quiet instrumental tunes, and Tom, who is from Ireland, plays folk music that nobody else understands. Last week, Tom's choice made the whole car sing along to a chorus they did not know, nodding wildly to the rhythm. The drive, which usually feels long, felt short that day, and they arrived at the office humming.

Whose turn is it to drive on Tuesdays?
It is Faiz's turn on Tuesdays.

Erin and her three flatmates set up a group chat to manage bills. It worked until the electricity bill arrived and nobody replied. Erin waited a day, then wrote, "Hi all, the bill is due on Friday. Can everyone send their share by Thursday night?" Two replied at once. Mark said he had forgotten. The fourth, Sophie, sent a message that evening apologising for being slow because of her exams. By Thursday, all the money was in. Erin noticed that clear dates, not reminders about being late, were what made people act, and she kept using the same style for the next bills.

What did Erin ask everyone to do in the group chat?
She asked everyone to send their share by Thursday night, since the bill was due on Friday.

The team's presentation was set for ten, and the projector refused to work. Anita, the group leader, tried the cable, the power switch and a different port. Nothing worked. The professor was already seated, watching the clock. Instead of apologising, Anita asked her team to gather around a single laptop and stand near the front row. She spoke clearly about the project, while Mohan held up the printed charts. Two students came closer to see the screen. By the end, the professor nodded and said he had rarely seen a team adapt so smoothly. The technician arrived with a new cable, but by then the talk was over.

What did Mohan hold up during the presentation?
He held up the printed charts.

Rani's father sold balloons, and every evening he came home exhausted. One day she asked if she could help, and he said no, because the crowd was rough. But she followed him to the market, hid behind a stall and watched. She saw him smile at every child, lifting balloons to each of them, even when they did not buy. A man shouted at him to move, and he moved without a word. Rani crept home before him. That night she gave him a glass of water and did not say a word about what she had seen, but she held his hand a little tighter.

Why did Rani hold her father's hand tighter?
Because she had seen how patiently and kindly he worked, and it made her proud and loving.

The expedition to the island began at dawn. Twelve students and two teachers sailed across the bay in a hired fishing boat. The sea was calm, and the captain, a tall man with a beard, pointed out dolphins breaking the surface. On the island, the group set up a camp near a freshwater spring. The students spent the day counting crabs on the shore and taking notes on seabirds. At night, they cooked rice over a driftwood fire. A teacher played a guitar, and everyone sang quietly. On the third day, the boat returned to carry them home, and they left the beach as they had found it.

How many students went on the expedition?
Twelve students went on the expedition.

Last winter, my grandmother took me to the mela in her hometown. She walked quickly through the crowd, greeting people at every corner. Sellers called out to her by name, and a woman pressed a handful of peanuts into my palm without charging anything. At the far end of the ground, we reached a small tea stall run by an old man. Grandmother stopped, and the two of them stood looking at each other for a long moment. Then they both began to laugh. She told me later that they had gone to the same school seventy years earlier, and had not met since. She talked about him all the way home.

How did Grandmother feel on meeting the old man?
She felt delighted and nostalgic, because they laughed and she talked about him all the way home.

Jamal had waited three years to see the sea. As soon as the family arrived at the beach, he ran to the water's edge and stopped. He stood very still with his arms hanging at his sides. His sister called him to come and paddle, but he did not answer. The waves rolled in, soaked his shoes and rolled out again. After a long minute, he turned around, his face wet, and said that it was bigger than he had imagined. He did not talk much for the rest of the afternoon. He just kept looking at the horizon as if he were trying to remember it.

How did Jamal feel when he saw the sea?
He felt amazed and deeply moved, because he stood still, did not answer, and kept staring at the horizon.

The group had been walking for hours when the guide suddenly stopped and raised his hand. Everyone halted. He pointed silently at a spot in the trees ahead, where a deer stood at the edge of a stream. Nobody moved. Even the youngest, a boy of six, held his breath, though his eyes were huge. The deer lifted its head, listened and looked straight at them for several seconds. Then it turned and slipped into the shadows. The guide lowered his hand. Only then did the boy let out a long, trembling whisper that he had never seen anything so beautiful.

What does the boy's whisper show about his feelings?
It shows he was amazed and thrilled to see the deer.

Every morning the bus to the college is crowded, and Suresh has learned a trick. He climbs on at the first stop, where the seats are still empty, and he gives up his place only when someone older enters. One day a woman with a heavy bag stood next to him, but he was studying for a test and did not look up. The conductor cleared his throat loudly. Suresh looked up, saw the woman, and jumped to his feet with a red face. She thanked him, and he spent the rest of the ride staring out of the window, no longer thinking about the test at all.

Why did Suresh's face turn red?
Because he felt embarrassed that he had not noticed the woman and offered his seat sooner.

The hot-air balloon ride over Cappadocia takes place at sunrise. Passengers meet at four in the morning, drink hot tea and walk to a field where the balloons lie flat on the ground. Fans inflate them slowly, and the burners roar with flame. When the basket lifts, the ground drops away quietly. The pilot, a Turkish man named Emre, steers by finding different wind levels. Below, the stone chimneys and cave houses glow pink. The flight lasts an hour. After landing, the crew serves cake and a sparkling drink, and each passenger receives a certificate signed by the pilot.

When do the balloon rides take place?
They take place at sunrise.

On my first day in London, I took the underground to a market near the river. The train was crowded, but a man gave me his seat and showed me how to read the map. At the market, I tried a pastry with cheese and spinach and watched a woman making pasta by hand. A street musician played the violin beside an old arch. By evening, my feet hurt, and I sat on a bench to eat apples from a paper bag. A friendly pigeon waited beside me. I took the underground back to my hostel and slept for eleven hours.

How did the writer travel to the market?
The writer took the underground train.

An old woman sells guavas at the bus stop, and she never raises her voice. She sits on a folded sack, cuts a guava into four, and hands the pieces out for free. Most people take a piece and walk away without buying. She does not seem to mind. When the afternoon bus is late and the sun is hot, however, many of those same people come back, and buy a whole bag. Her neighbour once asked why she gave away so much. She replied that fruit tastes better when someone has already chosen it for you, and that a free taste is only a small seed.

What does the old woman mean by calling a free taste a small seed?
She means the free taste may grow into later sales, because people come back and buy.

Pedro had saved for a year to take his mother to the mountains, and now they stood in line for the cable car. The line was long and the sky was darkening. A guard announced that the car would stop running in twenty minutes because of the wind. Pedro looked at his mother, whose hands were holding her scarf tight. She said nothing, but her eyes moved from the sky to the car and back. When the guard waved them forward, they were the last ones allowed on. Pedro stood close to the window. His mother gripped his arm all the way up, and neither of them said a word.

How did Pedro's mother feel in the cable car?
She felt nervous or afraid, because she gripped his arm tightly and said nothing.

The vegetable market in our town is run by a cooperative of women farmers. They arrive at dawn with baskets of spinach, brinjals and green chillies from their own fields. A large board shows the day's prices, written in chalk by a schoolgirl named Radha. Customers pay using coins or small notes, and change is kept in a tin box. Any vegetables that are not sold by noon are given to the community kitchen near the school. The cooperative has been running for eleven years, and it began with only five women and a borrowed handcart. Now there are sixty members, and they own a small truck.

Who writes the prices on the board?
A schoolgirl named Radha writes them in chalk.

At the antique market in the old town of Sonagarh, the shops stand side by side in a covered street. One sells old coins, another sells radios from the 1950s, and a third has a large collection of postcards and stamps. A man called Mr. Verma keeps a trunk full of brass door handles, which he polishes every day with a soft cloth. On Sundays, a group of retired teachers gather in his shop to drink tea and discuss history. A young couple came last month looking for an old gramophone. Mr. Verma found them one in a corner, covered in dust, and sold it at a fair price.

What does Mr. Verma polish every day?
He polishes brass door handles every day.

The mango seller at the roadside stall let customers taste a slice before buying, but one man took three slices and left without a word. The seller shrugged and turned to the next customer. An hour later the man came back with a large bag and asked for five kilos. He said the slices had reminded him of the mangoes in his mother's village, which he had not tasted in twenty years. The seller weighed the fruit slowly and added two extra mangoes at the end. He did not say why. The man only nodded, and carried the bag to his car with both arms.

Why did the seller add two extra mangoes?
Because he understood how much the taste meant to the man and was moved by his story.

Ayesha had promised her little brother that they would build the biggest sandcastle on the beach. They worked all afternoon with plastic buckets and a spoon from the picnic basket. Towers, walls and a wide moat took shape. Then the tide began to creep closer. Her brother stared at the water, his lip trembling, and Ayesha suddenly knew what he feared. Instead of telling him it would be fine, she said the sea wanted to visit the castle, and they should let it in as a guest. They stepped back and watched. When the first wave touched the moat, he clapped and shouted hello.

How did Ayesha help her brother handle the sea washing the castle away?
She turned it into a game, saying the sea was a guest, so he stopped being sad and clapped instead.

Before the lantern parade, the children of the school were told to walk slowly and keep their lanterns upright. Inside the hall, they stood in line, their paper lanterns glowing. Then the door opened, and a cold wind swept in. A dozen flames wavered. Some children gasped. A tall boy named Ravi quietly stepped to the front and shielded the smallest girl's lantern with his hand. The line moved forward. Outside, the wind eased, and the glow of a hundred small lights moved along the dark road like a slow river. The little girl turned to Ravi and whispered something that no one else heard.

What did Ravi's action show about him?
It showed he was kind and protective, because he shielded the smallest girl's lantern from the wind.

The village lit a hundred lamps along the river on the final night of the festival. Anita, who had lost her father that spring, stood at the edge with a single lamp in her hands. She had not planned to come. Her aunt had pushed her gently out of the door. As she knelt to place the lamp on the water, her hand shook, and a drop of oil fell on the stone. She watched the little flame float away, and she did not move until it joined the others and could not be told apart. Then she wiped her eyes, stood up and walked home slowly.

What was Anita probably thinking of as she set the lamp on the water?
She was probably thinking of her father, since she had lost him that spring and stayed until the flame vanished.

On our road trip, my father insisted on taking a shortcut. After half an hour, the road turned into a dirt track, and then into a field with a gate. My mother said nothing, but she looked out of the window very hard. My father drove on, and soon we reached a river with no bridge. He stopped the car and sat for a while with his hands on the wheel. Finally he turned the car around, and we drove back the whole way. At the main road, he said that we would be late for lunch. My mother passed him a biscuit without a word, and he took it and laughed.

What will the family probably do next?
They will probably continue on the main road, arriving late for lunch.

Christmas morning arrived, and the street outside Joel's house was silent, though the day before it had been loud with carols. He looked out of the window and saw that snow had fallen overnight, which almost never happens in his town. He pulled on his coat over his pyjamas and ran out. Soon, doors opened up and down the street, and neighbours came out in slippers, laughing and pointing. A woman made a tiny snowman on the wall. Joel scooped some snow in his hands and just stood there, with his mouth open. It was a long time before anyone remembered the presents inside.

Why did nobody remember the presents for a long time?
Because the surprising snow was so exciting that it took all their attention.

The old man at the next table in the train carriage had not moved for hours. He sat with his hands folded, looking at the passing fields. Whenever the train stopped, he leaned forward a little, as if he were looking for someone. At a small station near sunset, he stood up and pulled a battered suitcase from the rack. He walked slowly to the door. On the platform, an elderly woman waited, holding a small umbrella. They stood facing each other for a few seconds without speaking. Then she took his suitcase, and he took her arm, and they walked off together without looking back.

What can we guess about the old man and the woman on the platform?
They probably knew each other very well, perhaps a married couple, since they met quietly and walked off together.

The village of Mawlynnong in Meghalaya is often called the cleanest village in Asia. Bamboo dustbins stand at every corner, and the residents sweep the paths each morning. Many houses are built of wood and bamboo, and flower gardens grow in front of every door. Visitors are asked not to drop any litter, and children remind them politely. A walk through the village takes around an hour, ending near a living root bridge in the next village, made by the roots of rubber trees. The local women serve tea and fried banana in the shade. The village also runs a small school, and the tourist money helps pay for the teachers.

What is the living root bridge made from?
It is made from the roots of rubber trees.

Christmas in Kerala begins with a star hung from every house. Families make star-shaped lanterns from bamboo and coloured paper, and they hang them from trees and balconies in the first week of December. On Christmas Eve, midnight mass fills the churches, and the congregation sings carols in Malayalam. On the day itself, families eat appam with chicken stew, followed by a rich plum cake baked a week before. Children go from house to house in small groups, singing and collecting sweets. Our neighbour, Mr. Mathew, plays Father Christmas every year and hands out chocolates from a red cloth bag.

What do families use to make the star lanterns?
They make star-shaped lanterns from bamboo and coloured paper.

When the spring festival in Assam, called Bohag Bihu, arrives, the village women wear gold and white cloth woven at home. The dancing takes place in an open field after the afternoon meal. Drummers beat a fast rhythm on long drums, and the women sway with their hands raised. Young men blow on a horn made from a buffalo's horn and join the circle. The elders sit under a tree, drinking sweet tea and commenting on the steps. A small girl named Mala, who is five, tried to copy the older women and stumbled. They paused to let her catch up, and then the circle widened to bring her in.

What kind of cloth do the women wear?
They wear gold and white cloth woven at home.

The border guard looked at Tara's passport for a long time, then at her face, then at the passport again. She had been told to stay calm, so she smiled politely and waited. Behind her, the queue grew longer, and a man sighed loudly. Finally the guard stamped a page and handed the passport back without a word. Tara walked through the gate on legs that felt oddly light. Only when she reached the other side did she notice her hand had been shaking. She sat on a bench for a few minutes, drank some water, and laughed quietly at herself.

Why did Tara laugh quietly at herself?
Because she had been very nervous during the check, though nothing went wrong, and she found it funny afterwards.

Ananya's family drove from Bengaluru to Mysuru on a Sunday. The road was smooth, and they stopped once for coconut water at a roadside stall near Ramanagara. In Mysuru, they visited the palace first, where Ananya counted the pillars in the great hall and lost track at forty. After that, they walked through the market near the palace gate and bought sandalwood soap and a small wooden elephant. Lunch was a plate meal in a crowded restaurant. They started the drive back at four so that they would avoid the evening traffic, and Ananya fell asleep in the car before they reached the highway.

Where did the family stop for coconut water?
They stopped at a roadside stall near Ramanagara.

The shopkeeper in the lane always shut his stall at six, but on the evening of the carnival he stayed open late. Business was brisk. Around nine, a girl walked in, looking at the toys with big eyes and a few coins in her hand. She counted them twice, and her face fell. The shopkeeper looked at her coins, and at her face. Without asking her name, he picked up a small stuffed rabbit and put it in a paper bag. He named a price equal to what she had, and she handed over every coin. She ran out into the crowd, holding the bag against her chest.

Why did the shopkeeper name a price equal to her coins?
Because he wanted her to have the toy and was being kind.

A woman at the market picked up a mirror and looked at herself for a long time. The seller, who was folding scarves, noticed that her expression had turned sad. She put the mirror back, and he asked gently if she liked it. She said the frame was beautiful but that she did not look like the girl she once was. The seller thought. Then he held up a different mirror, small and round, and turned it to catch the sunlight so that a patch of gold fell on her face. She laughed in surprise. She bought the small mirror and left, her head high.

What did the seller's trick with the sunlight do for the woman?
It cheered her up and made her feel good about how she looked.

As soon as the rickshaw puller saw the foreign couple at the station, he waved and offered to take them anywhere. They looked at their map, whispered to each other, and finally asked for a price. He named a fair one. The woman said they would pay him double if he could also show them where locals eat. He grinned and took them to a lane where a man fried parathas on a huge flat pan. The couple sat on plastic stools, laughing at the heat of the green chutney. When they paid, the husband tipped the rickshaw puller generously. The man tucked the money away and said he would be at the station each morning.

Why did the husband tip the rickshaw puller generously?
Because the man took them to a good local place to eat and was helpful and honest about the price.

In Pune, the Ganesh festival is marked by large processions on the last day. Drummers walk in front, followed by decorated chariots carrying idols covered in flowers. People throw gulal, a red powder, into the air, and the streets turn pink. Police close the main roads from morning, and volunteers hand out water to the marchers. The processions pass slowly through narrow lanes, and families watch from balconies. The final immersion takes place at the river late at night, and the crowds do not go home until the early hours. My friend Aarav marched for nine hours with his drumming group and lost his voice.

How long did Aarav march with his drumming group?
He marched with his drumming group for nine hours.

The airport shuttle left at five, but Nora had arrived at half past four, with a small suitcase and a large worry. She had never flown alone. She watched the other passengers on the bench: a man reading a newspaper, a family arguing about snacks, a student asleep on his bag. Nora sat straight and held her boarding pass in both hands as if it might fly away. When the shuttle arrived she was the first one to stand. The driver gave her a friendly nod and said that she looked like someone who would not miss a plane. Nora smiled for the first time that day.

Why did the driver's words make Nora smile?
Because they made her feel capable and less anxious about flying alone.

Last summer, we rented a small cottage by a river in Himachal. The cottage had a stone fireplace, two beds and a porch with a swing. Each morning, the owner's daughter, Pinky, brought us fresh milk and warm bread. We spent the days wading in the cold river, picking wild berries and reading under a pine tree. In the evenings, Dad lit the fire, and we toasted corn on sticks. There was no internet, which none of us minded at all. We stayed for nine days, and on the last night, we counted shooting stars until we fell asleep on the porch.

Who brought the milk and bread each morning?
The owner's daughter, Pinky, brought them.

The village of Sarojini sets up a small market under the neem tree each Wednesday. Only five stalls are present, but each one has a specialty. One sells brooms made from coconut leaves, another sells earthen water pots, and a third sells hand-pounded rice. The fourth stall belongs to a woman who sells embroidered handkerchiefs and school bags. The fifth belongs to an old man who repairs bicycles. The market closes at noon because the sun is hot, and most sellers go home to eat lunch. On festival weeks, extra sellers come from nearby villages, and the market grows to fifteen stalls.

What are the brooms at the first stall made from?
They are made from coconut leaves.

The kite flying competition in our colony is taken seriously. Sixteen boys and girls signed up, and each had a secret method for keeping the thread strong. A shy girl named Anushka said nothing about hers. When the contest began, she stood at the edge of the roof and let her kite rise slowly, never pulling too hard. The others tugged and shouted, and one by one their kites were cut and fell. By evening, Anushka's kite was the only one still in the sky, a tiny yellow dot. She reeled it in and quietly accepted the trophy. When asked about her secret, she shrugged and said she had simply been patient.

Why did Anushka's kite stay in the sky longest?
Because she was patient and did not pull too hard, while the others tugged and had their kites cut.

Our family took a houseboat in Alappuzha for two nights. The boat had two bedrooms, a living area and a kitchen at the back where a cook named Joy prepared our meals. We ate rice with fish curry, banana fritters and sweet pumpkin soup. In the evenings, the boat stopped beside a coconut grove, and lights from the other boats shimmered on the water. My brother fished from the deck with a bamboo rod but caught only a boot. On the second morning, we saw kingfishers diving beside the boat. We disembarked on the third day at ten and our driver was waiting at the jetty.

Who prepared the meals on the houseboat?
A cook named Joy prepared the meals.

Two days before the trek, Imran stopped sleeping well. He packed and repacked his bag, checked the weather forecast on his father's phone, and asked the guide eight times if the route was safe. On the morning of the trek, he tied his shoes so tightly that his toes ached. The guide, a calm woman named Dolma, noticed and told him to loosen the laces. She said the mountain would still be there at the end of the day. Imran took a deep breath and walked beside her. After an hour of steady climbing, he found that he had stopped counting the steps and was enjoying the view.

How did Imran feel before the trek?
He felt nervous and anxious, because he slept badly, repacked his bag and kept asking if the route was safe.

A visit to the salt flats in Kutch takes you across a white world that stretches to the horizon. The ground is flat and cracked, and after the monsoon it is covered with a thin sheet of water that mirrors the sky. Visitors drive on a long straight road from the village of Dhordo, where small tents are set up on the edge of the flats. On full moon nights, a festival of music and folk dance is held, and the salt shines silver under the moon. Camel cart rides are popular with children. The best time to go is between November and February, when the air is dry.

Between which months is the best time to visit?
The best time is between November and February.

The little girl on the seat in front of me kept turning around to look at the tiffin box in my lap. She did not ask, but her eyes followed it each time I lifted the lid. The bus had been moving for three hours, and I could see that her mother had no food with her. At last I held out a paratha wrapped in paper. The mother started to refuse, then looked at her daughter, and accepted it with a quiet thank-you. The girl ate it in small bites, saving the last piece for her mother. They both fell asleep before we reached the next town.

What does the girl saving the last bite show about her?
It shows she is caring and thinks of her mother, because she saved the last piece for her.

The vegetable seller at the corner of Gandhi Road shouted his prices louder than anyone else, but by noon his basket of tomatoes was still almost full. Across the lane, Mrs. Dsouza had stacked hers in neat red pyramids and written the price on a small card. Shoppers stopped at her stall, picked up a tomato, pressed it gently and nodded. The loud seller watched them for a while, then wiped his hands on his shirt. The next morning he arrived early, washed every tomato, and sorted the soft ones into a separate box. He did not shout once, and by eleven his basket was empty.

Why did the loud seller start selling more tomatoes?
Because he washed the tomatoes and separated the soft ones, so shoppers could trust what they bought, as Mrs. Dsouza's neat stall had shown.

The camel fair at Moragarh brings thousands of visitors every year. Before the fair, the camels are washed, brushed and decorated with beads and bells. Owners tie bright cloths to their saddles. There is a competition for the best decorated camel, and the winner receives a trophy and a sack of grain. A magic show is held each evening in the open ground, and children sit in the first row. Meena, a girl from the nearby village, sells small glass bangles near the entrance. She said that in the three days of the fair she earned enough to buy a new school bag.

What does the winner of the best decorated camel contest receive?
The winner receives a trophy and a sack of grain.

A fisherman named Anil came to the fish market with only a small basket of sardines, because the sea had been rough all week. The other sellers had large catches from the previous days, stored on ice. Customers walked past him to the bigger stalls, and Anil sat with folded arms. A little later, a woman asked whether his sardines had been caught that morning. He said yes, at four, and showed her the shining eyes of the fish. She bought the whole basket. Soon, two more customers asked for the same, and by ten o'clock Anil was cleaning his empty basket with a smile.

Why did customers start buying Anil's sardines?
Because they were very fresh, caught that morning, and the shining eyes showed it.

The Mumbai local train carries more than seven million people a day. Each carriage has rows of seats and handles hanging from the roof. At peak hours people crowd right up to the open doorways. Regular travellers form small groups, often called train friends, who save seats for each other and share snacks. A man named Dilip sells combs and pens, walking from one carriage to the next as the train moves. Passengers jump off before the train fully stops, and new ones jump on in the same motion.

What do regular travellers form in a compartment?
They form small groups who save seats for each other and share snacks.

As the bus climbed the hill, the road narrowed until it was barely wider than the vehicle. Mrs. Pillai gripped the seat in front of her. Next to her sat a young boy who was eating chips and looking out of the window with perfect calm. She tried to copy him, breathing slowly. At each curve she glanced at him, and every time he was crunching peacefully. After half an hour, she realised her shoulders had come down. When the bus reached the top, she smiled at the boy and said, thank you. He looked puzzled and offered her a chip.

Why did Mrs. Pillai thank the boy?
Because his calm made her feel less afraid during the dangerous climb, though he did not know it.

In Japan, the cherry blossom season is celebrated with picnics under the trees. Families spread blue sheets on the grass in the park and share boxes of rice balls, pickles and sweet beans. People arrive early to reserve their spots, and sometimes a young employee is sent to sit and wait since dawn. When the wind blows, petals fall like pink snow. Mika, who lives in Tokyo, goes to the park with her grandparents every April. Her grandmother brings a thermos of green tea, and her grandfather takes photographs of the petals on the water. They stay until the light fades.

What do families spread on the grass?
Families spread blue sheets on the grass.

Neha was sure she had missed her stop. The train had passed two unfamiliar stations, and the sky outside had darkened. She asked the man opposite, who had been asleep, and he opened one eye, then shut it again. She asked the girl next to her, who shrugged. Her heart beat faster. Then the train slowed down, and a name came up on the board: her own station, a minute early. She jumped to her feet, grabbed her bag, and nearly hit the sleeping man's knee. As the door opened, she let out a long breath and laughed shakily at herself.

What was Neha worried about at the start?
She was worried that she had missed her stop.

On a mountain road between two towns, the road was blocked by a small landslide. The bus had to stop. Passengers got down, stretched their legs and looked at the heap of rubble. Some began to complain loudly. Others sat quietly. A man in a green jacket began to move stones to the side of the road, one by one. After a minute, a teenager joined him, and then two women. Soon, twelve people were working, passing stones from hand to hand. Within an hour the road was clear enough for the bus to pass. Nobody complained afterwards, and the driver gave a long honk of thanks.

What made the others join the man in the green jacket?
Seeing him start the work showed them it could be done, so they chose to help instead of complain.

The harvest festival Makar Sankranti is celebrated in many parts of India with different names. In Gujarat it is Uttarayan, and kites fill the sky. In Tamil Nadu, it is Pongal, and rice is cooked in new pots until it boils over. In Punjab, it is Lohri, and bonfires burn in the courtyards. People eat sweets made of sesame and jaggery, which are meant to keep the body warm in winter. Families exchange gifts and visit relatives. In our home, my grandmother prepares tilgul, small round sweets of sesame and jaggery, and we share them with neighbours, saying a short phrase that means speak sweetly.

What sweets does the grandmother prepare?
She prepares tilgul, small round sweets of sesame and jaggery.

On the road to the sea, a roadside stall sells fresh coconuts, piled in a green hill. The seller, a young man named Prabhu, cuts the top off each with one swing of a long knife. He pushes a straw into the hole and hands it to the customer. After the water is drunk, he splits the nut open and scrapes out the soft white flesh with a piece of the shell. A coconut costs thirty rupees, and he sells over two hundred on a hot day. His sister collects the empty shells in a sack for a dealer who makes coir rope.

What does Prabhu use to cut the top off the coconuts?
He uses a long knife.

We planned a picnic for Sunday at the botanical garden. My aunt packed lemon rice and potato chips, and my cousin brought a football. The garden opens at eight, and the entry ticket costs ten rupees. We found a shady spot under a huge banyan tree and spread out a bedsheet. After lunch, we walked to the glass house, where cactus plants of every shape stood on shelves. A guard blew a whistle at four, telling visitors that the gate would close soon. On the way home, the bus was so full that I had to stand all the way.

What did the aunt pack for lunch?
She packed lemon rice and potato chips.

Sana's grandmother had never been on an aeroplane. At the airport she gripped her handbag with both hands and stared at the moving belt of suitcases. She refused the offered wheelchair, saying she could walk perfectly well. When the plane began to move, she closed her eyes and whispered a prayer. Sana held her hand, and said nothing. Then the engines roared and the plane lifted into the air. After a minute Grandmother opened one eye, and then the other, and looked out of the window. The fields below were small green squares. She patted Sana's hand and said, in a surprised voice, that it was not so frightening after all.

How did Grandmother feel at the start of the flight?
She felt scared, because she gripped her bag, closed her eyes and whispered a prayer.

Behind the old clock tower is a lane where people sell second-hand clothes. Rows of shirts hang from ropes strung between two poles, and trousers are folded into piles on tarpaulin sheets. A shopkeeper named Zubair keeps a wooden box of buttons and offers free sewing for any shirt bought at his stall. His wife sits beside him with a hand machine and threads the needle without looking. Prices are low, from forty to two hundred rupees. Students and young workers from the nearby factory come on Sunday afternoons, when everyone has been paid. By evening, the ropes are almost bare.

What does Zubair offer for any shirt bought at his stall?
He offers free sewing for any shirt bought at his stall.

In a small French town, the Saturday market opens at seven in the morning. Stalls are covered with white canvas, and the vendors wear aprons. A baker named Henri sells long loaves with a crisp crust, and he stacks them in wicker baskets. Beside him, a woman sells goat cheese wrapped in leaves. Customers arrive with cloth bags and tap the loaves to check how fresh they are. There is a stand serving coffee in paper cups, and a street singer plays an accordion near the fountain. By noon, the baskets are empty, and the vendors sit down to eat a late lunch together.

What does Henri sell?
Henri sells long loaves of bread with a crisp crust.

The kite festival in Ahmedabad takes place in January. For days before it, the sky over the old city fills with colourful squares, and the shops sell thread coated with fine glass powder. On the festival morning, families climb to their rooftops with food, music and tall stacks of kites. Children shout when a kite is cut and drifts away. In our building, Mr. Shah keeps a record of how many kites each child catches. Last year, my cousin Dev caught eleven, which was the highest. The women upstairs make a sweet of sesame and jaggery, and everyone eats it as the sun goes down.

How many kites did Dev catch last year?
Dev caught eleven kites last year.

Richard had packed his bag the night before, but at the airport he realised that his passport was still on the kitchen table at home. He stood very still for a moment. Then he took a deep breath, called his neighbour, and asked her to check. She found it and sent a photograph. His flight was in four hours, and the taxi ride back would take two. He booked the cab, carried his bag back outside, and hoped the traffic would be kind. On the drive he did not say a word to the driver, who politely turned the radio down and kept his eyes on the road.

What can you tell about how Richard felt in the taxi?
He felt tense and worried, because he did not say a word on the drive and was hoping the traffic would be kind.

The Mutianyu part of the Great Wall of China can be reached from Beijing in about two hours by bus. At the entrance, a cable car carries visitors up the first slope, while the more energetic climb the steps. The wall winds over the ridges as far as the eye can see, with watch towers at regular intervals. Our guide, Mr. Wang, explained that soldiers once lit fires in the towers to send messages. At noon, we ate noodles at a small stall. The descent was by a long metal slide, which my brother rode three times. We reached the bus at five and slept all the way back.

How did the soldiers send messages, according to Mr. Wang?
They lit fires in the watch towers to send messages.

Lohri night in the neighbourhood always begins with a bonfire in the park. Children bring bags of peanuts and popcorn, and the elderly sit on folding chairs near the flames. This year it was unusually cold, and the wood was slightly damp. The fire sputtered and smoked and would not catch. Several men tried and failed. Finally, a girl called Jaspreet suggested using the dry paper from the dustbin as a starter. They gave it a try, and the flames leaped up so fast that everyone stepped back, laughing. The men clapped her shoulder, and one of them said that the girl would one day be a fire officer.

Why did the men clap Jaspreet's shoulder?
Because her idea of using dry paper worked and got the fire going.

The school fair at St. Mary's was held on the second Saturday of March. Each class ran one stall. Class Seven sold lemonade and paper fans, and Class Four ran a treasure hunt in the garden. The principal opened the fair at ten by cutting a ribbon tied between two gate posts. There was a small stage for songs and a corner for old books at five rupees each. A girl named Divya won the quiz and received a box of colour pencils. By three o'clock, all the lemonade had been sold. The money raised was given to the town library for new shelves.

What was the money raised at the fair used for?
It was given to the town library for new shelves.

At the Mapusa Friday market in Goa, women sit on the ground selling spices, dried fish and fresh bread. The bakers, known locally as poders, arrive on bicycles with baskets of pao, soft rolls that are best eaten warm. A man with a toothless smile sells coconut sweets from a glass jar. Tourists often buy cashew nuts, which are sold by the weight in small paper bags. Local customers prefer to buy fish early, before the heat. The market also sells plastic buckets, cloth and cheap sandals. By two in the afternoon, the sellers fold their mats and move on.

How do the bakers arrive at the market?
They arrive on bicycles with baskets of pao.

Samira walked past the antique stall three times before she stopped. A silver bracelet in the corner looked exactly like the one her grandmother used to wear. The seller noticed her look and turned it over, showing a tiny engraved peacock on the clasp. Samira's throat tightened, because her grandmother's bracelet had that same peacock. She asked the price quietly, and the seller named a figure that was more than she had. She said she would come back the next day. That night she counted her savings twice and decided to skip the school trip. The next morning she was at the stall at nine o'clock.

Why did Samira decide to skip the school trip?
Because she wanted to save enough money to buy the bracelet, which reminded her of her grandmother's.

Chitra boarded the train at Coimbatore with a heavy trunk and a cloth bag of oranges. Her seat was beside a window on the left side. A student with headphones sat opposite, tapping his knee to a beat only he could hear. At Erode, a large family got on, bringing three baskets and a goat on a rope. The conductor frowned but let them pass. By evening, the carriage smelled of lemon rice and coffee. Chitra shared her oranges with the family, and in return, the grandmother gave her a small steel box of sweet murukku. The train reached Chennai at ten at night, and her brother met her on the platform.

What animal did the large family bring on board?
They brought a goat on a rope.

The sweet shop at the end of the lane has been run by the same family for four generations. Every morning at five, the cook starts boiling milk in a huge copper pot. By seven, the first trays of rasgulla are ready, white and soft in sugar syrup. Customers line up with steel containers to take them home. On festival days, the shop stays open until midnight, and extra workers are hired to pack boxes. The current owner, Mr. Sen, says that his grandfather's recipe has never been changed. A photograph of the founder hangs over the cash counter, garlanded with a dry marigold chain.

At what time does the cook start boiling milk?
The cook starts boiling milk at five every morning.

In Sri Lanka, the New Year in April is celebrated with games and sweets. At the auspicious time, the family lights a clay stove and boils milk until it overflows, a sign of prosperity. Everyone wears new clothes of a colour chosen by an astrologer. Oil is placed on the heads of the elders, and children bow to receive blessings. Afterwards, the family plays games like pillow fighting while sitting on a pole, climbing a greased pole and breaking clay pots while blindfolded. Plates of kavum, a sweet fried cake, and kokis, a crispy snack, are shared with neighbours. The holiday lasts for two days.

What do families boil until it overflows?
They boil milk until it overflows.

The fastest way to cross the bay is by water taxi. A small motorboat leaves from the wooden jetty every ten minutes and takes six passengers at a time. Life jackets are stored under the seats. The crossing takes twelve minutes, and the boat bounces on the waves. The boatman, Mr. Fernandes, collects thirty rupees from each person and hands out a small ticket. On the other side, a narrow road leads to the fish market and a church built by sailors. The last boat returns at eight in the evening, but in rough weather it does not run at all.

How many passengers can the water taxi carry at a time?
It can carry six passengers at a time.

Eid at the old mosque in Delhi begins with prayers at eight. Thousands of people sit in rows on the red stone courtyard, and the imam's voice reaches them over the loudspeakers. Afterwards, the crowd walks out slowly, hugging one another three times, as is the custom. Sweet vermicelli is served in small bowls at the gate by volunteers, and children receive coins. Shops around the mosque sell perfume, caps and sweets, and a barber trims beards on the pavement. By ten o'clock, families begin returning home for the Eid meal. The streets of the old city are quiet by noon.

How many times do people hug at Eid, according to the custom?
They hug three times, as is the custom.

The mango auction in the coastal town of Ambewadi begins at dawn in a covered yard. Farmers bring crates of ripe Alphonso mangoes in tractors, and each crate is marked with the farmer's name. Buyers walk along the rows, pressing the fruit with a thumb and sniffing the stalk. The auctioneer calls the price for each lot, and the buyer lifts a hand to agree. Within an hour, the crates are loaded into trucks bound for big cities. The best mangoes are packed in wooden boxes lined with straw. A young farmer named Sachin said that the smell of the yard in May was the smell of his whole year's work.

How do buyers check the mangoes?
They press the fruit with a thumb and sniff the stalk.

The Sonepur cattle fair is one of the oldest in the country. It takes place on the bank of two rivers and begins on the night of the full moon in November. Horses, cattle and birds are brought for sale, and elephants were once traded here too. A long line of tents shelters the traders, and in the evening a small stage hosts folk singers and magicians. Visitors can ride on a horse-drawn cart through the fairground for ten rupees. A teacher from a local school, Mr. Prasad, brings his class on the second day to learn about the history of the place. They sit on the riverbank to eat their lunch.

In which month does the Sonepur fair begin?
The fair begins in November, on the night of the full moon.

In Kolkata, the days of Durga Puja are the happiest of the year. Large pandals, built from bamboo and cloth, rise on every street corner, each with its own theme. This year, our neighbourhood's pandal looked like a palace made entirely of clay pots. Every evening, people queue for hours to see the idol. The street fills with the smells of fried fish, sweets and incense. Children wear new clothes and run in groups from one pandal to the next. My friend Sohini's father drove us around the city at midnight so we could see the lights. We returned home after two, sleepy and happy.

What was the neighbourhood's pandal made to look like?
It looked like a palace made entirely of clay pots.

At the school sports festival, little Dhruv was sure he would lose his race. He was the smallest in the group, and his legs were short. The starting whistle blew, and he ran with all his might, but he fell behind. Near the finish line, he saw the others stop and turn around. Dhruv, sweating, kept running. When he finally crossed the line, a loud cheer broke out, and his classmates lifted him on their shoulders. Though he had come last, the crowd treated him like a champion. Dhruv's grin was so wide that his cheeks hurt.

Why did the classmates cheer for Dhruv?
Because he never gave up and kept running to the end even though he was last.

In our village the festival of Ram Navami is celebrated with a chariot procession. A cart is decorated with banana stems and flowers, and the images of Rama, Sita and Lakshmana are seated inside. Young men pull it by hand through the streets, and women pour water on the road ahead to cool it. At every house, the family offers a coconut and a garland. The procession stops at the temple for a reading from the epic. In the evening, buttermilk and sweet drinks are shared with the whole village. The children get a holiday from school and run along beside the chariot, shouting the name of the god.

What do the women pour on the road ahead of the chariot?
They pour water on the road to cool it.

The trek to the lake starts from a small village at the end of the road. On the first day we walked for six hours through oak and pine forests. Our guide, a quiet man named Pratap, carried a heavy pack and never seemed tired. We camped beside a stream, and he cooked khichdi on a small stove. It rained at night, and the tents flapped loudly. On the second day the trail came out above the trees, and we saw the lake, frozen at the edges and deep blue in the centre. We stood at the shore for half an hour without speaking. Then we turned around and walked back before the clouds closed in.

What did Pratap cook on the first night?
He cooked khichdi on a small stove.

The overnight bus from Delhi to Manali has twenty-four seats, and our seats were numbers seven and eight. The bus left at five in the evening and soon passed the city's outer lights. By nine the road was winding upward, and the driver turned off the interior lamps. Neha, my sister, put on her headphones and fell asleep against the window. I stayed awake because the stars outside looked so large. At two in the morning the bus stopped for tea at a roadside dhaba, and the cold air nearly took my breath away. I bought a cup and held it with both hands. We reached Manali at dawn.

What time did the bus leave Delhi?
The bus left at five in the evening.

When the monsoon came early, the street vendors in the old city were caught off guard. Within minutes, bright umbrellas of every colour appeared above the stalls. Shirin, who sells bangles, quickly pulled a plastic sheet over her tray, but not before a few bangles slipped to the muddy ground. A schoolgirl passing by crouched and picked them up, wiping each on her sleeve. She put them back on the tray and hurried on before Shirin could thank her. The rain grew heavier. Shirin watched the girl disappear into the crowd, and later that evening she set aside a pair of glass bangles with a note: for the girl in the blue uniform.

What will Shirin probably do with the set-aside bangles?
She will probably give them to the schoolgirl as a thank-you if the girl comes by again.

At the sugarcane juice stall, a heavy iron machine presses the stalks between two rollers. The seller, a man called Raju, feeds the cane through three times to extract all the juice. A glass costs fifteen rupees, and he adds a dash of lemon, ginger and a pinch of black salt. A bell is attached to the machine, and it rings whenever the rollers turn. In the hot months, the stall has a line of customers from noon until sunset. Raju's wife washes the glasses in a tub beside the cart, and his son helps by carrying the crushed stalks to a pile behind the stall.

How many times does Raju feed the cane through the rollers?
He feeds it through three times.

The potter at the village market never asked for a high price, but one day a woman bargained until he dropped to half. He agreed without a word. She paid, picked up her pots and walked away. A boy who helped the potter asked why he had accepted so little. The potter said that the woman had five children and, from the worn state of her sandals, little money. He added that clay was cheap and that a good deed was cheaper still. The next week, the woman came back with a bag of vegetables from her garden, and she left them at the potter's stall without a word.

Why did the woman bring vegetables to the potter's stall?
To thank him for the kind price he had given her.

The little mountain train to Ooty runs every day through tea gardens and tunnels. The little blue coach has wooden seats and large windows. At the start, a bell rings three times and the whistle gives a long wail. The driver, wearing a cap with a brass badge, leans out to wave at children standing by the track. The journey takes about five hours, and the train passes through sixteen tunnels. At a station halfway up, vendors sell hot corn and masala tea. The weather becomes cooler as the train climbs, and many passengers pull on their sweaters before reaching the top.

How many tunnels does the train pass through?
The train passes through sixteen tunnels.

Lena had always been afraid of deep water. On the holiday, her cousins swam far out and called her to join them. She waded to her waist and stopped. Her uncle, who was floating nearby, did not call or push. He simply turned onto his back and began telling a silly story about a fish with spectacles. Lena laughed, forgot to be afraid, and took another step, then another. By the time he reached the end of the story, the water was at her chest. She looked down in wonder, then grinned. She did not swim that day, but she stood in the sea.

How did her uncle help Lena without pushing her?
He told her a silly story that made her laugh and forget her fear.

Notice to passengers: Due to heavy fog in the morning, flights to Lucknow and Patna have been delayed by about two hours. Passengers are requested to remain in the departure hall and keep an eye on the display boards. Free tea and biscuits are being served near gate four. Those travelling with infants may use the quiet room on the first floor. Boarding passes will remain valid, and no new check-in is needed. The airport staff regret the inconvenience. Updates will be announced every thirty minutes over the speaker. Please do not leave your bags unattended, and report any unattended bag to the nearest officer at once.

Where are free tea and biscuits being served?
They are being served near gate four.

On Onam morning, Anu discovered that her pookalam, the flower carpet, had been disturbed in the night. Petals were scattered and the pattern was blurred. She stood at the door in silence. Her little brother came out behind her, rubbing his eyes, and she saw a small, guilty face. A cat's pawprints crossed the centre. Anu bit back her words, took a deep breath, and began to rearrange the petals. After a minute, her brother crouched beside her and started handing her the right colours. They finished in half an hour, and the new design was even brighter than the first.

Why did Anu not scold her brother?
Because she saw the cat's pawprints and chose to fix the design calmly instead of getting angry.

Our taxi to Shillong stopped on the way at a viewpoint called Elephant Falls. The water falls in three levels over dark rocks, and a path with metal railings leads to each one. The driver, Mr. Lyngdoh, said that the falls were named by the British for a rock that looked like an elephant, though it later fell in an earthquake. We took photographs and bought hot corn on the cob from a vendor. Then we drove another hour to reach the city, where a mist covered the streets. Our hotel stood on a hill, and from the balcony the lights of the town twinkled in rows.

Who told the writer how the falls were named?
The taxi driver, Mr. Lyngdoh, told them.

Karthik had always hated Ugadi because it meant long prayers and bitter neem leaves. This year his grandmother asked him to prepare the festival mix himself: neem flowers for sadness, jaggery for happiness, raw mango for surprise, salt, chilli and tamarind. He measured each carefully and stirred. When he tasted it, the flavours fought on his tongue, and he made a face. His grandmother laughed, and told him that this was exactly why the dish was made: the year would bring a bit of everything. Karthik looked at the bowl again, and for the first time, he did not mind finishing it.

What did Karthik understand about the dish after his grandmother spoke?
He understood the mix of flavours stands for the mix of good and bad things the year brings.

The beach at Gokarna is wide and clean, with black rocks at one end. Early in the morning the fishermen push their boats into the water, calling to one another to keep time. By seven they are far out, small dots against the orange sky. Tourists arrive later, carrying towels and hats. A woman named Shanta sells sliced raw mango with chilli powder from a basket. Next to her, a boy rents out plastic chairs. In the evening, everyone sits on the sand to watch the sun go down. A drummer sometimes comes and plays softly near the rocks.

What does Shanta sell on the beach?
She sells sliced raw mango with chilli powder.

The Teej festival is celebrated by women in Rajasthan during the monsoon. Swings are hung from the branches of banyan trees, and women in green saris sit on them and sing songs about rain and love. Their hands are decorated with mehendi in patterns of leaves and peacocks. Sweets, such as ghewar, a honeycomb-shaped cake soaked in sugar syrup, are sold in every shop. In Jaipur, a large procession with a decorated elephant and folk dancers moves through the old city. Mothers send gifts to their married daughters, and families visit each other.

Which sweet is a honeycomb-shaped cake soaked in syrup?
That sweet is called ghewar.

The boat ride through the backwaters began at nine. Our guide, a young man named Biju, steered the long wooden boat with a bamboo pole. Coconut palms leaned over the water on both sides, and white egrets stood on the banks. We passed a small village where women washed clothes at the edge of the canal and children waved from a floating pier. At noon the boat stopped at a house where a family served fish curry on banana leaves. After lunch, Biju let each of us try the pole, and I nearly dropped it in the water. We returned to the dock just before the heat grew too strong.

What did Biju use to steer the boat?
He used a bamboo pole.

The first day of Ramadan in the old city of Lahore begins with a pre-dawn meal. Families wake at three and eat parathas, eggs and sweet lassi. Mosques call out the time to stop eating, and everyone prays. During the day, shops open late, and the streets are quiet. At sunset, the call to prayer is heard, and families gather for iftar, breaking the fast with dates and water. Hot samosas and fruit chaat follow. Neighbours send plates of food to each other, and the streets fill with people going to evening prayers. The month ends with the festival of Eid.

What do families eat at the pre-dawn meal?
They eat parathas, eggs and sweet lassi.

The bangle seller in the narrow lane knew what every customer wanted before she said a word. A girl entering with her mother looked at the red ones for a long time but touched only the green. The seller slid a green set across the counter. The mother frowned and said red would be better for the wedding. The girl said nothing. The seller picked up a pair of red bangles and a pair of green, and put them together on the girl's wrist. They looked pretty. The mother paused, then bought both sets. The girl glanced at the seller with a grin she tried to hide.

What did the girl's grin show?
It showed she was pleased the seller had helped her get the green bangles she wanted.

Meera and her grandfather boarded the night train to Jaipur at half past nine. Their berths were in the middle of the carriage, next to a family with two small boys who kept asking for the window seat. Grandfather had packed puris, a jar of mango pickle and a flask of tea. Around midnight the train stopped at a small station for ten minutes, and a vendor walked along the platform selling hot samosas through the windows. Meera bought two with the coins in her pocket. They ate them slowly, watching the lamps of the station slide away behind them. By the time she lay down, the rocking of the carriage had already made her eyelids heavy.

Where were Meera and her grandfather travelling to?
They were travelling to Jaipur on the night train.

The little shop in the hill village stood at a crossroads, and the shopkeeper knew everyone. A stranger arrived one rainy evening, drenched and looking for the road to the next village. The shopkeeper gave him a cup of tea and pointed out the path, but he added that the stream would be too high to cross at night. The stranger frowned. Then the shopkeeper unrolled a mat in the corner of the shop and said he could sleep there. In the morning, the stranger woke to the smell of hot parathas. Before leaving, he left a note on the counter that said only: thank you, friend.

Why did the shopkeeper offer the stranger a place to sleep?
Because the stream was too high and dangerous to cross at night.

Last year, the neighbours of our building decorated for Diwali separately, and the stairs were dim. This year Mrs. Kapoor put up a sign asking everyone to light one lamp each on their landing. By evening, the stairwell glowed from the ground floor to the roof. Children ran up and down counting the lamps. At nine o'clock a man from the top floor, who rarely spoke to anyone, came down with a plate of sweets and offered it at every door. Mrs. Kapoor watched from her window and smiled. She told her husband quietly that the sign had worked better than she had hoped.

Why did Mrs. Kapoor smile at the man with sweets?
Because her idea had brought people together, even a quiet neighbour.

Every year on his birthday, Grandfather lights a lamp in front of the framed photo of his late wife. This year, he forgot. The family sat down to cake and sweets, and halfway through, his eight-year-old granddaughter Tia left the table without a word. She came back with a small clay lamp and a box of matches. She lit it carefully and placed it where it belonged. Grandfather watched her, then looked down at his hands. The room was very quiet. He took her hand and held it for a minute. After that, nobody said anything, but nobody ate cake for a while, either.

Why did nobody eat cake for a while?
Because everyone was moved by Tia's thoughtful act and the memory of Grandfather's wife.

The Sunday book bazaar in our old city stretches along a pavement for almost a kilometre. Sellers lay books on sheets, in neat piles organised by subject.
