A student can find old engineering manuals, children's stories and rare magazines. Buyers bend down to read titles, and bargaining is a daily sport. One seller, a man named Anwar, keeps a notebook where he writes down what customers ask for, in case a similar title comes his way. Many regular visitors have been coming for decades. Most shops close by four o'clock, as the light fades and the crowd begins to thin out.

What does Anwar write in his notebook?
He writes down what customers ask for, in case a similar title comes his way.

When the airline announced a two-hour delay, most passengers groaned and went to find a charging point. Mr. Okafor, seated near the window, simply took out a paperback and kept reading. A girl of about eight, sitting alone because her father had gone to buy water, watched him for a while. Then she asked what the book was about. He told her it was a story about a sailor who made friends with a whale. She listened closely. By the time her father returned, Mr. Okafor was reading aloud in a low voice, and several people near them had gone quiet to listen too.

How did the other passengers near them probably feel about the story?
They probably enjoyed it, because they went quiet to listen.

Every Thursday, a man with a bicycle cart visits our street, selling second-hand pots and pans. He has no sign and no bell. He simply stops at each gate, takes off his cap and waits. Most people buy nothing, yet he never seems disappointed. Last Thursday, my mother offered him a glass of water, and he sat on the step to drink it slowly. They talked for ten minutes about the price of onions and the weather. When he left, my mother bought a small steel ladle that we did not need. She said it was a fair price for good company.

Why did my mother buy a ladle she did not need?
Because she enjoyed his company and wanted to repay it with a small purchase.

On Easter morning, the village church was almost empty. Heavy rain had flooded the road, and only a few people had managed to wade through. The priest looked at the rows of vacant benches and smiled. He decided that they would hold the service outside under the large mango tree, since the rain had stopped. Within minutes, neighbours began to appear from side lanes, bringing chairs, umbrellas and cloths to sit on. By the time the singing started, forty people had gathered. The priest said that it was the best congregation he had had in years, and the children laughed as water dripped from the leaves.

Why did the crowd get larger after the move outside?
Because it became easier for neighbours to come, and the tree made the gathering open and welcoming.

When Mei arrived in Mumbai for the first time, she was frightened by the noise. Horns blared, vendors shouted and the crowd pushed at the station gate. She stood still, holding her suitcase and a paper with an address. A middle-aged woman noticed her and asked if she needed help. She read the address and then walked with Mei to the right bus, even though it was in the opposite direction from her own. She told the conductor to let Mei off at the correct stop. Mei wrote her a thank-you note that night and sent it with a box of tea, unsure whether it would arrive.

Why did Mei send the woman tea?
To thank her for the kind help, even though she was a stranger.

During the school festival, Arman's job was to hand out sweets at the gate. He had been told to give one to each person who came in. Soon he noticed that an old man, wearing a worn shawl, had arrived with no one and seemed lost. Arman gave him a sweet, and then walked with him to the seating area, finding a chair at the front. The old man looked at him, patted his hand, and said he had once been a student at this school. Arman beamed. He went back to the gate, and from that moment, he greeted each person with a little more warmth.

How did Arman's behaviour change after meeting the old man?
He became warmer and friendlier in greeting everyone, because the old man's words made him feel proud.

A boy named Naveen sat behind a table of old comics at the school bazaar. Nobody had bought anything for an hour. Beside him a girl was selling cupcakes, and her table was crowded. Naveen stared at her queue. Then he picked up a comic, walked over to the crowd, and began to read the funniest page out loud, using different voices. People turned and laughed. A few children hurried to his table and asked for that comic. By the end of the day he had sold twelve, and the girl with the cupcakes had given him one for the show. He decided that he would try the same trick next year.

What helped Naveen finally sell his comics?
Reading a funny page aloud in different voices drew a crowd and made children want the comics.

The courtyard of the housing society filled with people in bright clothes on the first night of Navratri. Children carried small sticks decorated with ribbon, and the older women brought brass plates holding lamps. At seven o'clock the drums began, and a circle formed around the picture of the goddess in the centre. Mr. Patel, who had practised the steps for a week, stumbled twice but kept smiling. The dancing went on until ten, when the secretary announced that the neighbours on the top floor needed to sleep. Everyone clapped, collected their shoes from the stairs, and promised to return the next evening.

What did the older women bring to the courtyard?
They brought brass plates holding lamps.

The tourist office in the desert town of Marupur is open from nine to six every day. A friendly clerk gives out free maps, and he can suggest hotels in any price range. On the wall there is a board with the day's weather and the timings of the fort. The office also sells tickets for a camel ride at the edge of the city, and a half-day cooking class with a local family. A rack by the door holds leaflets in six languages. Visitors who are lost are welcome to leave their bags for an hour while they look around. There is a small fee for lockers, which is twenty rupees.

What does the office give out for free?
It gives out free maps.

Our school bus is number twelve, and it picks up from seven different stops. The driver, Mr. Joseph, has worked on the same route for nineteen years. He knows every child's name and always waits for stragglers who run toward the road with their bags open. A conductor named Latha checks that all the children have their seat belts fastened. On Fridays, Mr. Joseph plays old songs through the speaker, and the children sing along. The bus reaches school at a quarter to eight. In the afternoon it leaves at four, and on rainy days it takes a little longer because of traffic near the bridge.

How many years has Mr. Joseph driven the same route?
He has driven the same route for nineteen years.

The district fair has a dog show on the last afternoon. Owners walk their dogs in a circle around the ring while two judges watch. Categories include the smallest dog, the best-behaved dog and the dog with the loudest bark. This year a brown street dog named Moti, brought by a girl called Alisha, won the best-behaved prize. He sat quietly while the judge checked his paws, and he did not bark once. Alisha received a medal and a bag of dog biscuits. She said Moti had been waiting outside her school every day for two years, and so she had decided to bring him home.

Which prize did Moti win?
Moti won the best-behaved prize.

The sleeper bus from Bengaluru to Goa departs at eight in the evening. Each passenger has a small bunk with a curtain, a pillow and a reading light. The bus makes two stops during the night, one at ten for dinner and one at five for tea. The conductor, a young man named Vinay, hands out bottles of water as passengers board. The road is smooth for most of the way, but the last stretch near the coast is full of curves. By seven in the morning, the bus reaches Panaji, where passengers get down in a quiet street lined with coconut palms.

At what time does the bus leave Bengaluru?
The bus leaves at eight in the evening.

Pooja's mother always packed too much food for train journeys. This time she had made twelve parathas, a tub of potato curry, boiled eggs, two kinds of chutney and a bag of laddoos, though the journey was only five hours. Pooja rolled her eyes and carried the bags. But when the train stopped for three hours because of a track repair, the other passengers in the carriage began to look hungry. Pooja opened the bags. By the time the train started again, a woman with a baby, an old man and two students had all eaten with her. Pooja said she would not complain about the food again.

Why did Pooja decide not to complain about the food again?
Because the extra food helped feed hungry passengers during the long delay.

The annual snow festival in the hill town begins in January. Carvers make sculptures of animals, birds and temples out of huge blocks of ice and snow in the central square. The sculptures are lit at night with coloured lights. A competition is held for the best design, and the winner gets a silver cup. Children make snowmen along the pavement, and shopkeepers serve hot soup and tea. An ice-skating rink is built near the town hall, and skates can be rented for fifty rupees an hour. Many visitors arrive by bus from the plains, wearing borrowed coats and woollen caps.

What does the winner of the design competition receive?
The winner receives a silver cup.

On New Year's Eve, the whole street in Chennai stayed awake. Ten minutes before midnight, Mr. Anand, who is usually grumpy, brought out a large speaker and a box of sparklers from his house. The children stared. He said nothing, only handed out the sparklers one by one. At midnight, the lights glowed, and the street filled with tiny golden circles in the air. Mr. Anand stood at the back with his arms folded, but his mouth was pulling into a smile. The next morning, the children left a drawing of a sparkler on his gate with the words: thank you, Uncle.

What does this suggest about Mr. Anand's real nature?
It suggests he is kind underneath his grumpy manner, because he gave the children sparklers and smiled.

The antique seller on Church Street kept a small card on his counter that said, Please touch gently. Most visitors ignored it and picked up the old clocks, the brass compasses and the glass inkwells as if they were toys. One afternoon a boy of about ten walked in with his father. The boy kept his hands behind his back and leaned close to look at each item. The seller noticed. He took down a small wooden music box, wound it, and handed it to the boy. The music was soft and slightly slow, as if the box were remembering a tune. The boy listened without moving, and the seller smiled for the first time that day.

Why did the seller let the boy hold the music box?
Because the boy was respectful and careful, keeping his hands behind his back, unlike the other visitors.

The fruit market in the town opens a little before dawn. Trucks from the orchards unload crates of apples, mangoes, guavas and pomegranates, depending on the season. The auctioneer stands on a wooden box and calls out bids in a fast, sing-song voice. Buyers raise their fingers to signal a number. In the corner, a boy hands out small cups of chilled buttermilk to the workers. By seven the best crates are gone, and the leftover fruit is sold cheaply to street vendors. The market is cleaned by nine, and the cleaners hose the floor until the water runs clear.

Who calls out bids at the fruit market?
The auctioneer calls out the bids, standing on a wooden box.

Setting up the Christmas crib is Valentina's favourite job. Every December, her father brings down a cardboard box from the attic, and inside are the small clay figures wrapped in cotton. There are Mary, Joseph, three kings, two shepherds, a donkey and several sheep. The baby is kept separately in a paper envelope until Christmas Eve. Valentina arranges the figures on a table beside the window, using dry straw from the garden. This year, her little brother wanted to add a toy car, and they agreed to park it behind the stable. On Christmas Eve, Valentina places the baby gently in the manger.

Where is the baby figure kept until Christmas Eve?
It is kept in a paper envelope.

When the rice harvest ends, the farmers of a village near Bhubaneswar gather in the village square for a feast. Women prepare dalma, a dish of lentils and vegetables, and large pots of rice are cooked on open fires. The oldest farmer offers the first sheaf of the new crop at the shrine, and everyone claps. Children run between the tables with leaf plates. A drummer plays the beat of the harvest, and men and women dance in a circle. The feast begins after sunset and lasts until the stars are bright. Next morning, the grain is carried to the market on bullock carts.

What dish do the women prepare for the feast?
They prepare dalma, a dish of lentils and vegetables.

The children had made a paper boat for each wish and planned to float them in the pond on the last evening of the festival. Rohan's boat, folded in a rush, was lopsided. When he set it on the water, it tilted and began to sink. He gasped. His sister quickly stepped in with a stick and nudged the boat upright. It wobbled, then floated, drifting slowly towards the middle. Rohan stood with his wet sleeves, staring at it. He did not say what he had wished, but he whispered thanks to his sister, and she shrugged as if it were nothing.

Why did Rohan whisper thanks to his sister?
Because she rescued his sinking boat by nudging it upright with a stick.

Rohan saved his pocket money for two months to spend at the school fair. He wanted to try the ring-toss, buy a paper kite and eat as many pakoras as possible. When the day came, he found a small girl crying beside the lemonade stall. She had lost her mother in the crowd. Rohan took her hand and walked with her to the announcement desk, where a teacher called out her mother's name. They waited together for ten minutes. By the time the mother arrived, the ring-toss line was long and the pakoras were nearly gone. Rohan only had enough left for one kite, but he walked home smiling.

What does this show about Rohan?
It shows he is kind and unselfish, because he gave up his fun to help a lost child.

The bus conductor shouted that the next stop was the last one, and the young man in the back row woke with a start. He looked out of the window at the dark road and a single lamp. His stop had been twenty minutes earlier. He did not panic. He asked the conductor how far the nearest tea stall was, and then if any bus returned that night. The conductor said one passed at ten. The young man bought a cup of tea, sat on the bench, and sent a message to his mother. He wrote that he would be late, but that he was fine and had a plan.

What does the way he acted show about the young man?
It shows he is calm and sensible, because he asked questions, made a plan and told his mother.

In the main bazaar of Leh, Tibetan women sit on rugs with piles of turquoise, coral and silver beads. The price of a turquoise necklace depends on the quality of the stone. The women are skilled at bargaining but also at telling stories about each piece. A bag of dried apricots, sold by a shop near the mosque, is a popular present to take home. Wool shawls and woven hats fill the stalls on the main street. The market is quietest in the afternoon, when the strong sun drives most people into the shade of the cafes.

What do the Tibetan women sell in the bazaar?
They sell turquoise, coral and silver beads.

The village fair at Kondapur happens every year after the rice harvest. This year it lasted three days. On the first day there was a bullock-cart race, which Ramesh's uncle won by a wide margin. On the second day the potters set up a long row of clay toys, whistles and tiny kitchen sets near the temple wall. The third day was for singing, and a boy of twelve named Imran got the loudest applause for a folk song his grandmother taught him. Each evening the sweet seller fried jalebis in a huge pan, and the smell drifted all the way to the river where the buffaloes rested.

Who won the bullock-cart race?
Ramesh's uncle won the bullock-cart race.

Our school trip to the Taj Mahal left at six in the morning from the school gate. There were forty-two students, three teachers and one very nervous bus driver. We stopped at a roadside restaurant for breakfast at eight, and Mrs. Iyer counted us twice before we climbed back on. At noon we reached Agra and ate lunch under a large neem tree. The guide, a tall man named Mr. Khan, walked us through the gardens and showed us where to stand for the best photograph. We returned to school at nine that night, and parents were waiting at the gate with torches and shawls.

How many students went on the trip?
Forty-two students went on the trip.

Just before the school's annual day, a storm knocked out the electricity. The hall was dark, and a hundred parents sat waiting. The principal came on stage with a torch and said that the show would have to be cancelled. A small voice from the back said, why not do it in the dark? The principal laughed, but then he paused. Within minutes, teachers had placed torches and lanterns around the stage. The children, who had expected disappointment, performed a story using shadows and flickering light. The audience was spellbound, and the programme was talked about for years afterwards.

Why was the programme talked about for years?
Because the shadow and lantern performance, born from the power cut, was unusual and beautiful.

The ferry to Elephanta Island leaves from the Gateway of India every hour between nine and two. The trip takes an hour, and the deck is open to the breeze. Gulls follow the boat, snatching at bits of bread thrown by children. At the island, a toy train carries visitors along the pier to the foot of a long stone stairway. There are one hundred and twenty steps up to the caves, where large carvings of Shiva stand in the dim light. Visitors must buy a ticket at the entrance. Monkeys on the steps are known to grab bags and bottles, so guides advise keeping things out of sight.

How long does the ferry trip to Elephanta Island take?
The trip takes an hour.

I have never forgotten the first time I travelled alone. I was fourteen, and my aunt had asked me to visit her in Nagpur during the summer holidays. My father put me on the train at Bhopal and handed me a packed lunch of puris and potato curry. A kind woman in the next seat promised to wake me before the station. I read a comic, looked out of the window, and ate slowly. When the train reached Nagpur at four in the afternoon, my aunt was standing right at the door of the compartment, waving a green scarf. I felt like a grown-up for a whole week afterwards.

Who was waiting for the writer at Nagpur?
The writer's aunt was waiting at the door of the compartment.

The Pongal pot is set on a stove of three stones in the open courtyard. Women of the house light the fire at sunrise, and a family member pours fresh milk into the pot. When the milk rises and boils over, everybody shouts, Pongalo Pongal, which means may it overflow. Rice, jaggery, cashews and cardamom are added next. The sweet dish is first offered to the sun, then shared with the family. The cattle are washed on the second day and decorated with garlands and paint. Families visit each other on the third day, and young people play games on the open ground.

What do people shout when the milk boils over?
They shout Pongalo Pongal, which means may it overflow.

The Eid morning in Hyderabad began early for the Qureshi family. Nasreen woke at five to help her mother prepare sheer khurma, a sweet dish of vermicelli, milk and dates. Her brother Zaid ironed the kurtas for everyone. After prayers at the nearby mosque, relatives began to arrive, one group after another, each carrying a box of sweets. Nasreen's grandmother gave small envelopes of money to all the children. By afternoon the house was full of voices, and the dining table had been extended twice. Nasreen sat in the corner with a plate on her knees, tired but very happy, listening to her cousins argue about cricket.

What dish did Nasreen help prepare?
She helped prepare sheer khurma, a sweet dish of vermicelli, milk and dates.

The Baisakhi procession in our town begins at the gurdwara at ten in the morning. Five men in saffron robes walk at the front, carrying swords and a large flag. Behind them march young men performing martial arts and children in blue turbans. Along the route, families offer cold drinks, snacks and sweets from tables set up outside their houses. The procession passes through the main road, the market and the railway crossing before returning to the gurdwara at two. Community kitchens serve free meals to everyone, and thousands of people sit in rows on the floor to eat together.

What time does the procession begin?
It begins at ten in the morning.

The sweet seller was preparing for a long afternoon when a bus full of tourists pulled in. They crowded around his stall, pointing at the trays and asking questions in several languages. He did not speak their languages, but he nodded, smiled and gave each person a tiny piece to taste. A teenage boy among them pulled out a notebook and began drawing the sweets. The seller leaned over to watch. After a few minutes the boy showed his sketch, and the seller touched it gently and called his wife to look. The tourists bought two boxes each, and the sketch was framed that evening.

Why did the seller call his wife to look at the sketch?
Because he was proud and pleased that someone had drawn his sweets so well.

At the pottery market in the small town of Mittipur, the shops are arranged along one long street. Each shop displays its plates, bowls and cups on shelves outside the door. The patterns are painted by hand, mostly in blue and white, with tiny flowers and birds. The shopkeepers wrap each piece in old newspaper and straw before handing it over. A set of six cups costs about three hundred rupees. Tourists often buy large decorated jars, which they say look good in a hall. The street is busiest in the winter months, when the weather is cooler and the kilns can be seen glowing in the lanes behind.

What colours are most of the patterns painted in?
Most patterns are painted in blue and white.

On the first of every month, a large pet market is held in the field near the river. Children arrive with their parents to look at puppies, rabbits and kittens. A few stalls sell goldfish in plastic bags, and one man offers colourful budgerigars in a cage. A volunteer from the animal shelter hands out leaflets about caring for pets. A small corner is reserved for adoption, where abandoned dogs wait on leashes. Last month, nine dogs found new homes. The market closes at noon, and the volunteers stay behind to clean the field and carry the unsold cages away in a van.

How many dogs found new homes last month?
Nine dogs found new homes last month.

The night before Raksha Bandhan, Kabir's sister Ira was away at college, and he had forgotten to remind her to send the thread. He spent the evening checking the post box, looking at his phone, and pretending not to care. In the morning, a small parcel arrived by courier. Inside were a thread, a packet of his favourite sweets and a note that said, Did you think I would forget, silly? Kabir read it twice. He tied the thread around his own wrist, since she could not do it, and called her. He could not say much, but she understood from his voice, and laughed.

How did Kabir feel when the parcel arrived?
He felt happy and touched, because he read the note twice and was too moved to say much on the phone.

The lane outside Sunita's building turns into a rainbow every year on Holi. Children chase each other with water guns while the adults dab coloured powder on cheeks. Sunita's neighbour Mr. Bose, who is eighty, usually sits on a chair at the gate and watches with a smile. This year, nobody threw colour near his chair. The older boys had agreed among themselves to keep a clear space around him. When Mr. Bose noticed, he stood up, walked to the middle of the lane, and gently put a pinch of pink powder on the head of the smallest child. The whole lane cheered.

Why did nobody throw colour near Mr. Bose's chair?
Because the older boys had agreed to keep a clear space around him out of respect for his age.

The boys on the beach at Puri started playing cricket at five in the afternoon. They used a bat cut from a coconut palm branch and a tennis ball wrapped in tape. The pitch was marked with the heel of a shoe. Two teams of five faced each other, and the loser had to buy lemon soda for everyone. The game continued until the sun touched the sea. When the final ball was hit into the waves, three boys ran into the water to retrieve it. The winning captain, a boy called Satya, bought the drinks anyway, saying that nobody should go home thirsty.

What did the boys use as a bat?
They used a bat cut from a coconut palm branch.

The little restaurant on the highway had only three tables, and the owner cooked everything himself. We were hungry, so we ordered whatever he suggested. He brought hot rotis, a bowl of spicy dal and a plate of fresh cucumber. A group of truck drivers at the next table ate quietly and thanked him by name when they left. When we asked how much we owed, he said to pay what we thought was fair. My father hesitated, then added a little more than he had planned to. Afterwards we sat in the car, and I realised we had not stopped talking about the meal for twenty minutes.

What does the truck drivers thanking the owner by name suggest?
It suggests they are regular customers who know and like him.

A Christmas market was set up in the town square in December. Wooden huts with red roofs sold hot chocolate, gingerbread and hand-carved toys. A brass band played carols near the fountain at six every evening. The mayor switched on the lights of the big fir tree on the first of December, and a crowd of nearly a thousand people watched. Anna, who had come from the next village, bought a knitted scarf for her father and a small wooden angel for the tree at home. She stayed until the band finished and then caught the last bus, carrying her parcels carefully.

What did Anna buy for her father?
She bought a knitted scarf for her father.

On the highway between Pune and Mumbai, there is a famous roadside stop called a food plaza. Buses and cars pull in throughout the day, and the parking area can hold two hundred vehicles. Under a long tin roof, a dozen small counters offer vada pav, samosas, tea, juice and ice cream. Plastic chairs are set out in rows, and travellers eat standing up or sitting. The toilets are cleaned every hour by a team of six workers. At night the plaza is lit with bright white lamps. Many families make a habit of stopping there for twenty minutes on each trip.

How many vehicles can the parking area hold?
It can hold two hundred vehicles.

The spice seller let each customer smell the cardamom before buying. A woman who had come to the market every week for years stopped at his stall and said the cardamom smelled different this time. The seller did not argue. He opened a second sack and a third, comparing them with her, until she pointed to the freshest. He sold her that one for the same price. Later, a young man watching from the next stall asked why he had taken so much trouble for a small sale. The seller said that a woman who trusts you is worth more than a quick profit, and that she brought her friends.

Why did the spice seller take trouble over a small sale?
Because he believed a customer's trust is worth more than a quick profit, and she brought her friends.

On the long train ride, Mr. Das kept to himself and read his newspaper. A little boy in the next seat stared at him for a long time and finally asked why he never smiled. Mr. Das lowered the paper. He said that the news was usually sad. The boy took out a paper aeroplane from his pocket and handed it to him. Mr. Das turned it over, and, after a pause, flew it down the aisle. The aeroplane landed at the feet of a woman, who laughed. Mr. Das folded the newspaper away and asked the boy to show him how to make another one.

What changed Mr. Das's mood?
The boy's gift of a paper aeroplane and the laughter it brought made him playful.

The fish auction at the harbour begins at four every morning. Boats arrive with their catch, and workers carry baskets up the steps to a long concrete floor. The auctioneer, wearing a yellow raincoat, calls the prices in a loud, sing-song voice. Buyers wave their hands and trade by gesture. The first lots are the largest fish, like tuna and kingfish. By six o'clock, the floor is wet and covered in scales. A cafe at the edge of the harbour sells hot tea and plates of fried fish to the workers. By eight, trucks have taken the catch to markets in the city.

What colour raincoat does the auctioneer wear?
He wears a yellow raincoat.

The little girl was told to sit quietly at the airport while her mother filled in a form. She sat with her hands in her lap for five full minutes. Then, from the corner of her eye, she spotted a toy aeroplane in a shop window. She stood and drifted toward it, her eyes wide. By the time her mother turned around, the child had vanished. The mother's face went white. She ran through the hall calling her name. A security officer found the girl pressed against the shop glass, whispering to the toy. The mother grabbed her tightly, and for a full minute did not say a word.

How did the mother feel when she could not see her daughter?
She felt frightened, because her face went white and she ran calling her name.

The journey from our village to the district town begins at the bus stop beside the school. Every morning at seven, a blue bus arrives, honking twice. It stops at the market, the post office and the old well before turning onto the highway. The ride takes forty minutes. Most passengers are farmers carrying sacks of onions or women carrying baskets of eggs. The conductor, Mr. Kumar, knows who will be late and holds the bus for them. On the way back, the bus leaves the town at five and often arrives after sunset. Children on the back seat sing film songs to pass the time.

What colour is the bus that comes to the village?
The bus that comes is blue.

On our visit to Bangkok, we took a long-tail boat along the canals. The boatman, a tanned man in a straw hat, steered with a long pole attached to the engine. We passed wooden houses on stilts, where children waved from the doors and washing hung over the water. At one spot, the boat stopped beside a floating shop selling mangoes and sticky rice. My sister bought a plate and shared it with me. By noon, a light rain fell, and the boatman passed us a plastic sheet. We reached the pier at one o'clock and walked to a temple with a very large golden statue.

What did the boatman use to steer?
He used a long pole attached to the engine.

Lakshmi had been practising her dance for the temple festival for three months. On the evening of the performance, she stood in the wings, listening to the drums, and felt her stomach tighten. Her teacher, who was standing behind her, said nothing but placed a hand lightly on her shoulder. Lakshmi walked onto the stage. For the first minute she moved stiffly, and then the rhythm took over her feet. When the last beat came and the audience began to clap, she realised she had not thought about being nervous since the first step. In the wings, her teacher gave a small nod.

What helped Lakshmi stop feeling nervous?
The music and rhythm took over once she started dancing, and her teacher's calm touch encouraged her.

A new weekend market has opened in the car park behind the library. Stalls will be open from eight in the morning until two in the afternoon on Saturdays and Sundays. Local farmers will sell vegetables, eggs and honey, and a bakery from the next town will bring fresh bread. There will be a free table where children can paint cloth bags. Visitors are asked to bring their own bags, as plastic will not be given out. Parking is free for the first two hours. The organisers, a group of neighbours led by Mrs. Gomes, hope to have thirty stalls by the end of the year.

Who leads the group of neighbours organising the market?
Mrs. Gomes leads the group of neighbours.

Before Diwali, Anjali's family cleans the house from top to bottom. Her father takes down the ceiling fans and wipes the blades, her mother washes the curtains, and Anjali is in charge of the shelves in the hall. On the day before the festival, they draw a rangoli at the door using coloured powder and flower petals. This year Anjali made a peacock with a long blue tail. At dusk they light a row of clay lamps along the windowsills. Her little cousin counted them aloud and got to twenty-six before losing track. Then everyone sat down for sweets, and the street outside filled with the sound of firecrackers far off.

What did Anjali draw at the door?
She drew a rangoli of a peacock with a long blue tail.

The ticket counter at the small railway station opens at six. Mr. Venkat, the clerk, arrives at half past five, sweeps the floor, and sets his stamp pad in a neat line beside the register. On the day of the festival, the queue stretched out of the door and around the corner. Mr. Venkat sold tickets without once raising his voice. A woman at the front asked about trains to Madurai, and he told her there were two, at nine and at two. She chose the nine o'clock train. By afternoon, the counter closed for lunch, and he ate his rice from a steel tiffin box under the fan.

At what time does the ticket counter open?
The ticket counter opens at six.

The tuk-tuk ride from the beach to the old town costs two hundred rupees if you bargain well. The driver, a man named Chaminda, decorates his vehicle with small paper flags and a framed picture of his daughter. He drives fast around corners but never touches the pedestrians. On the way, he points to a hill where monkeys gather in the afternoons. In the old town, he waits outside the market while passengers shop, reading a newspaper in the front seat. He will drive back to the beach for the same price. Many guests ask for him by name, and his phone number is printed on a card.

What does Chaminda keep in a frame on his vehicle?
He keeps a picture of his daughter.

The guide at the museum asked the visitors not to touch anything. A boy of about seven, standing at the back, kept his fingers curled into fists the whole time. Near the end of the tour, the guide stopped before a smooth stone statue and said that this one had been polished by visitors for a hundred years, so they might touch its foot if they wished. The boy's eyes lit up. He walked forward, and with one finger, touched the foot as gently as if it were a sleeping baby. Then he stepped back with a deep sigh, and whispered his thanks to the guide.

Why did the boy keep his fingers curled into fists?
Because he wanted to obey the rule and stop himself from touching the objects.

Baisakhi in Punjab marks the start of the harvest. In our village, the day begins with a visit to the gurdwara, where the sweet karah prasad is handed out in small portions. After that, the fair opens in the open ground behind the school. There are swings, a wrestling ring and stalls selling bangles, sweets and wooden toys. At noon the men perform bhangra, and the drumbeat can be heard from every corner. My cousin Harpreet, who is nine, won a small prize in a sack race. In the evening the whole family sat on the roof and ate sarson ka saag with maize roti.

What do people receive at the gurdwara?
They receive karah prasad, a sweet, in small portions.

On our last day in Colombo, my father hired a three-wheeler to take us to the fort. The driver, a cheerful man named Nimal, told us stories about each place we passed. He stopped at a corner shop so that we could taste a drink made from king coconut, which is orange outside and sweet within. After the fort, we visited a cloth shop and a bookshop. At three o'clock Nimal drove us back to the hotel, and my father paid him a little extra. The next morning we flew home, and I kept a coconut shell in my bag as a souvenir.

What did the writer keep as a souvenir?
The writer kept a coconut shell.

Joseph had planned the road trip carefully. He had maps, snacks, a playlist and a spare tyre. What he had not planned for was the flat tyre arriving on a lonely road at dusk, and the spare also turning out to be flat. He sat on the roadside with his head in his hands. A farmer on a tractor stopped and offered to tow the car to the village. In the village, the farmer's wife gave him dinner while a mechanic fixed both tyres the next morning. Joseph tried to pay, but the farmer refused. Joseph left, writing the name of the village in his notebook so he would never forget it.

Why did Joseph write the name of the village in his notebook?
Because the villagers had been kind to him and he wanted to remember them.

A woman had come to the market only to buy salt, but on her way she passed a stall of woollen blankets, and stopped. They were soft and thick, and she could almost feel their warmth. She thought about her father, who slept on the verandah and coughed at night. She asked the price, and it was more than she had expected. She turned, bought the salt and walked towards home. But a few steps on, she stopped again, turned, and walked back. This time she did not ask the price. She simply took the grey blanket, counted out the notes and asked to have it wrapped.

Why did the woman go back for the blanket?
Because she was thinking of her father and decided his comfort mattered more than the price.

On the flight to Singapore, the cabin crew handed out small boxes of rice and chicken curry. Dev, who was seated by the window, was given a cup of orange juice, and he spilled half of it on the tray. A flight attendant named Mei came with napkins and a fresh cup without any fuss. Later she showed him how to watch the flight path on the small screen. The plane was due to land at five in the evening, and it arrived ten minutes early. At the airport, Dev's cousin was holding a card with his name written in large letters, and they hugged each other near the baggage belt.

What did Dev spill on the tray?
He spilled half of his orange juice.

The Thrissur Pooram is held every spring. Decorated elephants, standing in two rows, carry golden ornaments and colourful parasols. Drummers play with great speed, while thousands of people watch from the streets around the temple. A famous part of the event is the fireworks display, which begins after midnight and lights the sky for almost an hour. Vendors sell sweets, balloons and cold drinks in the crowd. Families come from distant towns and rent rooms in advance. My uncle, who has attended every year for twenty years, says that the sound of the drums is something you feel in your chest.

What begins after midnight at the Thrissur Pooram?
The fireworks display begins after midnight.

Every Sunday morning, the flower market near the old bridge opens before sunrise. Trucks arrive from the villages with sacks of marigolds, roses and jasmine buds. The sellers sit on the ground and sort the flowers by colour. Marigolds are sold by weight, while jasmine is strung into long garlands and sold by the arm's length. Most of the buyers are temple workers and small shops. By eight o'clock the road is covered in loose petals, and the cleaners come with brooms made of dry grass. A boy named Tarun helps his aunt tie garlands there, and he earns enough to pay for his school notebooks.

How is jasmine sold at the flower market?
Jasmine is strung into long garlands and sold by the arm's length.

Our small railway station has one platform, a ticket window and a tea stall. The stationmaster, Mr. Ghosh, lives in a quarter at the back with his wife and two dogs. He raises the flag for each passing train and writes the time in a large register. Only four trains stop each day. The 7:10 to the city is the busiest, as students and office workers crowd into the carriages. In the afternoon, the platform is nearly empty, and the stationmaster sits on a bench shelling peas. A mango tree grows near the water tank and provides shade in the summer.

How many trains stop at the station each day?
Four trains stop each day.

The flower seller at the temple gate was in a bad mood and had no patience for beginners. A boy came forward and asked, in a hesitant voice, how to offer flowers properly because he had never done it. The seller sighed, but then she softened. She picked a small bunch of marigolds, wrapped them in a leaf, and showed him how to hold them with both hands. She told him to say a short prayer in his heart. The boy nodded and walked into the temple. Later she told her neighbour that she had needed that boy to remind her why she did this work.

Why did the flower seller say she had needed that boy?
He reminded her of the meaning of her work, which lifted her bad mood.

The guesthouse in the mountain village has only four rooms, and each one is named after a flower. Ours was the Rhododendron room, on the first floor. The owner, a retired army officer named Major Rawat, rises at five to feed the dogs and water the plants. Breakfast is served at eight on a terrace with a view of the snow peaks. It includes parathas, curd and apple jam made in the guesthouse. There is no television, and the only phone signal is on the roof. Most guests spend the afternoons on the terrace, reading. The Major has a shelf with two hundred old books.

What was the name of the room the writer stayed in?
The room was called the Rhododendron room.

In the main square of Marrakech, a juice seller stacks pyramids of oranges beside his cart. A glass costs only a few coins, and he squeezes the fruit in front of the customer with a hand press. Nearby, a water seller in a wide red hat rings a brass bell to call attention. Around the corner, a man teaches a snake to rise from a basket, though most visitors only watch from a distance. Women in colourful scarves sell dried figs and nuts, weighed on old scales with brass pans. The smell of mint tea comes from every corner, and the sellers insist that guests sit down.

What does the juice seller use to squeeze the fruit?
He uses a hand press.

Daniel arrived at the bus station in Pune with forty minutes to spare, and he felt proud of himself. He found the right platform, stood in line, and checked his ticket twice. When the bus finally pulled in, the conductor read out the names of the stops, and Daniel's village was not among them. He looked at his ticket again and noticed the small print: this was the express service. A woman beside him smiled and said the slow bus left from the far end of the station in fifteen minutes. Daniel picked up his bag and ran, his pride quite gone, hoping the slow bus had not already filled.

How did Daniel feel after hearing the conductor read the stops?
He felt worried and embarrassed, because his village was not named and his earlier pride disappeared when he ran for the slow bus.

The ticket seller at the station shook his head when Alex asked for a seat on the evening train. All the seats were sold. Alex looked at the departure board, thinking about his sister's wedding, which began at nine the next morning in the next city. He did not argue. He asked if there was a standing ticket, and the seller nodded. Alex bought it, thanked him, and boarded early to find a spot near the door. He stood for four hours, but a student shared half of her seat after the second stop. He reached the wedding hall by dawn, creased and tired, but in time.

Why was Alex willing to stand for four hours?
Because he badly wanted to reach his sister's wedding on time.

The cloth merchant waved at the young woman and invited her to see his new silks. She said she would only look, and he spread out seven rolls of cloth on the counter with a flourish. She touched each one but shook her head. He did not give up. He asked what she needed it for, and she said a friend's engagement. At that, he pulled out a plain deep blue cloth from under the counter and said that this was the one. She held it up against the light, and her eyes widened. The merchant folded it slowly and told her the price. She smiled and handed over the notes.

Why did the woman finally buy the blue cloth?
Because the merchant listened to what she needed and chose a cloth that suited the occasion.

When the train stopped for the third time between stations, the passengers began to look at each other. Someone said there was a cow on the track. Someone else said the signal had failed. An hour went by. The heat inside the carriage grew heavy. Then a man in the corner opened a bag of roasted chickpeas and passed it down the row. A woman offered water from a bottle. Soon people who had not spoken before were sharing stories about their villages. When the train finally began to move, there was a soft cheer, but a few passengers seemed almost sorry that the conversation would end.

What does this show about the passengers?
It shows people can become friendly and generous during a hard wait, because they shared food, water and stories.

The Rajdhani express leaves Delhi in the late afternoon and reaches Mumbai the next morning. Tickets for the air-conditioned coaches include dinner, breakfast and a small bottle of water. At about seven, a steward comes with a trolley of soup and bread, followed by a tray of rice, dal and vegetables. The bedding is provided in a sealed packet, with sheets, a blanket, a pillow and a towel. Passengers are asked to lower their voices after ten at night. My uncle, who travels on this train every month for his work, says the best sleep he gets is on the lower berth, when the wheels hum steadily.

What comes in the sealed bedding packet?
The packet holds sheets, a blanket, a pillow and a towel.

The riverside market at Varanasi sells brass bells, silk saris and small clay lamps. Boatmen wait by the steps, calling out to travellers in hope of a morning ride. Women sell flower garlands for the evening prayer, and a barber works on the stairs, with a basin and a cloth. Tea is poured from tall kettles into tiny clay cups. At dusk, priests prepare a large ceremony with fire, bells and chanting, and hundreds of people gather on the stone steps. The market stays busy until ten, and after the ceremony, the sellers sweep the steps clean for the next day.

What do women sell for the evening prayer?
They sell flower garlands for the evening prayer.

We reached the hill station at four in the afternoon, after a long climb through pine forests. The guesthouse stood at the edge of a cliff, painted yellow, with a red tin roof. A woman named Mrs. Thapa met us at the door with warm towels and a tray of ginger tea. Our room had two beds, a wooden desk and a window that looked over the valley. Dad unpacked the sweaters while my sister and I ran out to the garden. We could see the lights of a village far below, flickering like tiny stars. Dinner was served at seven: rice, dal and a spicy potato dish.

What colour was the guesthouse?
The guesthouse was painted yellow.

The seller of kites in Jaipur has a rule: he never sells a kite to someone who has not first asked about the thread. A customer in a hurry waved a bundle of notes and said he wanted the biggest kite. The seller crossed his arms. He asked what thread the man planned to use. The man blinked and said he had not thought about it. The seller then explained how a thick thread would tire the arms and a very thin one would break at the first gust. The man listened. He left with a medium kite and a good spool, and he came back the next day to say thank you.

Why did the customer come back to say thank you?
Probably because the seller's advice about the thread helped him fly the kite well, since he left with a good spool.

In the potters' lane, Gopi's grandmother shapes clay lamps on a wheel that she turns with a stick. Before Diwali she makes hundreds a day, and Gopi's job is to set them out in rows to dry in the sun. One afternoon a sudden shower began. Gopi ran for the plastic sheet, but his grandmother called to him to cover the rows nearest the road first, because those were the oldest and almost dry. He covered them and then the rest. Only a few of the newest lamps were spoiled, and those went back into the lump of wet clay. That evening his grandmother gave him the first lamp from the next batch to keep.

Why did the grandmother want the rows nearest the road covered first?
Because those lamps were the oldest and almost dry, so losing them would waste the most work, while the newest could go back into the clay.

Arjun landed in Dubai at two in the morning, and his connecting flight was not until nine. He found a quiet seat near a window and put his backpack under his head. A cleaner passing by smiled and pointed out that the water fountain was just around the corner. At six, a woman at the information desk told him that the lounge would open for transit passengers and offered him a free coupon for breakfast. He ate toast with cheese and drank two cups of coffee. At half past eight he walked to gate twenty-three, where the plane to Kochi was already boarding.

At what time did Arjun land in Dubai?
He landed at two in the morning.

After three days of rain, the road to the lake was a stream of mud, and the bus stopped at the edge. The driver announced that no vehicle could go any farther. Most passengers grumbled and turned back. Four of them, including a retired schoolteacher, decided to walk. It took them two hours, and their shoes were ruined, but when they came around the last bend, the lake lay still and silver below the grey clouds, and the mist drifted slowly over the water. The teacher took off her hat. She said it was worth every muddy step, and nobody disagreed.

Why did the four passengers think the walk was worth it?
Because the beautiful view of the silver lake and mist rewarded their effort.

The lantern festival in the small town of Hoi An, which I visited with my aunt, is held on the full moon night each month. Electric lights are switched off, and the streets glow with paper lanterns in red, yellow and green. Small boats with candles drift along the river. Tourists can buy a floating lantern for a few coins and make a wish before setting it on the water. My aunt chose a pink one. We sat on the stone steps beside the river and watched our lanterns join the hundreds of others. A local girl told us that the festival began many years ago to honour the town's ancestors.

When is the lantern festival held?
It is held on the full moon night each month.

The ferry across the lake runs every thirty minutes from the town pier. A ticket for an adult costs eighty rupees and a child pays half. On the other side, a path leads to a hill with a small white temple. Walking to the top takes about forty minutes, and monkeys wait near the steps for peanuts. Visitors are told to hold their bags tightly. A tea shop at the top sells hot pakoras and has a long bench facing the water. The last ferry back leaves at six, and the boatman rings a bell to warn latecomers that it is about to go.

How often does the ferry run?
The ferry runs every thirty minutes.

Diary, Tuesday. We checked into the hostel in Lisbon at noon, but our room was not ready, so we left our bags at the desk and walked uphill to find lunch. Ines, the girl at the desk, drew us a small map and circled a cafe she said the locals loved. It was tiny, with only five tables, and the owner brought us bread, olives and grilled fish without a menu. He said he cooked whatever came from the boats that morning. Neither of us had eaten so well in weeks. We went back to the hostel two hours later, full and sleepy, and decided not to plan anything else that day.

Why did they not plan anything else that day?
Because they were full and sleepy after a big lunch.

Our class went to a farm on a school trip. The farmer, a tall woman named Mrs. Alvares, welcomed us at the gate with a basket of guavas. She showed us how a cow is milked, and the children were allowed to try, although most of the milk missed the bucket. Then we fed the hens with grain and collected their eggs in a cloth bag. In the field, she explained the difference between wheat and rice. At noon we ate bread with fresh butter under a tree. When it was time to leave, she gave each child a small packet of seeds to grow at home.

What did the children feed the hens?
They fed the hens with grain, and then they collected the eggs in a cloth bag.

The Navratri dance floor in our colony has a rule: no one is allowed to sit out. Grandfather, who is seventy-eight, thought the rule did not apply to him, and he settled on a bench with a cup of tea. The dancers circled past him again and again. Each time, someone waved. After half an hour, he stood, put down his cup, tapped his foot twice, and stepped into the circle. His steps were slow but exact, and the younger dancers adjusted their pace to his. When the song ended, a loud cheer rose. Grandfather bowed and returned to his tea, looking like a young man.

Why did the younger dancers adjust their pace?
Because they wanted Grandfather to feel welcome and keep up with the circle.

The vegetable cart stood outside the school gate, and the seller noticed that a small boy lingered beside it every afternoon. He never bought anything. One day the seller asked what he was waiting for. The boy said his mother worked in the next building and would come out at four, and that he liked to look at the colours. The seller picked up a bright red tomato, polished it on his shirt and put it in the boy's hand. The boy stared. From that day, he stood a little closer to the cart, and each afternoon the seller set aside one fruit for him.

What does the seller's gift of the tomato show?
It shows he is kind and noticed the lonely boy, wanting to make him feel welcome.

The apple seller in Shimla looked at the clouds and then at his half-sold stock. A thin rain began, and the crowd thinned. Instead of covering the apples, he picked up a handful and walked through the lane, offering a free apple to every person without an umbrella. They looked surprised, but took them, and a few stopped under his plastic sheet to stay dry. Within minutes, a small group had gathered, eating apples and chatting. Several bought a kilo before the rain stopped. Back at his stall, the seller grinned and said that rain was only bad luck for those who waited.

Why did the seller give away free apples in the rain?
He wanted to draw people to his stall, and it brought in customers who then bought apples.

The old clock repairman at the market sat all day with a magnifying glass over his eye. A teenager came by with a broken wristwatch and asked how long it would take. The old man said that it might take a week, as it was a delicate piece. The teenager groaned, but he agreed to come back. After a week the watch was running perfectly. The teenager noticed that the glass had been polished and a new strap added. He asked how much extra it would cost. The old man shook his head and said that a watch given to him in trust should leave better than it came.

What does the repairman's answer show about his work?
It shows he takes pride in his work and cares about doing it well, beyond what was asked.

The whole class had practised the Republic Day song for a month. On the morning of the programme, rain began to fall, and the headmaster announced that the event would move into the hall. The hall was small, and the children had to stand close together. Some of them whispered that it would not feel the same without the flag outside. But when the music began, the voices rose and filled the room, louder and clearer than they had ever been in the open ground. The teachers at the back looked at each other in surprise. After the song, the headmaster said he would never again worry about the rain.

Why were the teachers surprised?
Because the children sang louder and better in the small hall than anyone expected.

Late in the day, the vegetable sellers at the market usually drop their prices. Today, a woman named Sheela did not. She stood behind her tomatoes with her arms folded, even though the sun was low and few customers were left. A man next to her asked why she did not follow the others. Sheela said the tomatoes were picked that morning and were worth the price. After a while, an elderly man stopped, looked closely at her tomatoes and bought a kilo without asking for a discount. He said they looked like the ones from his own garden many years ago. Sheela smiled, and the man next to her went quiet.

Why did the man next to Sheela go quiet?
Because a buyer paid full price for her fresh tomatoes, which showed she had been right not to drop her price.

The bus driver, Mr. Pinto, announced that the air conditioning was broken. Passengers fanned themselves with newspapers, and a baby began to cry. At the next stop he did not move on. Instead, he stepped down and bought a dozen cold bottles of water from a stall, handing one to each row. Some passengers refused politely, but he insisted. He paid with his own money, and he did not mention it afterwards. When the bus reached the last stop, several riders paused beside his seat to shake his hand. Mr. Pinto looked embarrassed and said that it was only water.

What does buying water show about Mr. Pinto?
It shows he is generous and cares about his passengers' comfort.

Our school's trip to the planetarium left at nine on Thursday. Each student carried a lunch box and a small notebook. The show started at eleven in a dome-shaped hall, where we lay back in tilted chairs. A man's voice described how the planets move, and the ceiling showed stars so clearly that someone whispered they were real. After the show, we visited a small museum with models of rockets. My friend Salma wrote down the names of all the planets in order. We ate lunch on the lawn under a tree, and returned to school by three o'clock. Our teacher asked us to write a page about the trip.

Where did students sit during the show?
They lay back in tilted chairs in a dome-shaped hall.

On the first Monday of each month, the cattle market is held outside the town of Kesarpura. Farmers lead camels, goats and buffaloes down the dusty road before dawn. Traders from three districts arrive in jeeps, carrying notebooks and rolls of notes. Each animal is inspected carefully: the buyers check the teeth, the legs and the shine of the coat. A boy named Arjun, who is twelve, helps his father hold the rope of their buffalo. They sold her by noon for a good price. Afterwards, his father bought him a glass of sugarcane juice and a cap with a wide brim.

Who helped hold the rope of the buffalo?
A twelve-year-old boy named Arjun helped his father hold the rope.

Ganesh Chaturthi lasts for ten days in our neighbourhood in Mumbai. On the first morning, a small clay idol arrives in a decorated truck and is carried into the tent by six volunteers. Every evening there is an aarti, and people bring plates of modaks. The children of the building perform a short play each year. This time they acted out the story of how Ganesha got his elephant head. On the last day, the idol is taken in a procession to the sea, with drums and loud cheering. Rina cried a little as the idol was lowered into the water.

How long does the festival last?
It lasts for ten days.

When her flight was cancelled, the airline gave Dina a voucher for a hotel and a list of other options. She was tired, and the queue was long. Behind her, a young father was struggling with a crying baby and three bags. Dina looked at her own single suitcase, put it down, and offered to hold the bags while he settled the baby. He accepted with surprise. They moved up the line together. At the counter, the father got his hotel voucher first because the clerk saw the baby. He turned and thanked Dina three times. She waved it off, and she felt less tired than before.

Why did Dina feel less tired after helping?
Because helping the young father lifted her mood and made her feel useful.

Early morning at the grain market in Indore is a noisy affair. Trucks arrive loaded with sacks of wheat, soybean and chickpeas. Porters, called hamals, carry the sacks on their backs and stack them in the sheds. Buyers dip long metal probes into the sacks and pull out a handful of grain to test. The auction is conducted in a shed with a tin roof, and the prices are chalked on a blackboard. By noon, most of the trade is over, and the porters sit on the sacks to eat their lunch from steel boxes. Dust hangs in the air until the evening.

What do buyers use to take a handful of grain from a sack?
They use long metal probes.

A boy sold peanuts outside the cinema hall, calling out in a loud voice. Every evening, a man in a suit walked past him without a glance. One evening, the man stopped and asked the price. The boy said ten rupees a packet. The man bought five, and when the boy tried to count the change, he waved it away. A week later the man came again, and the boy waved at him first. The man chuckled and said he had not expected such a friendly greeting. He bought five packets again. The boy later told his mother that he would always smile at the customers who walk past without looking.

What did the boy learn from the man's visits?
He learned that being friendly can win over customers who ignore you.

Greta spent the first week of her trip in Kyoto, and the second in Osaka. In Kyoto she stayed in a wooden house with sliding paper doors, and she slept on a thin mattress on the floor. She visited three temples each day and kept a list of their names in her notebook. The best moment was a morning walk through a bamboo grove, when the wind made the tall stems knock gently together. In Osaka she ate fried octopus balls at a street stall and rode a ferris wheel at night. She flew home on the fifteenth of April with a suitcase full of tea.

Where did Greta stay during her first week?
She stayed in a wooden house with sliding paper doors in Kyoto.

In the south of the city, the Durga idol-makers work through the night in the weeks before the festival. A young apprentice, Biplab, was asked to paint the eyes of an idol. He had watched the master do this for two years but had never been allowed to try. His brush shook as he approached the clay face. The master stood behind him, silent. Biplab breathed out slowly and painted the first eye, then the second. When he stepped back, the master looked for a long time, then said, simply, that tomorrow Biplab could paint the whole face. The apprentice walked out into the dawn feeling taller.

How did Biplab feel at the end?
He felt proud and confident, because the master trusted him with the whole face and he felt taller.

The bird market in the old quarter of the city opens before dawn. Wooden cages are hung in rows from ropes, and the air is full of chirping. Sellers offer parrots, pigeons, finches and tiny birds from the hills. Some people come just to look, others to buy a pair for a garden. A seller named Idris explained that each bird must be fed twice a day with seeds, and that parrots need fresh chillies. The market is also known for its wooden cages, which are made in a small workshop behind the lane. By eight, the crowd has grown, and the sound of chirping can be heard from two streets away.

What must parrots be given, according to Idris?
Parrots need fresh chillies, along with seeds twice a day.

The village drummer had not played for two years, since his hands had begun to shake. When the festival came, the villagers did not ask him. On the first evening, the other drummers started, but the beat was uneven. The old man listened from his doorway, then walked slowly to the square. He sat beside the drum, put his hands on it and, after a while, began a slow, steady beat. The shaking stopped as the rhythm rolled. The others fell in beside him. When the song ended, nobody spoke for a moment, and then the whole square rose to its feet.

Why did the whole square rise to its feet?
Because they admired the old drummer's courage and skill in returning to play.

A man in a long coat stood outside the book stall and read the same page for twenty minutes. The seller, a woman named Nalini, watched him. When he finally closed the book, he sighed and put it back on the shelf. She said that he could take it for half price, as the cover was already worn. He shook his head and said he could not afford even half. Nalini looked at him for a moment, then tore a page from her notepad, wrote the title on it and told him the library on the next street had a copy. He bowed, and walked away with the note in his hand.

What does Nalini's action show about her?
It shows she is kind and practical, because she helped him find the book for free.

Latif's tea stall near the vegetable market opens at four in the morning, long before anyone else. Porters, truck drivers and farmers stop for a glass before the day begins. Latif knows how each person likes his tea: strong for the driver, sweet for the porter, with ginger for the old farmer. One morning a new porter arrived and Latif handed him a glass without asking. The young man looked surprised, and Latif explained that he had guessed, from the way the man rubbed his shoulders, that he needed something hot and sweet. The porter nodded slowly. After that morning, he never went to another stall.

Why did the new porter keep coming to Latif's stall?
Because Latif noticed what he needed without asking, and the porter felt cared for.

Nobody wanted to pack on the last day of the family holiday. Dad folded clothes slowly. Mum kept finding reasons to take one more walk to the lake. My brother hid his shoes. At the car, we stood in a line looking back at the little wooden house and the hill behind it. Mum said that she would like to come again next year, and Dad nodded. As we drove off, my sister put her head on my shoulder. No one turned on the radio. The road wound down through the pines, and the quiet was a sort of agreement.

What does the quiet in the car show about the family's feelings?
It shows they were sad to leave and had enjoyed the holiday.

An old woman who sold bangles in front of the temple counted her coins each evening and sighed. One day a young girl in a school uniform stopped to look at the glass bangles. She said she had only five rupees. The old woman looked at the girl's thin wrists, and slipped on a pair of pale blue bangles for the five rupees, though they were worth more. The girl danced a little on the spot and ran off. The next week she returned with her mother, who bought a dozen sets. The old woman sighed again, but this time the sigh sounded like a laugh.

Why did the old woman's sigh sound like a laugh the next week?
Because her kindness was repaid with more sales, and she felt happy.

The mountain bus from Shimla to Kalpa takes most of the day, and the road is narrow, with a deep valley on one side. The driver honks at every curve, and passengers hold their breath as the bus edges past oncoming trucks. At noon the bus stops at a roadside stall for lunch. The menu is simple: rajma, rice and a glass of buttermilk. The conductor, who knows all the passengers by sight, collects the fares in a leather bag. By evening the sky is orange, and the first snow peaks come into view. Most passengers are quiet by then, looking out of the windows.

What does the driver do at every curve?
He honks at every curve.

The taxi driver had been quiet for the first hour, but when the road began to climb into the hills he started to hum. Priya noticed that he slowed down at every sharp bend and honked once before turning. At a tea stall he stopped, bought two cups, and handed one to her without asking. Then he pointed to the dark clouds gathering in the west. He said they would reach the guesthouse before the rain if they left right away. Priya finished her tea quickly. When the first heavy drops hit the windshield, they were already pulling into the gate, and she thanked him for being so careful.

What kind of driver does the passage show him to be?
He is a careful, thoughtful driver, because he slowed at bends, honked before turns, and got her to the guesthouse before the rain.

At the school carnival, Tanya volunteered to run the face-painting booth. She had practised on her little cousin all week and felt ready. But on the day, the first child to sit down was a boy who wanted to be a tiger, and Tanya's hand shook so much that the stripes came out crooked. The boy peered into the mirror and went silent. Tanya felt her cheeks burning. Then the boy grinned and said that a tiger with crooked stripes looked even fiercer. Other children lined up behind him, and by the end of the afternoon, Tanya had painted forty faces, and she was no longer worried about straight lines.

What made Tanya stop worrying about straight lines?
The boy's kind comment that crooked stripes looked fiercer, and the long line of happy children.

When the rickshaw stopped in the middle of the flooded street, the water was up to the wheels. The driver turned around and apologised, saying he could go no farther. Mr. Banerjee, wearing a clean white shirt and carrying a briefcase, looked at the water and then at his watch. He had an important meeting. Without a word, he rolled his trousers to the knee, took off his shoes, and stepped into the water. The driver stared, then jumped down and carried the briefcase for him. They waded together for a hundred metres. At the end, Mr. Banerjee handed the driver double the fare.

Why did Mr. Banerjee pay the driver double?
Because the driver helped him through the flood by carrying his briefcase.

At the floating market in Srinagar, vendors sell vegetables from small wooden boats on the lake. They start at five in the morning, and by six, the water is crowded with shikaras full of produce. Buyers also arrive by boat, calling out for lotus stems, turnips and tomatoes. Goods are passed from one boat to another. The boatmen know the lake so well that they rarely collide. When the sun rises over the mountains, the water turns pink and gold. Tourists wake early to see this, and many buy fresh flowers from a boat that carries nothing else.

How do vendors sell vegetables at the floating market?
They sell from small wooden boats on the lake.

The train from Siliguri to Darjeeling is called the toy train because it is so small. It runs on a narrow track that twists around the hillside, and the carriages are painted blue and cream. We bought tickets for the morning ride and sat on the left side for the best views. The engine puffs black smoke and whistles loudly before every bend. At one station called Ghum, the train stops for ten minutes so that visitors can take photographs. A boy sold roasted peanuts from a paper cone, and I bought two. The whole ride took more than six hours, but nobody complained.

Why is the train called the toy train?
It is called the toy train because it is so small.

The women of the lane make a giant rangoli every year for the festival, and every year it looks different. This time, Ruchi, the youngest, proposed a picture of a river. The elders hesitated, since rivers are difficult to draw in dots and lines. But Ruchi insisted, and she began laying blue powder in a long curve. Slowly, others joined in, adding fish, boats and reeds in different colours. When it was done, passers-by stopped to stare. An old neighbour said that she had not seen anything so lovely in years. Ruchi lowered her head to hide a smile, then went to fetch a broom to sweep the edges.

How can we tell the rangoli turned out well?
Passers-by stopped to stare, and an old neighbour said she had not seen anything so lovely in years.

Aisha had never danced at a wedding before, and when the drums began, she sat very straight on her chair. Her cousin took her hand and pulled her gently into the circle. At first she stood stiffly, copying the others. Then someone started clapping to the beat. Aisha's shoulders loosened. She spun once, then again, and her dupatta flew out behind her. The other girls cheered. When the song ended, she was out of breath, and she had a smile that she had to cover with her hand. Her mother, watching from the side, wiped her own eyes quickly.

Why did her mother wipe her eyes?
Because she was moved and proud to see her shy daughter dancing happily.

At the temple festival, the chariot would not move. Ten men pulled on the thick ropes, but the wheels remained stuck in the soft mud from the night's rain. The priest waited. The crowd murmured. Then, from the back, a group of schoolchildren stepped forward and took hold of the ropes beside the men. A woman started a rhythmic chant, and everyone pulled together on the beat. Slowly, the wheels came out with a wet sucking sound, and the chariot rolled on. The crowd cheered louder than it had all morning, and the priest raised his hands to bless the children.

What made the chariot finally move?
Everyone pulling together on the beat of a chant, including the children, got it out of the mud.

On Diwali night, Saira's family lit more lamps than usual, because her brother was returning from a year abroad. The door was left open, and a plate of sweets waited on the table. Saira kept glancing at the clock. At nine, there was a knock. Instead of rushing to the door, her mother put down the plate and smoothed her sari. Then she walked, not ran. Saira watched her mother open the door and, for a second, stand motionless. Then the two of them held each other without a sound, and Saira realised that she was crying too.

What did the mother's actions at the door show?
They showed she was overcome with emotion at seeing her son, too moved to speak.

Our walking tour of old Hyderabad began at the Charminar at nine in the morning. The guide, a retired teacher named Mrs. Fatima, carried a small flag so that we would not lose her in the crowd. First we visited the bangle market, where stalls glittered with glass and lac. Then she led us through a narrow lane to a bakery that has been making the same biscuits for eighty years. We tasted them warm. The tour ended at noon with a plate of biryani in a small restaurant. Mrs. Fatima told us that the best time to visit is early morning, before the traffic grows loud.

What did Mrs. Fatima carry so the group would not lose her?
She carried a small flag.

The Bonalu festival in Hyderabad takes place in July and August. Women dress in new saris and carry pots of rice, jaggery and curd decorated with neem leaves on their heads. They walk in a line to the temple of the goddess, accompanied by drums. At the temple gate, a woman in trance sometimes speaks in a loud voice, and the crowd listens quietly. Men dance in front with painted faces and bells on their ankles. Some families also make animal offerings, while many offer only cooked rice. At the end of the festival, the temple is cleaned and the pots are washed.

What do the women carry on their heads?
They carry pots of rice, jaggery and curd decorated with neem leaves.

A small boy was sitting alone on the toy train, clutching a paper bag, when the conductor noticed him. He asked where the boy's parents were. The boy said that they were in the next carriage and that he had come to count the tunnels. The conductor smiled, and said that there were exactly nine on this stretch. At the first tunnel, the boy raised one finger. At the second, two. By the sixth, other passengers had begun counting aloud with him. When the ninth tunnel came, a loud cheer filled the carriage, and the boy stood up and bowed, as if he had built them himself.

Why did the other passengers join the boy's counting?
Because his enthusiasm made it a fun game that everyone wanted to share.

Teresa had rehearsed what to say to the stall owner for a week. The scarf she wanted cost more than she could easily spend, and she planned to ask for a lower price with a firm voice. When she reached the stall, though, the owner looked at her and asked if she was buying for herself or for a present. Teresa told him it was for her mother, who was recovering from a long illness. The man was silent for a moment, then folded the scarf into paper and quoted a price that was almost half. Teresa's firm voice never came out; she simply said thank you and her eyes filled up.

Why did the stall owner lower the price?
Because he felt sympathy when he heard the scarf was for Teresa's mother, who was recovering from illness.

At the village fair, Rohit stood in front of a stall where players threw balls to knock down a pyramid of tin cans. He had three balls, and the owner told him he had to knock them all down to win a toy. Rohit missed with his first throw, and with the second. The owner smirked. Rohit took a long breath, closed one eye, and threw the third ball hard. Seven cans fell, but one stayed on the shelf. The owner shrugged and said better luck. Rohit looked at the leftover can for a long time. Then he walked away without complaint, and he did not look unhappy at all.

What can you tell from Rohit walking away without complaint?
He accepted the result like a good sport and was not angry about losing.

In Kerala, the Onam feast is served on a banana leaf. The leaf is placed with its tip pointing to the left of the person sitting down. First come the salt and pickles at the top corner, then the fried banana chips, then the different vegetable dishes in a neat row. Rice goes in the middle, and sambar is poured over it. After that, a thin sweet pudding called payasam is served from a large brass vessel. Thomas, who was visiting a friend's family for the first time, copied what the others did and ate with his fingers. He finished two helpings of payasam.

What is the Onam feast served on?
It is served on a banana leaf.

The cheese seller at the farmers' market let every customer taste before buying. One Saturday a little girl tasted a slice, made a face, and spat it into a napkin. Her mother looked mortified. The seller laughed so heartily that the whole row turned to look. He said that it was the most honest review he had had all year, and that cheese was not meant for everyone. He gave the girl a slice of mild cheese from another shelf. She chewed it carefully, then nodded. Her mother bought a large wedge, and the seller wrote the girl's verdict on his blackboard.

How did the girl's mother feel at first?
She felt embarrassed, because she looked mortified when the girl spat out the cheese.

In the weeks before Pongal, the farmers of the village argue about whose sugarcane is the sweetest. The elders say the argument is part of the festival. Selvi's grandfather insisted that his field had the best crop, so on the morning of the harvest he carried the first stalk to the temple himself. He did not sell any until it had been offered. Afterwards, he gave a piece to each neighbour, including the farmer with whom he had argued. That man chewed it slowly, and then admitted, with a grin, that it was not bad at all. Both men laughed so hard that Selvi had to sit down.

What does this show about the two farmers' argument?
It shows the argument was friendly and not serious, because they laughed together over the sugarcane.

The train had barely left the platform when the little girl began to cry. She had wanted to wave to her grandmother until the very last moment, but the crowd had hidden the old woman.
