Her father tried to give her a biscuit, but she pushed it away. After a while the crying became sniffles. A man in the opposite seat took a small cloth bird from his bag and made it hop along the window ledge. The girl watched, still sniffling. Then the bird bowed, and she gave a wet laugh. By the next station, she was holding it in both hands and asking its name.

What stopped the girl from crying?
The man's hopping cloth bird distracted her and made her laugh.

A stranger came to the toy stall and asked for a puppet, but he had only a large note, and the seller had no change. The seller thought for a moment, then said that the man could take the puppet and pay later. The man was surprised, but he took it and promised to come back. For three days the seller waited. His assistant said that the money was lost. On the fourth morning, the stranger returned, out of breath, and handed over the note, along with a small bag of sweets. He said he had been away on work. The seller's face lit up, and he never lost faith in people.

What does the stranger returning show?
It shows he was honest and kept his promise, so the seller's trust was rewarded.

Each week at a village haat in Bastar, the paths around the clearing are full of people walking in from the forest. Women carry baskets of mahua flowers and dried mushrooms on their heads. Men bring hand-made drums and small iron tools. Traders from the plains come on motorbikes with sacks of salt and soap. Some trade is done by swapping, a basket of mahua for a packet of salt. By afternoon, the haat smells of wood smoke and roasted corn. People who have sold everything buy cloth, sugar and cooking oil before walking home in groups, singing as the light fades.

What do women carry in baskets on their heads?
They carry mahua flowers and dried mushrooms.

The Saturday market in a small hill town sits in a narrow lane behind the bus stand. Sellers from the hills bring woollen caps, hand-knitted socks and small jars of wild honey. A man named Tenzin sells momos from a steel steamer at the entrance, and the queue for his stall often reaches the next shop. Buyers sit on low stools to eat, holding the plates close. Next to him, an elderly woman repairs umbrellas for ten rupees each. She works with a small kit of wire and thread and never seems to hurry. The market closes at dusk, when the mountain air turns sharply cold.

What does Tenzin sell?
Tenzin sells momos from a steel steamer.

The book fair opened in the school hall on Monday and ran until Friday. Each class was given a one-hour slot. Class Five went in at eleven, and Mrs. Nair gave each student a slip with a limit of one hundred and fifty rupees. Hari wanted a book on dinosaurs, but it cost two hundred, so he chose a smaller one about birds. Nisha bought a mystery story and a bookmark shaped like a fish. At the back of the hall, a retired teacher sat on a stool and signed copies of her own children's book. A line of shy students waited to say hello.

How much money was each student allowed to spend?
Each student could spend one hundred and fifty rupees.

The potato seller at the Tuesday market noticed that the same girl came to his stall every week and bought only two potatoes. One day he asked why she did not buy more. She said her grandfather lived alone, and she cooked for him in small amounts so nothing would be wasted. The seller thought about this. The next Tuesday, when she paid for her two potatoes, he quietly slipped in a third one and an onion, and said it was extra. She noticed but did not say anything. After that she smiled every time she arrived, and the seller began to keep his best potatoes aside for her.

How did the girl probably feel about the extra potato and onion?
She probably felt grateful, because she noticed the gift and smiled whenever she came back.

The night bazaar in our city comes alive after nine, when the day's heat has gone. Stalls sell embroidered bags, silver jewellery and colourful mirror-work cloth. A woman called Hansa sits in front of her stall hand-stitching cushion covers, and she can finish one in less than an hour. Customers watch her work and ask questions about the patterns. Next door, a man grills sandwiches on a hot iron plate, and the queue winds around the corner. Policemen on bicycles patrol the lane, and the bazaar stays open until one in the morning, making it a favourite of students on holiday.

What does Hansa make at her stall?
She hand-stitches cushion covers.

The bargaining at the carpet shop lasted almost an hour. Mr. Rao wanted a small woollen rug for his hallway, and the shopkeeper, Mr. Hamid, kept pointing to the fine knots on the back. Each time Mr. Rao mentioned a price, Mr. Hamid shook his head, but he poured another cup of tea. At last Mr. Rao stood up to leave. Mr. Hamid called him back, named a price a little above what Mr. Rao had hoped, and added a small cushion cover as a gift. They shook hands. Walking out with the rolled rug, Mr. Rao felt he had not been cheated, and he promised himself he would visit again.

Why did Mr. Rao feel good about the purchase?
Because the shopkeeper met him near his price and added a free cushion cover, so he felt the deal was fair.

Chor Bazaar in Mumbai is famous for second-hand goods. Narrow lanes are lined with shops selling old clocks, brass lamps, radios and antique furniture. A shopkeeper named Hussain is known for his large collection of old film posters, hung from the ceiling in plastic sleeves. Many customers are collectors who come on weekends, and some travel from other cities. Prices depend on mood and bargaining skill. Hussain says the best time to visit is just after the rainy season, when new stock arrives from old homes that have been cleared. A cup of chai, he says, always comes before any talk of money.

What does Hussain keep hung from the ceiling?
He keeps old film posters, in plastic sleeves.

When Sunil's family visited the village for the harvest festival, he did not want to go. The village had no internet and nothing to do, he thought. On the first morning his cousin handed him a sickle and took him to the field. Sunil cut a few stalks badly and laughed at himself. By noon his hands were blistered, but the older farmers praised him, and a small boy asked him to show how to tie the bundles. In the evening everyone sat around a fire and ate fresh roti with jaggery. When the family packed to leave, Sunil asked his father if they could come back next year.

What does Sunil's question at the end show?
It shows he enjoyed the village visit and changed his mind about it.

The passenger ship from Port Blair to Chennai takes three days and passes through open sea. The ship has dormitories on the lower deck and cabins on the upper deck. Meals are served at set times in a hall with long tables. A small shop sells biscuits, soap and postcards. On the second day, dolphins followed the ship for an hour, and everyone rushed to the rail to look. In the evening, the crew held a game of cards, and a passenger from Tamil Nadu won every round. When the steamer arrived, the passengers clapped as the coast came into view.

How long does the ship journey take?
The journey takes three days.

We started our trek at six in the morning from the foot of the hill. The path was lined with wild marigolds, and the air smelled of damp earth. After an hour we reached a stream and filled our bottles. At nine we stopped at a ledge to eat boiled eggs and bread. The guide, Ravi, pointed to a pair of eagles circling high above. By eleven we had reached a small flat meadow with a stone hut where shepherds rest. There we rested for an hour. The way down was faster but steeper, and I slipped twice. We reached the village by four in the afternoon, thirsty and cheerful.

At what time did the group reach the meadow?
They reached the meadow at eleven.

Before we left for Goa, my mother wrote a list of all the things to pack. The list ran to two pages. It included sunscreen, caps, a first-aid box, a torch and extra phone chargers. My father said he only needed a toothbrush and a hat. The bag was packed the night before and kept by the door. We caught the early train at six and found our seats near the window. The journey took twelve hours, and mother played cards with us to pass the time. At ten in the evening we arrived at the hotel, and I fell asleep before dinner.

How long did the train journey take?
The train journey took twelve hours.

The tourist guide in the fort spoke so quickly that most of the group stopped listening. Only Ishaan, who was nine, kept asking questions. He wanted to know where the soldiers slept, how the cannons were lifted, and why the walls had tiny holes. The guide slowed down and began to point things out to him. Soon the other children came closer, and even some adults put away their phones. By the time the tour ended at the high gate, the guide was telling stories rather than reciting facts. As the group dispersed, he shook Ishaan's hand and said that he had not enjoyed a tour so much for a long time.

Why did the guide slow down?
Because Ishaan's keen questions made the guide more interested in explaining and telling stories.

The Dasara festival in Mysuru ends with a grand procession led by a decorated elephant. The elephant carries a golden seat on its back, and a long line of musicians and dancers follows. Thousands of people line the streets to watch, many standing on rooftops. In the evening, the palace is lit with ninety-seven thousand bulbs, and the glow can be seen from the hill nearby. The festival lasts for ten days and includes concerts, wrestling matches and a flower show. On the final evening, a torchlight parade takes place in the open ground, and fireworks light up the sky.

What does the elephant carry on its back?
The elephant carries a golden seat on its back.

Fatima carried her mother's old brass pot to the market and asked the shopkeeper how much he would pay for it. He turned it over, tapped the base, and offered a low price. Fatima did not answer. Instead she asked if he had seen the pattern around the rim, and she told him it had come from her great-grandmother's wedding. The shopkeeper stopped tapping. He looked at the pot again, more carefully this time, and raised his offer. Fatima thanked him, wrapped the pot back in its cloth, and walked home. She had not wanted to sell it at all; she had only wanted to learn what it was worth.

What does this show about how Fatima felt about the pot?
It shows the pot mattered to her, because she did not really want to sell it and only wanted to know its value.

Two friends, Kiran and Aman, set off to cross the city by bicycle. After the first hour, Kiran's chain slipped and he had to push the cycle. Aman waited at every corner but did not complain. In the second hour, a puncture slowed them further. At noon, Aman stopped at a tea stall and bought two cups and a plate of biscuits. They sat on the kerb together and ate. When they finally reached the old fort, the sun was low and the gate was closed. They looked at each other and laughed. They agreed, without needing to say it, that the ride itself had been the best part.

Why did the friends laugh when they found the gate closed?
Because they had enjoyed the journey so much that missing the fort did not matter.

Rahul's uncle lives in a town near the coast, and every summer Rahul spends two weeks there. The journey takes six hours by bus and ends at a tiny stop beside a cashew orchard. His uncle waits there on a scooter, wearing the same faded cap. They ride home along a narrow lane, past a pond with ducks. Aunty always makes fish fry on the first night. Rahul sleeps on the roof under a mosquito net. Early each morning he walks to the beach with his cousin Gopal to watch the fishing boats return with the catch, and they help drag the nets ashore.

How long does the bus journey take?
The bus journey takes six hours.

The orange sellers of the small town of Santrapur set out their baskets in the early morning at the wholesale yard near the railway line. Oranges are sorted by size into three grades, and the best ones are wrapped in tissue paper for export. Workers use long wooden crates, each holding about forty kilograms. A man named Kishore keeps a small notebook in which he writes the weight of each crate in pencil. Trucks come from other states to collect large orders, and loading goes on until nine at night. In the winter months, the smell of oranges can be noticed from two streets away.

What does Kishore write in his notebook?
He writes the weight of each crate in pencil.

Under the railway bridge in Kantapur, a second-hand book market has been open for over fifty years. Rows of shelves lean against the pillars, and many books are stacked on the pavement in towers. Students come to find old textbooks at half the price. The seller Mr. Dutta knows where every title is, and can find a particular novel in less than a minute. He wears thick glasses and keeps a small radio playing songs from old films. When it rains, he covers the stacks with blue plastic sheets and the customers squeeze under the bridge to wait. Business slows then, but nobody seems to leave.

Where is the second-hand book market located?
It is located under the railway bridge in Kantapur.

In the lane where Aditi lives, nobody had ever hosted a Janmashtami programme because the lane was too narrow. This year, her mother had an idea. The families agreed to hang cloth between the rooftops, so a roof was made over the whole lane. Each house brought a chair, a mat or a lamp. Children dressed as Krishna and his friends ran along, balancing little pots of curd. A neighbour who usually complained about noise came out with a plate of butter. As the evening closed, the old and young sat on mats and sang together. Aditi's mother received many compliments for her idea.

What can you tell about how the neighbours felt about the programme?
They enjoyed it and felt united, because they all contributed and even the usually complaining neighbour joined in.

Raksha Bandhan was a few hours away when Zoya's cousin Imran realised that he had no gift for his sister. The shops were closing, and he had only a few coins. He wandered back home, sat on the steps and thought. Then he went to his room, took a sheet of paper and drew a small picture of the two of them as children, flying a kite. He wrote underneath, in careful letters, a short line of thanks. The next morning, his sister read the note, and her eyes filled with tears. She hugged him and pinned the drawing above her desk, where it stayed for years.

Why did the sister's eyes fill with tears?
Because the drawing and note were heartfelt and showed how much he cared.

After the long walk through the market, Dhanush realised that he was lost. Every lane looked the same, with the same bright cloth hanging from the same blue poles. He stopped under a tarpaulin and tried to think. A boy of about nine offered to help and asked where he needed to go. Dhanush said the clock tower. The boy looked at him sceptically, but then took his hand and led him through three turns and a narrow passage. When the tower came in sight, Dhanush searched his pockets for a coin, but the boy had already vanished into the crowd.

What can we tell about the boy who helped Dhanush?
He was helpful and kind, because he guided a stranger without waiting for a reward.

In the grain shop, a girl was weighing flour when a customer began to shout that the scale was unfair. The shopkeeper, her father, was away, and she was alone. Her hands trembled, but she kept her voice level. She explained that the weights were checked every month, and she showed the stamp. Then she placed the flour on the scale and let the customer see the needle for himself. The man peered at it, grumbled and fell silent. After he left, a woman who had watched the whole thing told the girl that she had handled it well. The girl blushed and went back to the sacks.

What does the way the girl handled the customer show?
It shows she is brave and calm, because she kept her voice level and let him see the scale himself.

The old tailor under the banyan tree has fixed clothes for forty years. On a rainy morning, a young man brought him a torn jacket and asked how soon it could be done. The tailor looked at the sky and said he could do it by the evening. The young man frowned, because he needed it by noon for an interview. The tailor looked at the jacket again, put aside his other work, and began to sew. By eleven, the jacket was mended so neatly that the tear could hardly be seen. The young man tried to pay extra, but the tailor refused and wished him luck.

Why did the tailor change his plan and finish by eleven?
Because he understood the young man needed the jacket for an interview and decided to help.

Hamza woke up on the morning of Eid to find that his new kurta had a tear in the sleeve. He held it up and stared. It was too late to buy another one. His sister came in, took one look, and went away. She returned with a needle, thread and a small patch of embroidered cloth that she had saved from an old scarf. She stitched it neatly over the tear, so that it looked like a deliberate flower. Hamza wore the kurta to prayers. Several relatives asked where he had bought it, and he said, with a wide smile, that his sister had made it special.

How did Hamza feel about the kurta in the end?
He felt proud and happy, because he smiled widely and told people his sister had made it special.

The temple in our town is built on a small hill, and a flight of one hundred and eight steps leads up to it. At dawn, priests ring a large brass bell and the sound travels down to the river. Visitors leave their shoes at the foot of the steps. Flowers, coconut and incense are sold from small stalls on both sides. In the main hall, a stone lamp has burned continuously for as long as anyone can remember. The temple gets most crowded on full moon days, when buses bring pilgrims from villages far away. On quiet mornings, monkeys sit on the wall and watch the visitors.

How many steps lead up to the temple?
One hundred and eight steps lead up to it.

The children of Gomti Nagar prepare for the festival of lights by making their own lamps from clay. They gather at the park, sit on mats, and shape small bowls with their fingers. Dev's lamp collapsed twice. Each time, his friend Mira patted her hands dry and showed him how to press the sides more gently. By the third try, his lamp stood neatly. Later they painted them with red and gold paint and left them to dry in the sun. On the festival night, Dev placed his lamp at the front, and when it flickered to life, he looked first at Mira and then at the flame.

Why did Dev look at Mira when the lamp lit?
Because she had helped him make it, and he was grateful to her.

The two sisters selling flowers beside the temple gate always argued about prices. The older sister, Kamala, wanted to keep the cost low so that people could afford offerings. The younger, Vimala, thought they should charge more on busy days. One festival morning, a long line of devotees arrived and the flowers were almost gone by nine. Kamala kept the usual price. Vimala grumbled, but she kept silent when she noticed an old man with trembling hands putting his small coins together. Kamala handed him the biggest garland. Vimala looked away and began sorting the remaining jasmine with a sigh that sounded more like agreement.

What changed Vimala's attitude?
Seeing the old man with trembling hands paying with small coins made her understand why Kamala kept prices low.

The ferry to the island leaves only twice a day, and Kavya had missed the morning one by three minutes. She stood at the jetty watching the white boat grow smaller. An old fisherman sitting on an upturned crate looked up from his net and told her not to worry. He said the afternoon ferry was never full, and she could sit in the shade of the tea stall until then. Kavya bought a glass of tea, took out her notebook, and began to sketch the boats tied along the pier. By the time the afternoon ferry came, she had filled four pages and no longer minded the wait.

Why did Kavya stop minding the wait?
Because she used the time to sketch the boats and became absorbed, filling four pages in her notebook.

Mina was embarrassed because she had spent most of her allowance on a snow globe at the market, and it turned out to be cracked at the base. She did not want to complain, but she did not want to keep it either. After standing at the stall for several minutes, she held it up and quietly showed the seller the crack. He took it, turned it over, and handed her another, saying nothing at all. Mina's relief was so great that she nearly dropped the new globe. She hurried away, and later she thought about how a few brave words had cost her nothing.

What did Mina learn from the experience?
She learned that speaking up politely about a problem can solve it easily.

The big weekly market in the lake town of Kesargarh is held near the water. Sellers from the surrounding villages spread cloth on the ground and arrange tiny mirrors, silver anklets, leather sandals and printed bedsheets. A man with a small harmonium sings old songs to attract customers to his brother's shop of fabrics. Behind the rows is a food corner where women make fresh bhajiyas and serve them in newspaper cones. A tourist from Germany, named Lukas, bought a puppet and a wooden spoon. He said that the best part was not the shopping, but the way the shopkeepers explained the story behind each item.

What did Lukas buy at the market?
He bought a puppet and a wooden spoon.

Our camel safari in Jaisalmer started at four in the afternoon. A guide named Bhanwar Singh lifted each of us on to a camel, and the animals rose with a lurch that made everyone gasp. We rode for two hours across the dunes, with the sun sinking red behind us. At the camp, there were low cots, a fire and a cook preparing dal baati on hot stones. A man played a stringed instrument, and a boy danced in a flowing skirt. We slept outside under a blanket of stars. At dawn, the cook brought us warm tea in clay cups, and the dunes turned gold.

What did the cook prepare at the camp?
The cook prepared dal baati on hot stones.

On the night train to Kolkata, we were given a compartment with six berths. I was on the upper berth and my sister on the lower. Across the aisle sat a man who spent the whole night sketching in a notebook. He drew quick pictures of the sleeping passengers, the window and a cat that had boarded at a small station. At seven in the morning the train rolled over the long bridge across the river, and I woke up to see the water shining like silver. The man tore a page from his notebook, drew the bridge and gave it to me. I still have it, folded in a book.

What did the man across the aisle do all night?
He sketched in a notebook.

Every autumn the riverside town of Ban Lom holds a lantern night. Thousands of paper lanterns rise from the riverbank at once and drift upward like slow orange stars. Before the release, families write wishes on the paper with a black pen. Volunteers stand beside the crowd to hold lanterns while the flame inside warms the air. A young woman named Noi sold bamboo frames from a table near the bridge, and the line stretched forty people deep. The festival ends at midnight with a drumbeat from the temple. Early next morning, local students walk the fields to collect any fallen lanterns.

Who collects the fallen lanterns the next morning?
Local students walk the fields to collect them.

The tea market in the small town of Bagicha has a very early start. Auction buyers gather at six in the morning around a long table covered with tiny bowls of dry leaf. Each bowl is labelled with the name of a garden. The buyers pick up a pinch, smell it, then brew a small cup and taste it with a loud slurp. A man in a grey cap explained to me that the loud slurp spreads the tea around the tongue. Prices are called out in a soft voice, and a clerk writes the winning bids on a large board. By ten, most of the tea has been sold and loaded into trucks.

Where do auction buyers gather at six in the morning?
They gather around a long table covered with small bowls of dry tea leaf.

A man selling balloons stood at the gate of the weekly market, and he never seemed to run out. A child tugged at her mother's hand, and the mother sighed, but bought a red one. The balloon man tied it to the girl's wrist. After the family left, he turned to a small boy standing nearby with empty pockets. Without a word, he blew up a blue balloon, twisted it into the shape of a dog and gave it to him. The boy stared, then grinned, and ran off to show his friends. A woman who had seen this smiled to herself, and bought two balloons from the man before she left.

Why did the woman buy two balloons?
Because she saw the man's kindness to the poor boy and wanted to support him.

On Christmas Eve, the church bells in the old part of Goa rang at ten, and families began walking up the hill with candles. Maria had been carrying her baby brother for half the climb, and her arms were aching. She said nothing. Halfway up, her uncle, who had been walking behind, quietly took the baby from her and told her to hold the candle instead. Maria let out a long breath. At the top, they found a place in the third row, and she watched the flame in her hands shake with each step she had taken. She sang the carols louder than she had expected.

How did Maria feel when her uncle took the baby?
She felt relieved, because she let out a long breath once her aching arms were free.

At the fish market in Kochi, an old woman named Leela has sold sardines from the same spot for thirty years. One morning a boy of about ten arrived alone, holding a folded note and a cloth bag. His mother was unwell, he said, and had sent him for fish. Leela read the note, chose the sardines herself and cleaned them with quick strokes of her knife. When the boy held out his coins, she took exactly what was needed and pushed the rest back into his palm. Then she tucked a lime and a few curry leaves into the bag. The boy walked off holding the bag with both hands, and Leela watched him until he turned the corner.

Why did Leela probably watch the boy until he turned the corner?
She probably wanted to be sure he was safe, because he was young, alone and shopping for his sick mother.

Our guide in the desert told us to keep our eyes on the horizon and not to talk. We trudged up the dune in silence, sand pouring into our shoes. At the top, he held up a hand. Below us, a pool of water gleamed in a small valley between rocks, and a few palm trees leaned over it. For a moment nobody breathed. Then the youngest of us, a girl of ten, burst into laughter. The guide, who had never smiled before, smiled broadly. We ran down the slope, shoes and all, and splashed in the pool like children, even the grown-ups.

What does the group's reaction show about how they felt?
They were delighted and relieved to find water, because they laughed, ran down and splashed like children.

Dear Nani, the mela here was wonderful. It was held on the riverbank, and we reached it by bullock cart. There was a giant wheel with wooden seats, and Chotu was too scared to ride it, so I went alone with Uncle. I ate hot jalebis from a leaf bowl and bought a tin whistle for four rupees. In the evening a puppet show told the story of a clever crow, and all the children sat cross-legged in the sand. I wish you had come with us. Please tell Dadu that his old umbrella kept the sun off Aunty the whole day. With love, Rekha.

How did Rekha and her family reach the mela?
They reached it by bullock cart.

The night market on the hill road begins at seven, once the heat of the day has faded. Strings of yellow bulbs hang between the stalls, and the smell of roasted corn drifts through the air. One stall sells mirrors with embroidered frames, another sells leather belts and wallets. A girl named Pooja runs a stand with cold lemon soda and rock salt. She has a small speaker that plays old songs at low volume. By nine the lane is so crowded that people walk sideways. The sellers pack up around midnight, loading their goods onto handcarts and pulling them slowly down the hill.

What does Pooja sell at her stand?
She sells cold lemon soda with rock salt.

The street food lane near the station is open from five in the evening. A man named Gopal sells pani puri from a glass-fronted cart. He fills each crisp shell with potato, chickpeas and spicy water and passes it into the customer's hand with a small flourish. Beside him, a woman fries corn fritters in a wide pan, and a boy sells lemon tea in tiny glasses. The lane gets crowded after office hours, when people come straight from work. Most stalls shut by ten, and the cleaners come with hoses to wash the road before midnight.

What does Gopal sell?
Gopal sells pani puri from a glass-fronted cart.

Ravi's grandfather ran a small shop in the market, and every evening he counted the money alone. One night Ravi sat with him and noticed that his grandfather set aside a few coins in a tin box before counting the rest. Ravi asked what it was for. His grandfather said it was for whoever came by without enough. Ravi watched for a week. Two times, he saw a customer short by a few rupees, and each time his grandfather quietly took a coin from the tin. Ravi said nothing to him, but the next week he dropped his own pocket money into the box.

Why did Ravi put his pocket money into the tin box?
Because he admired his grandfather's kindness and wanted to help in the same way.

The Sagar Lodge is a small family inn near the harbour of a busy port town. It has twelve rooms, a dining hall and a roof where guests can watch the ships. Breakfast is served between seven and ten and includes idli, vada and filter coffee. The owner, Mrs. Rao, greets every guest at the door and remembers their names. Checkout time is at eleven, but she lets late travellers keep their bags in a locked room until evening. A walk to the beach takes five minutes. Rooms with a sea view cost a bit more, and they are booked well in advance in the holiday season.

What time does breakfast end at the hotel?
Breakfast ends at ten in the morning.

At the science fair, Meghna's model of a water filter did not work. The sand and gravel clogged, and the water that came through was almost as cloudy as before. The judges were already walking towards her table. She felt her ears turning hot. When they arrived, she did not hide the dirty cup. Instead she explained what she had tried, why she believed the sand was too fine, and how she would use a coarser layer next time. One of the judges wrote a few lines on her sheet and smiled. Meghna did not win a prize, but she was given a special mention for honest thinking.

Why did the judges give Meghna a special mention?
Because she was honest about the failure and explained clearly what went wrong and how to fix it.

Meera lives in a small town near Mysore, and every morning a family of langurs sits on the wall behind her house. Last week she noticed that the smallest langur, a baby with pale fur, was clinging to its mother's belly and not moving much. The mother kept stopping to look down at it. Meera put a plate of cut cucumbers on the wall and went back inside. When she looked out again, the mother had taken one piece and was holding it close to the baby's mouth. The baby nibbled a little and then opened its eyes wide. By noon the whole group had moved on to the tall tamarind tree.

Where does the langur family sit every morning?
They sit on the wall behind Meera's house.

Tobias found a tiny hedgehog in his garden in Hamburg on a cold evening in October. It was curled in a ball under a pile of dry leaves and it did not unroll when he leaned closer. His grandmother told him not to touch it with bare hands. Instead, they set a shallow dish of water near the leaves and left a small cardboard box with straw beside it. Then they went indoors and watched from the kitchen window. An hour later the hedgehog crept out, drank for a long time, and walked into the box. Tobias grinned and wrote the date on a card.

Why did Tobias and his grandmother put out water and a box?
They wanted to help the cold hedgehog. The water gave it a drink and the box with straw gave it a warm place to rest, and the hedgehog used both.

In the science room at Sunrise School, Ms. Fernandes held up a glass of water and a small clear marble. She asked the class what would happen if she dropped the marble into the glass. Ravi said it would sink, and he was right. Then she poured six big spoonfuls of salt into a second glass, stirred it well, and dropped in a fresh egg. The egg floated near the top. The children gasped. Ms. Fernandes explained that salty water is heavier than the same amount of plain water, so it pushes things up more strongly. Priya wrote this in her notebook and drew a picture of the floating egg.

What did Ms. Fernandes drop into the second glass?
She dropped a fresh egg into it, after stirring in six big spoonfuls of salt.

For years, old Mr. Banerjee had tied a long string to his reading glasses so they would not get lost. One afternoon his grandson Arun noticed that the string kept catching on the chair and pulling the glasses off his nose. Arun took two thin wires from his craft box and bent them into small hooks. He fixed one hook to each arm of the glasses so that they curled behind the ears. Mr. Banerjee tried them on and walked around the veranda twice. The glasses stayed in place. He laughed, took off the string, and put it in a drawer, saying he would never need it again.

What did Mr. Banerjee do with the string at the end?
He took it off and put it in a drawer.

A baker in a village in Kerala once left her dough on the counter and forgot about it for most of the day. When she came back, the dough had grown to twice its size and smelled sweet and a little sour. She was worried it was spoiled, but she did not want to waste the flour, so she shaped it into small rounds and steamed them anyway. The buns came out soft and light, much softer than her usual ones. Her neighbours asked how she had made them, and soon she was leaving a bowl of dough out on purpose every evening.

Why did the baker begin leaving dough out on purpose?
Because the forgotten dough made softer, lighter buns than usual, and her neighbours wanted to know how she made them.

Every evening at six, a heron lands on the same flat rock in the middle of the pond behind Hana's school in Osaka. It stands on one leg without moving for so long that some children think it is a statue. Then, quick as a flash, it darts its neck into the water and comes up with a small silver fish. Hana has counted the heron's catches in her notebook for three weeks. On the best evening it caught five fish, and on the worst evening, after a heavy rain made the water cloudy, it caught none and flew away early.

On which evening did the heron catch no fish?
It caught none on the evening after heavy rain, when the water was cloudy.

Kofi poured some vinegar into a bowl and then added a spoonful of baking soda. At once the mixture hissed and foamed up over the rim and onto the table. His little sister Ama jumped back and laughed. Kofi wiped the table with a cloth and explained what his teacher had said: when the two things meet, they make a gas, and the gas makes the bubbles. Ama wanted to try, so he gave her a smaller bowl and showed her how to add the soda slowly. This time the foam stayed inside the bowl, and she clapped her hands.

How did Ama feel when the foam first rose over the rim?
She was surprised and amused. She jumped back, but she also laughed, and then she wanted to try it herself.

The first umbrella in Dhruv's village was owned by the postman, and it was black, large and very old. When the monsoon came, children followed him along the lane just to stand under its edge. One day a strong wind turned the umbrella inside out and bent two of its metal ribs. The postman was sad, but a tailor named Salma offered to fix it. She sewed a new cloth cover and straightened the ribs with a pair of pliers. The next morning the postman walked through the rain with the umbrella open again, and a line of small children walked behind him.

Who repaired the postman's umbrella?
A tailor named Salma repaired it.

When Leila lifted the lid of the old rice tin, she found a thin line of ants carrying tiny white grains across the shelf. She followed them with her eyes and saw that they all went into a crack in the wall behind the cupboard. Her mother wanted to wash the shelf at once, but Leila asked her to wait a day. She put a small saucer of sugar a little way from the crack. By the evening a much bigger crowd of ants was around the saucer, and none of them went near the rice tin. Leila smiled, pleased with her small experiment.

What did Leila learn from putting out the saucer of sugar?
She learned that the ants would go to the sugar instead of the rice tin, since the crowd gathered around the saucer and left the rice alone.

Mr. Okafor took his class to the school field at five o'clock on the morning of the lunar eclipse. The sky was dark and the air was cool. Each child carried a blanket and a notebook. They lay on their backs and looked up at the moon, which was big and bright at first. Slowly a shadow crept across it from one side until the moon turned a deep orange-red. Mr. Okafor said that the shadow was made by the earth, standing between the sun and the moon. The class stayed silent for several minutes, and then Chidi whispered that the moon looked like a copper coin.

At what time did the class go to the school field?
They went at five o'clock in the morning.

Before she had a bicycle bell, Anjali used to shout "Excuse me!" to people on the narrow road to the market. Often they did not hear her, and once she almost hit a man carrying eggs. That evening she took a spoon and an old steel cup from the kitchen. She tied the cup upside down to the handlebar and hung the spoon from a string so that it would tap against it when she pressed a lever she had made from a clothes peg. The next day the little clang rang out clearly, and the man with the eggs stepped aside and waved.

Why did Anjali make a bell for her bicycle?
Because people on the narrow road did not hear her shouting, and she had almost hit a man carrying eggs.

Dr. Haldar was cleaning her old microscope slides when she noticed that one of them had a patch of blue-green mould growing on the glass. Around the patch, the small dots she had placed there earlier, which were bacteria, had vanished. She looked at it for a long time and then called her assistant to take a photograph. They wrote a note in the log book with the date, the shelf number and a drawing of the slide. Later that week they began to grow the same mould in dishes to see whether it would clear the bacteria again.

What did Dr. Haldar notice on the old slide?
She noticed a patch of blue-green mould, with the bacteria gone from the area around it.

A stray dog named Bholu used to sleep beside the tea stall at the corner of Station Road. When the stall owner, Mr. Kapoor, opened his shutter at dawn, Bholu would stand and wag his tail until he got a biscuit. One monsoon morning the shutter did not open. Bholu waited for a long time, whined, and then trotted down the road. He came back with Mr. Kapoor's neighbour, pulling at her sari with his teeth. She found Mr. Kapoor lying on his kitchen floor with a twisted ankle and helped him to a doctor. Afterwards, Bholu got a whole packet of biscuits.

What does Bholu's behaviour show about him?
It shows he was smart and loyal. He noticed something was wrong when the shutter stayed closed, and he fetched help.

Ishaan's project for the science fair was a small lemon battery. He pushed a copper coin into one side of each of three lemons and a zinc nail into the other, and then joined them in a row with thin wires to a tiny light. The class waited. The light gave a faint red glow. The judges leaned closer, and one of them asked him to explain. Ishaan said that the two different metals and the lemon juice together make a small electric current. He had also tried an orange and a potato, and he showed the judges a chart of how brightly each one lit the light.

What did Ishaan push into the lemon?
He pushed a copper coin into one side of each lemon and a zinc nail into the other.

Grandfather Ramu kept his matchboxes on a high shelf because the damp kitchen made them go soft. Still, every monsoon, half of them would not light. His granddaughter Tara noticed that the salt jar never got wet because it had a tight lid. She found an old glass jam jar with a screw lid, filled it with matchboxes and closed it firmly. A week later she opened it and struck a match, and it lit at once. Her grandfather stared, then fetched three more jars from the pantry and told her to help him pack all the rest.

Why did Grandfather Ramu fetch more jars?
Because Tara's jar kept the matches dry and they lit, so he wanted to store all the other matchboxes the same way.

An elephant calf at the sanctuary near Coorg stepped into a muddy ditch and could not climb out. It trumpeted loudly, and the older females gathered at the edge. Two of them knelt and pushed against the calf's back with their heads, while another reached down with her trunk and tugged at its ear. The keepers watched from a distance with a rope ready, but they did not need it. After ten minutes of pushing and pulling, the calf scrambled up the bank. It was covered in mud from head to foot, and the herd led it to the river to wash.

Where did the herd take the calf after it climbed out?
They led it to the river to wash.

Sam left a metal spoon in a cup of hot tea while he went to answer the phone. When he came back, the handle of the spoon felt hot and he pulled his hand away quickly. He tried a wooden spoon next, and its handle stayed cool. His mother told him that metal carries heat along itself very well, while wood does not. Sam put the metal spoon on a plate and used the wooden one to stir. The next day he told his friends at school, and one of them brought a plastic spoon to test it too.

Why did Sam's metal spoon handle feel hot?
Because metal carries heat well, so the heat from the hot tea travelled up the spoon to the handle.

Drying red chillies on his roof in Rajasthan, a man was busy with the harvest when a sudden shower began. He rushed to cover them with a sheet, but several fell into a clay pot of pickled mangoes that stood nearby. Weeks later, when he opened the pot, the pickle was hotter and smelled richer than any he had made before. His wife tasted it and said it was wonderful. From that year, they added a handful of dried red chillies to every batch, and relatives began to order jars from the next village.

How did the man find out that chillies improved the pickle?
By accident. Some chillies fell into the pot during a shower, and when he opened it weeks later the pickle tasted hotter and richer.

The crows near Lalitha's apartment block in Chennai had learned that the water tank on the roof leaked a little every afternoon. At about three o'clock they would gather by the drip and take turns drinking. One day Lalitha put a wide bowl under the leak. The crows hesitated, hopping around the edge and tilting their heads. Then the oldest crow, one with a torn feather, stepped forward and drank. The others followed. After that, the bowl was never empty on hot afternoons, because Lalitha refilled it from a bucket every time she saw it low.

What does the old crow's action show?
It shows that the old crow was the bravest or most trusting one. It drank first from the new bowl, and the others copied it.

During a power cut, Ben lit a candle and placed it on the dining table. He noticed that the flame moved upward and that a little black smoke curled from its tip. His sister Nora put a glass jar over the candle, and within seconds the flame grew small and went out. Ben lit it again and this time left a gap by tilting the jar slightly with a coin. The flame stayed alive for much longer. Their uncle said that fire needs air to keep burning, and he warned them never to play with matches without a grown-up nearby.

What did Nora put over the candle?
She put a glass jar over it.

Arjun's grandmother had trouble opening the tight lids of jars because her fingers were stiff in the morning. Arjun cut a wide strip from an old bicycle tube and wrapped it round the top of a jar. When his grandmother twisted, the rubber gripped the lid and it turned with a soft pop. She was delighted and asked him to make three more strips for the kitchen. He cut them in different widths for the big pickle jar and the small spice jars. Since then she has called the strips "Arjun's helpers" and keeps them in a basket by the stove.

How did Arjun's grandmother feel about the rubber strips?
She was very pleased. She was delighted, asked for three more, and gave them a special name.

Chen noticed a spider building a web between the gate and a rose bush one windy afternoon. It first let out a long thread that drifted on the breeze until it stuck to the bush. Then it walked along that thread and added a second one below it, making a Y shape. Over about an hour, it laid spokes like those of a wheel and then wound a spiral around them. By the time the sun began to set, the web was finished and shone in the evening light. Chen did not touch it and told his father to walk around the gate.

What shape did the spider make with its first two threads?
It made a Y shape.

While washing dishes, Zoya saw that when she dropped a little oil into a bowl of water, it did not mix. It stayed in round, shiny drops on the top. She added a drop of dish soap, and the oil slowly broke into smaller bits and spread out. She called her brother to watch. Together they tried shaking the bowl, and the oil mixed even more. Their mother said this was why soap helps to clean greasy plates. Zoya thought about all the times she had scrubbed pans without knowing why the soap worked so much better than water alone.

What does this event show about soap?
It shows that soap breaks oil into small bits so it can mix with water, which is why it cleans greasy plates better than water alone.

Marta was digging a small vegetable bed when her spade turned up a flat grey stone with a perfect round hole in the middle. She rinsed it under the tap and showed it to her teacher, who said it looked like an old fishing weight. Marta's town had no water nearby now, but her teacher explained that a lake had once stood nearby. The class marked the spot on a map and wrote a short note about the find. Marta felt proud, and she kept looking at the ground more carefully on her walk to school every morning.

What does the stone tell us about Marta's town long ago?
It suggests there was once a lake nearby, since the stone looked like an old fishing weight.

A mother duck led her ducklings across a busy road in Bengaluru early one Sunday morning. There were seven of them, all small and yellow, walking in a straight line behind her. A man on a scooter stopped and held up his hand, and soon an auto-rickshaw and a milk van stopped as well. The mother duck did not hurry. She waddled across, climbed onto the grass verge, and waited until every duckling had come through the railing gap. Then the cars slowly moved again, and the man on the scooter took off his helmet and clapped.

How many ducklings were there?
There were seven ducklings.

Siddharth held a magnifying glass over a dry leaf on a sunny day and moved it slowly until a small, bright dot of light appeared on the leaf. After a short while, a tiny wisp of smoke rose and the leaf began to turn brown at the spot. He pulled the glass away at once and stamped on the leaf. His father, who had been watching, praised him for acting quickly. He explained that the glass gathers the sunlight into one point and makes it very hot. Siddharth decided to use the glass only to look at insects from now on.

Why did Siddharth pull the glass away and stamp on the leaf?
Because the leaf began to smoke and burn. He knew it could start a fire, so he stopped it quickly.

The first wheelbarrow at Farmer Selvam's field was a wooden box on two uneven wheels. It wobbled badly, and the load of sugarcane often fell off. His daughter Janani, who liked to draw, sketched a new design. She drew just one wheel at the front and made the handles longer and straighter. The village carpenter built it in two days from her drawing. When Selvam loaded it with cane and walked across the field, the barrow rolled smoothly and did not tip. He hugged Janani and said he would buy her a set of paints with the first money from the harvest.

What did Selvam promise to buy Janani?
He promised her a set of paints, bought with the first money from the harvest.

When Pablo's grandfather washed a new red shirt together with his white ones, everything came out pink. He was upset, but he noticed that the pink was gentle and rather pretty. His wife, Lucia, suggested washing the red shirt on its own in cold water until the rinse water ran clear. It took three washes, but after that the shirt went in with the white ones and nothing turned pink. Lucia wrote a note for the neighbours explaining the trick. The following weekend three families washed their new dark clothes on their own first.

What did the family find out about washing new red clothes?
They found that washing the new shirt alone in cold water until the water ran clear stopped its colour running into other clothes.

At the farm, the buffalo calf would not stop crying every night after the herd came home. Farmer Gulab felt sure that something was wrong, but the vet found nothing. His wife suggested that the calf was lonely because its mother slept at the far end of the shed. They moved the calf's straw bed next to the mother's. That night the calf made a few soft sounds, pressed against its mother's side and soon fell asleep. The shed was quiet until the cock crowed in the morning. Gulab laughed and said that even animals need to sleep next to someone they love.

Why did the calf stop crying?
Because it was moved beside its mother, so it was no longer lonely and could sleep close to her.

On Tuesday, Mr. Alvarez placed a single bean seed between a damp paper towel and the wall of a clear plastic cup. By Thursday the seed had split open, and a pale root was pointing downward. On Saturday a small green shoot appeared at the top and bent toward the window. The students wrote the date and drew the seed in their science books each time. They learned that the root always grew down and the shoot always grew up and toward the light. On Monday morning, they planted it in a pot and set it on the sill.

On which day did the green shoot appear?
It appeared on Saturday.

Hamid kept dropping his pencil when he drew in bed because it rolled off the slanted board. One day he stuck a strip of old chewing gum, dried and stiff, along the lower edge of the board. The pencil stopped against it and stayed. His brother Yusuf thought it was messy, so he suggested bending a thin strip of cardboard instead and taping it. It worked just as well and looked better. Soon both boys had a small ledge on their drawing boards, and the floor of the room was never covered in pencils again.

Why did Yusuf suggest cardboard instead of gum?
Because he thought the gum was messy, and a cardboard strip would work as well and look neater.

The old well in Ratna's village had a strange green stain on its stones that kept growing every summer. The village elder said it was moss, and children were told not to lean over it. One day a visiting scientist took a small bit of the green growth in a jar and looked at it through a microscope. She said it was algae, which makes its own food from sunlight, and that it grew only because the well was open to the sky. She suggested covering half of the well with a board. By the next summer the stain had shrunk to a thin line.

What did the scientist say the green growth was?
She said it was algae.

Biscuit, a small brown pony, lived at a riding school in Ooty. Whenever a new child arrived, Biscuit would walk slowly and stop at every puddle to look at its own reflection. Instructors found that nervous children laughed at this and forgot their fear. One shy boy, Imran, came for his first lesson and gripped the reins hard. When Biscuit paused at the first puddle and bent its head, Imran giggled out loud. By the end of the hour he was sitting up straight and asking if he could come again the next week.

How did Imran's mood change during the lesson?
He began nervous and shy, but he giggled at Biscuit and by the end he felt confident enough to ask for another lesson.

Everyone in the building complained about the squeaky lift door, and the caretaker, Mr. Dsouza, was tired of the noise. He had tried oil, but the squeak came back. One afternoon, he noticed a thin line of dust packed into the track at the bottom. He cleaned it with a thin stick and a wet cloth before putting just a drop of oil. The door slid without a sound. The residents noticed it the next morning, and a small group stopped to thank him. Mr. Dsouza smiled and said the trick was patience, not more oil.

What did Mr. Dsouza mean by saying the trick was patience?
He meant that cleaning the dust carefully from the track, not just adding more oil, was what fixed the squeak.

A girl named Pooja was making tea when she dropped a pinch of dried tulsi leaves into the hot water by mistake. She was about to throw it out, but the smell was fresh and pleasant, so she tasted a little. It was mild and slightly peppery. She made a cup for her grandmother, who said it reminded her of her own childhood and that tulsi tea was often given in winter in her village. Pooja wrote down the recipe on the back of a calendar page and stuck it on the fridge door so everyone could try it.

Where did Pooja write the recipe?
She wrote it on the back of a calendar page and stuck it on the fridge door.

For three nights, a small owl hooted from the neem tree in front of Rohan's house. On the fourth morning, he found a pile of tiny bones and fur at the foot of the tree. His uncle showed him that it was a pellet, which owls cough up after eating mice. Rohan broke it open carefully with a stick and found the skull of a mouse inside. He took a photograph and drew the bones on paper. Afterwards, he noticed that fewer mice came into the grain store by the gate, and he understood that the owl was helping his family.

Why did Rohan think the owl was helping his family?
Because fewer mice were coming into the grain store after the owl began hunting near the house.

At home, a boy named Dylan filled a plastic bottle to the top with water and put it in the freezer. The next morning, he found that the bottle had swollen and its sides were bulging. He took it out and put it on the table. His father said the water turns bigger when it freezes, which is why a full bottle can crack. Dylan wrapped a towel around the bottle and put it back on a tray. That afternoon he and his friends watched the ice melt slowly and fill the tray with water.

What had happened to the bottle after a night in the freezer?
It had swollen, and its sides were bulging.

A fisherman named Anand had trouble keeping his lantern lit on the boat because the wind blew out the flame. One evening, his young daughter Devi cut the bottom off a glass bottle and slid the neck over the wick, making a chimney. The flame stood tall and steady, even when the wind gusted. Anand tied the lantern to the mast and fished late into the night. In the morning, he brought home a full basket and a big smile for Devi. He gave her the first and finest fish for supper.

Why did Anand give Devi the first and finest fish?
He was grateful to her. Her bottle chimney kept the lantern lit, which let him fish late and bring home a full basket.

A scientist visiting a hill station from far away left a bowl of milk uncovered in a cool pantry by mistake over a long weekend. When she returned, the milk had thickened into a soft, creamy mass with a mild sour smell. She was about to throw it away, but one of the cooks taught her it was just curd, which people in the region had made for centuries. She tasted it, and it was smooth. Then she carried a spoonful to the lab and looked at it under the microscope to see the bacteria that had done the work.

What had the milk turned into?
It had turned into curd, a soft, creamy mass with a mild sour smell.

When Zara cycled past the field every day, a flock of green parrots was always perched on the same wire. One day, a boy flew a kite so close that the parrots all burst into the air, screeching. Zara stopped to watch them circle over the field and settle again, a little further down the wire. The boy lowered his kite and looked ashamed. He said sorry to Zara even though she was not the one he had disturbed. After that, he flew his kite on the other side of the field, well away from the wire.

How did the boy feel after the parrots flew off?
He felt ashamed, because he lowered his kite and said sorry, then moved to the other side of the field.

At the school pond, Meena dipped a clear jar into the water and held it up to the sun. Inside the jar, dozens of tiny creatures twitched and darted. Her teacher Mr. George handed out hand lenses and asked the group to count how many kinds they could find. They found round ones, long ones, and some with little tails. Meena drew each one on a page, with a short name she made up, such as "wiggler" and "spinner." Back in the classroom, they looked at a drop under the microscope and talked about what the animals might eat.

What did Meena name the creatures she drew?
She gave them short names she made up, like wiggler and spinner.

Sanjay hated waiting for his hot soup to cool, and he often burned his tongue. One evening he poured a little into a wide plate instead of the deep bowl. His mother noticed that the soup in the plate was cool enough to sip in a minute or two. Sanjay learned that more of the soup touches the air in a wide plate, so the heat escapes faster. He began using a plate for his dinner soup and a bowl for his breakfast porridge, which he liked to keep warm for longer. His sister called him the soup scientist.

Why did the soup cool faster in the plate?
Because more of it touched the air in the wide plate, so the heat escaped faster.

Layla was clearing out an old cupboard in her grandmother's house in Cairo when she found a small brass compass. The needle was stuck, but when she tapped it gently, it swung and pointed firmly in one direction. Her grandmother told her that her own father had carried it on his journeys along the river. Layla took it to the roof and found that the needle pointed toward the old minaret. She compared it with a map and saw that this was north. For the rest of the week, she carried the compass in her pocket on every walk.

Where did Layla find the compass?
She found it in an old cupboard in her grandmother's house in Cairo.

Farmers in the village of Nandur saw that their goats became restless a few minutes before the ground shook slightly one afternoon. Two weeks later, it happened again. The goats stopped eating, bleated and ran toward the open ground just before a small tremor. An old shepherd, Vikram, said he had seen this happen before. The village council asked a geologist to visit and look at the area. She told them that animals may sense small vibrations before people do, but that no one can use it to predict an earthquake. The council still decided to keep an eye on the goats.

Why did the council decide to keep an eye on the goats?
Because the goats seemed to sense tremors before people did, and the village found that useful, even though it cannot predict an earthquake.

Rukmini walked to the river each morning to fill her brass pots, and she often saw a kingfisher sitting on a bamboo pole over the water. The bird was small and bright blue, with an orange chest. It stared at the water without moving, then dived and came up with a fish before she could blink. One morning the pole was empty, and so was the next. On the third day Rukmini found the bird on a different pole, much closer to the bank. She learned later that the river had risen overnight, and the old pole stood too deep in the water.

What colour was the kingfisher's chest?
Its chest was orange.

Tomas set up a small bird feeder outside his window in Lisbon and filled it with sunflower seeds. For two days no bird came. On the third day a single sparrow landed on the edge, looked around, ate one seed and flew away. Tomas stayed very still behind the curtain. By the end of the week, a dozen sparrows were visiting at every hour. He noticed that they never fed all at once. One always stood on the railing, looking left and right, while the others ate, and then they swapped places.

Why did one sparrow always stand on the railing while the others ate?
It acted as a lookout, watching for danger so the others could eat safely, and then they swapped places.

The kitchen scale in Mrs. Thomas's house was old and its pointer always shook before it settled. Her grandson Jacob thought he could do better. He took a small spring from a broken pen, a flat tin lid and a ruler. He fixed the spring to a stand, placed the lid on top and marked the ruler where the spring stopped when different things sat on it. After a week of tests with bags of rice and sugar, his scale gave the same marks each time. Mrs. Thomas called it "Jacob's scale" and kept it beside the stove.

What did Jacob use to make his scale?
He used a spring from a broken pen, a flat tin lid and a ruler.

A girl named Amrita watched a snail cross the garden path after the rain. It left a thin, shiny trail behind it. Amrita put a pinch of dry ash in front of it to see what it would do. The snail stopped, waved its two long feelers and then turned sharply to the left, going around the ash. She tried again with a small twig, and the snail simply climbed over it. Amrita wrote in her diary that snails do not like dry, dusty places and that they are good climbers.

What did the snail do when it met the ash?
It stopped, waved its feelers and turned left to go around the ash.

The telescope that Mr. Gill built was made from two lenses and a cardboard tube from a roll of wrapping paper. He taped the lenses at each end and painted the inside of the tube black. On the first clear night, he took it to the roof and pointed it at the moon. The craters stood out sharply, and the edge of the shadow looked jagged. His neighbours queued on the stairs to take a turn. A small girl who looked last said nothing for a full minute and then asked if she could come back every night.

What does the little girl's reaction show?
It shows she was amazed and fascinated. She stayed silent for a minute and then wanted to come back every night.

While planting beans, Haruki accidentally dropped some seeds into a tray with a wet sponge instead of soil. He forgot about them. After four days, he found long white roots poking out of the sponge, and green leaves already opening. He took out a ruler and measured the tallest root. Then he planted the sponge, seeds and all, in a pot of soil on the balcony. A week later the plants were twice as tall as the ones his friend had planted straight in the soil. Haruki now starts all his seeds on a sponge first.

Where did Haruki plant the sponge in the end?
He planted it in a pot of soil on the balcony.

Dilip was in the kitchen when the milk began to boil over, so he grabbed a wooden spoon and laid it across the top of the pan. The foam sank back down at once. He told his aunt, who said she had heard about the trick but never tried it. She tested it with the next pan. This time the milk simmered quietly for a long while without spilling. Dilip explained that the wood is cooler than the metal rim and breaks the bubbles as they touch it. His aunt put the spoon in a special place on the stove for next time.

Why did the milk stop boiling over?
Because the wooden spoon across the pan was cooler than the metal and broke the bubbles as they reached it.

When the clouds turned dark one afternoon, a group of cows in Anil's field began to lie down on the grass. Anil's grandfather looked up and said it would rain soon, because cows often lie down before a storm. The boys laughed and went on playing cricket. Within twenty minutes, thick drops started falling, and the boys ran for the shed. They were soaked by the time they reached it. Grandfather smiled from the doorway with a dry towel in his hands, and nobody laughed at him again that day.

What did the cows do before the rain?
They lay down on the grass.

The village of Kothur had no clock, so Chandra's father woke each morning when the cock crowed. One day the cock fell silent and the family overslept, missing the early bus to the market. Chandra took an old tin bowl, filled it with water and made a small hole at the bottom. She marked the sides with a knife where the water level fell after each hour, using the school bell to check. The next morning she woke before dawn to check the bowl and called the family. They caught the bus with time to spare.

Why did Chandra make a water clock?
Because the cock stopped crowing and the family overslept and missed the bus, so she needed another way to tell the time.

Dr. Okonkwo walked along the beach at low tide with a bucket and a notebook. Among the rocks, she found a pool full of small creatures: crabs, anemones and tiny striped fish. She sat beside it for an hour and counted them. When the tide began to creep back, the water rose into the pool, and the fish scattered into the wider sea. Dr. Okonkwo noted the time on her watch and checked it against the tide table. The next week she brought her students to see the pool and showed them how to measure its size with a rope.

What did Dr. Okonkwo count at the rock pool?
She counted the small creatures in it, such as crabs, anemones and tiny striped fish.

Ritu's grandmother had a habit of putting an apple in the same bag as the green bananas to make them ripen. Ritu did not believe it, so she set up a test with two paper bags. In one she put only a green banana, and in the other she put a banana and a ripe apple. After three days, the banana with the apple had turned yellow and soft, while the other was still firm and green. Ritu showed her results to her class. Her teacher explained that ripe fruit gives off a gas that helps other fruit to ripen.

What did Ritu's test show about ripe apples?
It showed that a ripe apple helps green bananas ripen faster, because the banana in the bag with the apple turned yellow first.

A stray kitten wandered into the school library in Nairobi on a rainy Monday. It was wet and shaking and sat under a table near the heater. The librarian, Mrs. Njoroge, gave it a saucer of water and wrapped it in an old scarf. By Wednesday, the children had named it Page. They took turns reading aloud to it during lunch. When a boy named Kamau found that he was too shy to read to his classmates, he read his book to Page instead, and soon his voice grew steady.

What did the children name the kitten?
They named it Page.

A farmer in Punjab saw that the sparrows in his wheat field kept landing on the scarecrow's hat. Instead of scaring them away, the scarecrow seemed to be a good perch. His son Harpreet suggested tying old silver sweet wrappers to the arms. The wrappers flashed and fluttered in the wind, and the sparrows kept away from the scarecrow. The wheat was left to ripen in peace. When the harvest came, the farmer weighed the grain and found that it was heavier than the previous year's. He hung a few more wrappers on the fence as well.

Why did the sparrows stay away after Harpreet's idea?
Because the shiny wrappers flashed and fluttered in the wind and frightened them off.

Nadia put an ice cube in a glass of juice and watched it for a while. Water drops formed on the outside of the glass. She wiped them off, and soon they came back. She asked her mother if the glass was leaking, but her mother showed her that the juice was still at the same level. The drops came from the air, she said, because the cold glass cools the air next to it, and the water in the air turns into small drops. Nadia drew the glass with the drops in her notebook and wrote the word "condensation" under it.

Where did the water drops on the glass come from?
They came from the air. The cold glass cooled the air next to it and the water in it turned into drops.

The paper boats that Femi made always sank after a minute because the water soaked into them. Then he remembered the wax candle on the shelf. He rubbed the candle over the paper, covering every fold, and then set the boat on the pond. This time it stayed afloat all afternoon and drifted from one side to the other. Femi's friends begged him for some wax. He shared a stub from the candle and showed each of them how to rub it thinly. By evening the pond had a small fleet of shiny paper boats.

What did Femi use to make his paper boats stay afloat?
He rubbed a wax candle over the paper.

When Gita's cat, Mishri, was only a year old, she began spending her afternoons on the window sill, staring at the street. Gita thought she was bored. One day a boy walking home from school stopped to wave at her, and Mishri meowed in reply. After that, the boy appeared at exactly the same time every day. He stopped, waved, and the cat answered him. Gita noticed that Mishri started waiting at the sill from one o'clock, though the boy came at half past two. She said the cat seemed to know when to expect him.

What does Mishri's early waiting show?
It shows the cat had learned the boy's routine and looked forward to his visit, since she began waiting well before he came.

An engineer named Mrs. Pillai was fixing a leaking pipe in her kitchen when her wrench slipped and hit the floor with a clang. She noticed that the sound was different from the clang of other tools. It was higher and lasted longer. She picked it up and saw that it was made of a different metal. Curious, she tapped each tool in the box and listed what each sounded like. Later, her son used the list to guess which metal each tool was made of, and then checked the labels. He got six right out of eight.

How many tools did her son identify correctly?
He got six out of eight right.

A beekeeper named Mr. Rao noticed that the bees at his hive were busy and loud in the early morning but quiet by noon in the heat. On a very hot day, he saw a group of bees standing at the entrance of the hive, all fanning their wings in the same direction. He put his hand near the door and felt a cool breeze coming out. He learned that the bees were moving air through the hive to keep it from getting too hot. He put a shade of palm leaves over the box that afternoon.

Why were the bees fanning their wings at the entrance?
They were moving air through the hive to keep it cool in the heat.

On Diwali night, Karan lit a small clay lamp and put it on the window sill. He noticed that the flame flickered whenever someone opened the door. He watched his baby cousin put her hand close to the lamp, and he gently pulled her back. That evening, his grandfather told him that a lamp made from clay is meant to hold oil and a cotton wick, and the clay keeps the flame safe. Karan set a second lamp on the steps, where it stayed lit all night because there was no draught. In the morning he collected the cool lamps in a tray.

Where did Karan put the second lamp?
He put it on the steps.

A man in Chile noticed that his dog always began scratching at the door a few minutes before his daughter arrived home from school. The dog never did that for anyone else. One afternoon, the man looked at his watch and found that the dog started well before the bus came into sight. He asked his neighbours, and they said their dogs did something similar when family members returned. A vet said that dogs learn the times when people come back and can hear familiar sounds a long way off. The man laughed and said the dog was a better clock than the one on the wall.

Why did the dog scratch at the door before the girl came home?
Because it had learned the time she usually came back and could hear familiar sounds from far away.

The first thermos flask that Dev's family owned was a heavy steel one that kept tea hot for a whole day. Dev wondered how it worked, so he asked his uncle, a plumber, who opened an old broken flask. Inside there were two walls with a gap between them. Almost no air was left in the gap, so little heat could pass through. His uncle said that a thin layer of silver on the inner wall also reflected heat back in. Dev made a model with two paper cups, one inside the other, and kept a cube of ice in it for two hours longer than in a single cup.

What did Dev make to copy the flask?
He made a model with two paper cups, one inside the other.

When Isha was seven, she found a smooth round pebble on the road to the temple and put it in her pocket. At home, she held it up to the light and noticed little silver sparkles inside it. Her teacher said it was granite, with bits of mica in it. Isha rubbed the pebble with a soft cloth and watched the sparkles shine brighter. Then she looked at some other stones and noticed that each had its own colour and feel. She started a collection in an egg carton, with the name of each stone and the place she found it.

What did Isha put her stones in?
She put them in an egg carton.

Neelam saw a lizard on the wall catch a moth with a flick of its tongue. It had been standing very still for a long time, and its colour was almost the same as the wall's. She came closer, and the lizard slowly edged away into the dark behind the cupboard. Her brother said lizards are scary, but Neelam said they help by eating insects. She put a small saucer of water on the floor and moved the lamp that drew the moths away from the wall. Later that evening, she saw the lizard drinking from the saucer.

What does the lizard's colour tell us about how it hunts?
It shows the lizard hides by blending into the wall, staying still and unseen until it can catch an insect.

A baby sea turtle hatched on a beach in Odisha at night. It was no bigger than a child's palm. It struggled out of the sand and began crawling toward the water, guided by the bright shine of the moon on the waves. Volunteers had put a ring of small flags around the nest to keep dogs away. They switched off their torches and watched quietly as the small turtle reached the foam and was swept into the sea. One volunteer, a girl called Sneha, wiped a tear from her eye and said it was the best night of her life.

Who put flags around the nest?
Volunteers did, to keep dogs away.

Ayesha noticed that her pot of mint grew taller when it sat on the sunny sill but turned thin and pale when she moved it behind the curtain. She asked her uncle, a gardener, what was wrong. He said that plants need light to make their food, and that without enough light, they stretch toward any glow they can find and grow weak. Ayesha moved the pot back to the sill and turned it a quarter turn each day so all sides got sunshine. Within two weeks, new dark green leaves had appeared, and the stems were stronger.

Why did the mint become thin and pale behind the curtain?
Because it did not get enough light to make its food, so it stretched toward any glow and grew weak.

On Friday afternoon, Sofia and her father carried a long plank to the park and propped one end on a low wall. They set a toy car at the top and let it roll down. Then they made the slope steeper by raising the plank, and the car rolled faster and went further. Sofia wrote down the distance for each slope with chalk marks on the path. Her father smiled and said she had just done what real scientists do. On Saturday she took her notes to school and her teacher pinned them on the board.

What did Sofia use to mark the distances?
She used chalk marks on the path.

A potter in Khurja found that his cups cracked when he baked them too quickly in the kiln. His apprentice, Zaid, suggested leaving the cups in the sun to dry for two full days before baking. The potter doubted it, but he let the boy try with six cups. All six came out perfectly whole. The potter, who was a proud man, rubbed his chin and then thanked Zaid in front of the whole workshop. From that day, he let the cups dry slowly before every baking, and the number of cracked ones dropped to almost none.

How did the potter feel about Zaid's idea in the end?
He was grateful and impressed, because he thanked Zaid in front of everyone and began drying all cups slowly.

The goats on the hillside above Lakshmi's home always went to the same spring each morning. One morning the spring was dry. The leader goat, a white female with a bell around her neck, stood sniffing the cracked ground and then turned and walked up the hill. The herd followed. Lakshmi followed them as far as she could and came to a small pool under a rock, hidden by bushes. She had never seen it before. She told her father, and the village built a low wall around it so that it would stay clean.

Who found the hidden pool first, Lakshmi or the goats?
The goats found it first. The leader goat led the herd to it and Lakshmi followed.

Yusuf was eating a peach when he dropped the stone in the garden and forgot about it. The following spring, a small green shoot came up through the soil in the same place. His mother recognised it at once as a peach sapling and moved it to a larger bed. Yusuf gave it water twice a week and kept the snails away with a ring of crushed eggshells. Four years later, the tree gave its first fruit, and he picked one with a beating heart. He said it was the sweetest peach he had ever tasted.

What did Yusuf use to keep the snails away?
He used a ring of crushed eggshells.

At night in the forest near Kaziranga, a researcher named Dr. Bora set up a camera trap beside a muddy path. The next morning, she checked the pictures. There were deer, a wild boar and a small fox. In one picture a rhino stood with her calf only a metre from the lens. Dr. Bora printed that photograph and pinned it on the wall of the field office. Visitors often stopped to look at it. She said that the camera showed her more than days of walking ever did, because the animals did not know they were being watched.

Why did the camera show Dr. Bora more than walking in the forest?
Because the animals did not know they were being watched, so they behaved naturally.

The first pair of spectacles that Hari's village ever saw belonged to the schoolmaster. They were round and heavy and slid down his nose whenever he looked at the blackboard. Hari, who liked to fix things, made two small pads from soft cloth and sewed them onto the nose bridge. The schoolmaster put them on and moved his head from side to side. The glasses did not move at all. He tapped the blackboard with his stick, and all the children cheered. He gave Hari a shiny pencil as a reward.

What did the schoolmaster give Hari?
He gave Hari a shiny pencil.

While walking home in a light drizzle, Esme saw a rainbow curve over the fields. She stopped at the gate and stared. Her older cousin said that a rainbow only appears when the sun shines from behind you while it rains in front of you. Esme turned around and saw that the sun was indeed low behind her.
