That evening she took a water spray bottle into the garden, stood with her back to the sun and sprayed a fine mist in front of her. A tiny rainbow shone in the spray for a few seconds, and she shouted for her mother to come and look.

Where was the sun when Esme saw the rainbow?
It was low behind her.

Lalan the bullock refused to pull the cart on market day. Its owner, Mr. Mishra, tugged and shouted, but the animal stood still with its head down. A passing vet looked at its feet and found a small thorn deep in one hoof. Mr. Mishra had not seen it because the bullock had walked so carefully. The vet pulled the thorn out and cleaned the spot with clean water. The bullock gave a loud snort and took a few steps, then pulled the cart with ease. Mr. Mishra rubbed its neck and said he was sorry for shouting.

Why did Mr. Mishra say sorry to the bullock?
Because the bullock had stood still due to a thorn in its hoof and not out of stubbornness, and he had shouted at it.

Linh left a wet towel on the bathroom floor for a few days, and soon a tiny white fuzz had started to grow on one corner. She told her mother, who said it was mould. It grows where things stay damp and warm, and it spreads by tiny spores that float in the air. Linh hung the towel in the sun and washed the floor with soap. She also opened the bathroom window every day after her bath. After two weeks there was no more fuzz, and the towel smelled fresh. Linh promised never to leave it on the floor again.

Where does mould grow, according to Linh's mother?
It grows where things stay damp and warm.

A boy named Eli kept a jar of ants in the classroom to learn how they dig. After two days, the ants had built long, winding tunnels along the glass. The children watched in wonder. Mrs. Sharma told them that the ants shared the work: some dug, some carried dirt, and some took care of the eggs. On Friday, the class took the jar outside and tipped the ants gently onto a flower bed. Eli said he felt sad to say goodbye, but Mrs. Sharma said that ants are happier in a garden than in a jar, and he nodded.

Why did the class set the ants free?
Because Mrs. Sharma said that ants are happier in a garden than in a jar.

It was Grandmother Sara's idea to save the water that came out of the rice-washing bowl. She poured it onto the roots of the tomato plants instead of throwing it away. Her grandson Omar was not sure it was a good idea, but within three weeks the tomatoes on her plants were bigger and redder than those on the neighbour's. Omar asked a teacher at school, who said the water holds small bits of starch and minerals that plants can use. Omar then began to collect the water from the vegetable washing too, and he kept it in a bucket by the back door.

What did Grandmother Sara pour onto the tomato plants?
She poured the water used to wash rice onto the roots.

The new swing in the park squeaked terribly. Children covered their ears every time it moved. A girl named Tamsin noticed that the sound came from the metal hook where the chain went through. She asked the park keeper for a drop of oil, and he gave her a small can with a thin spout. Tamsin put two drops on each hook and pushed the swing. It glided without a sound. The park keeper laughed and asked if she wanted a job. She said she would think about it, but only if he gave her free swings in the evenings.

How did the park keeper react to Tamsin's fix?
He was impressed and amused. He laughed and joked about offering her a job.

Mr. Kamath was cleaning the attic in Udupi when he found a bundle of old letters tied with string. Each one had a stamp and a postmark from a different city. He carefully sorted them by date and found that the oldest came from 1950. His daughter helped him read the faded handwriting. The letters were from his own grandfather, who had worked on a ship and written to his wife each month. Mr. Kamath took them to a shop and had them placed in clear sleeves. He hung two of them on the wall of the hall.

Who wrote the old letters?
They were written by Mr. Kamath's grandfather, who worked on a ship.

A crow in the courtyard of Bhaskar's school kept dropping walnuts onto the road. At first, Bhaskar thought it was careless. Then he saw that the crow waited at the edge of the zebra crossing until the traffic light turned red. The cars stopped, and the crow hopped onto the road, picked up the cracked nuts and flew back to the tree. Bhaskar told his teacher, who said that crows use passing cars to crack nuts that are too hard for their beaks. The whole class went out at lunchtime to watch the clever bird at work.

Why did the crow drop the walnuts on the road?
It used passing cars to crack the nuts, which were too hard for its beak.

On a chilly morning in Shimla, Pema noticed that her breath made small white clouds in the air. She breathed out slowly, again and again, and then tried to blow a cloud onto the cold window. A patch of mist appeared on the glass. Her father said the warm, wet air from her mouth cooled quickly in the cold, and the water in it turned into tiny drops. Pema used her finger to draw a smiling face in the mist, and then watched as it faded back into clear glass when the room grew warm.

What did Pema draw in the mist on the window?
She drew a smiling face.

In her grandmother's village, Kiran saw women wash their clothes on flat stones by the river. The clothes took a long time to dry on the grass, and some blew away in the wind. Kiran took a long rope and tied it between two trees. She then used wooden clothes pegs from the kitchen to hold each piece on the line. The clothes dried faster in the breeze, and nothing blew away. The women stopped to look, and within a week, ropes were stretched between trees all along the riverbank. Kiran grinned and said it had been her best idea of the summer.

What did the women do after seeing Kiran's rope?
They stretched ropes between trees all along the riverbank, copying her idea.

A beaver in the pond near Elsa's cabin in Canada spent every night dragging branches to the same spot at the edge of the water. In the morning, a small wall of sticks and mud rose higher than the day before. After a week, the water behind the wall had grown deep and still, and a round lodge of sticks stood in the middle of it. Elsa's grandfather said that beavers build dams to make deep water, and the lodge is safe from wolves because the door is under the surface. Elsa counted the branches in the wall and gave up at two hundred.

Why does the beaver's lodge have its door under the water?
So that wolves and other enemies cannot easily get in, which keeps the beavers safe.

When Tarun poured hot water into a glass jar that he had just rinsed under the cold tap, the jar cracked loudly. His mother cleaned up the pieces and warned him to be careful. She said that glass expands quickly where it is hot, but the cold part stays small, so it breaks. The next time, Tarun warmed the jar slowly with a little warm water first, then poured in more. The jar did not crack. He told his friend at school, who did not believe him until Tarun showed her at lunchtime with a spare jar from his bag.

Why did the jar crack the first time?
Because the hot water made one part of the glass expand while the other part stayed cold and small.

Ashok needed to keep his school notebooks dry on the long walk through monsoon rain. His plastic bag had a hole, and the books got wet. On the road he passed a man selling vegetables who had wrapped his onions in a large banana leaf. Ashok bought one leaf for two rupees and wrapped his books in it, tying it with a string. At school, the books were dry and flat. The teacher admired the idea and asked him to show the class. Soon half the children in his lane carried leaf-wrapped books in the rainy season.

What did Ashok wrap his books in?
He wrapped them in a large banana leaf.

Children in Kolkata noticed that every evening at dusk, hundreds of bats flew out from the old banyan tree by the temple. They flapped across the sky in a long, dark line. One boy, Debu, wondered where they went. His teacher told them that bats feed at night on fruits and insects and return before dawn. The next evening the children followed the line on bicycles until they reached an orchard of ripe guavas. They sat quietly at the edge, watching the bats swoop down. One girl whispered that the bats looked like a river in the sky.

Where did the bats go in the evening?
They flew to an orchard of ripe guavas to feed.

A girl named Vera was frying an egg on a hot pan when she noticed that a drop of water that fell into the oil jumped around and spat. She jumped back, and the oil spat again. Her uncle turned off the flame and told her that water sinks under hot oil and turns to steam suddenly, which pushes the oil out. Vera dried the pan completely before using it again. After that, she wiped every vegetable well before frying it, and she stood a little further away from the stove, holding a lid like a shield.

Why did Vera begin to wipe vegetables dry before frying them?
Because she learned that water in hot oil turns to steam and makes the oil spit, which can be dangerous.

Wei's grandfather had a small rice farm near a stream, and every year the frogs began to sing in the paddy a few nights before the rains. Wei used to hear them from his bed. One night, the frogs were silent, and Wei lay awake wondering if they had left. By morning, the sky was grey and a gentle drizzle had started. His grandfather said the frogs knew the rains were close, and they had stopped singing because the air had changed. The next night, the whole paddy filled with their croaking again.

What did the silence of the frogs mean for Wei's grandfather?
He took it to mean the rain was coming, because the frogs stopped singing when the air changed just before the drizzle.

The balloon in Pritha's hand rubbed against her woollen sweater and, when she held it near her hair, her hair stood up and followed it. She giggled and showed her little brother, who held out his hand to touch the balloon. His hair stood up too. Their mother told them that rubbing gave the balloon a tiny charge, like a small spark that does not hurt. Pritha stuck the balloon on the wall, where it stayed without falling for the whole evening. At bedtime, she peeled it off and put it carefully on a shelf for another day.

What happened to Pritha's hair when the balloon came close?
Her hair stood up and followed the balloon.

A fisherman's son, Joseph, loved to sit beside the tidal river and watch the crabs scuttle on the mud. They all walked sideways with one claw held high. He noticed that some had one claw much larger than the other and that those crabs waved the large claw in the air. Joseph's uncle told him that these were male fiddler crabs, and they wave to attract a mate or to scare away other males. Joseph tried waving his arm at the crabs. They backed away into their holes, and Joseph laughed so much that he nearly fell off the log.

Why do male fiddler crabs wave their big claw?
They wave it to attract a mate or to scare away other males.

The first time Ivan saw a tiny seed stuck to his sock after a walk in the field, he thought it was a bit of dirt. His grandmother pointed out the little hooks on its surface. She said seeds like that hang on to animals' fur and travel far away before dropping. Ivan examined it under a magnifying glass and saw that the hooks were curved like fish hooks. He later learned that this was the idea behind the hook-and-loop fastener on his shoes. He pressed the fastener and felt how it gripped, then drew a picture of a seed beside it.

What invention did the hooks on the seed remind Ivan of?
They reminded him of the hook-and-loop fastener on his shoes.

A heavy load of bricks needed to go up to the roof of the new school building in Jaipur, and the masons were tired of carrying them up the ladder one by one. A mason named Pappu tied a rope over a wheel fixed to a beam. He fastened a basket to one end of the rope and pulled the other end from the ground. The basket rose smoothly with twenty bricks in it. By the end of the day, the masons had saved hours of work, and they took an early tea break. The foreman patted Pappu on the back and said he had earned a day's extra pay.

Why did the foreman want to reward Pappu?
Because Pappu's rope and wheel saved the masons hours of hard work carrying bricks.

A cuckoo lays its eggs in the nests of other birds. In the garden of Mrs. Lobo, a small brown bird called a babbler had built a nest in the hedge. One morning, the children saw a large baby bird, much bigger than the babbler, sitting in the nest and opening its beak wide. The tiny babbler parents hurried back and forth with insects, working all day to feed it. The children watched the nest for a week until the young cuckoo flew away. Mrs. Lobo said the babblers had been very hard-working foster parents.

Whose nest did the young cuckoo grow up in?
It grew up in a babbler's nest in Mrs. Lobo's hedge.

When Mehmet's family moved to a flat in Istanbul, he found that his basil plant on the balcony drooped every afternoon, even though he watered it in the morning. He moved it into the shade of a larger pot, and it perked up. Then he realised that the afternoon sun on that side was very strong and dried the soil quickly. He started watering it in the early evening as well. The plant grew thick and green. Mehmet kept a small notebook for his plants, with notes on what each one liked, and he was proud of the long list of tips.

What did Mehmet decide to do once he understood the afternoon sun?
He decided to water it in the early evening as well, because the strong sun dried the soil quickly.

One summer afternoon in Karachi, Saira's grandfather asked her to put two cloths on the roof: one dry and one wet. After an hour, the wet cloth was cooler to touch, though the sun had been on both. He asked her why. She guessed that water must be cold. He shook his head, and said that when water dries into the air it takes some heat from the cloth. He then draped a wet cloth over the clay pot of drinking water. By evening, the water inside was pleasantly cool, and Saira drank three glasses.

Why was the wet cloth cooler than the dry one?
Because as the water dried into the air, it took heat away from the cloth.

A fox cub in the hills near Dehradun came to the edge of the camp one evening, and the campers noticed that it limped. One of them, a girl named Ritika, saw a thin wire wound around its paw. She called the ranger, who arrived with a blanket and gloves. Together, they held the cub gently while he cut the wire. The cub shook its paw, gave a short bark and ran into the bushes. Ritika sat for a long time looking at the dark trees. The ranger told her she had a good eye for noticing small things.

What was wrong with the fox cub's paw?
A thin wire was wound around it.

Zubin was making a kite for the festival in Ahmedabad but could not find glue. He looked in the kitchen and found a bowl of cooked rice left over from lunch. He mashed it into a paste and used it to stick the paper onto the thin bamboo frame. When it dried, the paper was firmly stuck. The kite flew high above the rooftops all afternoon. Zubin's friend asked how he had fixed the paper so well, and he said it was rice. His friend laughed and said he would try it the next day.

What does Zubin's use of rice show about him?
It shows he was resourceful. He used what was in the kitchen to solve a problem when he had no glue.

In the paddy field near her home, Latha spotted a small bird standing on the back of a buffalo. Each time the buffalo moved, the bird hopped along, picking at the insects the animal's feet stirred up. The buffalo did not seem to mind at all. Sometimes the bird pecked at its back, and the buffalo flicked its ear but stayed calm. Latha's mother said that these birds, the egrets, follow cattle everywhere. Latha thought of them as friends who helped each other, because the buffalo got rid of pests and the bird got a meal.

How did Latha think the buffalo and the egret helped each other?
The egret ate the insects that bothered the buffalo, and the buffalo's walking stirred up food for the bird.

While brushing his teeth, Nikhil spilled a few drops of toothpaste on the mirror. Later, he saw that the spots had dried into hard white dots. He wiped them off, but they left faint marks. His father said that toothpaste contains tiny grains that clean teeth by rubbing, and these grains can leave dull marks on glass too. Nikhil cleaned the mirror with a soft cloth and plain water, then rinsed his brush more carefully. He made a small sign for the bathroom wall that read "Wipe drops at once!" and stuck it above the basin.

What did Nikhil write on his sign?
He wrote "Wipe drops at once!"

A group of geese flying in a V shape passed over the field near Sunita's school. They honked loudly as they went. Sunita counted twelve of them. Her teacher explained that the bird at the front breaks the wind for those behind it and that they take turns leading. When one grows tired, it drops back, and another moves to the front. Sunita made a V-shape with her hands and tried to flap along, and the rest of the class joined in. From then on, whenever geese flew overhead, the class stopped to watch and cheer them on.

Why do the geese take turns leading the V?
Because the front goose has the hardest work breaking the wind, so they swap when one gets tired.

After a rainstorm, Daniel noticed a wide band of worms on the pavement in front of his house in Kampala. He carefully picked up a few and put them on the soil by the hedge. His sister asked why he bothered. Daniel said that worms often come up when the ground is soaked with rain, and they cannot get back to the soil when they cross a hard surface. They dry out in the sun. His sister helped, and they saved about thirty. In the evening, a thrush hopped down to the soil, and Daniel decided it was a fair bargain.

Why did worms come out onto the pavement?
Because the ground was soaked with rain.

Doctor Chaudhary held a small rubber hammer and tapped Rahul's knee, just below the kneecap. His leg kicked forward, though he had not meant to move it. Rahul's eyes widened. The doctor said that this quick jerk is called a reflex and that it happens without thinking, to protect the body. Then he showed Rahul how to test it on his father. When the leg of his father kicked too, Rahul laughed and tapped again and again until his father asked him to stop. The doctor smiled and put the little hammer back in the drawer.

What did Rahul do after he saw his father's leg kick?
He laughed and tapped again and again until his father asked him to stop.

A kind old man named Mr. Pinto made a bird bath out of a broken clay pot and put it under the mango tree. For a few days nobody came. Then a pair of bulbuls landed on the rim, dipped their beaks and splashed the water onto their wings. Soon, other birds arrived, from tiny sunbirds to a large mynah that scared all the others away. Mr. Pinto scooped out the muddy water each evening and put in fresh. A neighbour asked him why he took so much trouble, and he said that birds also need to be clean and cool in the heat.

What does Mr. Pinto's daily care of the bird bath show about him?
It shows he is kind and thoughtful about animals, since he cleaned the water every evening so the birds could stay clean and cool.

Lucia held a spoon under the tap and noticed that the thin stream of water bent toward the spoon and curled around its back. She tried again with the back of a bigger spoon and saw the same thing. Her father said that water likes to stick to surfaces, so it follows the curve. He asked her to hold a comb with a plastic handle, rub it on her hair and bring it near the stream. The water bent to the comb as if pulled. Lucia lifted her eyebrows and said it was like magic, but he told her it was science.

What did Lucia's father say was behind the bending of the water?
He said that water likes to stick to surfaces, so it follows their curve.

A pair of storks built a huge nest on the roof of the village school in Spain, and the headmaster worried that the weight might damage the tiles. A local engineer, Mr. Ruiz, climbed up and looked at it. He said the roof beam was strong and the nest was held by sticks woven in a tight pattern. He suggested adding a flat board to give the nest more support. The headmaster agreed. By spring, three white storks stood in the nest, and the children watched them from the playground every morning without making a noise.

Why did the headmaster agree to Mr. Mehta's suggestion?
Because Mr. Ruiz said the roof was strong, and the board would support the nest and protect the roof, so the storks could stay safely.

The old woman at the corner of the street in Hanoi had no refrigerator, but her fish stayed fresh all day. She packed each fish in a layer of cracked ice and wrapped it in wet cloth. She covered the pile with a thick sack and set it in the shade of an umbrella. Her granddaughter Mai watched her turn the fish and add more ice when needed. When Mai opened a small notebook in school, she wrote that cold keeps things fresh for longer, and she drew the ice, the cloth and the sack in a row.

What did the old woman cover the pile of fish with?
She covered it with a thick sack, in the shade of an umbrella.

When Felix first learned that a firefly's light is made without heat, he did not believe it. He caught one in a jar one evening in the garden and held it against his cheek. It glowed, but his skin felt nothing. His grandfather told him that this is called cold light, and that the insect makes it with a special chemical inside its body. Felix let the firefly go and watched it drift into the dark. He said he wished that lamps could be made in the same way, so that they would never become hot.

What did Felix wish about lamps?
He wished lamps could be made to give cold light like the firefly's, so that they would never get hot.

One winter morning in Leh, the water in Tsering's bucket was frozen on the top. He broke the ice with a spoon and filled his kettle. His aunt said that on a very cold night even tap water in the pipes can freeze, and when it freezes, it expands and can burst the pipe. So each evening, they left a tap dripping slowly. In the morning the water was still running, and the pipes were safe. Tsering was proud to be in charge of leaving the tap open and checking it as soon as he woke.

Why did the family leave a tap dripping at night?
To keep the water moving so it would not freeze and burst the pipes.

A girl named Beatriz saw an anteater at the zoo licking up ants with its long, sticky tongue. Its tongue flicked in and out faster than she could follow. She read on the board that the tongue is longer than its head and can flick about one hundred and fifty times a minute. She tried to flick her own tongue as fast as she could and gave up after ten seconds. Her brother laughed so much that the guard came to see who was making noise. They apologised and went to see the sleepy sloth instead.

What did Beatriz and her brother do after the guard came?
They apologised and went to see the sleepy sloth.

Hira noticed that her father's phone charger felt warm while it was plugged in. She asked him if it was broken. He said no, and that every electric thing makes a little heat when it works, because some of the energy turns into warmth. He told her to leave the charger on a hard shelf and not under a pillow, so the heat could escape. Hira moved it to the desk. She then felt the fan and the lamp and found that each was a little warm too. She told her friends at school that everything that works gets warm.

Why did Hira's father tell her to keep the charger on a hard shelf?
So the heat it makes could escape instead of building up under a soft thing like a pillow.

In a hill village in Nepal, a man carried loads of firewood on his back down a steep slope every day. His son, Dawa, watched him struggle. Dawa set up a long steel wire from the top of the slope to a tree at the bottom, and hung a pulley with a basket on it. His father put in the wood at the top, and the basket slid down by itself. At the bottom, a boy took the wood out. In a week, the work that once took a whole morning was done before breakfast.

How did Dawa's invention change his father's work?
It made the work much quicker and easier, because the basket carried the wood down by itself.

A tiny hummingbird visited Camila's garden in Bogota at the same time each morning. It hovered by the red flowers, its wings a blur, and dipped its long beak into each one. Camila counted that it visited thirty flowers in five minutes. When she put out a bottle of sugar water with a red cap, the bird drank from it in less than a minute and then came back every day. She wrote the times in her notebook. After a month, she noticed that the bird arrived two minutes earlier than at the start.

What colour was the cap on the bottle of sugar water?
It was red.

In Mrs. Iyer's class, the students placed an old coin in a cup of vinegar with a pinch of salt. After an hour, the coin was shiny and clean. Mrs. Iyer said that the vinegar removes the dull layer that forms on the coin when it touches air. Pritesh left his coin in for the whole day and found it covered in a thin green film. Mrs. Iyer said that was also a chemical change, one he could learn about in higher classes. She asked them to write what they saw, not what they guessed.

What did Mrs. Iyer want the students to write?
She wanted them to write what they saw, not what they guessed.

When a monsoon flood covered the road to the village, Salim's grandfather used a large tractor tyre as a boat to carry children to school. He tied a rope around the tyre and pulled it through the shallow water, with two children sitting inside holding their bags above their heads. Other families brought their own tyres the next day. A teacher from the school stood at the far end with dry towels and counted heads. By the end of the week, every child in the village had crossed safely and no class was missed.

Why did other families bring their own tyres the next day?
Because Salim's grandfather's tyre boat carried children safely across the flood, and they wanted their children to get to school too.

A mongoose and a cobra faced each other on the path behind Lal's farm. Lal watched from a safe distance behind a wall. The snake raised its hood and swayed. The mongoose darted left and right, never staying in one spot, and when the cobra struck, the mongoose was already somewhere else. After several tries, the snake grew tired. The mongoose jumped in, bit the back of its head and ran off. Lal felt his heart pounding and let out a long breath. He did not walk on that path again for the rest of the week.

Why did Lal stay behind the wall?
Because he was afraid of the snake and wanted to be safe while he watched.

On the school trip to the planetarium in Hyderabad, the children lay back in soft chairs and looked at the dome above them. The lights dimmed, and stars appeared one by one. A voice told them that the planets in the sky move slowly across the stars over many nights, and that is why the ancient people called them wanderers. Sara tried to find the red dot that was Mars and spotted it near the edge of the dome. She whispered to her friend, who nodded. On the bus ride home, nobody spoke for a long time.

What did the children do on the bus ride home?
They were quiet and did not speak for a long time.

Yuki noticed that when she stirred sugar into hot tea, the sugar vanished. She tried the same with a spoonful of sand, but the sand sank to the bottom and stayed. Her mother said that sugar dissolves because it breaks into tiny bits that mix with the water, while sand does not. Yuki then tried a spoon of salt and watched it disappear as well. She tasted the water to be sure and made a face. Her mother reminded her not to taste science experiments, and Yuki laughed and said she would remember next time.

What did Yuki's mother remind her about?
She reminded Yuki not to taste science experiments.

The village potter, Mr. Pandit, found that the clay by the river made strong bowls, but the clay from the hill cracked in the kiln. A student of geology, Aditi, visited and tested both. She mixed some sand into the hill clay and found that it did not crack. She explained that the sand gives the clay room to shrink without breaking. Mr. Pandit tried mixing the sand into all his clay for a week. His bowls came out smooth. He told Aditi she could take any bowl she liked, and she chose the smallest one with a blue rim.

Why did Mr. Pandit offer Aditi a bowl?
To thank her, because her sand trick fixed the cracking in his bowls.

At a hospital in the city, a nurse named Sister Grace showed children how to wash their hands properly. She spread a small amount of glitter on their palms and asked them to rinse as they usually did. Most still had glitter on their wrists and between their fingers. Then she taught them to rub with soap for as long as it takes to sing a short song. This time, the glitter was gone. The children stared at their clean hands, and a small boy said he would sing the song at home every day.

What did Sister Grace spread on the children's palms?
She spread a small amount of glitter.

Tara left a piece of bread in a closed box at the back of the cupboard for two weeks as part of a school project. When she opened it, the bread was covered with grey and green fuzz. It smelled strange. She wrote down the date and took a photograph before putting the box in a bin with the lid closed tightly, as her teacher had told her. Her friend Jai kept his bread in the fridge and found no change after two weeks. Tara and Jai agreed that cold slowed the fuzz and that warm, damp places were worse.

What did Tara and Jai learn from their two pieces of bread?
They learned that cold slows the mould, and that warm, damp places make it grow more.

A big wasp's nest hung from the eaves of Mr. D'Souza's house in Goa. His children wanted to knock it down with a stick, but he stopped them and called the forest office. A man arrived in a thick coat with a long pole and a bag. He waited until dusk, when the wasps were quiet and inside the nest. Then he bagged the nest gently and carried it away to the woods. Mr. D'Souza thanked him and told the children that the right way is often the slow way.

Why did the man wait until dusk to remove the nest?
Because the wasps are quiet and inside the nest at that time, so it is safer to remove.

Nasir often found it hard to hear his teacher at the back of a noisy classroom. One day, his teacher showed him how to cup his hand behind his ear. Nasir was amazed at how much louder the voice became. He found that the curve of his hand caught more sound and sent it toward his ear. He then made a paper cone and put the narrow end near his ear. It worked even better. After that, he used a paper cone in the quiet corner of the library as well to hear the librarian whisper.

How did Nasir feel when he cupped his hand behind his ear?
He was amazed, since the teacher's voice became much louder.

Every Sunday, Mr. Verma took his old dog, Sheru, to the park by the lake. This Sunday, Sheru would not climb out of the car. He lay down on the back seat and looked at the floor. Mr. Verma tried a biscuit, then a ball, but nothing worked. He finally lifted the dog out and placed him on the grass. Sheru took three slow steps and sat. A young woman nearby offered a bowl of water. Sheru drank and wagged his tail a little. Mr. Verma decided to take him to the vet the next morning instead of walking him further.

Why did Mr. Verma decide to visit the vet?
Because Sheru refused his usual walk, ignored his treats and moved slowly, so Mr. Verma thought something might be wrong.

A boy named Omar from Muscat tied a long thread to a small piece of cork and let it float on a bowl of water. When he brought a magnet near the cork, nothing happened. Then he pushed a small iron needle through the cork, and the magnet pulled it across the water. He tried again with a needle that had been rubbed on the magnet. This one turned slowly and always pointed the same way. Omar's teacher told him that he had made a simple compass. He drew a picture of his invention and wrote his name on it.

What did Omar push through the cork to make the magnet pull it?
He pushed a small iron needle through it.

When the first monsoon clouds arrived in Thrissur, the gardener Mr. Nair noticed that the ants on his path were carrying their eggs uphill in a long dark line. He pointed it out to the children. By the evening, heavy rain had filled the low part of the path with water. The children ran to see the ants, which were safe on the high ground by the wall. Mr. Nair said that insects often move to higher places before heavy rain. He watched the line of ants till the last one reached safety.

Why were the ants moving their eggs uphill?
They were getting ready for heavy rain, and moving to higher ground kept the eggs safe from the water.

At Bruno's grandmother's house in Lyon, a pot of soup sat on the stove with the lid on. When the soup boiled, the lid rattled and puffed steam. Bruno asked why. His grandmother said that the steam wants more room and pushes the lid up. Bruno remembered that a train engine works the same way, and he told her about the model he had seen at the station museum. She lifted the lid with a cloth and let the steam out. Then she gave him a small bowl and told him to blow on the soup before tasting it.

What did Bruno's grandmother tell him to do with the soup?
She told him to blow on it before tasting it.

For her science project, Dhara grew two sets of radish seeds, one on a sunny window sill and one in a dark cupboard. After a week, the seedlings in the cupboard were long, thin and almost white. Those on the sill were short, sturdy and green. She noted her results and drew both sets with coloured pencils. Her teacher asked her what she thought the plants needed. Dhara said sunlight, because the dark ones looked sick and stretched upward. The teacher praised her answer and then gave her a larger pot so she could move her healthy plants outdoors.

What clue led Dhara to say that plants need sunlight?
The seedlings in the dark cupboard were long, thin and pale, while those on the sunny sill were short, sturdy and green.

Veer found a tiny frog on the wet steps of the stairwell after the rain. It was small, as small as his thumbnail, and its skin was a bright, shiny green. He picked it up with a leaf and set it in a bucket of damp soil. His mother said that frogs need to stay wet and should not be held with dry hands. Veer watched it hop around for a few minutes. Then he carried the bucket to the garden and tipped it over beside the pond. The frog leapt into the grass and was gone.

Where did Veer release the frog?
He released it in the garden beside the pond.

Hamza needed a way to keep his small brother's toy boats from drifting away in the pond. He found a long, thin rope and tied each boat to a stick pushed into the mud. Whenever the boats floated too far, the brother pulled the rope to bring them back. Soon, other children asked for ropes, too. Hamza spent the evening cutting lengths of string and tying loops at the end. He kept a roll of string in his pocket from then on, and the children called him the Rope Captain.

Why did the children call him the Rope Captain?
Because he made and gave out ropes that kept their toy boats from drifting away.

A researcher named Dr. Menon dropped a feather and a stone at the same time from a high balcony. The stone fell fast, but the feather drifted slowly side to side. Then she put both inside a tall clear tube, and used a pump to take the air out. This time, the feather and the stone fell side by side and hit the bottom together. The students clapped. Dr. Menon told them that air slows down the feather, and without it, everything falls at the same speed. She let each student take a turn working the pump.

What did Dr. Menon take out of the tube?
She took the air out of it with a pump.

Oleg watched a spider spin a web in the corner of the shed. It worked for hours, and the web gleamed in the sun. A fly buzzed in and stuck to a thread. The spider ran across and wrapped it carefully. Oleg wanted to free the fly, but his grandfather said the spider also had to eat. Oleg frowned and stayed quiet. The next morning, he came back to look at the web again. Then he sat down to draw the web in his book.

How did Oleg feel when the fly was caught?
He felt sorry for the fly and wanted to free it, because he frowned and stayed quiet when his grandfather said the spider had to eat.

Miriam spilled a little cooking oil on the kitchen floor. She did not notice until her brother stepped on it and slid across the room. He landed on the mat with a thump, and they both burst out laughing. Their mother came running in with a cloth and a bucket. She poured a little washing powder on the spot and scrubbed until the floor was no longer slippery. Then she asked the children to be careful and made them promise to tell her at once the next time anything spilled.

What did their mother ask the children to promise?
She asked them to tell her at once the next time anything spilled.

When the first lightbulb in the village of Raipur was lit in the community hall, hundreds of people gathered to look at it. Some were afraid and stayed near the door. An elderly woman, Dadi Kamla, walked right up to it and held out her palm below the glass. She said it was warm but did not burn. Then she laughed, and everyone else began to laugh with her. By the end of the evening, the children were dancing under the light. The headman said they would soon have bulbs in every house.

What did the elderly woman's action show the villagers?
It showed them that the bulb was safe, because she stood close, felt its warmth and was not hurt.

A shy owl lived in the old clock tower in Prague. Every night, as the bells rang twelve, the owl flew out through a gap in the stone. One night a boy named Pavel was awake and watched it from his window. The owl glided over the square without a sound and landed on the roof of the baker's shop. Pavel wrote down the time and, in the following nights, saw it do the same each time. On Saturday, he invited his cousin to watch with him, and they wrapped themselves in a blanket and shared a flask of warm milk.

At what time did the owl fly out?
It flew out when the bells rang twelve, at midnight.

A girl named Chitra boiled an egg for too long, and when she cracked it, the yolk had a green-grey ring around it. She thought it was spoiled and threw it out. Her aunt, a cook, laughed and told her that this ring comes from cooking an egg a little too long, and the egg is still safe to eat. She showed Chitra a pan, with a timer set for ten minutes. Chitra tried again and got a bright yellow yolk. She ate it with salt and pepper and said the trick was in the timer.

What did Chitra learn about the green-grey ring?
She learned that it appears when an egg is cooked a little too long, and the egg is still safe to eat.

In a village in West Bengal, fireflies filled a mango grove each June. Children walked there at dusk with jars, but the elders told them not to catch the insects. Mala asked why. Her grandfather said that fireflies live only a few weeks and use their light to find each other. If they are caught, they cannot find a mate. Mala went back that evening with an empty jar. She sat on a log, held it open and watched the lights blink around her. When she went home, she told the others that watching was better than catching.

Why did Mala's grandfather say not to catch fireflies?
Because they live only a few weeks and need their light to find a mate, which they cannot do if caught.

A man named Mr. Choudhury kept bees on his roof in Guwahati. Early in spring, he noticed that fewer bees returned each evening. He checked the hive and saw a small, dark beetle crawling over the honeycomb. He put on gloves and a veil, removed the beetles with a pair of tweezers, and added a tray of oil underneath the hive to catch any more. Within two weeks, the bees were back in full numbers. Mr. Choudhury wrote down in his book what he had done, in case another keeper asked for advice.

What did Mr. Choudhury use to remove the beetles?
He used a pair of tweezers, wearing gloves and a veil.

The class pet at Cedar School was a tortoise named Tilly. Every morning, the children set her on a patch of lawn and watched her slowly eat a lettuce leaf. When it rained, she pulled her head and legs in. One day the children found that Tilly had not moved from her shell for hours. The teacher said that tortoises sometimes rest and the weather had been chilly. They carried her inside to a box with warm straw and a lamp. By afternoon, Tilly stretched her neck out and looked around, and the whole class cheered.

Why did the teacher move Tilly inside?
Because it was chilly, and Tilly was staying in her shell, so she needed a warm place.

Priyanka was drawing on a sheet of paper laid on a wooden table when she noticed that the pencil lines showed up on the sheet below. She had pressed hard. Then she placed a piece of carbon paper between two sheets and drew once more. A copy of her drawing appeared on the lower sheet in dark blue. Her father said that people used this method to make copies of letters before photocopiers existed. Priyanka decided to make copies of her hand-drawn birthday cards for all her classmates, taking a clean sheet for each one.

What did Priyanka put between two sheets of paper?
She put a piece of carbon paper between them.

While walking through the market in Marrakech, Soraya saw a man carrying a tray of fresh mint above his head. Bees buzzed all around him, but he did not seem bothered. Soraya asked him how he avoided being stung. He grinned and said that bees only sting when they feel threatened, and he moved slowly and never swatted at them. He gave her a sprig of mint to smell and told her to walk slowly past the next stall. She did, and the bees ignored her too. She walked home with her mint, feeling very brave.

What does the mint seller's advice show about bees?
It shows that bees usually sting only when they feel threatened, so slow, calm movement keeps people safe.

The snow leopard that lives in the cold hills near Spiti has thick, pale fur with dark spots. Rangers placed a camera near a rock, and for months it showed nothing. Then, one grey morning, the camera snapped a clear photograph of a leopard sitting on top of the rock with a long tail curled around its feet. The rangers were thrilled. The picture was sent to the town council, which decided to place a sign by the road asking visitors to be quiet on the path and to take their rubbish home.

Why did the council put up a sign?
To ask visitors to be quiet and not leave rubbish, so the snow leopard would be left in peace.

A girl named Maya noticed her shadow in the schoolyard was long in the morning and short at noon. She asked her teacher, who gave her a chalk and a stick. Maya pushed the stick upright into a patch of soft ground and, at each hour, drew a line along its shadow. The lines made a fan shape on the ground. By the afternoon, the shadow pointed the other way and grew long again. The teacher said that this was an old way of telling the time, and Maya called her little tool a sun clock.

What did Maya push into the ground?
She pushed a stick upright into a patch of soft ground.

Hearing a faint scratching in the wall, Mrs. Kulkarni worried that a rat was living in her kitchen. Her son, Sandeep, listened closely and said it sounded too light. They stood by the wall for a few minutes and saw a tiny gecko come out of a hole near the stove. Sandeep said that geckos eat mosquitoes, so it was welcome. Mrs. Kulkarni made a face but let it stay. That night, there were fewer mosquitoes by the window, and in the morning she told Sandeep that she had been wrong.

What changed Mrs. Kulkarni's mind about the gecko?
There were fewer mosquitoes that night, and she realised the gecko was helping.

A Japanese boy named Kenji folded a sheet of paper into a long, narrow shape and found that it flew far across the room. He folded another with the wings bent up at the tips, and it flew even farther. His sister folded one with the nose pressed flat, and it dived straight to the floor. Kenji took notes about each fold and told her that wings and weight matter. They set up a competition in the corridor, with a line of tape as a start and a ruler to measure distance. Kenji won, but only by a little.

What did Kenji's sister's flat-nosed plane do?
It dived straight to the floor.

The oldest well in a village near Hampi had a rope with a wooden bucket, but the rope kept fraying where it rubbed against the stone. A villager named Basavaraj fixed a smooth round log across the top of the well so that the rope rolled over it. The rope no longer rubbed against the rough stone. After that, the rope lasted for three years. Visitors to the village still ask about it. Basavaraj likes to show them how it turns, and he explains that a small change can solve a long-standing problem.

How did the log help the rope?
The rope rolled over the smooth log instead of rubbing on the rough stone, so it stopped fraying.

A calf was born in the middle of the night at Gopal's dairy in Anand. By morning it was already standing on its wobbly legs. Gopal's daughter, Sheetal, was delighted. She was allowed to give the calf a bottle of warm milk, and she held it with both hands. The calf butted her and drank greedily. Then it lay down on the straw and shut its eyes. Sheetal wanted to stay in the shed all day, but her father reminded her that she had to go to school. She promised to come back to visit the calf as soon as her class ended.

What did Sheetal promise her father?
She promised to visit the calf as soon as her class ended.

While travelling by train to Chennai, Aanya noticed that the telephone poles beside the track seemed to rush past, but the distant hills barely moved. She asked the old man sitting opposite why. He said that things that are close seem to go by faster than things far away. He suggested she hold up her thumb and shut one eye, then the other. Aanya's thumb seemed to jump from side to side. She tried it again and again, giggling, until the old man took out a sandwich and offered her half. She took it, still smiling.

Why did the poles seem to move faster than the hills?
Because things that are close seem to go by faster than things that are far away.

A small team of volunteers in Jamaica collected plastic bottles from the beach and made them into a floating platform. They tied the bottles together in nets and covered them with a wooden board. Then they pushed it into the water near a mangrove. The next morning, they found that pelicans were using the platform as a place to rest. Soon crabs and small fish gathered under it, too. The volunteers pinned a notice to a post on the beach asking visitors to bring their bottles to the net instead of dropping them in the sand.

What did the volunteers make from plastic bottles?
They made a floating platform.

Baby elephants in the sanctuary sometimes hold each other's tails when they walk through the long grass. Keeper Mohan noticed that the smallest calf, named Gudiya, always held the tail of the biggest, an older female called Rani. When Rani was moved to a different part of the camp for a day, Gudiya refused to eat and stood near the fence. Mohan brought her a bunch of bananas, but she ignored it. When Rani returned in the evening, Gudiya rushed up and wound her trunk around Rani's, and then ate her whole dinner.

What does Gudiya's behaviour show about her feelings for Rani?
It shows she was strongly attached to Rani, since she stopped eating when Rani was away and ate again once she returned.

During a school camp near a river, the children were asked to find out how fast the water was flowing. Mr. Singh handed each group a piece of cork and a stopwatch. The children dropped the cork into the stream and ran along the bank, timing how long it took to travel between two trees. They repeated the test three times and wrote the numbers on a chart. The groups found the same answer within a second, which pleased Mr. Singh. He told them that checking a result several times is what makes it trustworthy.

What did each group get from Mr. Singh?
Each group got a piece of cork and a stopwatch.

A farmer's wife named Parvati was grinding wheat when a few stones got into the flour. Everyone who ate the roti complained about the grit. She worked out a way to prevent it. She spread the wheat on a large tray, tilted it and tapped the edge so that the small stones rolled to one side and the grains stayed. After a few days of doing this, the roti was soft again. Her sister-in-law noticed and borrowed the tray. By the end of the month, all the women on the lane were using the same trick.

Why did all the women in the lane begin to use Parvati's trick?
Because it removed the stones from the wheat, so the roti came out soft and free of grit.

Camille found an old thermometer in a drawer and wondered how it worked. She put it in a glass of cold water and watched the red line shrink. Then she put it in a bowl of warm water, and the line rose. Her father told her that the liquid inside gets bigger when it is warm and smaller when it is cold, and the tube is marked to show how much. Camille took readings in the shade, in the sun, and in the fridge, and wrote all of them in a table. She stuck the table on her bedroom door.

Where did Camille stick her table of readings?
She stuck it on her bedroom door.

One morning, a peacock walked into the courtyard of an old house in Jodhpur and began spreading its tail. The household stopped what it was doing. Even the cook came out with a ladle in his hand. The peacock turned slowly so that everyone could see the feathers shimmer, blue and green. A small boy clapped and the bird gave a loud cry. It then walked to the water tap, drank and flew up onto the wall. Later the cook said that he had never before stood still for five whole minutes in the morning.

What does the cook's comment show?
It shows the peacock's display was so beautiful that it made even a busy cook stop and watch.

A dentist named Dr. Pereira visited the school to talk about teeth. She showed the children a hard-boiled egg in a cup of cola for a day, and it had turned brown and rough. She said that sugary drinks do the same to teeth if they are not brushed. Then she gave out small mirrors so the children could look at their own teeth. Ravi found one with a small dark spot and asked if he should worry. Dr. Pereira said to ask his parents to bring him to the clinic for a check, and she gave him a card with the address.

What did Dr. Pereira tell Ravi to do about the dark spot?
She told him to ask his parents to bring him to the clinic for a check.

Dhruv spotted something strange at the bottom of the garden pond in the morning. A brown, wriggling mass of tadpoles had gathered beneath a large leaf. By the end of the week, some had started to grow tiny legs. A few weeks later, small frogs, still with short tails, sat on the pond's edge. Dhruv took photographs every Sunday and made a poster to show how the tadpoles changed over time. His teacher gave him full marks and hung it in the corridor. A smaller child asked if frogs go back into the water, and Dhruv said they do, whenever they want to.

When did Dhruv take his photographs?
He took them every Sunday.

Ekta noticed that the new bicycle bell would not ring when the weather was damp. It made a dull thud rather than a bright ring. Her brother opened the cap, wiped away the moisture and found a tiny speck of rust on the spring. He rubbed it away with fine sandpaper and oiled it lightly. The bell rang clear again. Ekta decided to wipe her bicycle with a dry cloth after rainy rides and to keep it under the stairs. She also told her friends so that their bells would not go dull.

Why did the bell make a dull thud?
Because moisture and a small speck of rust had got into the spring.

A dog named Kaalu was very good at finding lost things. When Mrs. Fonseca's glasses went missing, her grandson took Kaalu to the room and held up her scarf for him to sniff. Kaalu went straight to the sofa and put his nose under a cushion. There lay the glasses. Mrs. Fonseca gave him a treat and a pat. Kaalu then sat beside the cushion as if to say there might be more. The grandson looked and found two buttons and an old pen. Mrs. Fonseca said she must clean the sofa more often.

How did Kaalu find the glasses?
He sniffed the scarf and followed the smell to the sofa, then put his nose under the cushion.

The inventor of the safety pin was a man who needed to repay a debt, and he twisted a piece of brass wire into a coil with a clasp. The idea was simple. The point of the pin was covered by a guard so that it could not prick the fingers. The pin could be opened and closed again and again. He sold the idea for a small sum. For many years afterward, safety pins were used on babies' clothes, torn shirts and even costumes. Kajal's grandmother still kept a card of them in her sewing box.

What did the inventor make the pin from?
He made it from a piece of brass wire.

When a storm knocked out the electricity in Ghazala's street, her neighbours came out with torches. Ghazala brought a large glass bowl and filled it with water. She laid a torch on its side against the glass so that the beam shone up through the water. Light spread out in the bowl and lit up the whole table. The neighbours gathered to eat their dinner under it. A small boy said it looked like a moon in a bowl. Ghazala's father said it was a clever trick and that he would remember it for the next power cut.

Why did the neighbours gather around Ghazala's bowl?
Because the torch light shining through the water lit up the whole table, so they could eat dinner together.

A researcher counted the number of stars she could see from a field outside the city, and then repeated the count from the middle of the city. In the field, she counted hundreds. In the city, she counted only twelve. The city's bright street lamps and shop signs wash out the faint stars. She gave a talk to a group of schoolchildren, who were surprised. A girl in the front row asked if the stars were really gone. The researcher laughed and said they were still there, just hidden by the glare, and invited them all on a night walk outside the city.

Why could the researcher see fewer stars in the city?
Because the bright street lamps and signs washed out the faint stars.

Siblings Joel and Ruth were playing near a stream when they saw a bird with a long beak poking into the mud. It pulled out a wriggling worm and swallowed it. Joel thought it looked funny. Ruth took out her small notebook and sketched the beak. Later they looked in a book and found that it was a snipe. The book said that a snipe's beak has nerves at the tip, which help it find food it cannot see in the mud. Joel stopped laughing and looked at the bird with new respect.

Why did Joel look at the bird with new respect?
Because he learned that the snipe's beak can feel food in the mud, so it was cleverer than he thought.

A shopkeeper named Mr. Dutta in Siliguri found that the tea he stored in a tin box lost its smell after a few months. His daughter, Rina, suggested lining the tin with thick paper and sealing the lid with tape. A month later, he opened the tin, and the smell was strong. He tried the same with a tin of spices and the same thing happened. Soon, Mr. Dutta was selling tins lined with paper and sealed with tape, with a card on top saying that the tea was fresh. Customers came from far away to buy it.

What did Rina suggest to Mr. Dutta?
She suggested lining the tin with thick paper and sealing the lid with tape.

Some children watched a black ant carry a dead beetle three times its size across the garden. It went up a small hill of mud, slipped, and began again. A second ant came and held one end of the beetle. Together they carried it over the hill and toward a crack in the wall. A little girl clapped and said they were a team. The boy next to her said that the ants must be strong. Their teacher said that the secret was in sharing the work, and she asked the children what they could carry together at school.

What does the story of the two ants show?
It shows that sharing the work makes hard jobs possible, since the two ants together carried the beetle over the hill.

A sailor in Kochi told the children about a trick for finding north at night. He said to look for a bright star that does not seem to move while the others circle round it. The children went out onto the beach that evening and looked up. They found the star and used a stick to mark the direction on the sand. Then they walked along the line toward the palm trees and found that it led to the lighthouse. One of the children said it was like having a map in the sky.

How did the children mark the direction on the sand?
They used a stick to mark the line toward the star.

A buffalo in a village near Nashik was found stuck in a muddy pond. Every time it tried to pull itself out, it sank deeper. Men from the village made a bridge of planks and wrapped a rope around its body. They pulled together on the count of three. The buffalo came out with a loud sucking sound, covered in black mud, and shook itself so hard that everyone was splashed. People laughed and wiped their faces. The owner was close to tears and thanked them all. He promised to bring sweets for every man who had helped.

How did the owner feel when his buffalo was safe?
He felt grateful and relieved, because he was close to tears, thanked everyone and promised sweets.

Radha took some lime juice and a cotton bud and wrote a message on a sheet of white paper. When it dried, the writing disappeared. Her friend Sonal held the paper over a warm bulb, and the words slowly turned brown and became easy to read. Radha explained that the acid in the juice makes the paper burn faster at that spot than the rest. The two girls wrote secret notes to each other all week, until the teacher saw one and asked them to show her the trick. She was delighted and asked them to demonstrate it for the class.

What did Sonal hold the paper over to show the message?
She held it over a warm bulb.

When the monsoon failed one year in a village near Bhuj, the pond dried up. The villagers noticed that pigeons still gathered each morning at a corner of the old fort. Curious, a young man named Hassan followed them and found a small pool of cool water at the bottom of a broken wall, fed by a hidden spring. The village gathered at the spot, cleared the stones and built a small enclosure. The pool gave enough water to last until the rains came, and Hassan was invited to the village feast.

Why was Hassan invited to the village feast?
Because he followed the pigeons and found the hidden spring that gave the village water.

On a sweltering afternoon, a monkey slipped into Mrs. Kaur's kitchen in Amritsar and grabbed a bunch of bananas. Her dog barked at it but did not dare to go close. The monkey sat on the window sill, peeled one banana at a time and dropped the skins down into the yard. Mrs. Kaur held a broom but did not wave it, because she knew monkeys bite when frightened. She waited until the monkey had finished and jumped over the wall. Then she locked the window, picked up the skins and went back to the kitchen.

Why did Mrs. Kaur not wave her broom at the monkey?
Because she knew monkeys can bite when they are frightened.

The old bridge in a hill town in Himachal was made of wooden planks tied with ropes. A boy named Sunil noticed that it swayed more when many people walked on it together, but swayed less when people spread out. He mentioned this to the bridge keeper, who put up a notice asking travellers to cross in small groups with space between them. After that, fewer people complained of feeling dizzy, and the ropes lasted longer. Sunil felt proud when he saw the notice and read it aloud to his younger sister, who pointed at each word.

What did Sunil notice about the bridge?
He noticed that it swayed more when many people walked on it together and less when they spread out.

A little girl named Asha was walking to the market with her father when she saw a squirrel carrying a nut across a wire. The wire swayed. The squirrel stopped, held the nut tightly in its mouth and moved on carefully, one paw at a time. When it reached the far pole, it dashed down the trunk and buried the nut in a pile of leaves. Asha wondered if it would remember where the nut was. Her father said that squirrels hide many nuts and forget a few, and so help new trees to grow. Asha looked at the leaves and smiled.

How do squirrels help new trees grow?
They hide many nuts and forget some of them, and those nuts can grow into new trees.

Lars left a glass of water on the ledge outside his window overnight in Oslo, and in the morning it had a thin sheet of ice on top. He tapped it with his finger and it cracked. His mother told him that the air outside was much colder than the room. He then put a second glass in the middle of the kitchen table, and it stayed liquid. Lars measured the room and the sill with a thermometer and wrote the numbers on a card. The ledge was well below zero, and the table was well above. He pinned the card above his bed.

Where did Lars put the second glass?
He put it in the middle of the kitchen table.

For many years, Mr. Fernandes washed the family car with a bucket and sponge, and the water ran across the road. One day he made a spray from an old plastic bottle by poking holes in the cap. When he squeezed the bottle, it sprayed a fine mist that wet the whole car using only a little water. His neighbour borrowed the bottle to water her seedlings. Soon the whole street was using bottle sprays, and the water bill of the neighbourhood fell. Mr. Fernandes was invited to explain the idea at the residents' meeting, and he brought three bottles to show.

Why was Mr. Fernandes invited to the residents' meeting?
Because his bottle spray saved water and the whole street began using it.

At night, the old village of Pochampally was quiet, except for the sound of looms clacking. In the morning, Revathi noticed that the cat that lived under the loom was missing. She searched the house and found it on the shelf above the cloth, curled around four kittens. Revathi gave the cat a bowl of water and a little fish. She put a cloth down for the kittens and told her mother. The family chose names for each kitten: Kajal, Chandni, Moti and Shera. Revathi drew a picture of the family and hung it above the loom.

How many kittens did the cat have?
She had four kittens.

A young scientist, Dr. Bhatt, studied the way sunflowers turn to face the sun. She set up a camera that took a picture of a sunflower every hour for a day. In the morning, the flower faced east. By noon, it faced upward, and by evening, it faced west. During the night, it slowly turned back to the east. She showed the pictures as a quick film to schoolchildren, who laughed when the flower seemed to dance. She said that young sunflowers do this, but older ones stop moving and face the east all day.

Which direction did the sunflower face in the morning?
It faced east.

Parrots in Mr. Das's compound loved to eat the guavas in his garden. He spread a net, and the parrots ate through it. He tried a scarecrow, and they sat on its head. Then his niece, Moni, noticed that the parrots never came while the neighbour's dog was in the garden. Mr. Das asked his neighbour if the dog could spend the mornings in his yard. The dog sat under the guava tree each morning, and the parrots stayed away. The guavas ripened fully, and Mr. Das sent a basket to his neighbour with a thank-you note.

Why did the parrots stay away when the neighbour's dog was in the garden?
They were afraid of the dog, since they never came when it was there.

Grandmother Elena used a clothespin to hold her glasses to her collar when she worked. Her granddaughter, Isabel, thought it looked silly. She made a small cord from beads and linked it to the glasses. Her grandmother put them on and wore them for the day. In the evening, a friend visiting from the next street asked where she had bought the cord. Elena said her granddaughter had made them. The friend asked for one and offered to pay. Isabel took three orders that week and used the money to buy her grandmother a new pair of spectacles.

What did Isabel do with the money she earned?
She bought her grandmother a new pair of spectacles.

A pair of swans lived on a pond in the middle of a busy town. Every spring, they built a nest on a little island and laid eggs. Last year, one of the eggs rolled out and sank in the water. The male swan dipped his head under the water again and again, but could not find it. The female sat quietly on the other eggs. A child on the bank threw bread, but the swans did not eat. Then, a few weeks later, five cygnets followed their parents onto the water, and the male swan swam with his neck held high.

What does the swans' refusal of bread suggest?
It suggests that they were sad or worried about the lost egg, because they did not eat even when food was offered.

A researcher placed a mirror in front of a small fish in a tank. The fish flared its fins and swam at the glass, thinking it was a rival. After a few minutes, it seemed to grow tired and backed away. The researcher covered the mirror with a cloth, and the fish settled. When she removed the cloth the next day, the fish no longer attacked its reflection but swam slowly in front of it. She wrote that fish can learn that a reflection is harmless after seeing it many times, though no one knows what they think.

What did the fish do at first when it saw the mirror?
It flared its fins and swam at the glass as if the reflection were a rival.

Sumi accidentally left her wet raincoat folded in her bag overnight. In the morning, it smelled musty. Her mother hung it in the sun for an hour, and the smell vanished. She said that wet cloth gets a bad smell when it stays damp and closed in. Sumi began to open her bag as soon as she reached home on rainy days and to spread out anything wet. Her friends followed her habit. Their mothers said they had never seen the school bags so tidy, and the teacher asked Sumi to give a short talk on the subject.

Why did the raincoat smell musty?
Because it was wet and stayed folded in a closed bag overnight.

The family in a small house in Kerala heard a strange hissing sound from the kitchen in the middle of the night. The father took a torch and found a cobra curled up beside the water pot. Everyone stayed calm. He called the local snake rescuer, Mr. Hari, who arrived in twenty minutes with a long hook and a cloth bag. Mr. Hari gently lifted the cobra into the bag and tied it. In the morning, he released it in a forest far from houses. The family thanked him and gave him a plate of hot idlis.

Who came to remove the cobra?
A snake rescuer named Mr. Hari came and took it away.

Marco noticed that the small paper cup he used as a lid on his tea kept the tea hot much longer than leaving it open. He asked his grandmother, who said that the cup stops the warm steam from escaping and also stops cold air from touching the tea. Marco tried covering the tea with a plate instead and found it worked just as well. Then he put a thick towel over the cup and plate, and the tea stayed hot even longer. He told his cousins and they tried the same with their cocoa on a winter evening.

Why does a cover keep tea hot for longer?
Because it stops the warm steam from escaping and keeps cold air away from the tea.

Amara watched a woodpecker hammer on the trunk of an old tree outside her window in Accra. Its head moved so quickly that she could not see it clearly. She wondered why the bird did not get a headache. She asked the science teacher, who explained that the woodpecker has strong neck muscles, a thick skull and a small brain held snugly inside it. Amara drew a diagram and showed it to her class. They all agreed that woodpeckers were the toughest birds in the world.

Why does the woodpecker not get a headache?
Because it has strong neck muscles, a thick skull and a small brain held snugly inside it.

Mr. Roy, a shopkeeper, noticed that a customer could not read the labels on his jars because the light was dim. He moved a mirror to the wall behind the shelf, and the light from the window bounced onto the jars. The labels were suddenly clear. Customers began to praise the brightness of his shop, and some came back just to see it. Mr. Roy cleaned the mirror every morning with a soft cloth, so that the shine would never fade. His wife teased him that the mirror got more attention than she did, and he laughed.

What did Mr. Roy do to brighten his shop?
He moved a mirror to the wall behind the shelf so that light from the window bounced onto the jars.

When Ben dropped a ball of clay into a bowl of water, it sank at once. Then he rolled the same clay into a flat boat shape with high edges and put it in the water. It floated. His teacher asked him why. Ben said that the boat had air inside and was not so heavy for its size. The teacher nodded. He loaded the boat with small pebbles one by one until it finally sank, and Ben counted fourteen before it went down. The class cheered as the boat disappeared, then Ben fished the clay out and dried it with a towel.

Why did the flat clay boat float when the ball sank?
Because the boat shape held air and spread the clay's weight out, so it was not too heavy for its size.

A small crab in a rock pool near Goa hid under a stone whenever a shadow passed. Rita crouched beside the pool, so still that she hardly breathed. After a while, the crab edged out and began picking at a piece of seaweed. Rita saw it hold the weed with one claw and pass it to its mouth with the other. She did not try to touch it. When her mother called, she stood up slowly. The crab ducked back under the stone. Rita wrote in her notebook that patience was the secret to seeing animals.

What did Rita write in her notebook?
She wrote that patience was the secret to seeing animals.

An old man in a village used a long bamboo pole with a hook to pick mangoes from high branches. Boys who climbed the tree sometimes fell and scraped their knees. His grandson, Tanmay, thought it was too slow, so he tied a net bag below the hook. Now the mangoes fell into the bag and did not bruise. The old man showed it to the other farmers, and they were delighted. The next season, the market was full of unbruised mangoes, and the price they fetched was better than ever.

Why did the mangoes fetch a better price the next season?
Because they were picked into a net bag and did not bruise.

A cat in Tashkent named Barsik used to sit near the bakery door each morning. When the baker opened it, Barsik walked in and sat beside the oven. The baker said that the cat liked the warmth. Customers began to drop in just to see the cat, and the baker sold more bread. One winter morning, Barsik did not appear, and the baker closed the shop early to look for him. He found Barsik asleep in a box that a child had set out near the school. The baker took him back with a hot loaf under his arm.

Where did the baker find Barsik?
He found him asleep in a box that a child had put near the school.

A new student in Mrs. Das's class, Imran, said that metal always sinks in water. To test this, the class placed a steel pin on a piece of tissue paper and set it on the surface of a bowl of water. When the tissue sank, the pin stayed floating on top. They stared. Mrs. Das explained that the surface of water acts like a thin skin, strong enough to hold a light thing. Imran poked the pin gently, and it sank. He looked at the teacher and said that he had learned two things that day.

Why did the pin float on the water?
Because the surface of water acts like a thin skin that can hold up a very light thing.

A shepherd named Birju noticed that his flock grew scared when thunder was near. He carried a long staff with a small brass bell and began to ring it as he walked ahead of the flock. The bell's sound made the sheep follow him in a calm line. When the thunder came, they did not run. Birju led them to a cave on the hillside and waited until the storm passed. Later, other shepherds in the valley made bells for their own flocks, and the hills rang with the soft sound every evening.

Where did Birju take the flock during the storm?
He took them to a cave on the hillside.

Hanna let a drop of ink fall on a wet paper towel and saw the colour spread in a ring. She noticed that the ink was not one colour but many: purple, blue and a little yellow. Her older brother said that the paper towel pulls the water, and the water carries the different colours at different speeds. Hanna tried a different pen and found a different set of colours. She tested every marker in her pencil box and made a chart of the results. Her art teacher hung the chart on the wall.

What did Hanna discover about the ink?
She discovered that the ink was made of several colours, such as purple, blue and yellow, which spread at different speeds.

In a fishing village in Tamil Nadu, a man noticed that when he threw a net at sunset, he caught more fish than at noon. His son, Murugan, asked why. The man said that fish come nearer the surface in the cool evening, and they hide in deeper water when the sun is strong. So he began to fish only in the early morning and at dusk, and rested in the heat of the day. His catches grew larger, and he had more time to mend his nets and teach Murugan how to knot them.

Why did the man catch more fish at sunset?
Because fish come nearer the surface in the cool evening and go deep when the sun is strong.

A bat swooped into the school hall during the evening choir practice. It zigzagged around the lights, and the children shrieked. The music teacher, Mr. Pinto, told them to stay calm and sit down. He opened both doors wide and switched off the lights. In a few minutes, the bat flew out into the dark, and the children laughed with relief. Mr. Pinto said that bats find their way mostly by sound, and bright lights and noise confuse them. The practice began again, and the choir sang louder than ever, as if it were celebrating.

Why did Mr. Pinto switch off the lights and open the doors?
So the bat could find the way out into the dark and leave the hall.

An American boy named Caleb learned that cooks used baking soda to make a cake rise. He decided to test it. He baked two small cakes, one with baking soda and one without. The first came out soft and tall. The other was flat and hard. His aunt Julie tasted both and chose the tall one. Caleb wrote in his book that tiny bubbles of gas in the batter make it rise. He then made a third one with double the soda, and it tasted bitter. He wrote down that too much is as bad as none.

What did Caleb write after the third cake?
He wrote that too much baking soda is as bad as none, because the cake tasted bitter.

Ayaan had a habit of blowing across the top of an empty bottle to make a low sound. One day, he poured in a little water and blew again. The note was higher. He added more water and the note grew higher still. He lined up five bottles with different amounts of water and made a row of notes. His sister tapped them with a spoon, and the notes were different from the blown ones. Together they played a simple tune. Their mother clapped and said that if they practised, they could play at the school function.

What happened to the sound when Ayaan added water?
The note became higher.

Farida's goat kept getting loose and eating her neighbour's plants. She tried a rope, but the goat chewed through it. Then she mended the gap in the fence with thick bamboo poles, so the goat could no longer squeeze through. The neighbour stopped complaining. Farida also gave the goat a pile of fresh leaves each morning so it would not be tempted by the garden. After a few days, the goat began to wait by the gate for its leaves and no longer wandered.

Why did the goat stop wandering after a few days?
Because it got fresh leaves each morning and waited by the gate for them instead of looking for the garden.

A visitor to the coast of California saw a young sea otter playing with a smooth stone. The otter tossed it into the air, caught it and rolled it along its chest as it floated on its back. It dropped the stone several times, dived to pick it up and then started again. A girl by the shore laughed so loudly that the otter looked toward her. Then it swam off, still holding the stone. Her father told her that sea otters have favourite stones that they carry for a long time and use as tools to crack open shells.

What did the otter play with?
It played with a smooth stone.

When Rhea poured a spoonful of honey into a glass of water, it sank to the bottom in a thick sticky blob. Then she added a layer of oil, and it floated on top. She added a drop of coloured dye, and it stayed in the water. The three layers looked like a tall, striped drink. Her father told her that honey is heavier than water and oil is lighter, so each settles where it belongs. Rhea added a small grape and watched it rest between two layers. She called it her rainbow tower.

What does the order of the layers show?
It shows that honey is heavier than water and oil is lighter, since the honey sank, the oil floated and the water stayed in the middle.

A kind of fruit bat lived in the old fig tree in a Mumbai suburb. At dusk, dozens of them unfolded their wings and flew off to find fruit. One evening, a boy named Nikhil put a small basket of overripe bananas on the wall at the top of the steps, and some of the bats landed for a bite. He filmed them with his father's camera. At school the next day, he showed the film, and everyone gasped. His teacher asked if he had touched the bats, and Nikhil said no, he had stayed very still.

What did Nikhil put out for the bats?
He put out a small basket of overripe bananas.

A boy named Idris sat by the roadside in Kano and watched a small whirlwind pick up dust and leaves. It spun for a few seconds and then vanished. Idris asked his uncle what made it. His uncle said that the hot ground heats the air just above it, and the warm air rises in a twisting column. Idris ran to the field and tried to spin round like the dust. He grew dizzy and fell down laughing. His uncle helped him up and said that a whirlwind is a sort of dance that the wind does when the ground is hot.

What causes a small whirlwind, according to Idris's uncle?
Hot ground heats the air just above it, and the warm air rises in a twisting column.

The old streetlamp near Mrs. Bose's house flickered every night. At first, it seemed like a problem with the wire. A repairman found small moths trapped inside the glass that were bumping against the bulb. He cleaned the glass and fitted a finer mesh over the gaps. The light burned steadily after that, and the street felt safer. Mrs. Bose brought him a cup of tea. He said that the moths had been drawn by the glow, and that moths have flown to lamps for as long as there have been lamps. He drank the tea in the shade of the lamp.

What caused the streetlamp to flicker?
Small moths had got inside the glass and were bumping against the bulb.
