While exploring a cave in Meghalaya with her father, Dolly found a long thin rock hanging from the roof, dripping water. Below it, a smaller rock rose from the floor. Her father said they were made by water that drips for thousands of years, each drop leaving a tiny bit of mineral behind. Dolly asked how long it takes for one of them to grow a finger's width. He said it might take a hundred years. Dolly looked at the rock for a long time and then whispered that she felt very small. Her father squeezed her hand.

Why did Dolly feel very small?
Because she realised how very long it takes for the rocks to grow, which made her own life seem short.

A girl named Beena put a ripe tomato and a hard, green one side by side on a shelf. A few days later, the green one had started to turn red. She wondered whether all fruits ripen the same way. She tried mangoes, bananas and papayas. All of them ripened faster when they were closed in a paper bag than when left in the open. Beena wrote that a closed bag keeps the ripening gas close to the fruit. She told her mother, who started wrapping unripe fruit in paper and leaving it in a dark cupboard.

Why did her mother start wrapping unripe fruit in paper?
Because Beena found that a closed bag keeps the ripening gas near the fruit, so it ripens faster.

A dog sled team in a snow village in Alaska pulled a heavy load of food to an isolated cabin. At one point, a storm covered the trail. The lead dog, a big grey husky named Bear, stopped and sniffed the air. He turned left, away from the marked route. The driver trusted him and followed. After an hour, they came to the cabin's smoking chimney. The driver told the family that without Bear, they would have been lost. The family fed the team and put out clean straw in the shed for the night.

Why did the driver follow the lead dog off the marked path?
Because he trusted the dog, and the storm had covered the trail so the dog's sense of smell was the best guide.

A child named Ola from Lagos placed a small mirror on the floor beneath a sunbeam and watched a bright spot dance on the ceiling. She tilted the mirror, and the spot slid across the wall. Her friend held another mirror, and together they sent the light across the room and onto a poster. Their teacher stepped in and was delighted. She told them that light always travels in straight lines and bounces off a smooth surface at the same angle that it arrives. The two girls drew arrows on a sheet of paper to show how the light moved.

What did the girls draw on the sheet of paper?
They drew arrows to show how the light moved.

When Mr. Saldanha noticed that his rooster crowed earlier each morning in the summer, he thought something was wrong with the bird. He took him to the vet, who said he was healthy. The vet explained that roosters crow when it becomes light, and in summer dawn comes earlier. Mr. Saldanha laughed and went home. He pinned a card on the door that said the rooster was simply an early riser. His neighbours complained at first but soon got used to waking with the sun, and some even said they felt better for it.

Why did the rooster crow earlier in summer?
Because roosters crow when it gets light, and dawn comes earlier in summer.

In an old workshop, a carpenter named Mr. Ghosh made a toy from two wooden discs joined by a short peg, with a string wound round the peg. When he let it drop, it spun down the string and climbed back up again. The children called it a yo-yo. A boy named Shiv spent the entire afternoon learning to make it roll down and climb back. He finally managed to make it sleep, spinning in one place at the end of the string. The carpenter was pleased and said he would make one for each child in the street.

What did Shiv manage to do with the yo-yo?
He made it sleep, spinning in one place at the end of the string.

Katie noticed that the leaves on her family's plants in Dublin curled and dropped when winter came. She asked her father if the plants were dying. He said that some trees drop their leaves to save water and energy when it is cold and there is less sunlight. In spring, new leaves would open. Katie marked the tree in her garden with a bright ribbon and wrote down the date of the first fallen leaf. When April came, she sat under the tree and counted the new buds. She was delighted and told everyone it had come back to life.

Why did the trees drop their leaves in winter?
To save water and energy when it is cold and there is less sunlight.

A drongo is a small black bird with a long forked tail, and it lives in the fields near Maya's village. Maya noticed that the drongo sat on the back of a cow and rode it from one end of the field to the other. Whenever the cow's feet disturbed an insect, the drongo swooped down, caught it and flew back. Maya's grandfather said that a drongo can also copy the sound of other birds. Maya tried to imitate the drongo, whistling and twittering, and the bird tilted its head and looked at her.

Where did the drongo sit while the cow walked?
It sat on the back of the cow.

In Mr. Thapa's school in Darjeeling, there was a day when the clouds came down so low that the playground vanished in white mist. The children gasped. Mr. Thapa said that fog is a cloud that touches the ground and is made of tiny water drops. He took them out in a line to walk through it, holding a rope. They came back with wet hair and wet faces. A boy said he had walked inside a cloud. Mr. Thapa wrote this sentence on the blackboard and asked each child to copy it into their notebook.

What did Mr. Thapa say fog is?
He said fog is a cloud that touches the ground and is made of tiny water drops.

A fox came to the edge of a farm in England every evening for scraps. Farmer Gill left a plate of leftover bread outside the barn. One evening, he put an unripe apple on the plate instead, just to see what the fox would do. The fox sniffed the apple, pushed it aside with its nose and ate the bread. The next evening, the farmer gave a piece of bread and the apple, and the fox took only the bread again. Farmer Gill chuckled and told his wife that foxes know what they like better than most people do.

What did the fox do with the apple?
It sniffed it, pushed it aside with its nose and ate the bread instead.

When a power cut stopped the fridge, Gauri's mother worried that the milk would go sour in the heat. Gauri wrapped the milk bottle in a wet towel and placed it in a large clay pot in the shade. The pot's walls kept the heat out, and the wet towel cooled the bottle a little as it dried. After three hours, when the power came back, the milk was still cool and fresh. Gauri's mother was amazed and hugged her. Gauri said she had read about it in a book on village life, where people used clay pots to cool water all through the summer.

What does the milk staying cool show about the clay pot and wet towel?
It shows that together they kept the milk cool, since the pot kept heat out and the drying towel cooled it.

A beekeeper wearing a white suit smoked the hive with a small can of burning leaves before lifting the lid. Rani, who stood a safe distance away, asked why he did that. He said that the smoke calms the bees and masks the smell that they give off when alarmed. After that, he took out a frame full of honey and showed her the cells sealed with wax. He cut a small piece of comb and handed it to her. Rani tasted the honey and her eyes lit up. She asked if she could come back to help him at the next harvest.

Why did the beekeeper use smoke?
The smoke calms the bees and covers the smell they give off when alarmed.

Henry's grandfather said that if you see a spider's web covered in dew in the morning, the day will be fine. Henry did not believe him. For a week, he went out every morning to check the webs near the shed and wrote down whether the day turned out sunny or wet. Six of the seven times, the dewy web was followed by a fine day. Henry told his grandfather that the saying seemed mostly right, and his grandfather chuckled. He said that dew forms on clear, calm nights, and these are often followed by fine days.

Why do dewy webs often come before fine days?
Because dew forms on clear, calm nights, and those are often followed by fine weather.

A group of boys in Jaipur found a baby parrot lying on the ground beneath a tree after a strong wind. It was alive, but its wing looked bent. The boys carried it to a veterinary clinic in a small box lined with cloth. The vet looked at it and said it had only a small bruise. She told them to keep it in a quiet place and feed it soaked grain. A week later, the parrot flapped its wings and flew to a branch. The boys cheered, and the youngest boy, Ali, said goodbye with tears of joy.

How did Ali feel when the parrot flew off?
He felt happy and emotional, because he said goodbye with tears of joy.

Mr. Simon planted a row of tall sunflowers next to the vegetable bed in his garden in Cape Town. His wife asked why. He said that the flowers draw bees, and the bees help the vegetables to bear fruit. That summer, the courgettes and beans grew larger than ever. Mr. Simon counted over thirty bees on a single flower one morning. His wife went out and photographed it. At the end of the season, they left the heads of the sunflowers for the birds to eat, and they stood in the garden like tall watchmen.

Why did Mr. Simon plant sunflowers beside the vegetables?
Because sunflowers draw bees, and the bees help the vegetables bear fruit.

A group of students in Pune built a small solar cooker from a cardboard box, foil and a sheet of glass. They placed a few tomatoes inside it and set the box in the sun. After three hours, the tomatoes were soft and cooked. The students cheered and tried a potato next, but it was still hard after the same time. Their teacher said that denser foods take longer and that the cooker needs a clear day. They agreed to start earlier the next time and to cut the potato into thin slices.

Why did the students plan to cut the potato into thin slices?
Because thick, dense foods take longer to cook, and thin slices would cook faster in the solar cooker.

A man digging a well in his courtyard in Lucknow struck something hard about two metres down. It was a clay pot with a narrow neck. Inside there were a few old copper coins, green with age. The man carried them to the museum, where an expert looked at them and said they were more than two hundred years old. She wrote down the details and thanked him. The museum asked if it could keep the coins. The man agreed, on the condition that his name would be written on the card beside them, and the museum said it would.

What was inside the clay pot?
A few old copper coins, green with age.

A baby kangaroo, called a joey, was brought to the zoo in Perth after its mother was hit by a car. The keepers placed it in a soft cloth pouch, hung it on a wall and kept it warm. Every few hours, they fed it with a tiny bottle. The little joey grew quickly. After a few months, it began to hop out of its pouch and back. Keepers laughed to see it disappear head-first into its pouch whenever a loud noise sounded. They said it still thought of the pouch as home.

Why did the joey dive into its pouch when it heard a loud noise?
Because it still saw the pouch as its safe home and went there when it was frightened.

While cleaning the attic, Mr. Alam found a dusty gramophone with a big brass horn. He wound its handle and placed a heavy black disc on the plate. A thin, scratchy music came out of the horn. His grandchildren gathered around in amazement, as they had never seen anything like it. Mr. Alam explained that a needle follows a groove on the disc and shakes, making the sound. One child touched the needle and the music jumped. He told them to be gentle. They played the same song again and again until the sun went down.

What made the music jump?
A child touched the needle.

Ines was making lemonade when she squeezed a lemon onto a purple cabbage juice that her brother had left in a glass. The juice turned bright pink. She added a pinch of baking soda to another glass of the same juice, and it turned blue-green. They were both amazed. Their aunt told them that the juice changes colour depending on whether something is sour or not. Ines made a chart with a row of glasses, and each one showed a different colour. She labelled each glass with what she had added, and her brother copied it neatly.

What colour did the cabbage juice turn when Ines added lemon?
It turned bright pink.

Sita's grandfather kept hens in a coop behind the house. Every evening, the hens walked into the coop by themselves as the light faded, and he closed the little door. One evening a storm arrived early, and the sky turned dark long before sunset. The hens hurried inside while the grandfather was still at the market. When he came home, he found the door open and every hen sitting on its perch, huddled together. He shut the door, gave them a handful of grain and told Sita that hens go to bed when it gets dark, not when the clock says so.

What does the hens' behaviour in the storm show?
It shows that hens go to roost when the sky gets dark, because they went into the coop early when the storm darkened the sky.

A girl named Yara put a few drops of water on a flat leaf of a lotus after a shower. The drops rolled around like silver beads and did not soak in. She tilted the leaf, and the drops rolled off, taking small specks of dust with them. Her teacher said the leaf has a surface covered with tiny bumps that keep water from spreading. The dust on the leaf gets washed away each time it rains, so the leaf stays clean. Yara said she wished her school bag were made of the same stuff, and her teacher laughed and said that someone had already tried.

Why does the lotus leaf stay clean?
Because the water drops roll off it and carry away the dust each time it rains.

Jun was fishing from a small boat when he noticed that his line was tugging in a strange rhythm. He lifted it up and saw a small octopus holding the bait with its arms. It looked at him and changed from brown to a pale pink. He gently untangled the line and put the octopus back in the water. It squirted a cloud of dark ink and jetted away. Jun laughed and wrote in his logbook that he had been outwitted by something with eight arms. His father, in the next boat, rowed over to hear the whole story.

How did the octopus escape?
It squirted a cloud of dark ink and jetted away after Jun put it back in the water.

Mrs. Khan found that the food in her son's lunch box was always warm and soggy by lunchtime. Then she saw that the box lay in his bag next to a flask of hot soup. She moved the soup to the side pocket and wrapped the lunch box in a cloth. The next day, the food was cool and still fresh. Her son said that his friends envied him because their lunches were hot and damp. Mrs. Khan told other parents about it at the school gate, and they said they would try it.

Why was the lunch warm and soggy before Mrs. Khan changed the bag?
Because the lunch box sat next to a flask of hot soup, which warmed it.

Zeynep's cat kept pushing glasses off the table. She decided to find out why. She placed a plastic glass, a small bowl and a paper cup in a row. The cat tapped the glass and watched it roll. It tapped the bowl, then the cup. It stopped only when something made a noise or moved far. Zeynep's mother said that cats are curious and enjoy making things move. Zeynep set a ball on the table instead, and the cat spent the whole afternoon chasing it. The glasses stayed where they were from then on.

Why did the cat push things off the table?
Because cats are curious and enjoy making things move, as it kept tapping what rolled or made a noise.

When the school sports day dawned, a heavy shower had made the track slippery. The teachers worried that the children might fall. The caretaker, Mr. Joseph, spread a thin layer of dry sawdust along the track. The children ran in their bare feet and did not slip. The races went on as planned, and a girl named Dipti won the long race by a small margin. The headmaster thanked Mr. Joseph in his speech at the end and gave him a small trophy. The caretaker blushed and said that sawdust costs almost nothing.

What did Mr. Joseph spread on the track?
He spread a thin layer of dry sawdust.

A boy named Kiran noticed that the old tap in the yard dripped and the drip made a hollow in the soft soil below. Next to it lay a flat stone that had sat under the tap for years, and it had a tiny smooth dent where the drops fell. His grandfather said that this was how water wears away rock over many years. Kiran placed a bucket under the tap instead and used the water for the plants. His grandfather mended the tap that weekend. Kiran kept the stone with its dent on his shelf as a souvenir of what a slow drip can do.

Why did Kiran keep the stone on his shelf?
Because its dent showed how slow dripping water can wear away rock, and it reminded him of that.

At a village fair in Odisha, a man showed the crowd a small clay whistle shaped like a bird. When he filled it with water and blew, it made a trilling sound like a real bird. Children crowded around him and begged their parents for one. Rina bought one and took it home. She blew it all evening, until her father asked her to stop. The next day, she took it to school and showed her teacher how it worked. The teacher said it works because air moving over the water breaks into tiny bubbles, which make the trill.

What did the whistle sound like?
It made a trilling sound like a real bird.

A cow in the field behind Mr. Pillai's house suddenly started mooing and walking in circles. The children saw it and ran to tell him. Mr. Pillai looked and saw that her calf was missing from the herd. He told the children to look in the bushes at the edge of the field. They found the calf tangled in a bramble. Together they freed it, and it ran straight to its mother. The cow stopped mooing and began licking its calf. The children went home with scratched hands, but they were proud and told the story at supper.

Why was the cow mooing and walking in circles?
Because her calf was missing, and she was upset and looking for it.

A girl named Pari noticed that her pet rabbit thumped its back foot on the floor whenever the doorbell rang. She watched this for a week. Her uncle, who had kept rabbits, said that rabbits thump to warn the others of danger. Pari held the rabbit and spoke softly to it each time the bell rang, and slowly it thumped less. After a month, it hardly reacted to the bell. Pari was happy and gave the rabbit an extra carrot. She wrote in her diary that animals learn to feel safe when they are given time.

Why did the rabbit thump its foot?
To warn others of danger, since it did so when the doorbell rang.

A cook in a small restaurant noticed that his rice stuck to the bottom of the pot. He asked his mother, who told him to wash the rice until the water ran clear and to put a lid on the pot while it cooked. The next time, the rice was fluffy and each grain stood apart. He thanked her and wrote the steps on a card near the stove. His customers praised the rice that evening, and one of them asked for the recipe. The cook smiled and said that it was not a secret, only a matter of washing and waiting.

What did the cook's mother tell him to do?
She told him to wash the rice until the water ran clear and to cover the pot with a lid while it cooked.

The class had planted two identical bean plants. One was watered every day and the other once a week. After a month, the first plant had yellow leaves and a soft stem. The second one was green and strong. The children were puzzled because they had thought more water would be better. Their teacher said that plants can drown if their roots sit in water, since roots also need air. The class stopped watering the first plant for a few days. Slowly, the leaves began to turn green again, and the children cheered.

Why did the plant that was watered every day turn yellow?
Because its roots sat in too much water and could not get enough air.

A group of village women in Gujarat began placing shallow bowls of water on their rooftops for the birds in summer. At first, only pigeons came. Then sparrows, crows and even a few green parrots started arriving at the same time each morning. A child, Mehul, counted the birds each day and drew a chart. On the hottest day, there were fifty birds at one bowl. The women filled the bowls twice a day after that. They said the sound of the birds splashing was a better alarm than any clock.

Who counted the birds each day?
A child named Mehul counted them and drew a chart.

Paul's little sister was afraid of the dark, so he decided to make her a nightlight. He took a glass jar and filled it with water, then dropped in a few glowing sticks from his party box. The jar glowed softly green. She stared at it from her bed and slowly her fear faded. Their mother found the two of them asleep, with the jar between them. In the morning, his sister asked if she could keep it forever. Paul said yes and wrote her name on the lid with a marker.

How did Paul's sister feel after seeing the jar?
She felt calmer and safer, since her fear faded and she fell asleep, then asked to keep it forever.

A researcher put some honey on a plate and watched ants find it. The first ant walked around in loops until it found the honey, and then it went straight back to its nest, leaving an invisible trail. Within minutes, a line of ants came along the same path. The researcher moved the plate a short way and watched how the ants lost the trail and wandered until a new one was formed. She wrote that the ants share information by leaving scent trails, and that they all follow one another so quickly that the line looks like one animal.

What happened when the researcher moved the plate?
The ants lost the trail and wandered until a new trail was formed.

When Ramesh pulled his bicycle out after the rain, the chain was brown and sticky. It creaked as he pedalled. He took a cloth and wiped the chain, then put a drop of oil on each link. After that, the bicycle moved smoothly and without noise. His younger brother asked if he could do it too, so Ramesh handed him the cloth. They spent the morning cleaning both bicycles and the chains shone in the sun. Their father, who watched them from the doorway, said that he was proud to see them care for their own things.

Why did the bicycle stop creaking?
Because Ramesh cleaned the chain and put a drop of oil on each link.

A girl named Lena saw that ice cubes in a glass of water melted faster when she stirred them. She asked her uncle about it. He said that stirring brings warmer water against the ice, so it melts sooner. Lena tried it with cold water and warm water, and measured the time with her watch. In warm water the ice was gone in four minutes with stirring and six minutes without. She wrote the numbers on a card. The next day, she showed it to her class, and her teacher asked her to put the card on the science board.

How long did the ice take to melt in warm water when stirred?
It took four minutes.

While walking in a forest in Sikkim, a boy noticed a trail of tiny footprints in the mud. They were round, with five toes and a larger pad. He followed them and found droppings full of chewed bamboo. His guide said that a red panda had passed that way. The boy crouched and looked around, but all he saw was a tree with some bamboo leaves nibbled. The guide told him that red pandas sleep in tree hollows during the day, and are shy of people. The boy decided to stay quiet and walk on his toes.

Why did the boy walk quietly after the guide's words?
Because red pandas are shy of people, and he did not want to disturb it.

Grandpa Joe kept a jar of water by the window for his plants, and every few days a new layer of green slime formed at the bottom. He asked his granddaughter Lily to look at a drop under the school microscope. She found tiny green threads and round cells swimming in it. Her teacher told her that algae grow in still water where sunlight reaches. Lily took a photograph of her sketches to show Grandpa. He peered at the picture through his glasses and said that he had never imagined so much life in a glass of water.

What did Lily find in a drop of the water?
She found tiny green threads and round cells swimming in it.

One morning, the children in a small town in Peru saw a llama standing on the roof of a shed. It had climbed up the slope of a pile of dirt beside the wall. The llama stared at the town below with calm eyes. The owner came with a bucket of corn and shouted. The llama looked at him, chewed slowly and did not move. The children fell about laughing. When the owner finally pulled the dirt away, the llama stepped down with a bored look. The children said the llama had enjoyed the view more than the corn.

What does the llama's calm look suggest?
It suggests the llama was not worried at all and was enjoying itself, because it chewed slowly and ignored the owner.

At the foot of a mountain in Uttarakhand, a girl called Gauri noticed that the spring water was warm in winter and cool in summer. She told her teacher. He said that water underground stays about the same all year, so it feels warm when the air is cold and cool when the air is hot. Gauri dipped a thermometer in the spring on a snowy morning and wrote down the number. Then she did the same on a hot afternoon and found that the two numbers were close. She presented her notes at the school science show.

Why did the spring water feel warm in winter?
Because water underground stays at about the same temperature all year, so it feels warm compared with the cold air.

Aditya's mother always shook the bottle of salad dressing before pouring it, because the oil and vinegar separated into two layers. One day Aditya added a spoonful of mustard and shook the bottle hard. This time, the dressing stayed creamy for the whole meal and did not split. His mother tasted it and raised her eyebrows. She said she had cooked for thirty years and had never tried mustard. Aditya explained that his teacher had said some things help oil and water to mix. His mother wrote the new recipe on a card and thanked him with a kiss on the forehead.

What does his mother's reaction show about her?
It shows she was surprised and willing to learn from her son, because she raised her eyebrows, admitted she never tried it, and wrote down the recipe.

A herd of wild boar crossed the road near a forest in Coorg, and a bus stopped to let them pass. The passengers leaned out of the windows to watch. At the back of the herd, one small piglet was limping. The mother boar turned around, walked back and nudged it forward with her snout. She stayed beside it until it reached the trees. The bus driver waited with the engine off. When the road was clear, he started the engine and said softly that he would remember that sight for a long time.

Why did the bus driver wait with the engine off?
He wanted to let the boar cross safely and not frighten them, especially the limping piglet.

For years, farmers in the village of Sundar carried water in two pots hung from a pole across the shoulder. A visiting engineer saw them and drew a small cart with two wheels and a drum on top. The village carpenter built it from the drawing. A boy could pull it with one hand. The first morning, three families used the cart, and by evening, the whole village was queuing. The elders set a rule that the cart would be shared in turns. A woman who had carried water for forty years was the first to walk beside it, laughing.

Why did the whole village queue for the cart by evening?
Because it made carrying water much easier, and the first families who used it showed how well it worked.

Mira lined a shoe box with black paper, cut a small hole in one end and put a thin piece of tissue paper at the other. She aimed the hole at a bright window and looked at the tissue from behind. A small, upside-down picture of the window shone on it. Mira gasped. Her father told her that she had made a pinhole camera, and that light passing through a tiny hole forms an upside-down picture. Mira turned the box toward the garden and saw the trees upside down. She laughed and called her friends to look.

What did the picture on the tissue paper look like?
It was a small, upside-down picture of the window.

A farmer in Karnataka noticed that his hens laid fewer eggs in the winter months. His niece, a student, said that hens need about fourteen hours of light a day to lay well. He hung a small lamp in the hen house and switched it on in the evening for a few hours. A few weeks later, the hens were laying nearly as many eggs as in summer. He sold the extra eggs at the market and gave his niece a share of the money. She used it to buy a book about farm animals.

Why did the hens lay more eggs after the lamp was hung?
Because the lamp gave them the extra hours of light that hens need in order to lay well.

A pair of sparrows built a nest inside the old street signal near Lakshman's house in Nagpur. The workers who came to repair the signal climbed up and saw three small eggs among the wires. The foreman told his crew to stop. They put a cloth over the lamp and went to have tea. Two weeks later, the eggs hatched, and the workers came back with a ladder and carefully moved the nest to a box beside the pole. Lakshman watched from the balcony with his grandmother. She said it was kind of strangers to wait for baby birds.

Why did the foreman tell his crew to stop?
Because there were eggs in a nest among the wires, and he did not want to harm them.
